Text of the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* (*AP*) based upon Bühler’s edition (*Bombay Sanskrit Series* Nos. LIV and L), 3rd ed., 1932.
Variant readings are provided in parentheses at the conclusion of each sūtra, following the edition of the Kashi Sanskrit Series No. 93 (K), edited by A. Chinnaswami, Benares 1932.
Examples:

KSS reads "ccccc.ddddd" instead of "aaaaa bbbbb".
3) --- aaaaa#1 ----- bbbbb#2 ( K 1:ccccc, 2:ddddd ) KSS reads "ccccc" instead of "aaaaa", and "ddddd" instead of "bbbbb".
4) Ap.a.a.a.5 ----- / (= K 6) a.a.a.5 in BSS corresponds to a.a.a.6 in KSS.
In the BSS, a.a.a.5 corresponds to both a.a.a.5 and a.a.a.6 in the KSS.
KSS a.a.a.5 corresponds to BSS a.a.a.5 and a.a.a.6.
KSS omits the / (daṇḍa).
Sandhi variations have been disregarded and obvious typographical errors have been corrected.

Now, therefore, [the rules] concerning customary conduct. (ApDhS 1.1.1.2–3) The consensus of those who know the Dharma is authoritative, as are the Vedas.
(ApDhS 1.1.1.4–5) There are four castes: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. Among them, each preceding one is superior by birth.
(ApDhS 1.1.1.6) For those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not defective, there is initiation, Vedic study, the establishment of the sacred fires, and fruit-bearing rituals.

ApDhS 1.1.7: Service is the duty of the Śūdra toward the other castes. ApDhS 1.1.8: For each preceding caste, there is greater ultimate spiritual welfare. ApDhS 1.1.9: Initiation is the sacrament for one seeking knowledge, according to the revealed scripture.
"From all the Vedas the *sāvitrī* is to be recited," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

"He indeed enters from darkness into darkness who initiates one who is ignorant and who is himself ignorant," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, one should seek a preparer who is endowed with noble birth and learning, and who is composed.

And in that very person who has not deviated from the duties ending with sacred knowledge; for he is an *ācārya* because he gathers (*ācinoti*) the *dharmas* for one. One should never act treacherously toward him.
For he (the father) begets him through knowledge;
that is the most excellent birth.
The mother and father beget only the body.

ApDhS 1.1.1.19: One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring, a Rājanya in the summer, and a Vaiśya in the autumn; specifically, a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception, a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception. ApDhS 1.1.1.20: Now follow the optional initiations. ApDhS 1.1.1.21–26: In the seventh year, one desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa); in the eighth, one desiring long life (āyus); in the ninth, one desiring splendor (tejas); in the tenth, one desiring food (annādya); in the eleventh, one desiring sensory power (indriya); in the twelfth, one desiring cattle (paśu).

ApDhS 1.1.27: Until the sixteenth year for a Brāhmaṇa, until the twenty-second for a Kṣatriya, and until the twenty-fourth for a Vaiśya—provided he is capable of observing the vows which we shall describe—there is no lapse of time. ApDhS 1.1.28: Once the time for the Sāvitrī has passed, he should observe the student’s life (*brahmacarya*) pertaining to the three Vedas for one season. ApDhS 1.1.29: Now follows the initiation (*upanayana*).

ApDhS 1.1.1.30: After that, there shall be bathing in water for one year. ApDhS 1.1.1.31: Then he may be initiated. ApDhS 1.1.1.32: Now, those whose father and grandfather have not been initiated are declared to be equal to slayers of a Brahmin.
One should avoid their arrival, their eating together, and their marriage (ApDhS 1.1.1.33).
For those who desire it, there is an expiation (ApDhS 1.1.1.34).
Just as the first transgression is equal to the period of a *ṛtu*, so too is a year (ApDhS 1.1.1.35).

ApDhS 1.1.1.36: Now follows the initiation (*upanayana*); after that, the touching of water. ApDhS 1.1.2.1: He shall count the years according to each individual person, as many as may be those who have not yet been initiated. ApDhS 1.1.2.2: [He shall purify himself] with the seven *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "That which is near and that which is far," with these [mantras], with the *yajus-pavitra*, with the *sāma-pavitra*, and with the *āṅgirasa*.

Or rather, [he should initiate him] with the *vyāhṛtis* alone. Then he should be taught [the Veda]. Now, those for whom the initiation ceremony is not remembered from their great-grandfather onwards are designated as "associated with the cremation ground."

One should avoid their arrival, eating with them, and marriage. If they so desire, the penance is twelve years of the *brahmacarya* discipline according to the three Vedas (*traividyaka*). Then follows the initiation (*upanayana*), after which comes the ritual touching of water (*udaka-upasparśana*) with the *pāvamānī* verses and others.

Ap1.1.2.7: Now follows the instruction regarding the Gṛhamedha sacrifice. Ap1.1.2.8: There is no teaching of the Veda. Ap1.1.2.9: Then, for one who desists from it, the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) is performed as in the case of the first transgression.
ApDhS 1.1.2.10: From that point onward, it is according to the original rule.
ApDhS 1.1.2.11: For one who has approached [the teacher], the residence as a student (brahmacārin) in the teacher’s household [is required].
ApDhS 1.1.2.12: It lasts for forty-eight years.
Ap1.1.2.13–15: [The time for study may be] less by one quarter, or by half, or by three quarters.
Ap1.1.2.16: It shall not be less than twelve years. Ap1.1.2.17–18: For a religious student seeking knowledge, there is no fasting with others. (= K 17, K 18: Now, the rules for studentship.)

ApDhS 1.1.2.19: He shall remain dependent on his teacher, except in cases involving acts that cause loss of caste (*patanīya*). ApDhS 1.1.2.20: He shall do what is beneficial for his teacher and not oppose him with his speech. ApDhS 1.1.2.21: He shall sit and sleep on a lower seat.

ApDhS 1.1.2.22: He shall not eat what has not been assigned [to him]. ApDhS 1.1.2.23: Likewise, he shall avoid alkaline substances, salt, honey, and meat. ApDhS 1.1.2.24: He shall not sleep during the day.
25. He shall not indulge in perfumes. 26. He shall not engage in sexual intercourse. 27. He shall abandon all boastfulness.
ApDhS 1.1.2.28: One should not wash one’s limbs. ApDhS 1.1.2.29: However, one may wash those parts that are smeared with impurity, provided it is out of the teacher’s sight.
ApDhS 1.1.2.30: One should not bathe in water while praising oneself; if one must bathe, one should do so by floating like a staff.

One who has matted hair (*jaṭila*) or whose hair is matted in a topknot (*śikhājaṭa*) should have the others shaved. A girdle made of *muñja* grass is for the Brāhmaṇa; a bowstring is for the Kṣatriya; and a girdle of *muñja* grass or a woolen thread is for the Vaiśya.

Ap1.1.2.37–38: A staff made of *sairī* wood for a Brāhmaṇa; one produced from the branch of a *nyagrodha* tree and bent downwards for a Rājanya; one made of *bādara* or *audumbara* wood for a Vaiśya; some teachers, however, prescribe a wooden staff without regard to caste.
Ap1.1.2.39: [The rules for] clothing. Ap1.1.2.40: [These are] garments of hemp, linen, and skins.
ApDhS 1.1.2.41: Some prescribe that the garment be dyed with a decoction (kaṣāya).
ApDhS 1.1.3.1: That of a Kṣatriya should be madder-red (māñjiṣṭha). ApDhS 1.1.3.2: That of a Vaiśya should be turmeric-yellow (hāridra).
ApDhS 1.1.3.3: For a Brāhmaṇa, the skin of a black antelope or of a black deer.
ApDhS 1.1.3.4: If it is the skin of a black antelope, he must not lie down on a bed or sit on a seat that has been spread out.
ApDhS 1.1.3.5: For a Rājanya, the skin of a ruru deer.

A goat-skin is for a Vaiśya. A sheep’s wool garment is for all castes. One desiring the increase of Brahmanical power should wear only skins; one desiring the increase of Kṣatriya power should wear only clothes; one desiring the increase of both should wear both—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
However, he should always wear a skin as the upper garment.
ApDhS 1.1.3.11: He shall not look upon dancing. ApDhS 1.1.3.12: He shall not go to assemblies or social gatherings. ApDhS 1.1.3.13: He shall not be habituated to gossiping about people.
ApDhS 1.1.3.14: He should be habituated to solitude. ApDhS 1.1.3.15: He should not imitate the teacher’s mannerisms, nor perform independent actions.
ApDhS 1.1.3.16: He may converse with women only as much as is necessary.
He should be gentle, calm, self-controlled, modest, firm in resolve, untiring, free from anger, and free from malice.

Bringing all his gains to the teacher, he should practice the begging of alms in the evening and in the morning without using a formal mantra; when begging, he should avoid those with defective vessels and those who have been accused of crimes.

When women refuse [to admit a student], one who is concentrated, a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), takes away their sacrifice, their gift, their oblation, their offspring, their cattle, their Vedic splendor, and their food.
Therefore, one should not refuse a group of celibate students as they wander about; for even among them there may be one who is such a knower and observes such a vow—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Alms are not considered "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa) when obtained through inference, but rather through what has been seen or heard. A Brāhmaṇa should beg with the word "bhavat" placed at the beginning; a Rājanya, with it placed in the middle.
With the word "bhavat" at the end, he should address a Vaiśya (ApDhS 1.1.3.30).
Having gathered that [food] and placed it before the teacher, he should announce it to him (ApDhS 1.1.3.31).
He should eat what is served by him (ApDhS 1.1.3.32).
ApDhS 1.1.3.33: When separated from his guru, he may seek it from the family of a teacher (ācārya).
ApDhS 1.1.3.34: If separated from them, he may seek it from other learned brahmins (śrotriya).
ApDhS 1.1.3.35: He should not act for his own sake.
ApDhS 1.1.3.36: Having eaten himself, he should wash the vessel. ApDhS 1.1.3.37: And he should not leave it as food-remnant (ucchiṣṭa). ApDhS 1.1.3.38:
If he is unable, he should bury it in the ground.
Ap1.1.3.39: Or he should cause it to enter the waters.
Ap1.1.3.40: Or he should hand it over to an Ārya. Ap1.1.3.41:
Or to a Śūdra who acts as an intermediary.
ApDhS 1.1.3.42: One who has gone abroad should eat after having offered alms-food into the fire.
ApDhS 1.1.3.43: Alms-food is declared to be equivalent to an oblation; in that regard, the teacher serves as the deity.
ApDhS 1.1.3.44: And he serves as the Āhavanīya fire.
ApDhS 1.1.3.45: Having fed him, he eats what remains as leavings.
ApDhS 1.1.4.1: That which he eats as leavings— ApDhS 1.1.4.2: that is indeed the leavings of the sacrificial oblation (*havir-ucchiṣṭa*).

Whatever other substances he offers according to his means, these indeed constitute the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). This is the sacrifice of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), which is perpetually extended.
And one should not give him leavings that are prohibited by the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
ApDhS 1.1.4.6: For example, "alkali, salt, honey, and meat.
ApDhS 1.1.4.7: By this, other restrictive rules are explained.
ApDhS 1.1.4.8: For direct revelation (śruti) is more authoritative than customary practice (ācāra) based on inference.
And a cause for engagement is indeed observed;
for pleasure is experienced.
The remnants of the father and the eldest brother are to be eaten.
ApDhS 1.1.4.12: When there is a conflict regarding dharma, [the food is] not to be eaten.
ApDhS 1.1.4.13: Morning and evening, he should fetch a water-pot.
ApDhS 1.1.4.14: Having always brought firewood from the forest, he should place it below.
ApDhS 1.1.4.15: One should not go out to fetch firewood after the sun has set.
ApDhS 1.1.4.16: Having kindled the fire and swept around it, one should place fuel sticks upon it in the evening and in the morning, according to the instruction.
ApDhS 1.1.4.17: Some say that the worship of the fire should take place only in the evening.

ApDhS 1.1.4.18: One should stir a well-kindled fire with the hand, not with a stirring-stick. ApDhS 1.1.4.19: But before that, one may act as one pleases. ApDhS 1.1.4.20: One should not perform useless acts with water remaining from [use for] the fire, nor should one sip water [for *ācamana*] with it.
ApDhS 1.1.4.21: One should not sip water that has been stirred by the hand, nor water that has been drawn up by a single hand.
ApDhS 1.1.4.22: And one should avoid sleep.
ApDhS 1.1.4.23: Furthermore, day after day, he should serve his teacher with actions consistent with dharma and artha.
ApDhS 1.1.4.24: Having protected [the teacher] and having gone to bed, he should say: "I have protected the guardian of Dharma. ApDhS 1.1.4.25:

If the teacher should transgress a rule, whether through negligence or intentionally, the pupil should point it out to him in private. ApDhS 1.1.4.26–27: If the teacher does not desist, the pupil himself should either undertake the duties or cause them to be abandoned.
ApDhS 1.1.4.28: Now, regarding one who rises early and goes to bed late, they say of him, "He does not sleep.
ApDhS 1.1.4.29: For a religious student (*brahmacārin*) who has thus directed his self, all his actions—even those belonging to the householder—become fruitful and attained right here.
ApDhS 1.2.5.1: The word *tapas* (asceticism) refers to the observances (*niyamas*).
ApDhS 1.2.5.2: When that is transgressed, knowledge and ritual action flow away from this person, along with his offspring.
ApDhS 1.2.5.3: His progeny becomes ruined and he lacks long life. ApDhS 1.2.5.4: Therefore, sages are not born among later generations due to the transgression of the rules.

However, some become *śruta-ṛṣis* (heard-of seers) through the remainder of the fruit of their past actions when they are reborn, such as Śvetaketu. Whatever one who is concentrated applies toward Brahman from a teacher, the fruit in that case becomes exactly like that of Brahman itself.

Moreover, they teach that whatever one intends with the mind, speaks with speech, or perceives with the eye—whether one forms a mental resolve (*saṅkalpayati*), meditates (*dhyāyati*), speaks (*āha*), or looks upon (*abhivipaśyati*)—that very thing comes to be so. (While forming such resolves,) the student should perform those acts that propitiate the teacher, as well as rites for prosperity and the completion of his studies.
Other than these, the student’s ritual duties cease.
A student who maintains his private Vedic study, delights in dharma, practices austerity, is upright, and gentle succeeds as a *brahmacārin*. (K.
*ajur*) Always rising during the latter part of the night, he should stand before his teacher in the morning and offer a respectful greeting, saying: "O sir, I am so-and-so. (K.
*abhivādanam*) And this applies even to others who are older than himself living in the same village, prior to their morning meal.
ApDhS 1.2.5.14: And upon returning from a journey, when meeting [others].

ApDhS 1.2.5.15: Desiring heaven and long life. ApDhS 1.2.5.16: A Brāhmaṇa should salute by extending his right arm level with the ear; a Rājanya level with the chest; a Vaiśya level with the waist; and a Śūdra with his palms joined low.
ApDhS 1.2.5.17: Furthermore, there shall be the sprinkling of water on the name, as well as the salutation and the return-salutation for those of the preceding castes.
ApDhS 1.2.5.18: But when the sun has risen, having met with his teacher, he shall clasp his feet.
ApDhS 1.2.5.19: He shall always perform the salutation.
ApDhS 1.2.5.20: "Having grasped [the feet], [one addresses him as] 'Teacher'—so say some.
ApDhS 1.2.5.21: "With his right hand, having touched the teacher's right foot from below, he should grasp it together with the toes.
ApDhS 1.2.5.22: "Both [feet] should be grasped by both [hands], pressing them down"—so say some.

ApDhS 1.2.5.23: One who is diligently engaged in study should not recite immediately after [eating] until the end of the day. ApDhS 1.2.5.24: Likewise, one should not recite while performing services for the teacher. ApDhS 1.2.5.25: And one should not recite mentally during a period when formal study is prohibited.
And he should be one who studies when summoned.
He should always cause his teacher to lie down at night after washing and massaging his feet;
being permitted, he himself should lie down.
And one should not stretch out toward him (the teacher). Some say that there is no stretching out while sitting on a couch.
Nor should one speak while lying down in his presence.
When addressed, one should respond while remaining seated if the teacher is seated; one should not respond by standing up if the teacher is standing.
One should follow him when he walks and run after him when he runs.
One should not sit down wearing sandals or with the head wrapped, nor with hands tucked under the armpits.
Ap1.2.6.11: But one who has set out on a journey may sit down while engaged in his work.
Ap1.2.6.12: Provided that he does not sit too close.
Ap1.2.6.13: He should attend upon the teacher as if he were a god—refraining from idle chatter, with a clear mind, and listening attentively to his speech.
Ap1.2.6.14: [The act] not performed with the lap [as a support].

Ap1.2.6.15–17: [The fire] blowing from behind (*anuvāti*), [the wind] having ceased (*vītaḥ*), [the vessel] not supported by the hand (*apratiṣṭabdhaḥ pāṇinā*), and [the sacrificer] not leaning against anything (*anapaśritaḥ*)—except in the case of [the wind] blowing from behind.
Ap1.2.6.18: Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), [he should be] one who has two garments (*dvi-vastraḥ*).

Ap1.2.6.19: Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder and under the left arm (*adhonivīta*), he should be clad in a single garment. Ap1.2.6.20: Facing [the teacher], he should not face away from him. Ap1.2.6.21: He should not stand too close, nor too far; [and he should remain neither too near nor too distant].
ApDhS 1.2.6.22: [As long as he can reach with his arms while sitting];
ApDhS 1.2.6.23: [Not against the wind];
ApDhS 1.2.6.24–25: A single student should sit facing the right arm; many may sit according to available space.
Ap1.2.6.26: And while standing, one should not sit down, except when engaged in the practice of standing or sitting.
Ap1.2.6.27: And while sitting, one should not lie down. Ap1.2.6.28: And while moving about, one may act toward that which is within the scope of one's capacity to accomplish.
And one should not clasp the feet of a person who stands in a subordinate position (*anvak-sthānin*) in his presence (ApDhS 1.2.6.29).
Or, one may address him by his *gotra* name (ApDhS 1.2.6.30).
And one should not rise up to meet him, nor follow after him when he departs (ApDhS 1.2.6.31).
Even if his teacher should be present, (31–32) he should rise from his seat and move away from his place.
(32) Some say that he should address even his own teacher as "Teacher" by name only when the latter is in the presence of another teacher. (33)

ApDhS 1.2.6.35: But toward one who is not related to him as a teacher, yet toward whom he behaves with respect, even though he stands in a subordinate position, he should behave as toward a teacher. ApDhS 1.2.6.36–37: After eating in his presence, he should not rise after him nor give him his leftovers; or he may rinse his mouth (*ācāmet*). ApDhS 1.2.6.38: Having addressed him, saying "What shall I do?", he should then rise, or he may rise silently. (1.2.7.1)
ApDhS 1.2.7.1: He should rise either silently or [with a word of greeting].
ApDhS 1.2.7.2: He should not turn his back toward his teacher; having circumambulated him from left to right, he should depart. ApDhS 1.2.7.3: He should not look at a naked woman.
ApDhS 1.2.7.4: One should not smell herbs or trees after having plucked them. ApDhS 1.2.7.5: One should avoid shoes, an umbrella, and a vehicle.
ApDhS 1.2.7.6: One should not smile.
ApDhS 1.2.7.7: If he should smile, he should do so covering his mouth; for thus says the Brāhmaṇa. ApDhS 1.2.7.8: He should not kiss a woman with his mouth.
ApDhS 1.2.7.9: He should not desire her with his heart.
One should not touch water without a specific reason (ApDhS 1.2.7.10).
One who is menstruating should have red teeth and speak the truth; for so says the Brāhmaṇa (ApDhS 1.2.7.11).
Those who teach him a branch of knowledge under his teacher are also his teachers, as well as those who belong to the lineage of that teacher in that branch (ApDhS 1.2.7.12).
Ap1.2.7.13: When he sees others whom he might otherwise greet by clasping their feet, then these [others] should be greeted by clasping their feet.
Ap1.2.7.14: When a multitude of teachers is present and alms have been obtained, the one to whom he is attached is the one upon whom the alms depend.
Ap1.2.7.15–17: Upon returning from his studies, he should give [the alms] to his mother; the mother should send them to her husband; the husband [should send them] to the teacher.
ApDhS 1.2.7.18: Or he may employ it for religious duties.
ApDhS 1.2.7.19: Having acquired as much knowledge as he is capable of, he shall receive the Vedic fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the law and according to his ability.
ApDhS 1.2.7.20: But if the teacher is in distress, he may receive it from a fierce person or from a Śūdra.
ApDhS 1.2.7.21: Some say that it is lawful to obtain the teacher’s fee from a Śūdra or an Ugra at any time.
ApDhS 1.2.7.22: Having given it, he should not speak of it again.
ApDhS 1.2.7.23: Having performed it, he should not remember it again.

One should avoid self-praise and the censure of others. (ApDhS 1.2.7.24) When commanded, one should perform exactly that which was assigned. (ApDhS 1.2.7.25) And in the absence of a scriptural injunction from the teacher, one's livelihood may be sought elsewhere. (ApDhS 1.2.7.26)
ApDhS 1.2.7.27: Except for clasping the feet and eating the leftovers, one should behave toward the teacher’s wife as toward the teacher himself.
ApDhS 1.2.7.28: Likewise [the same behavior is required] toward one who instructs him [in the Veda]. ApDhS 1.2.7.29:
And likewise toward a fellow student who is older than oneself.
ApDhS 1.2.7.30: One should behave toward the teacher’s son as toward the teacher himself, with the exception of eating his leftovers.

ApDhS 1.2.7.31: For one who has returned home from studentship (*samāvṛtta*), this same conduct prescribed by custom (*sāmayācārika*) remains the same as that of the religious student (*brahmacārin*).

One who wears garlands, one whose face is smeared with unguents, one whose hair and beard are anointed, one who is anointed or rubbed with oil, one who is wrapped or dressed in a turban, one wearing a tunic, one wearing sandals, or one wearing shoes— among these,
he should neither perform nor cause others to perform such acts during formal religious observances,
nor during acts performed at will.
ApDhS 1.2.8.5: For example, [he should not mention] the washing of teeth, the rubbing of the body with unguents, or the scraping of the nails.
ApDhS 1.2.8.6: And the teacher should not speak of those substances when they have come into contact with himself.
ApDhS 1.2.8.7: But when he has bathed at the proper time, if the food has been brought according to rule, whether he is invited or comes of his own accord, some say that he should not refuse it.
One should not sit higher than [another], nor on something with many legs, nor on anything firmly established on all sides.
One should not occupy a bed or seat already used by another. When commanded, one may mount a vehicle while traveling on a road.
One should avoid sitting on the same seat as the teacher, nor on a stone slab, a mat, or a bed.
One should not speak to the teacher unless addressed first; and one should not say anything other than what is pleasant.

One should avoid poking him, whispering to others in his presence, laughing at him, calling out to him, mentioning his name in a disrespectful manner, and giving him commands. (K: *vyupajāpa* = whispering to others in his presence).
Ap1.2.8.16: In times of distress, he should make himself known for the sake of his purpose.
Ap1.2.8.17: Living together with him, he should go to see the teacher in the evening and in the morning, even if unsummoned.
Ap1.2.8.18: And having traveled abroad, he should see him on that very day.

Ap1.2.8.19–20: When an *ācārya* and a *prācārya* meet, one should desire to clasp the feet of the *prācārya* after having already clasped those of the *ācārya*; the other (the *ācārya*) should forbid him.
Ap1.2.8.21: Furthermore, honor toward the *ācārya* is suspended in the presence of the *prācārya*.

And he should go frequently to the teacher’s household for the purpose of seeing him, bringing with him, according to his ability, whatever can be carried by hand—even if it be merely mouth-washing sticks. (K inserts: One should not approach one's mother, father, teacher, the sacred fires, or the houses with empty hands; nor should one approach a king unless one has something learned to offer. Regarding that [teacher], this is the conduct toward the guru. (K 24)
Desiring him as if he were his own son, and not concealing anything among all duties, the teacher should, being well-disciplined, cause him to grasp the knowledge.

(K = 25) And he should not obstruct him with obstacles to study for the sake of his own interests, except in times of distress. (= K 26) A pupil who fails to apply himself skillfully toward his teacher becomes a non-pupil, having failed to surrender his self to him. (= K 27)
ApDhS 1.2.8.27: Even a teacher ceases to be a teacher if he neglects what he has heard [from his own teacher].

(K 28) ApDhS 1.2.8.28: And one should constantly reprove him for his transgressions. (K 29) ApDhS 1.2.8.29: Threatening, fasting, touching water, and exclusion from sight are the punishments, applied according to the gravity of the offense, until [the offender] desists. (K 30)

ApDhS 1.2.8.30: Having completed his period of student celibacy (*caritabrahmacarya*) and having turned away from other duties, he should grant permission [to leave], saying, "Become one who is not separated [from me].
ApDhS 1.3.9.1: Having performed the opening ceremony (*upākaraṇa*) on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, he shall not study during the first watch of the night for one month.
ApDhS 1.3.9.2: He shall cease [the study] on the full moon day of the month of Taiṣya, or under the asterism Rohiṇī.
ApDhS 1.3.9.3: Some say [the study period lasts] four months and a half.
ApDhS 1.3.9.4: One should avoid Vedic study at the *nigamas* (sacred sites).
ApDhS 1.3.9.5: Or one may study after having smeared [the ground] with a lump of cow-dung from a bull.

ApDhS 1.3.9.6: Within a cremation ground, one must not study at a distance of one throw of a yoke-pin (śamyā) from any side. ApDhS 1.3.9.7: There is no suspension of study because of a village that has been settled upon, nor because of a field.
ApDhS 1.3.9.8: However, when that [cremation ground] is known to be present, one should not study in that very place.
A Śūdra and an outcast (patita) are like a cremation ground. Some say they are like a cremation ground only within the same house.
However, in the case of a Śūdra woman, there is a suspension of study only during mutual looking and being looked at.

Likewise, if he has sexual intercourse with another woman who has transgressed her caste, when he is about to study the Veda and desires to speak with a woman wearing soiled clothes, he should first speak with a Brāhmaṇa and then speak with her; but having spoken with her, he must speak with a Brāhmaṇa again before he may study. In this way, there is the highest welfare for his offspring.
ApDhS 1.3.9.14: Within a corpse.
ApDhS 1.3.9.15: Within a *caṇḍāla*. ApDhS 1.3.9.16: But there is no suspension of study for those who have been carried out beyond the boundary. (Variant: *abhinissṛtānām*)
And when they have come into sight in the forest;
on that day, even if they have arrived in the village from outside;
and even if they are already present there.
ApDhS 1.3.9.20: When there is thunder during the twilight, [the suspension of study lasts for] the night. ApDhS 1.3.9.21: When there is lightning until the end of sleep.

ApDhS 1.3.9.22: Until dawn, or for as long as it takes to perceive a dark or red cloud from the distance of a *śamyā*-throw; at that time, if lightning flashes, the day including the evening is a period of non-study (*anadhyāya*).
Ap1.3.9.23: [The study of the Veda is suspended] in a small room during the latter part of the night when there is thunder.
Ap1.3.9.24: According to some, [it is suspended] after midnight. Ap1.3.9.25: And when cattle are being penned.
Ap1.3.9.26: And for those who are to be executed, [one should not study] as long as they are being executed.
Ap1.3.9.27: One who has mounted upon the backs of animals should not study.
Ap1.3.9.28: [One should not study] for a day and a night on the new moon days.
And during the Cāturmāsī festivals;
the three-day periods consisting of the Vairamaṇa, the Aṣṭākya, and the Aupākaraṇa rites performed for one's gurus;
and likewise when there are kinsmen who are relatives.
In the case of a mother, a father, or a teacher, the period of impurity lasts twelve days.
During those days, there shall be ritual bathing in water for that same duration.
Furthermore, for those who survive [the deceased], there shall be the shaving of the hair.

ApDhS 1.3.10.7: "Some say that those who have returned from their teacher's house should not shave, except at the sacrificial ground. ApDhS 1.3.10.8: Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "He who is shaven is indeed empty and uncovered; this topknot (*śikhā*) is his covering. ApDhS 1.3.10.9: However, in the case of sacrificial sessions (*satra*), there is shaving of the topknot because of a specific scriptural injunction.
ApDhS 1.3.10.10: Regarding the death of a teacher, some say [the impurity lasts] for three days and nights.

ApDhS 1.3.10.11: At the funeral of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) who has not been dead for a full year, [the impurity lasts] for one day. ApDhS 1.3.10.12: Some say this applies when the deceased was a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*).

Ap1.3.10.13: Upon the arrival of a *śrotriya*, one who desires to learn (*adhi-jigāṃsamāna�*), or one who is already studying (*adhīyānaḥ*), should study after having obtained permission (*anujñāpya*).
Ap1.3.10.14: Or he may teach (*adhyāpayet*).
Ap1.3.10.15: And in the presence of his teacher, he should study after having said, "Recite, sir! (*adhīhi bho iti uktvā*).
ApDhS 1.3.10.16: Or he may teach [the Veda]. ApDhS 1.3.10.17: One who desires to learn [the Veda] should clasp both [feet of the teacher], and likewise after having studied it.
ApDhS 1.3.10.18: Or, while others are studying, if another person should intervene, one should continue reciting, omitting only that specific word.

The barking of dogs and donkeys, the howling of jackals, the cries of the *ekasṛk* bird and the owl, all sounds of musical instruments, and the sounds of weeping, singing, and the *sāman* chants; (ApDhS 1.3.10.19).
Furthermore, there is no study of the *sāmans* according to other recensions (ApDhS 1.3.10.20).
And in all cases involving vocal actions, where they might overlap (ApDhS 1.3.10.21).
ApDhS 1.3.10.22: Having vomited, he should sleep until the end of the dream.
ApDhS 1.3.10.23: Or, having consumed clarified butter.
ApDhS 1.3.10.24: A foul odor. (K: *pūti*)

Ap1.3.10.25: And when there is sour gruel; and when one is in contact with oneself; Ap1.3.10.26: And having eaten at nightfall; (K adds: one should not study); Ap1.3.10.27: And when the two hands are wet with water.

ApDhS 1.3.10.28: Having eaten food prepared for the deceased (pretasaṃkalpita), there shall be no study for that day along with the preceding evening. ApDhS 1.3.10.29: [This applies] until its digestion. ApDhS 1.3.10.30: However, one may finish [the meal] with food not intended for a śrāddha.
ApDhS 1.3.11.1: And at the commencement of a *kāṇḍa*, one who has no mother;
ApDhS 1.3.11.2: And at the completion of a *kāṇḍa*, one who has no father;
ApDhS 1.3.11.3: And at a sacrifice to deities who have human forms, some say that one may eat.
Ap1.3.11.4: There is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) on account of stale rice or raw meat. Ap1.3.11.5: Likewise, there is no suspension of study on account of herbs, trees, roots, or fruits.

Ap1.3.11.6: On the day one performs the *upākaraṇa* (the formal commencement) of a section (*kāṇḍa*), or on the day one performs the *anuvākya* (the recitation) of a section, one should not study that same section on that day.
And during the commencement and conclusion of the *pārāyaṇa* recitation of that specific Vedic knowledge;
when there is a loud sound of wind on the ground or a rustling of grass; where it rains or where streams flow;
and at the boundary between a village and the forest.
ApDhS 1.3.11.10: And on a high road;
ApDhS 1.3.11.11: And having returned from a journey, one should not study that day;
ApDhS 1.3.11.12: And during the performance of voluntary rites.
Ap1.3.11.13: For example, [the times for study suspension include] washing the feet, massaging, and anointing the body—(K 11, 1: hands; 2: ointments). Ap1.3.11.14:
For that duration of time, one should neither study nor teach. Ap1.3.11.15:
[This applies] during the two twilights.
Likewise, one who has climbed a tree;
one who has plunged into the waters;
and one who is uncovered at night. (16+17+18 = K 14: likewise, one who has climbed a tree, one who has plunged into the waters, and one who is uncovered at night.)
Ap1.3.11.19: And also during the day, when it is not covered.
Ap1.3.11.20: The recitation of Vedic lessons (*anuvāka*) is not prescribed during the months of Āṣāḍha and the spring.
Ap1.3.11.21: And also for the daily recitation (*nityapraśna*), except in accordance with the rule.
Ap1.3.11.22: The rule for that [is as follows].

Ap1.3.11.23: Having not yet eaten his morning meal, having gone to the edge of water, being pure in a clean place, he should study according to the lesson, either reciting it aloud or [mentally], while suspending [other activities]. Ap1.3.11.24:
And he should study mentally during times when formal study is prohibited.
ApDhS 1.3.11.25: When lightning is near, during thunder, when there is a lack of ritual purity, regarding the food of the deceased, and during mist, they declare that mental study is prohibited.
(K = 21) ApDhS 1.3.11.26: Some say this applies specifically to the time of eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony.
(= K 22) ApDhS 1.3.11.27: Where lightning, thunder, and rain should coincide outside of the rainy season, there shall be a three-day suspension of study. (= K 23)

ApDhS 1.3.11.28: According to some, [the suspension of study lasts] as long as the ground remains wet. ApDhS 1.3.11.29: For one or two of these [causes], the suspension lasts until the time [the ground becomes dry].
ApDhS 1.3.11.30: During an eclipse of the sun or moon, an earthquake, thunder, a meteor, or a portentous fire, the suspension of all branches of learning lasts for the entire duration of that time.

ApDhS 1.3.11.31: In the case of a cloud when it is not the rainy season, an aura around the sun and moon, a rainbow, a mock-sun, a fish-shaped phenomenon in the sky, a foul odor in the wind, and mist—in all these instances, one must wait for that same duration of time.
ApDhS 1.3.11.32: If the wind has ceased, one must wait for a *muhūrta*.
ApDhS 1.3.11.33: Upon hearing the cry of a female jackal or a one-eyed animal, one must wait until the end of the dream.

Ap1.3.11.34: Nor at night in the forest, nor when there is no fire, nor when there is no gold. Ap1.3.11.35: One should not study a Vedic text that has not been formally taught, nor out of season, nor during the twilight. Ap1.3.11.36: And also at the onset of evening.
Ap1.3.11.37: It is prescribed as being for all times. (K 33) Ap1.3.11.38: Other than this, it is as stated regarding assemblies. (K 34) Ap1.4.12.1:
"Austerity and Vedic study"—this is the Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding this, it is heard in scripture: "If he recites his daily study while standing, sitting, or lying down, he performs austerity; for the daily study is indeed austerity."

Moreover, there is the Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa: "This private recitation (*svādhyāya*) is indeed the sacrifice to Brahman; these are its *vaṣaṭ*-calls: when it thunders, when it lightens, when it crashes, and when the wind blows. Therefore, one should study while it thunders, lightens, crashes, or when the wind blows, so that there may be no failure of the *vaṣaṭ*-calls. In another recensional branch (*śākhā*), the sentence concludes with this.

Ap1.4.12.5: Now, if wind should blow, or if there should be thunder, or lightning, or a clap of thunder, he should recite one Ṛg-verse, or one Yajus-formula, or one Sāman-chant, saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Truth! Austerity! I offer this into faith. By this very means, his Vedic study for that day becomes properly undertaken. (Ap1.4.12.6:
This being so, it is not contradicted by the traditional practice of the Āryas.)
For they teach what constitutes a day of study and a day of non-study; that would be purposeless if one were to regard the *Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa*.
For the convention of the Āryas is not based on an apprehensible cause.
Regarding knowledge, a suspension of study is prescribed, but not regarding the application of mantras in ritual action.

Ap1.4.12.10: Regarding those injunctions stated in the Brāhmaṇas, their recensions having been lost, they are inferred from usage. Ap1.4.12.11: But where activity proceeds from the perception of pleasure, there no scripture exists.
Ap1.4.12.12: One who follows such [activity] prepares himself for hell.
ApDhS 1.4.12.13: Now, the rules for the Brāhmaṇas have been stated.

ApDhS 1.4.12.14: These are praised as the "Great Sacrifices" (mahāyajña) and the "Great Sessions" (mahāsattra). ApDhS 1.4.12.15: Every day, one should offer the bali-oblation to the beings and give gifts to men according to one's ability.

ApDhS 1.4.13.1: The utterance of *svāhā* for the gods extends as far as the sacrificial wood; for the ancestors, the utterance of *svadhā* extends as far as the water-vessel; and likewise for Vedic study. ApDhS 1.4.13.2–3: Honor should be shown to those of superior caste and to those who are older.
ApDhS 1.4.13.4: One who is joyful becomes arrogant; one who is arrogant transgresses the Dharma; and indeed, upon the transgression of Dharma, there is hell.
Ap1.4.13.5: There is no instruction for one who has returned [from his teacher].
Ap1.4.13.6: The syllable *oṃ* is the gate to heaven; therefore, one about to study the Veda should begin with this. Ap1.4.13.7:
And by engaging in other idle talk, the Veda is turned away from him by means of worldly speech.

Ap1.4.13.8: And at sacrifices, these and similar utterances are the *prasavas* (authorizations). Ap1.4.13.9: And in the world, in rites for prosperity (*bhūtikarma*), these very same types of sentences should be used, such as "May it be an auspicious day," "May there be well-being," and "May there be success.
Ap1.4.13.10: One should not perform a difficult rite (*kṛcchra*) out of season, except by omitting the threefold proclamation and the threefold simultaneous recitation.
Hārīta says that one should proceed without hesitation as far as the Brahman [is to be reached].
There is no going outside of the Veda. One should clasp the feet of the teacher who has been instructed and is teaching, for as long as the study lasts.
Ap1.4.13.14: [The word *arhantam* is] always [used; some say it refers to one who is worthy].
Ap1.4.13.15: No movement [is possible].
Ap1.4.13.16: But [it applies] to those who are aged.
ApDhS 1.4.13.17: There is no way [to avoid] mutual engagement in the Veda.

ApDhS 1.4.13.18: They teach that the Veda increases [in this way]. ApDhS 1.4.13.19: Śvetaketu says: "When his residence [at the teacher's house] has been completed, he should live for two months every year in the teacher’s family with a concentrated mind, desiring further learning."

"For by this very method, I have heard more than before: 'I did not perform [the sacred recitation]' (ApDh 1.4.13.21). That is contradicted by the scriptures (ApDh 1.4.13.22), for once the settling [of the household] has taken place, the obligatory rites are prescribed."
The Agnihotra sacrifice and guests;
and whatever else is similarly appropriate.
He should not refuse one whom he may invite for the purpose of study.

And one should not perceive any fault in this; for when no other means of subsistence is available, there is simply no alternative course of action. One must serve one's mother and father as one would an *ācārya*.
Ap1.4.14.7: Upon returning from his studies, one should clasp the feet of all teachers.
Ap1.4.14.8: And likewise upon meeting them after having been away on a journey.
Ap1.4.14.9: Among brothers and sisters, the clasping of the feet is performed according to seniority.

And daily worship should be performed according to the instructions. (K 9) One should rise to greet a priest, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, or a maternal uncle who is younger than oneself, and address them with a greeting.
(K 10) Or one may silently clasp their feet in salutation. (K 11)
Friendship among fellow citizens lasts for ten years; that of a wandering performer (*cāraṇa*), five years; and a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) who is three years senior deserves a salutation.

(ApDhS 1.4.14.13) When the difference in age is known, one must salute an elder. (ApDhS 1.4.14.14) One need not salute someone who is in a precarious position, nor one who is not an *ācārya*. (ApDhS 1.4.14.15)
Ap1.4.14.16: Or, having ascended [the same vehicle], one should offer salutation.
( = K 15) Ap1.4.14.17: But in all cases, one must rise up before offering salutation.
( = K 16) Ap1.4.14.18: One should not offer salutation to someone who is impure.
Likewise, [one should not respond] to one who is impure;
nor should one respond to a greeting from one who is impure. (ApDhS 1.4.14.19–20) [One should not respond to a greeting from] women whose husbands are living. (ApDhS 1.4.14.21)
ApDhS 1.4.14.22: One should not salute while wearing shoes, nor with one's head wrapped, nor with hands not placed in the *avahita* position.

ApDhS 1.4.14.23: Women, as well as Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, should be addressed by their full name; one should not address them by their personal name alone. ApDhS 1.4.14.24: According to some, this applies to one's mother and the wife of one's teacher as well.

A ten-year-old Brāhmaṇa and a hundred-year-old Kṣatriya should both be understood as father and son; of these two, the Brāhmaṇa is the father. One should ask a younger person or a peer about their *kuśala* (well-being). One should ask a Kṣatriya about his *anāmaya* (freedom from illness).
Ap1.4.14.28: [He should ask] "Is the Vaiśya not lost? (= K 25). Ap1.4.14.29: "Is the Śūdra healthy?
(= K 26). Ap1.4.14.30: He should not pass by a Śrotriya without conversing with him. (= K 27).
ApDhS 1.4.14.31: And [one should avoid speaking] with a woman in the forest.

(= K 28) ApDhS 1.5.15.1: In the presence of teachers, elders, guests, during the fire-oblation, in the performance of *japa*, while eating, when sipping water (*ācamana*), and during Vedic study, one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*).
ApDhS 1.5.15.2: Having sipped water from water that has reached the ground, one becomes pure.
Or he may cause one who is pure to rinse his mouth for him.
He should not rinse his mouth in streams of rain,
nor likewise in water from a fissure in the ground.

ApDhS 1.5.15.6: And one should not touch water that has been heated without a specific reason. ApDhS 1.5.15.7: With empty hands, one should not approach a person of high standing; having raised water, one should sip it. ApDhS 1.5.15.8–9: When capable of doing so, one should not remain impure even for a moment, nor should one remain naked.
ApDhS 1.5.15.10: For one who is in water, there is no cleansing. ApDhS 1.5.15.11: But having emerged, one should sip water.
ApDhS 1.5.15.12: One should not place un-sprinkled fuel into the fire.
And on a bed of grass used by the ignorant, one who is pure should consider himself pure even while not touching others who are impure. Likewise, this applies to grass and wood that have been buried.
Or, having sprinkled it with water, he may use his garment.

ApDhS 1.5.15.16: One who has been struck by a swelling should immerse himself in water along with his clothes. ApDhS 1.5.15.17: Or, having washed that spot and touched it with fire, and having washed his feet again and sipped water, he becomes pure.
ApDhS 1.5.15.18: One should not sit near the fire while impure.
According to some, [the distance] should be at least the length of an arrow (ApDhS 1.5.15.19).
One should not blow upon him (ApDhS 1.5.15.20), nor should one place him upon a bed (ApDhS 1.5.15.21).

ApDhS 1.5.15.22: In a village where fuel and water are abundant, a Brāhmaṇa’s dwelling is lawful provided that the means of purification are under his own control. ApDhS 1.5.15.23: Having voided urine or feces, having washed away the smears of urine and feces, the smears of food, the smears of impurity from eating, and whatever smears of semen there may be, and having washed both feet and sipped water, he becomes pure. ApDhS 1.5.16.1: He should sip water while standing or while stooping forward.
Seated, he should sip water three times with water that reaches his heart;
he should wipe his lips three times—some say twice;
he should touch [the organs] once—some say twice.
ApDhS 1.5.16.7: Having sprinkled his left hand, his feet, and his head with water from his right hand, he should touch his sense organs—the eyes, the nostrils, and the ears.
ApDhS 1.5.16.8: Then he should touch water.
ApDhS 1.5.16.9: But when about to eat, even if he is already pure, he should sip water twice, wipe his mouth twice, and touch water once.
Having touched the lips at their dark edges, one should sip water for purification (*ācāmet*).

One does not become impure (*ucchiṣṭa*) by the presence of beard hairs within the mouth, as long as one does not touch them with the hand. Regarding those drops which are perceived falling from the mouth, sipping water (*ācamana*) is prescribed for them.

ApDhS 1.5.16.13: Some say that one should not sip water when [the discharge] falls upon the ground. ApDhS 1.5.16.14: Upon dreaming; upon sneezing; upon smelling the breath from the nose; upon touching tears; upon touching blood, hair, fire, a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, or a woman; upon having traveled along a high road; upon touching something impure; upon touching a person who is not ritually pure; upon putting on the *nīvī* (the lower garment); and upon touching water—one should sip water. ApDhS 1.5.16.15: Or [one may touch] fresh dung, plants, or the earth.
Meat cut with a knife intended for killing is unfit to be eaten.
One should not cut off a portion of a cake with one's teeth.
If someone dies in a family, one must not eat there until ten days have passed.
Likewise, when the woman who has recently given birth has not yet emerged [from confinement];
and when there is a corpse inside [the house];
and food that is defiled by one who is impure—though it is impure, it is not, however, unfit for consumption.

ApDhS 1.5.16.22: But food offered by a Śūdra who is not self-restrained is unfit to be eaten. ApDhS 1.5.16.23: Nor is that food in which there is hair. ApDhS 1.5.16.24: Nor any other impure substance.
[If food is] touched by impure things;
or if a worm that frequents impure places [is found in it];
or if there is a limb of a mouse [in it].
Or [food] struck by a foot (ApDhS 1.5.16.28);
or [food] touched by a fringe (ApDhS 1.5.16.29); or [food] seen by a dog or by one who uses a discarded vessel (ApDhS 1.5.16.30).
Or [food] brought by a female messenger; or brought at night by a female slave;
or while he is eating.
ApDhS 1.5.17.1: Where a Śūdra might touch [the food];
ApDhS 1.5.17.2: Or where there are those unworthy to sit in the same row;
ApDhS 1.5.17.3: Or where, while people are eating, someone stands up and gives them the leavings or sips water [for himself].
ApDhS 1.5.17.4: Or where they might give food after having reviled it; ApDhS 1.5.17.5:
or food smelled by humans or by other impure things; ApDhS 1.5.17.6: one should not eat on a boat.
Likewise, in a palace;
but one should eat on ground that has been prepared;
and one should eat from an unbaked earthenware vessel.
If it is scorched, it is purified by being sprinkled with water; if it is burnt, it is purified by being thoroughly scrubbed; iron is purified by being cleansed;
and wood is purified by being scraped.
According to tradition, one should eat at a sacrifice;
one should not eat food that has been purchased. Likewise, among savory substances, one should avoid meat, honey, and salt.
One should place oil and ghee into water before using them.

Food that has turned sour, as well as food that has become stale, is unfit to be eaten, drunk, or consumed; this includes all fermented substances. However, one may consume the following even if they have turned sour: molasses, flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), rice grains, *karambha* (curd mixed with barley meal), parched grain (*bharūja*), roasted barley flour (*saktu*), vegetables, meat, flour-based preparations, products of milk, medicinal herbs, forest plants, roots, and fruits—provided these are not fermented. *(Note: Regarding the term *karambha-bharūja*, there are variants such as *bharuja* and *bharija*.)*
And fermented sour gruel that has undergone further fermentation; all intoxicating liquor is forbidden to drink; likewise, the milk of a sheep.
The milk of a camel, the milk of a female deer, the milk of a cow in heat, the milk of a cow that has twin calves, and the milk of a cow that miscarries;
likewise, the milk of a cow within ten days of calving;
and similarly, the fermented liquor (kīlāla) and the juices of plants.
The *karañja*, the *palaṇḍu*, and the *parārīka*;
and whatever else they censure, for the Brāhmaṇa says: "That which is called 'kyākva' is not to be eaten."
The meat of single-hoofed animals, camels, gayals, village pigs, śarabhas, and cows is edible; likewise, that of milch-cows and oxen. According to the Vājasaneyaka, the flesh of an ox is pure.
The cock is the foremost among birds that scatter their food; the water-fowl is the foremost among birds that peck;
and those that eat raw flesh [are the foremost among carnivorous birds].
The *haṃsa*, *bhāsa*, *cakravāka*, and *suparṇa* [are permitted],

with the exception of the *kruñca*, *krauñca*, *vārdhrāṇasa*, and *lakṣmaṇa*. Among five-toed animals, [they are permitted] with the exception of the *godhā*, *kacchapa*, *śvāvit*, *śalyaka*, *khaḍga*, *śaśa*, and *pūtikaṣa*.
ApDhS 1.5.17.38: Among fish, the *ceṭa* is not to be eaten.
ApDhS 1.5.17.39: The *sarpaśīrṣī*, the *mṛdu*, the *kravyāda*, and others that are deformed, such as those with human heads, are forbidden. ApDhS 1.6.18.1:
Honey, raw meat, venison, land, roots and fruits, protection, pasture, a dwelling, and fodder for draft animals may be accepted from a fierce person.

Hārīta says that even these [foods] are not [permissible] if they have not been brought by a resident pupil (anantevāsī). Or they may take raw food (āma), or food that has been prepared but is devoid of its flavor (virasa).
The regions shall not be well-supplied with food.
Even when he himself is unable to subsist, he may enjoy [the property] by giving gold or a beast;
however, he must not settle there permanently.
Having obtained a means of subsistence, he should cease [from begging].
He must not eat the food of the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya once he has returned from his teacher’s house.
By nature, the food of a Brāhmaṇa may be eaten; it is inedible only for a specific reason. (Alternatively: It may be eaten except for a specific reason.)
ApDhS 1.6.18.11: Where one performs an act that is not subject to expiation while it is actually subject to expiation;

ApDhS 1.6.18.12: Food may be eaten from one who has performed the penance; ApDhS 1.6.18.13: Some say that food may be eaten from all castes when they abide in their own duties, with the exception of the Śūdra.

Even for that [one who has been brought by Dharma], having given gold or a cow, he may enjoy [the property]; he should not settle there permanently; once he has obtained a means of livelihood, he should desist. Food belonging to a *saṅgha* (an assembly) is unfit to be eaten.
And [the food] of one who calls out for alms;
(ApDhS 1.6.18.17) and of all those who live by manual crafts; (ApDhS 1.6.18.18) and of those who live by weapons. (ApDhS 1.6.18.19)
And those who practice sorcery;
a physician; a usurer.
Ap1.6.18.23: [The initiated one] who has not yet purchased the King Soma; Ap1.6.18.24: Only at the conclusion of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice;
Ap1.6.18.25: Or, when the omentum has been offered, the initiated one may eat. (K omits *vā*)

ApDhS 1.6.18.26: Or, when it has been designated for the sake of the sacrifice, they may eat from the remainder; for so says the Brāhmaṇa. ApDhS 1.6.18.27: A eunuch. ApDhS 1.6.18.28: One who carries out the commands of kings.
One who does not perform the sacrifice of oblations;
one who wanders as a mendicant; and one who has gone forth [into homelessness] contrary to the prescribed rule.
He who abandons the sacred fires;

he who avoids all [Vedic study]; a learned Śrotriya who is a *nirākṛti* (one who has renounced his duties); a husband of a Śūdra woman (*vṛṣalīpati*); one who is intoxicated, insane, bound, or without a king; and he who causes another to sit in protest (*pratyupaveśayate*) for that duration of time.
Ap1.6.19.2: What is his food? (Kāśyapa says:
It is whatever he desires; thus says Kaṇva. Ap1.6.19.3:
It is that which is meritorious; thus says Kautsa.
Vārṣyāyaṇi says that anyone may give [such food].

If the impurity (*rajas*) in the person is stationary, it must be consumed; but if it is mobile, one becomes free from fault through giving it away. Pure alms may be eaten by the followers of Eka-kuṇika, as well as by the Kaṇvas, the Kutsas, and Puṣkarasādin.
Ap 1.6.19.8: The Vārṣyāyaṇīya school maintains that one may eat food that is endowed with excellence in every respect. Ap 1.6.19.9: One should eat food that is meritorious and desired.
Ap 1.6.19.10: One should not eat food that is meritorious but undesired.
ApDhS 1.6.19.11: Food may be eaten from anyone when it is offered.
ApDhS 1.6.19.12: "Not if it was previously intended for someone else," says Hārīta.

ApDhS 1.6.19.13: Now they cite two verses from the Purāṇas: "(a) Prajāpati considered alms that are being offered, brought forth, and not previously announced as fit to be eaten even from one who has committed evil deeds. (b) His ancestors do not eat for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblations, for him who holds such food in contempt."
The food of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a fowler, an unchaste woman, and a eunuch—these are not to be eaten.

Furthermore, they cite this: "The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the eater of his food; the innocent man is defiled by the slanderer; and the thief who has escaped punishment transfers his guilt to the king when he begs for alms."
One should not practice religious duties by placing this worldly purpose at the forefront;
for they become fruitless with respect to spiritual elevation (*abhyudaya*).
Just as when a tree is planted for the sake of its fruit, shade and fragrance arise as secondary effects, so too when one practices religious duty, worldly benefits arise as secondary effects.

ApDhS 1.7.20.4: If they do not arise [in him], there is no loss of *dharma*. ApDhS 1.7.20.5: He should be free from envy and difficult to deceive regarding the talk of deceivers, rogues, nihilists, and fools. ApDhS 1.7.20.6: Neither gods, Gandharvas, nor ancestors say, "We two practice *dharma* and *adharma*"; nor do they declare, "This is *dharma*, this is *adharma*."
ApDhS 1.7.20.7: That which the noble ones (*ārya*) praise when it is being performed is *dharma*; that which they censure is *adharma*. ApDhS 1.7.20.8:

One should follow the conduct (*vṛtta*) of those who are consistent in all regions, who are noble, well-disciplined, aged, self-controlled, free from greed, and devoid of hypocrisy; one should adhere to their similarity of conduct.
ApDhS 1.7.20.9: In this way, one conquers both worlds.
Trade is not prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa.
In times of distress, however, he may engage in commerce, avoiding those goods that are forbidden for sale.

These include: human beings, liquids, dyes, perfumes, food, hides, a barren cow, phlegm, water, sprouts, fermenting agents, long pepper and black pepper, grain, meat, weapons, and the hope of a good reputation.

One should especially not sell sesame and rice among grains. Furthermore, the mutual exchange of these items is not prescribed. Nor should there be an exchange of food for food, humans for humans, liquids for liquids, fragrances for fragrances, or knowledge for knowledge.
One should engage in trade with goods that have not been purchased:
with *muñja* grass, *balbaja* grass, roots, and fruits; and with grass and wood that have not been processed.
One should not settle down permanently;
having obtained a livelihood, one should desist from worldly activity.
No social intercourse with outcasts is permitted.
Likewise, [one becomes an outcast] by sharing a vessel with those who have lost their caste.
Now, the causes for falling [from one's status] (patanīyāni) are:

theft, calumny, killing a human being, abandoning a Veda-student, destroying an embryo, sexual intercourse with the mother, the father, or other female relatives connected by birth—including their offspring—and drinking liquor, as well as having sexual intercourse with those with whom it is forbidden.

Having approached the wife of a teacher, the female friend of a teacher, and other women whose husbands are away, one does not fall [from his caste] if it is not the bed of a Guru— so say some. However, the constant practice of unrighteous acts [leads to such a fall].
ApDhS 1.7.21.12: Now, the acts that cause impurity.
ApDhS 1.7.21.13: Having sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman when one is an Ārya.
ApDhS 1.7.21.14: Eating the meat of animals whose consumption is forbidden.
ApDhS 1.7.21.15: [The same penance applies for] consuming the urine or excrement of a dog, a human, domestic fowl, or pig, or of carnivorous animals.
ApDhS 1.7.21.16: [The same applies for] consuming the urine or excrement of humans.
ApDhS 1.7.21.17: [The same applies for] consuming the leavings of a Śūdra, and for Āryas receiving food from one who has been excluded from the company of diners (apapātra).
ApDhS 1.7.21.18: Some maintain that even these [other acts] are causes for falling (patanīya).
ApDhS 1.7.21.19: Other than these, there are other faulty acts that cause impurity.
ApDhS 1.7.21.20: Having recognized a fault, one should not be the first to proclaim it to others regarding someone who has fallen; rather, one should avoid him in religious matters.
One should practice spiritual disciplines that are consistent with reason and free from worldly attachment.
There is nothing superior to the attainment of the Self.
In this regard, we shall cite verses concerning the attainment of the Self.

All living beings are indeed the cave-dwelling city of the one who lies in the cave, who is never slain and is free from stain. Those who attend upon that which is immovable yet has its abode in the moving world are immortal.
Whatever is here in this world is called an object of sense; having shaken off this, the wise man should attend upon that which lies in the cave.

Not finding this Self within yourself, practice what is beneficial and avoid what is harmful. Then, with no expectation of reward, I shall seek among others that state of the virtuous—the great body of splendor, the Lord established everywhere.

He who is eternal among all beings, wise, immortal, and firm; limbless, soundless, bodiless, intangible, great, and pure—he is everything, he is the supreme goal, he is the equinox. He who would abide in him, always practicing his path everywhere, being disciplined and perceiving that which is difficult to see and subtle, shall rejoice in the world.
Seeing all beings in the Self, the wise man who reflects shall not be deluded; he who sees the Self everywhere—he indeed shines as Brahmā upon the back of the firmament.

He who is subtle, subtler than the fiber of a lotus stalk, and who stands pervading all; who is greater than the earth, firm, and stands grasping all—he is the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhī*), distinct from the knowledge of this world by means of the senses, yet not different from that which is to be known; he is the divider. From him all bodies originate; he is the root, eternal, and everlasting.
But in this life, the eradication of faults has its root in yoga; having removed those things that burn living beings, the wise man attains security.
Now we shall set forth the defects that lead to the burning of living beings:
anger, joy, wrath, greed, delusion, hypocrisy, malice, falsehood, overeating, slander, envy, lust, resentment, lack of self-control, and lack of yoga; the eradication of these is rooted in yoga.

Absence of anger, absence of exultation, absence of resentment, absence of greed, absence of delusion, absence of hypocrisy, absence of malice, truthful speech, moderation in eating, absence of backbiting, absence of envy, sharing with others, renunciation, straightforwardness, gentleness, tranquility, self-control, non-opposition toward all beings, yoga, nobility, kindness, and contentment—these are the fundamental rules for all stages of life (*āśrama*). By practicing these according to the prescribed rule, one becomes one who attains all goals.
Having killed a Kṣatriya, one should give a thousand cows as a means of expiation for the enmity; a hundred for a Vaiśya; and ten for a Śūdra.
And in all these cases, a bull is additionally required for the purpose of expiation.
And it is the same regarding women of these [classes].
Having killed a student of the Veda belonging to either of the two former castes, or one who has gone to a Soma-sacrifice, or even a mere Brāhmaṇa, one is accused (and must perform penance).
And [the penance for killing] an embryo whose sex is unknown, and for killing a woman of the Ātreya clan, is as follows:

having built a hut in the forest, remaining silent, with the head of a corpse as his banner, and covering himself with a garment made of half-wool from below the navel to above the knees; this is his expiation.
His path is between the two tracks.
Having seen another [person], he should step aside.
He should enter the village with a broken, reddish earthenware dish.
Ap1.9.24.15: "He should go for alms to seven houses while being accused. Ap1.9.24.16:
That is his means of subsistence.
Ap1.9.24.17: If he does not obtain anything, he shall fast.
And he should tend the cows;
for their going out and coming in, a second [stay] in the village is permitted.
Having practiced this for twelve years, he becomes perfected and attains association with the virtuous.

Or, having built a hut on the path of battle, he may dwell there desiring to win back the property of Brahmins or cows; or, having been thrice defeated, he is released upon winning them back. Or, having performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Ashvamedha sacrifice, he is released. This same penance applies to one who seizes wealth when both dharma and artha are in conflict.

Having killed a teacher or a *śrotriya* who has completed his ritual studies, one shall perform penance according to this very rule until the final breath. For such a person, there is no restoration to his former status in this world; however, his stain is removed.
One who has violated the teacher’s bed shall cut off his penis together with the testicles, place them in his joined palms, and walk toward the southern direction from which there is no return.
ApDhS 1.9.25.2: Or, having embraced a glowing iron image (*sūrmi*), he shall complete his penance.
ApDhS 1.9.25.3: One who has touched liquor or water containing liquor shall drink liquor.

ApDhS 1.9.25.4: A thief, with disheveled hair and carrying a wooden pestle on his shoulder, shall go to the king and confess his deed; the king shall strike him with it, and by that blow, he is released from the guilt. (Having placed [the pestle] upon him...)
ApDhS 1.9.25.5: If permission is granted, he incurs sin against the one who grants it.
ApDhS 1.9.25.6: Or he may enter fire, or undertake severe austerity. ApDhS 1.9.25.7: Or he may emaciate himself by reducing his food.

Or he may perform the *kṛcchra-saṃvatsara* penance. Furthermore, they quote this: "Having committed theft, drunk liquor, or violated the teacher's bed, but not having committed the murder of a Brahmin, they should eat measured food at the fourth meal-time and enter the water according to the ritual of the *savana*s. Alternating between standing and sitting, they remove their sin after three years. (ApDhS 1.9.25.8–10) (Note: 1 = K 10, 11; 2: inserts /; 3: *nundante*)

ApDhS 1.9.25.11: Having abandoned the first caste—that is, having killed a member of the first caste—one should go to battle; there they should kill him. ApDhS 1.9.25.12: Or alternatively, having caused his hair, skin, and flesh to be offered as an oblation, he should enter the fire.

ApDhS 1.9.25.13: For killing a crow, a peacock, a peacock-of-the-forest (*barhiṇa*), a ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), a swan (*haṃsa*), a vulture (*bhāsa*), a frog, a mongoose, a *ḍerika*, or a horse, the penance is the same as for a Śūdra.

ApDhS 1.9.26.1: And for killing a milch cow or a bull without a valid cause; ApDhS 1.9.26.2: And for causing the death of other living beings that are capable of bearing a yoke or being used for transport; ApDhS 1.9.26.3: Having reviled one who should not be reviled, or having spoken an untruth, one shall subsist for three nights on food that is neither milk, nor pungent, nor saline.
ApDhS 1.9.26.4: For a Śūdra, there shall be fasting for seven nights.
ApDhS 1.9.26.5: And the same applies to women.
ApDhS 1.9.26.6: In cases where there is a charge of grievous sin, one limb shall be cut off [provided no injury to life occurs].

ApDhS 1.9.26.7: Having committed an ignoble act, slander, or any prohibited conduct; having consumed what is unfit to be eaten, tasted, or drunk; having discharged semen into a Śūdra woman or into a non-vaginal opening; or having intentionally or unintentionally performed a blameworthy act—one should touch water with verses addressed to the Waters (*ap-liṅga*), or with verses addressed to Varuṇa (*vāruṇī*), or with other purificatory mantras (*pavitra*), according to the repetition of the act.
ApDhS 1.9.26.8: One who has violated the vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*) should sacrifice to Nirṛti with a donkey using the *pākayajña* ritual.
ApDhS 1.9.26.9: A Śūdra should consume the sacrificial remains of that offering.
[The expiation for studying falsely:

For one year, while remaining intent on the welfare of his teacher, he shall restrain his speech, except when reciting his own Vedic study; and the teacher [shall likewise restrain his speech] toward the teacher’s wife and when going on alms-rounds.
In this same manner, for other sinful acts involving loss of caste (*patanīya*) which we shall describe hereafter, the subsequent [penances] apply.
Or he may offer oblations with the two mantras "Desire has done it" and "Anger has done it," or he should mutter them, saying, "Desire has done it; Anger has done it.

Or, on a sacred festival day (parvan), having fasted while consuming sesame seeds, or having fasted until the next day, he should touch water and repeat the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times, either with each breath-control (prāṇāyāma) or without breath-control.

On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, having fasted on that day or on the following day, one should touch the waters of a great river and either offer a thousand pieces of fuel while reciting the Sāvitrī verse or mutter it.
Or, one should perform purificatory *iṣṭi* sacrifices, *yajña*s, or *kratu*s.
Having eaten food that is unfit to be consumed, one should undergo the *naiṣpurīṣya* penance.
That is accomplished by a seven-night fast;
or one may touch water at both twilights during the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira;
or one may perform the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance.

ApDhS 1.9.27.7: For three days he eats without oil and does not eat during the day; then for another three days, he observes the vow of eating only what is unasked for; and for three days he does not eat anything at all—this is the rule for the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance. ApDhS 1.9.27.8: If one should practice this very same rite for a year, that constitutes a *kṛcchra* performed over a year. ApDhS 1.9.27.9: Now, another rule: even after committing many acts that cause loss of caste (*apataniya*), one becomes purified by having performed the penance through three recitations of the Veda while fasting.

ApDhS 1.9.27.10: He who supports an ignoble woman on his bed, he who bestows interest upon one who drinks fermented liquors, and he who, having paid homage like a non-Brāhmaṇa, sits down upon blades of grass with his back scorched by the sun—[these are the punishments]. ApDhS 1.9.27.11: Whatever sin a Brāhmaṇa incurs in a single night by serving a man of dark complexion, he destroys that sin in three years by eating only at the fourth mealtime and subsisting on water.
"Whoever considers another's property as his own becomes a thief," so say Kautsa, Hārīta, Kaṇva, and Puṣkarasādi.
Vārṣyāyaṇi says that there are exceptions regarding such possessions:
"Fodder for a yoke-animal and fuel do not prohibit one from taking them from their owner."
Excessive taking away results in failure.
Hārīta says that in all cases it must be preceded by permission. One should not go to see an outcast teacher or a kinsman.
And he should not enjoy these pleasures;
having accepted what comes by chance, he should pass by in silence.
A mother undertakes many actions for the sake of her son's status.
One should always attend upon her even when she has fallen from grace;
however, there should be no joint performance of religious duties (*dharma-saṃnipāta*). (Or: there should be no cohabitation.)

ApDhS 1.10.28.11: Having consented to enjoyments acquired through unrighteous means, and having declared, "Neither we nor unrighteousness," he shall cover himself from below the navel to above the knees, touch water three times a day, eat food that is neither milk, nor pungent, nor saline, and for twelve years he shall not enter a house. (K: 1. adho nābhi; 2. jānvācchādya; 3. akṣīrākṣārālavaṇaṃ; 4. na āgāraṃ). ApDhS 1.10.28.12:
From that, perfection is attained. ApDhS 1.10.28.13:
Then there may be association with noble persons.
This same [penance] applies to others who have committed *patanīya* sins as well.
However, one who has violated the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpagāmī*) shall enter a hollow metal image (*sūrmi*), set fire to both ends, and burn himself.
Hārīta says this is false.
For he who considers himself superior to another is indeed accursed.
By this very rule, he should perform penance until his final breath; there is no restoration for him in this world, but his taint is removed.

One who violates the fidelity of his wife shall put on a donkey skin with the hair turned outward and beg for alms from seven houses, saying, "Alms for one who has violated his wife. This shall be his mode of livelihood for six months.
But for a woman who has transgressed against her husband, there is the practice of the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights for that same duration of time.

Now, a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*), having put on the skin of a dog or the skin of a donkey with the hair turned outward, and having taken a human head for the purpose of drinking [the blood] against the current [of the river],...

Carrying a bedstead leg as a staff and announcing his occupation by saying, "Who will give alms to the slayer of a learned Brahmin? he should wander about. Having obtained means for sustaining life in a village, he should take refuge in an empty house or at the root of a tree, thinking: "I have no association with noble men. By this very rule, he should live until his final breath; for him there is no restoration to his former status in this world, but his taint is indeed removed.

He who, being negligent, kills one who has arrived [as his victim], incurs the fruit of the offense; this is all the more so when accompanied by a deliberate intention. The same applies to other actions that involve faults.

Likewise, even for the sake of meritorious deeds, a Brāhmaṇa should not take up a weapon, even for the purpose of testing it. For it is said in the Purāṇa: "He who strikes one who has already attacked him for the purpose of harming him touches only wrath with wrath; there is no fault in that."

Now, those who have been accused of a grave sin may live together after resolving, "We shall act according to dharma. Having agreed upon this, they may act as sacrificers for one another, as teachers to one another, and intermarry among themselves.
After they have produced sons, they should say: "O Brahmins, depart from us; for it was thus that our ancestors entered into this state.
Furthermore, he does not fall [from his caste] so long as he remains possessed of his virile power.
This is to be understood by this: for one who is deficient in a limb begets a child with complete limbs. Hārīta says that this is false;
a woman possesses the same characteristics as a vessel for curd.

For when one churns impure milk in a vessel for curds after it has been curdled, no religious duty is accomplished by that act. Likewise, there is no association with that which is impure once the pure portion has been separated. (Kāṭañcya) Malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and curses (*anuvyāhāra*) cause impurity, but they do not entail loss of caste (*apatanīya*). Hārīta, however, maintains that they do entail loss of caste.

ApDhS 1.10.29.17: But for those who perform acts causing impurity, the conduct leading to downfall consists of twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of seven days, twelve periods of three days, twelve days, seven days, three days, and one day. (K 1: inserts *dvādaśa dvahān* between *tryahān* and *dvādaśāhaṃ*; K 2: inserts *dvyaham*) ApDhS 1.10.29.18: Thus is the expiation for acts causing impurity, according to the repetition of the act.
"By means of knowledge he bathes," say some;
likewise, "by means of the vow measured at forty-eight years";
and "by means of both knowledge and the vow," say others.
ApDhS 1.11.30.4: In all of these cases, the conduct is that of a *snātaka*.
ApDhS 1.11.30.5: Due to differences in concentration and differences in the sacred texts (*śruti*), there is a difference in the fruit regarding the worship.
ApDhS 1.11.30.6: Now, the vows of a *snātaka*.
One should practice exiting and entering the village by the eastern gate, or by the northern one. At both twilights, one should sit outside the village, restraining one's speech.
In case of a conflict between two rules, that which is based on direct Vedic revelation (śruti) is more authoritative.
One should avoid all dyed garments; likewise, one should avoid a garment that is naturally black. One should wear a garment that is not dazzlingly bright.
And one should not cover the head while within range of one's ability to do otherwise. During the day, one should avoid covering the head, except during the act of voiding urine or excrement.
However, when voiding urine or excrement at night, one should do so on the ground after covering the head and placing some material as a barrier between oneself and the earth.
One should avoid performing the act of voiding urine or excrement in the shade (of a tree). However, one may void urine in one's own shadow.
One should not void urine or excrement while wearing shoes, nor on ploughed land, on a path, or in water.
Likewise, one should avoid spitting and sexual intercourse in water.
(ApDhS 1.11.30.19) One should avoid performing the acts of urination and defecation while facing fire, the sun, water, a Brāhmaṇa, cows, or deities.
(ApDhS 1.11.30.20) For the cleansing after urination and defecation, one should avoid using a stone, a clod of earth, fresh herbs, or trees by cutting them from above. (ApDhS 1.11.30.21)
One should not, within one's power, turn away from fire, water, a Brāhmaṇa, cows, deities, a door, or the wind.
(ApDhS 1.11.30.22) Furthermore, they also cite this:

(ApDhS 1.11.31.1) "One should eat food facing the east; one should discharge excrement facing the south; one should urinate facing the north; and the washing of the feet is toward the west. (ApDhS 1.11.31.1)
One should void urine and feces at a distance from one's dwelling, toward the southern direction or slightly south of it.

After sunset, one should avoid performing the act of voiding urine or feces outside the village or at a distance from one's dwelling. Furthermore, one who is impure should not utter the names of the deities.
One should avoid touching a man who belongs to both classes of deities and to the king;
one should avoid touching the foot of a Brahmin or a cow; and one should avoid touching with the hand without a specific reason.
One should avoid speaking ill of cows, sacrificial fees, and virgins; one should not point out a cow that is licking [the calf],
nor a cow that is excessively fond of her calf, unless there is a specific reason.
One should not say of a non-cow, "a non-cow"; one should rather say, "one that is to become a cow.
One should not say of what is auspicious, "the auspicious"; one should rather say, "meritorious" or "well-governed. And one should not walk over a rope to which a calf is tied.
One should not pass between the two *pleṅkha* poles.
One should not say, "This one is my rival. If one were to say, "This one is my rival," he would produce an enemy and a hostile kinsman.
One should not point out a rainbow to another, saying, "It is Indra’s bow."
One should not look at [the sun] when it is falling [behind the horizon]. One should avoid looking at the sun while it is rising or setting, as far as it remains within sight.

By day the sun protects living beings, and by night the moon; therefore, on the night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), one should desire greater protection for oneself through self-restraint, the period of celibacy, and proper conduct.
For on this night, Sūrya and Candramas dwell together.
(K 22) One should not enter a village by a shortcut. If one should enter, he should mutter this *ṛc*: "Homage to Rudra Vāstoṣpati," or another verse addressed to Rudra.

(K 23) One should not give the remains of food (*ucchiṣṭa*) to a non-Brahmin. If he should give them, he should first bite off the tips of the grains, place them upon that [non-Brahmin], and then give them. (K 25–26)
He should avoid anger and other defects that burn living beings. (ApDhS 1.11.31.23) One engaged in sacred study should avoid sexual intercourse during the rainy season and autumn.
(ApDhS 1.11.32.1) Having engaged in sexual union, he should not sleep with her for the remainder of the night. (ApDhS 1.11.32.2)
And while lying down, he should avoid teaching. Nor should he teach on that same bed upon which he himself lies.
He should not wear visible garlands or apply ointments.
