He should always adorn himself for his wife at night;
he should avoid immersing his head in water;
and he should not bathe after sunset.

He should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, wooden sandals, and the cleaning of his teeth. He should also avoid praising his teacher in his presence, such as saying, "He has bathed well. And he should remain awake until nightfall.

ApDhS 1.11.32.12: There is no study during the night, except for the instruction of students in the Dharma. ApDhS 1.11.32.13: Or one may study mentally by oneself. ApDhS 1.11.32.14: Teaching may take place after midnight.

ApDhS 1.11.32.15: Having risen after the latter part of the night, one should not go back to bed thinking, "It is a time unfit for study. ApDhS 1.11.32.16: One may, however, lie down on one's side. ApDhS 1.11.32.17: Or one may recite the Veda mentally.
One should not frequent low-born people, nor regions inhabited by such low-born people; one should avoid assemblies and social gatherings.
If one must go to a social gathering, one should circumambulate it clockwise before departing.
He should avoid entering cities,
he should not answer questions,
and furthermore, they cite this:

"The root and the tuft of the one who speaks ill are torn out; he destroys his offspring, cattle, and his abode. O Dharmaprahrāda, Death did not speak this question for the sake of harming a child, even while weeping."
He should avoid mounting a donkey vehicle, as well as ascending or descending uneven heights. He should not cross a river with his arms,
nor should he board a boat that is in a state of uncertainty.
Cutting grass, crushing clods of earth, spitting, and so forth, without a valid reason;
and whatever else they censure, and whatever else they censure.
ApDhS 2.1.1.1: From the taking of the hand [in marriage], the vow of the householders begins.
ApDhS 2.1.1.2: Eating [is permitted] at two times of the day.
ApDhS 2.1.1.3: And there must be no satiety with food.
Ap2.1.1.4: On the festival days (parvan), there is fasting for both [husband and wife].
Ap2.1.1.5: Eating at another time constitutes the very state of fasting (aupavasta).
Ap2.1.1.6: And there must be satisfaction with food.
Ap2.1.1.7: And whatever may be dear to these two, that they should eat on this day; Ap2.1.1.8: and they should sleep on the ground;
Ap2.1.1.9: and there must be avoidance of sexual intercourse.
Ap2.1.1.10: On the following day, there is the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering). Ap2.1.1.11: Its procedure is explained by [the rules of] the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha]. Ap2.1.1.12:
They teach that this is obligatory for worldly life.
Ap2.1.1.13: Wherever one intends to kindle the fire, there one should draw three lines each directed toward the east and the north, sprinkle them with water, and then kindle the fire.
Ap2.1.1.14: Having poured out this water, one should place another vessel to the north or to the east.
Ap2.1.1.15: Water-vessels must always remain unfilled with water; this is the vow for the householder and his wife.

ApDhS 2.1.1.16: On the day [of the wedding], they shall not sleep together. ApDhS 2.1.1.17: And during the fertile period, he shall have union with his wife according to the prescribed rule. ApDhS 2.1.1.18: Even during the intervening periods, he shall have union only with his wife.

ApDhS 2.1.1.19: And the act of lying down together occurs because of the word of a Brāhmaṇa. ApDhS 2.1.1.20: The sexual union should take place with her wearing only her woman’s garment. ApDhS 2.1.1.21: And they shall share the same bed only as long as the sexual union lasts.
Ap2.1.1.22: After that, [the teacher says] "Nānā" (separate).
Ap2.1.1.23: [The students] perform the ritual touching of water (*udakopasparśana*).
Ap2.1.2.1 / Alternatively, having washed the smears and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), there is the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the limbs.
Ap2.1.2.2 / For all social classes (*varṇas*), there is supreme and immeasurable happiness in the performance of their own duties (*svadharma*).

Ap2.1.2.3 / Upon returning from that [state], by means of the remainder of the fruits of one's actions, one obtains birth, form, class, strength, intelligence, wisdom, wealth, and the performance of duty; like a wheel, this revolves for the sake of happiness in both worlds.

Ap2.1.2.4: Just as there is an increase in the fruit of herbs and trees through specific treatments of the seed and the field, so it is here. Ap2.1.2.5: By this, the increase in the fruit of faults has been explained. Ap2.1.2.6: A Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya who is a thief or one accused of a heinous crime is born in the next world, after a limited period in hell, as a Caṇḍāla if he was a Brāhmaṇa, a Paulkasa if he was a Rājanya, or a Vaiṇa if he was a Vaiśya. (K: *parimitaṃ*)

ApDhS 2.1.2.7: By this same principle, others who have fallen away due to actions resulting in defects are born in wombs that result in defects, specifically in those castes that have fallen away from their status.
ApDhS 2.1.2.8: Just as there is a defect incurred by touching, conversing with, or looking upon a *caṇḍāla*, so too is there a penance for that.
ApDhS 2.1.2.9: For touching water, the penance is immersion; for conversation, it is conversing with a Brāhmaṇa; and for looking, it is looking at the luminaries (the sun).
Ap2.2.3.1: During the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the Āryas who prepare the food should be pure.
Ap2.2.3.2: One should avoid facing food while speaking, coughing, or sneezing.
Ap2.2.3.3: Having touched one's hair, limbs, or clothing, one should touch water.
Or, Śūdras presided over by Āryans may perform the consecrations.
For them, the same rule for sipping water (ācamana) applies;
additionally, they must shave their hair, beards, body hair, and nails every day.

And there shall be a touching of water along with the garment. Or rather, they may sow [the seeds] only on the eighth days or on the festival days. Having placed the prepared food out of sight over the fire, one should sprinkle it with water; that is called the "divine purifier" (*devapavitra*).
Ap2.2.3.10: When the food is ready, [the wife], standing [over it], should announce to the master, "It is prepared.
Ap2.2.3.11: The response is, "May that well-prepared food, which is the Virāj, never diminish for me.
Ap2.2.3.12: For the two householders, whatever offerings and oblations of edible food are connected with heaven and prosperity—[these belong to] the householder.
Ap2.2.3.13: When these mantras are employed, for twelve days there shall be sleeping on the ground, celibacy, and the avoidance of pungent and salty foods.
Ap2.2.3.14: For the final [mantra], there is a fast for one night.
Ap2.2.3.15: Regarding the offerings (balis), the consecration at each respective place consists of wiping with the hand, sprinkling water, placing [the food], and finally pouring water around it.
Ap2.2.3.16: At the *aupāsana* fire or the cooking fire, one should offer oblations with the hand using the first six mantras, one by one.
Ap2.2.3.17: There is sprinkling of water around the fire at both the beginning and the end, as prescribed previously.
Ap2.2.3.18: Likewise, for the *bali* offerings gathered in their respective places, there is a single sprinkling of water around the fire at the end.
Ap2.2.3.19: [The rites] are to be performed with [the formulas] well-conjoined when [the condition] exists.
Ap2.2.3.20: To the west of the fire, [he performs the rites] with the seventh and eighth [formulas], ending towards the north.
Ap2.2.3.21: In the vicinity of the water-vessel, he performs [the rite] with the ninth [formula].
Ap2.2.3.22: In the middle of the house, [he should offer] with the tenth and eleventh [formulas], ending toward the east.
Ap2.2.3.23: In the north-eastern part of the house, [he should offer] with the four following [formulas].
Ap2.2.4.1: In the place of the bed, [he should offer] with the formula containing the word *kāma* (desire).
Ap2.2.4.2: [He places it] on the threshold with a verse containing a word for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
Ap2.2.4.3: [He places it] on the north side of the cover.
Ap2.2.4.4: With the following verses, [he places it] on the seat of the Brahman priest (*brahmasadana*).

Ap2.2.4.5: To the south, with the *pitṛ-liṅga* formula, wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), and with his hand turned downwards (*avācīna-pāṇiḥ*), he should perform [the rites].
Ap2.2.4.6: The northern [rite] is dedicated to Rudra, according to the respective deities.
Ap2.2.4.7: For these two, the sprinkling around is performed separately because of the difference in their ritual rules (*dharma-bheda*).
Ap2.2.4.8: At night alone, with the last [verse], he should perform the Vaihāyasa [offering].
Ap2.2.4.9: He who performs these [rites] constantly, without distraction and according to the instruction, attains heaven and prosperity.
Ap2.2.4.10: And the first portion should be given away.
ApDhS 2.2.4.11: He should feed the guests first.
ApDhS 2.2.4.12: [He should feed] children, the elderly, those afflicted by disease, and women who are pregnant.
ApDhS 2.2.4.13: At the proper time, the two masters (husband and wife) should not refuse one who comes seeking food.

Ap2.2.4.14: In the absence [of other things], the earth, water, grass, and kind words—these indeed never fail in the house of a virtuous man. Ap2.2.4.15: For one who conducts himself in this manner, there are infinite worlds.
Ap2.2.4.16: To a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied [the Veda], a seat, water, and food should be given; one should not rise to greet him.
One should rise specifically for the purpose of greeting [if the person to be greeted is present].
This applies to both a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya.
As for a Śūdra who has arrived as a guest, one should employ him in work and then give him food.
Ap2.2.4.20: Or, having brought a Śūdra from the royal palace, they should honor him like a guest.
Ap2.2.4.21: An upper garment must always be worn. Ap2.2.4.22: Or else, a thread alone may serve the purpose of the sacred thread (upavīta).

Ap2.2.4.23: Where it has been eaten, that place should be swept together, cleared away, and sprinkled with water; having scraped off the smears from the vessels and mixing them with water, one should pour them out toward the north in a clean spot for Rudra. In this way, the site becomes auspicious. Ap2.2.4.24: However, a Brāhmaṇa is traditionally remembered as the teacher. Ap2.2.4.25:
In times of distress, study may be undertaken by a Brāhmaṇa under a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.
Ap2.2.4.26: And following behind [the corpse] occurs afterwards.

(K 27) Ap2.2.4.27: After that, the Brāhmaṇa alone should be at the front as they proceed. (K 28) Ap2.2.5.1: Having commenced the study of any of the Upaniṣads among all the sciences, there shall be no study on that day.

Ap2.2.5.2: Having completed his studies, he should not depart immediately. Ap2.2.5.3: If, however, he is in haste, he may go at will after having recited the Veda while in the presence of the teacher; in this way, welfare accrues to both. Ap2.2.5.4: If the teacher should come to him after he has returned home, he should go out to meet him face-to-face, clasp his feet, and without feeling any aversion, touch water, place him in front, and honor him according to the instructions.
ApDhS 2.2.5.5: When sitting, lying down, or when food to be chewed, food to be eaten, or clothing is present, he should adopt a more humble manner.
ApDhS 2.2.5.6: Standing and supporting the teacher with his left hand, he should cause him to sip water for purification (*ācamana*).
ApDhS 2.2.5.7: Or he may cause another person of equal status to do so.
When he desires to imitate [the teacher's] standing, sitting, walking, or smiling, [he should do so].

(ApDhS 2.2.5.8) In the presence [of the teacher], he should avoid passing wind, voiding urine or excrement, speaking loudly, laughing, spitting, grinding his teeth, yawning, frowning, clapping his hands, and spitting. (ApDhS 2.2.5.9) Regarding his wife and children, he should avoid touching them or speaking to them with excessive familiarity. (ApDhS 2.2.5.10)
One should avoid contradicting a sentence with another sentence, as well as the teacher’s words; likewise, one should avoid contradicting those who are superior,
and all forms of reviling or abuse directed at living beings.
And by means of one branch of knowledge, he may study all branches of knowledge.
(ApDhS 2.2.5.14) If, through a particular branch of knowledge, he does not shine forth, he should approach his teacher once again and master it with strict discipline.

(ApDhS 2.2.5.15) From the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) until the conclusion (*utsarjana*), the teacher must observe restrictive rules. He should avoid shaving the hair on his body, eating meat, performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and sexual intercourse. (ApDhS 2.2.5.16)
Or, for the sake of a religious rite, he may take a wife (ApDhS 2.2.5.17).

He should be devoted to the transmission of knowledge to his disciples and to the observance of rules according to the tradition (ApDhS 2.2.5.18). Behaving in this manner, he secures the welfare of his ancestors, his descendants, and himself. (ApDhS 2.2.5.18). By means of the mind, speech, breath, sight, hearing, and by refraining from the discharge of semen through the restraint of the penis, stomach, and hands, he becomes fit for immortality (ApDhS 2.2.5.19).

Ap2.3.6.1. When there is doubt regarding a person’s caste or conduct, one should kindle a fire for the sake of determining the dharma and, having done so, inquire about their caste and conduct. Ap2.3.6.2. If they profess their integrity, saying, "Agni is the witness, Vāyu is the listener, Āditya is the observer; he professes his integrity," then, having said, "May integrity be ours; this sin is false," one should proceed to instruct them. Ap2.3.6.3. A guest approaches like a blazing fire.
ApDhS 2.3.6.4: Having studied one branch of each of the Vedas according to the law, one becomes a *śrotriya*.
ApDhS 2.3.6.5: A householder who approaches another while engaged in his own duty, motivated by righteousness and having no other purpose, is an *atithi* (guest).
ApDhS 2.3.6.6: Through honoring him, there is peace and heaven.
Having approached him face-to-face and gathered together according to their age, he should offer him a seat.
Some say that, within one's capacity, the seat should not have many legs.
He should wash his feet; some say that this should be done by a Śūdra couple.
Ap2.3.6.10: One or the other [of the two] should participate in the consecration. Ap2.3.6.11: Some say that one should cause water to be brought for him in an earthen vessel.
Ap2.3.6.12: One who has not yet returned home from his teacher’s house should not be made to sip water.
And here, the means of subsistence for study is also included.
Having consoled them, one should satisfy them with liquids, foods, and water, at least with the lowest grade of offerings.
One should provide a dwelling, a bed above, a mattress, a pillow, a coverlet, and an ointment.
Ap2.3.6.16: Having summoned the preparer of the food, he should pour out rice or barley intended for that purpose.
Ap2.3.6.17: He should look at the portions of food that have been drawn out, saying: "Is this more? Is this more? Ap2.3.6.18: He should say: "Draw out more."
One should not eat the food of one who hates him, or of one who is hated; nor of one who suspects him of a fault, or of one who has been suspected.
For it is known from tradition: "He indeed consumes the evil of that person."
Ap2.3.7.1. This very sacrifice of the householder belongs to Prajāpati; it is perpetually extended. Ap2.3.7.2.
That fire which is for guests is the Āhavanīya; that which is in the household is the Gārhapatya; and that upon which food is cooked is the Anvāhāryapacana. Ap2.3.7.3.
He who eats before the guest eats away the strength, the prosperity, the offspring, the cattle, and the merit of both sacrificial and charitable works belonging to his house.

Food with a pouring of milk is commensurate with the Agniṣṭoma; with clarified butter, it is commensurate with the Ukthya; with honey, it is commensurate with the Atirātra; and with meat, it is commensurate with the Dvādaśāha. With water, there is an increase of progeny and of life-span.
It is known from tradition that dear and even non-dear guests cause one to go to the heavenly world.
When he gives at morning, midday, and evening, those gifts become the very Soma-pressings (savana).

Whatever he performs, that is indeed the *udavasanīya* sacrifice. Whatever he conciliates (*sāntvayati*), that is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the praise. Whatever he accomplishes, those are the *viṣṇukrama* steps.

"That which he turns toward is the *avabhṛtha*," for so says the *Brāhmaṇa*. If a guest should arrive while the *rājasūya* is being performed, he should cause a more excellent honor to be bestowed upon him than that which he has prepared for himself.

Ap2.3.7.13: If a guest should arrive at one who has established the sacred fires, he himself should rise to meet him and say: "O Vrātya, where did you stay? "O Vrātya, here is water. "O Vrātya, satisfy yourself. Ap2.3.7.14: Before the Agnihotra oblation is offered, he should mutter softly: "O Vrātya, may it be according to your mind. "O Vrātya, may it be according to your will. "O Vrātya, may it be according to your pleasure. "O Vrātya, may it be according to your desire."

Ap2.3.7.15: If a guest should arrive when the fires have been taken out but not yet offered, he himself should rise to meet him and say, "O Vratya, give me leave; I shall sacrifice. Only when permitted may he sacrifice. If he should sacrifice without being permitted, the Brāhmaṇa declares that there is a fault.

ApDhS 2.3.7.16: "If one should lodge guests for one night, he conquers the earthly worlds; by a second night, the atmospheric worlds; by a third, the celestial worlds; by a fourth, the distant worlds; and by an unlimited number of nights, he conquers unlimited worlds—so it is known. ApDhS 2.3.7.17:

"If a guest who is not well-versed in the Vedas should arrive claiming to be such, one should give him a seat, water, and food with the thought, 'I am giving this to a *śrotriya*'; in this way, his act becomes complete."

ApDhS 2.4.8.1: One should not rise up for or descend from one's seat to greet a guest by whom a lodging has already been provided, provided that he was greeted first. ApDhS 2.4.8.2: He should eat only the remnants of what remains after the guests have eaten. ApDhS 2.4.8.3: He should not consume flavorful foods in his house without leaving some for the guests.
ApDhS 2.4.8.4: One should not cook delicious food for one's own sake.

ApDhS 2.4.8.5: A student who has completed his Vedic studies is worthy of the cow, honey, and the *madhuparka* offering. ApDhS 2.4.8.6: So too are the teacher, the officiating priest, the *snātaka*, and a king who is righteous.
ApDhS 2.4.8.7: To the teacher, the officiating priest, the father-in-law, and the king—when they visit after a year has passed—a cow and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) are offered.
ApDhS 2.4.8.8: The honey-mixture consists of curds mixed with honey, or milk mixed with honey. ApDhS 2.4.8.9:
In the absence of these, water is used.

ApDhS 2.4.8.10: The Veda has six auxiliary limbs (aṅgas). ApDhS 2.4.8.11: These are prosody (chandas), ritual science (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), astronomy (jyotiṣa), etymology (nirukta), phonetics (śīkṣā), and the analysis of meters (chando-viciti). ApDhS 2.4.8.12: However, the term "Veda" applies to the collection of rites that have words and meanings as their basis, upon the completion of the traditional recitation (samāmnāya). In that regard, the aforementioned number [of six limbs] is contradicted.
"However, it is the consensus of those who know the principles of logic that the subsidiaries (aṅga) are not designated by the same terms as the primary acts (pradhāna).
Having neglected a guest, if one remembers this while the meal is already underway, one should stop eating from that point and fast."
Ap2.4.9.1: On the following day, having gratified [the ancestors] according to his inclination, he should perform the *saṃsādana* rite.
Ap2.4.9.2: [He should do so] until the traveler has reached his vehicle. Ap2.4.9.3: Until the other [the host] gives permission.
Ap2.4.9.4: In case of a lack of confidence, he should desist at the boundary.
Ap2.4.9.5: At the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, he should make all participants sharers, even down to dogs and Caṇḍālas.
Ap2.4.9.6: Some say that one should not give to those who are unworthy.

ApDhS 2.4.9.7: One who has been initiated should avoid the remnants of food from women and from those who have not been initiated. ApDhS 2.4.9.8: All gifts should be preceded by the offering of water.
ApDhS 2.4.9.9: In the sacrificial rite, one should act according to the revealed scripture.
ApDhS 2.4.9.10: A distribution of shares has been ordained for those who are permanent dependents and those who receive a share by virtue of their status, provided it does not cause them hardship.
ApDhS 2.4.9.11: One may, at will, cause hardship to oneself, one's wife, or a son, but never a slave or a laborer.

ApDhS 2.4.9.12: Furthermore, one should ensure that no hardship is caused to oneself such that one becomes incapable of performing one's duties. (K: ...such that one remains capable of performing one's duties.)

Moreover, they cite this: "Eight mouthfuls are the meal of a sage (*muni*), sixteen for a forest-dweller, thirty-two for a householder, and an unlimited amount for a student (*brahmacārin*). (These are the quantities of food to be eaten.
"The one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the ox, and the student—these three achieve success only while eating; there is no success for them through fasting."

ApDhS 2.5.10.1: The occasions for begging are: when one’s teacher is away, at a marriage, at a sacrifice, when one’s parents desire to support [one], and when there is a lapse in the observances of an Arhat.
ApDhS 2.5.10.2: In those cases, having considered one’s qualities, one should give according to one’s ability.
ApDhS 2.5.10.3: But begging for the sake of gratifying the senses is without cause; one should not heed that.

Ap2.5.10.4: The specific duties of a Brāhmaṇa are studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, receiving gifts, inheritance, and gleaning ears of grain or picking up single grains. (K 5: *śiloñchaḥ*) Ap2.5.10.5: And other things that have not been specifically forbidden. (K 6) Ap2.5.10.6: These same duties apply to a Kṣatriya, with the exception of teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts; however, these are supplemented by the authority to wield punishment and engage in battle. (K 7)

ApDhS 2.5.10.7: The duties of a Vaiśya are like those of a Kṣatriya, with the exception of bearing arms and fighting; they additionally include agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. (K 8) ApDhS 2.5.10.8: One should not appoint as a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*) one who has not studied the Vedas, nor one who is haggling for a fee.
(9) ApDhS 2.5.10.9: One who has not studied the Vedas is unworthy to perform sacrifices. (K 10)

In battle, one should act according to the methods they teach for those purposes. (K 11) Noble people condemn the killing of those who have laid down their weapons, those with disheveled hair, those with joined palms, or those who have turned their backs. (K 12) For those who have mastered the scriptures but deviate from them due to weakness of the senses, the teacher should prescribe penance as prescribed for each specific act. (K 13)
If he should transgress the sacred law, one should cause him to go to the king; (K 14) the king [should send him] to the domestic priest who is skilled in dharma and artha;
(K 15) he [the priest] should appoint Brāhmaṇas [to deal with the case]. (K 16)

ApDhS 2.5.10.16: According to the specific gravity of the offense, he should cause the offender to wither away through restrictive penances, with the exception of corporal punishment or slavery. ApDhS 2.5.11.1: Regarding other castes, the king, having considered their actions, should inflict punishment until the end of life.
ApDhS 2.5.11.2: And he should not inflict punishment when there is doubt.
ApDhS 2.5.11.3: Having thoroughly investigated [the case], up until the divine ordeals, the king should proceed with the infliction of punishment.
ApDhS 2.5.11.4: A king who conducts himself in this manner conquers both worlds.
ApDhS 2.5.11.5: The path belongs to the king, except when meeting a Brāhmaṇa.
ApDhS 2.5.11.6: But when they meet, the path belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone.
ApDhS 2.5.11.7: Way must be yielded by everyone to one in a vehicle, to one burdened with a load, to a sick person, and to a woman.
ApDhS 2.5.11.8: And way must be yielded by lower castes to those of higher castes.
ApDhS 2.5.11.9: To those who are undisciplined, fallen, intoxicated, or insane, [the inheritance] must be given by all [relatives] for the sake of their own welfare.
ApDhS 2.5.11.10: Through the practice of righteousness (*dharma-caryā*), a lower caste attains each successive higher caste during the transformation of birth (*jāti-parivṛtti*).
ApDhS 2.5.11.11: Through the practice of unrighteousness (*adharma-caryā*), a higher caste falls to each successive lower caste during the transformation of birth.
ApDhS 2.5.11.12: One should not take another wife while one already has a wife who is endowed with both virtue and offspring.

ApDhS 2.5.11.13: In the absence of either of these, another may be taken before the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya). ApDhS 2.5.11.14: For once the fire-ritual has been performed, she becomes connected with those rites for which this [wife] is an essential constituent.

One should not give one’s daughter to a man of the same *gotra*, nor to those related through the mother’s lineage (*yoni-sambandha*). In the *brāhma* form of marriage, having ascertained the man’s kinship, character, learning, and health, one should bestow the daughter upon him— adorned with ornaments according to one’s means— for the sake of his offspring and for joint religious duties.
In the *ārṣa* rite, a pair of cattle should be given to the father of the daughter.
In the *daiva* rite, one should bestow the bride upon the officiating priest during the course of a sacrifice.
When a man and woman unite with each other out of mutual desire, that is the *gāndharva* rite.

Ap2.5.12.1: Having given away goods within the scope of one's power, they should marry her off; that is the Āsura [form]. Ap2.5.12.2: Having caused the father of the daughter to gamble, they should marry her off; that is the Rākṣasa [form]. Ap2.5.12.3: Among these, the first three are commendable; each preceding one is better than the next.
ApDhS 2.5.12.4: As the marriage is contracted, so the offspring becomes. ApDhS 2.5.12.5:
One should not step upon the hand-grasped [fire] of a Brāhmaṇa unless it has been sprinkled with water.
ApDhS 2.5.12.6–7: One should not pass between the fire and a Brāhmaṇa, nor between Brāhmaṇas.
Ap2.5.12.8: Or, having obtained permission, he may pass through.
Ap2.5.12.9: He should not hold fire and water simultaneously.
Ap2.5.12.10: And he should avoid the bringing together of different fires (or their confluence).

Ap2.5.12.11: One should not circumambulate the fire being brought forward while it is facing oneself, nor before it has been established upon the ground. Ap2.5.12.12: And one should not let one's hands touch each other behind one's back.

Ap2.5.12.13: Having fallen asleep or having woken up at sunset, one should remain seated for the night, restrained in speech, until dawn; on the following day, having touched water, one may release the vow of silence.
Ap2.5.12.14: Having slept, or having risen [from sleep], or having failed to eat, or having failed to eat for two days, one should remain silent during the day.
Ap2.5.12.15: Some say that one should restrain the breath until sunset. Ap2.5.12.16: Or [one should do so] after seeing an evil dream.
Or when one desires to accomplish a specific purpose; or when there is a transgression of another rule;
or when there is doubt regarding the consequences of a fault—one should not perform that [act].
The same applies to permitted and forbidden days for Vedic study (ApDhS 2.5.12.20).
One should not speak as if one were an eyewitness when there is doubt (ApDhS 2.5.12.21).

Among those who have been overtaken by sunset while studying, those who have studied at sunrise, those with deformed nails, those with black teeth, the younger brother whose elder brother is unmarried, the elder brother whose younger brother has married first, the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried, the younger brother who marries before the elder, the elder brother who marries after the younger, and the younger brother who performs the marriage rites while the elder is still living—among these, each subsequent person incurs a heavier penance for the removal of impurity than the preceding one (ApDhS 2.5.12.22).
And that sign, some say, should be removed after having performed the penance.

ApDhS 2.6.13.1: For those who approach their wife of equal caste, as prescribed by the prior scriptural injunctions, during her fertile season, there is a connection with their sons through their ritual acts. ApDhS 2.6.13.2: And there is no deviation regarding the inheritance for both [husband and wife]. ApDhS 2.6.13.3:
There is fault in sexual intercourse with one who has not been consecrated (uninitiated) or with one of a different caste, even if she possesses the aforementioned qualities.
Even in that case, the son belongs to the one who commits the fault. For it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "The son belongs to the progenitor.
Furthermore, they cite this example: "O Janaka, it is only now that I am jealous of women, not before; for when they were in the abode of Yama, they declared the son to belong to the progenitor."
The depositor of seed leads the son away after death to the abode of Yama; therefore, fearing the seed of another, they guard their wives.
"Be vigilant and guard this lineage; let no one sow the seeds of another in your field. In the life hereafter, the son belongs to the progenitor; the sower makes this lineage in vain."
Transgression of the law and acts of violence were observed among the ancients.
Due to their extraordinary spiritual power (*tejas*), no sin (*pratyavāya*) accrued to them.
Examining that precedent, one who applies it today meets with downfall.

The giving away or the act of purchase regarding offspring is not permitted. Regarding marriage, it is heard in the sacred texts that the gift given to the father of the daughter is optional; however, for the sake of dharma, it is prescribed that "one hundred [cows] plus one chariot should be given to the father of the daughter. To do otherwise would be false. In this context, the term "purchase" is merely a figurative praise, for the relationship [between the bridegroom and the family] arises from dharma.

ApDhS 2.6.13.12: Having gratified the eldest son with the "single-wealth" share; ApDhS 2.6.14.1: While living, he shall divide the inheritance among his sons equally, excluding one who is impotent, insane, or an outcast. ApDhS 2.6.14.2: In the absence of sons, the nearest *sapiṇḍa* shall receive it.

In the absence of that [heir], the teacher [should take it]; in the absence of the teacher, the pupil [should take it and], having taken it, employ it for the sake of those [funeral] rites or for religious duties.
Or the daughter [may do so].
In the absence of all these, the king shall take the inheritance.
"Only the eldest is the heir," say some. In certain regions, gold, black cows, and black land belong to the eldest;
likewise, the chariot and the household utensils of the father [belong to him].
"Ornaments and the paternal wealth of the kinsmen belong to the wife," say some. (K:
"to the wife") This is contradicted by the sacred scriptures.
It is heard in the *śruti* without qualification: "Manu divided his inheritance among his sons."
Moreover, it is also heard in the scriptures that "therefore they exclude the eldest son from his share of the wealth," as if treating him as a single unit.

Furthermore, those who know the principles of logic say that this is a perpetual restatement (*nitya-anuvāda*) and not an injunction (*avidhi*), just as: "Therefore goats and sheep graze together among cattle"; "Therefore the mouth of a *snātaka* seems to reverb (*rebhāyati*)"; and "Therefore the goat and the learned scholar (*śrotriya*) are most desirous of women."

For all those who are endowed with righteousness are entitled to shares. However, even if he is the eldest, one should deprive him of his share who distributes wealth through unrighteous means. No division of property exists between husband and wife.
For from the taking of the hand, there is indeed jointness in ritual acts;
likewise in the fruits of merit,
and in the possession of property.
For they do not teach that there is theft when a gift is made on account of a specific occasion during the absence of the husband.
ApDhS 2.6.15.1: By this, the religious duties (*dharma*) of regions and families are explained.

ApDhS 2.6.15.2: Among those related to the mother by blood-connection and those related to the father up to the seventh person, or for as long as the connection is known—if they have died, one should perform the touching of water (*udaka-upasparśana*), excepting fetuses that have not yet reached one year of age.
ApDhS 2.6.15.3: Regarding these [deceased persons], the duty falls upon the mother and the father alone.
And they shall be the ones to carry [the body].
When the wife has died, as well as when a supreme guru has passed away, there shall be fasting at improper times.
They shall assume the appearance of those who are afflicted.

Having scattered their hair and strewn dust over themselves, wearing a single garment, they face south, immerse themselves once, emerge, and sit down; thus three times. Having splashed water toward that [direction], they return to the village without looking back and do whatever women tell them to do.
Regarding other [deaths], some teachers prescribe this very same procedure.
ApDhS 2.6.15.11: One should feed those who are pure and learned in the mantras at all ritual acts.
ApDhS 2.6.15.12: Gifts are bestowed with respect to place, time, purity, and the recipient.
ApDhS 2.6.15.13: That food which is not offered into the fire and the first portion of which is not given away should not be eaten.
There is no offering of alkaline substances or salt. Likewise, there is no offering for those of lower status or for one who has come into contact with them.
When there is an offering of non-sacrificial food, one should remove the hot ashes toward the north and offer it therein; that offering becomes both offered and unoffered in the fire.
A woman shall not offer the oblation;
nor one who has not been initiated;
nor embryos until the ceremony of first feeding with solid food; they do not become impure.
Some say until one year has passed;
others say as long as they do not recognize the directions;
another view is until the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
For in this matter, authority is derived from the scriptures;
that is the finality;
and it is also based on tradition (smṛti).

Ap2.7.16.1. In ancient times, gods and humans existed together in this world. Then, by means of their ritual actions (*karma*), the gods ascended to heaven, while humans were left behind. Those among them who likewise undertake such actions come to exist in that world together with the gods and Brahman. Now, Manu has declared this rite under the name *śrāddha*, for the sake of the ultimate welfare of progeny.
Ap2.7.16.2–3. In this rite, the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are the deities, while the Brāhmaṇas serve the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire.
It should be performed month by month. (K 3) The latter part of the fortnight and the afternoon are preferable. (K 4) Likewise, the final days of the fortnight are even more so. (K 5)

Ap2.7.16.7: By performing [the rite] on all the days of the latter fortnight, one gratifies the ancestors; however, for the performer, there is a distinction in the fruit resulting from the restriction regarding the time. Ap2.7.16.8: When performed on the first day, offspring is born that is predominantly female.
Ap2.7.16.9: On the second day, [offspring] becomes thieves.
In the third year, they are endowed with Vedic luster (*brahmavarcas*).
In the fourth, they possess small livestock.
In the fifth, they produce male offspring; they have many children and do not die childless.
In the sixth [year], he becomes habituated to travel and habituated to dice.
(ApDhS 2.7.16.13) In the seventh, there is success in agriculture. (ApDhS 2.7.16.14) In the eighth, there is prosperity. (ApDhS 2.7.16.15)
In the ninth [section], single-hoofed animals;
(K 15) in the tenth, success in legal proceedings;
(K 16) in the eleventh, black iron, tin, and lead. (K 17)
In the twelfth year, one possesses cattle.

(ApŚS 2.7.16.19) In the thirteenth year, one has many sons, many friends, and handsome offspring; however, they die young. (ApŚS 2.7.16.20) In the fourteenth year, there is success in weaponry. (ApŚS 2.7.16.21)
On the fifteenth day, there is nourishment. (K 21) In that regard, the materials are sesame, beans, rice, barley, water, roots, and fruits.
(K 22) However, when the food is oily, the gratification of the ancestors is more intense and lasts for a longer period of time. (K 23)

Likewise, there is satisfaction for one year by means of wealth acquired through righteous means and bestowed upon a worthy recipient; greater satisfaction than that is obtained through the gift of a cow,
and even greater still through the gift of a buffalo.
By this, the sacrificial purity of the meat of both domestic and wild animals has been explained. (ApDhS 2.7.16.28) (= K 27).
With the meat of a rhinoceros served as a base, one attains an infinite duration of time;
likewise with the meat of the *śatabali* fish. (ApDhS 2.7.17.1–2)
And also [the meat] of the *vārdhrāṇasa* (ApŚS 2.7.17.3).

[The host], being self-restrained (*prayata*), serene in mind (*prasannamanas*), and invited (*sṛṣṭa*), should feed Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda, provided they are not related by birth (*yoni*), lineage (*gotra*), mantra, or studentship (*antevāsī*).
However, if others are deficient in [necessary] qualities, even a uterine brother (*sodarya*) who is superior [in merit] should be fed.

By this, the resident pupils (*antevāsinaḥ*) have been explained. Now, they also cite this: "The alms-begging known as *saṃbhojanī* is the food of a *piśāca*; it goes neither to the ancestors nor to the gods. Having its merit exhausted, it wanders right here like a cow that has lost its calf within the stall.
"Right here, by eating together, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) perishes from family to family."
Among those of equal qualities, one who is advanced in age is superior, as is one who is destitute of wealth if he desires [to perform the rite].
On the previous day, there is the announcement;
on the following day, the second [announcement].
ApDhS 2.7.17.13: The third invitation is performed.
ApDhS 2.7.17.14: Some teachers prescribe that the Śrāddha rite should be repeated three times.
ApDhS 2.7.17.15: Just as the first [invitation] is performed, so too are the second and the third.

Ap2.7.17.16: Having taken portions from all [the cooked foods] in every respect, he should eat of the remainder at least one mouthful, as previously prescribed. Ap2.7.17.17: According to the northern custom (*udīcya-vṛtti*), however, there is the bringing of a water-pot to the hands of those seated. Ap2.7.17.18:
He addresses them, saying, "Let [the food] be lifted up, and let [the oblation] be made in the fire."
Ap2.7.17.19: If [the host] gives permission, saying, "Let it be lifted up at will; let it be offered into the fire at will," one may lift it up and offer it.
Ap2.7.17.20: One should avoid the sight of dogs and those excluded from the community (apapātra) during a *śrāddha*.

Ap2.7.17.21: A person with white leprosy (*śvitra*), a hermaphrodite (*śipiviṣṭa*), one who approaches the bed of another's wife, the son of a soldier, and one born of a *śūdra* woman by a *brāhmaṇa*—these are defilers of the row (*paṅktidūṣaṇa*) when they eat at a *śrāddha*.

One who has mastered the *Trimadhu*, the *Trisuparṇa*, the *Triṇāciketa*, the *Caturmedha*, the *Pañcāgni*, one who chants the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who has studied the Veda, and the son of such a learned man (*anūcāna*)—these, when eating at a *śrāddha*, become purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).
(ApDhS 2.7.17.22) And one should not perform a *śrāddha* at night. (ApDhS 2.7.17.23) Once it has begun, there shall be no eating until its completion. (ApDhS 2.7.17.24)
Except during an eclipse of the moon.
One should avoid melted butter, curdled milk, oil-cake, honey, and meat;

black grain, the food of a Śūdra, and whatever else is considered unfit to be eaten by others. One who desires memory, fame, intelligence, heaven, and prosperity should avoid these twelve things: that which is not fit for an oblation, falsehood, anger, and whatever causes one to become angry.

Ap2.8.18.4: Covering the area from below the navel to above the knees, touching water at the three daily libations, subsisting on food not cooked by fire, avoiding the shade, and remaining either standing or sitting, one should observe this vow for a year. This is said to be equivalent to forty-eight years. Ap2.8.18.5: There is the obligatory *śrāddha* offering. Ap2.8.18.6: Outside the village, the pure ones prepare it in a pure place.
In that regard, there are nine types of substances:
those by which food is prepared and those in which it is eaten;
these he should give to those who have eaten.
He should feed those who have risen together [with him].
He must not give the remains of the food to one who does not possess those same qualities. He should do this for a year.
Among these, the highest [penance] should be performed with a copper goat;
one should also cause a covered vessel to be made;
and in its northern half, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas.

Ap2.8.18.16: They see both; they teach that Brahmins are eating and the ancestors are being honored. (K 17) Ap2.8.18.17: From this point forward, the rite may be performed or left unperformed. (K 18) Ap2.8.18.18:
For through the *śrāddha*, the ancestors are made known as being satisfied. (K 19; note: *hi* is omitted in some versions, and *nivedayante* is used for *vedayante*)
Ap2.8.18.19: One who desires prosperity should perform [the rite] under the asterism Tiṣya.

(K 20) Ap2.8.19.1: Having had the flour of white mustard seeds prepared, he should wash his hands and feet with them, rinse his mouth and ears, and then, sitting in a place where the wind does not blow too strongly, he should eat facing south while remaining silent; the skin of a goat is the first choice for his seat. Ap2.8.19.2: However, they teach that eating in such a manner—with the face turned [toward the north]—is detrimental to longevity for one's mother. (K: *tvaivaṃmukhasya*?)
A cup made of udumbara wood with a golden navel is prescribed for the *praśāstṛ*.
It must not be used by anyone else; he should consume from it only as much as fits in a single mouthful.
[He should] not skip [a verse];
[he should] not omit [a verse];
or [he may] omit [a verse].
One should swallow the entire morsel together with the thumb;
one should not make a sound with the mouth,
nor should one shake the hand.
Ap2.8.19.12: Having sipped water, he should hold his hands raised until they become wet with perspiration.
Ap2.8.19.13: Then he should touch fire.
Ap2.8.19.14: And during the day he should not eat, except for roots and fruits.
One should avoid those items that are to be served from the *sthālīpāka* (ApDhS 2.8.19.15).
He should eat while wearing the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītin*) and covered with an upper garment (ApDhS 2.8.19.16).
However, at the obligatory *śrāddha*, one should provide food that contains oil (ApDhS 2.8.19.17).

Clarified butter and meat constitute the primary rule. In their absence, oil and vegetables may be used. Furthermore, during the Maghā asterism, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with clarified butter according to the ritual procedure for Śrāddha.
Ap2.8.20.1. At the monthly *śrāddha*, one should employ a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds by whatever means possible that one is able to do so.
Ap2.8.20.2. One should feed those who possess the required qualities, and they should not give the remnants of the food to one who lacks those qualities.

Ap2.8.20.3. During the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), in the waxing fortnight, having fasted for at least one night, one desiring prosperity should cook a *sthālīpāka* under the asterism Tiṣya; having sacrificed to Mahārāja and fed a Brāhmaṇa with that [food] mixed with clarified butter, he should cause the Brāhmaṇa to pronounce a blessing for the attainment of prosperity.
In this manner, day after day, until the last Tiṣya; two [verses] on the second day; three on the third day.
In this manner, for a year [by way of accumulation],
he nourishes great prosperity;
from the very beginning, there is fasting.
Ap2.8.20.10: One should avoid eating food from which the vital energy has been taken away. Ap2.8.20.11: One should avoid standing upon ashes or chaff.
Ap2.8.20.12: One should avoid washing one foot with the other, as well as standing upon it.
Ap2.8.20.13: And swinging the feet;
Ap2.8.20.14: And placing the shank upon the knee;
Ap2.8.20.15: And scratching the nails with the nails.
And [there are] the acts of causing pain without cause;
and whatever else they censure; and that which has been declared regarding those engaged in dharma and regarding the acquisition of property.
He shall be one who causes [the goods] to be delivered at a proper crossing; he shall be a driver when there is no proper crossing, provided that there is no danger;
and he shall be a gatherer of men.
And he enjoys pleasures that are not contrary to dharma;
thus he conquers both worlds.

ApDhS 2.9.21.1: There are four stages of life (āśrama): that of the householder, that of the teacher’s family, that of the silent sage, and that of the forest-dweller. ApDhS 2.9.21.2: By conducting oneself without distraction in all of these according to the instructions, one attains security.
ApDhS 2.9.21.3: For all of them, from the time of initiation onwards, there is residence in the teacher’s family.
ApDhS 2.9.21.4: There is no relinquishing of the pursuit of knowledge for anyone.
ApDhS 2.9.21.5: Having understood the ritual acts, he may undertake whatever he desires.
ApDhS 2.9.21.6: Just as there is a rule for one seeking knowledge, by that very same rule a student (brahmacārin) remains until the end, casting off his body in the teacher's household.
Now, concerning the wandering mendicant (parivrāja): he departs from this very state while still observing the vow of studentship (brahmacarya). Regarding him, they teach as follows.

ApDhS 2.9.21.10: A sage (*muni*) should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling; he should be without shelter and without protection. Abandoning all speech except for the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), and obtaining his livelihood by begging in a village, he should wander without anger and without looking toward the hereafter. ApDhS 2.9.21.11: For him, a discarded garment is prescribed as clothing.
ApDhS 2.9.21.12: Some say he should seek liberation from everything.
Having renounced truth and falsehood, pleasure and pain, these Vedas, and this world as well as the next, one should seek the Self.
When it has been realized, there is the attainment of security;
that [attainment] is not contradicted by the scriptures.
Ap2.9.21.16: If the attainment of security were found upon awakening, one would not experience suffering even here in this world.
Ap2.9.21.17: By this, the subsequent stage is explained. Ap2.9.21.18: Now, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
Therefore, one who is still a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacaryavān*) goes forth [into the life of a wandering ascetic].

To him they teach: "The sage (*muni*) should possess a single fire, have no fixed abode, and be without shelter or protection; he should abandon all speech except for the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*).
For him, clothing made from forest materials is prescribed.
Then he should subsist on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses; finally, he should subsist on whatever comes his way. Thereafter, he should take refuge in water, air, and space.
Among these, each subsequent stage of union is superior in terms of its fruit.
Alternatively, some teachers prescribe the sequence for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) alone:
having completed his studies, taken a wife, and established the sacred fires, he undertakes those ritual acts that are prescribed as being subsequent to the *soma* sacrifice.

Having built a house, he should dwell outside the village together with his wife, his offspring, and the sacred fires; or he may live alone. He should subsist by gleaning ears of grain or picking up individual grains.
And from this point forward, he should not accept gifts.
Once consecrated, he should offer oblations.
He should descend into the water slowly, striking it gently, and touch the water while facing the sun.
ApDhS 2.9.22.14: Thus is the rule for touching water in all cases.

ApDhS 2.9.22.15: Some teachers prescribe that he should take pairs of objects for the purpose of cooking and eating—namely, a mortar and pestle, a knife and axe, and a sickle and goad. ApDhS 2.9.22.16: Having taken one from each pair and having given away the others, he should depart for the forest.
From this point forward, his fire-oblation, means of subsistence, looking toward [the guests], and covering [of the body] shall be performed with forest products alone.
In those rites where there are sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) or oblations of boiled rice (*caru*), these [forest products] are to be used.
And everything, including the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), is to be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Ap2.9.22.20: One should not call out toward the forest.
Ap2.9.22.21: A shelter for the sake of the fire.
Ap2.9.22.22: [The fire] itself in the open air.
[He should use] an unspread bed and seat. When new grain has been obtained, he may permit the use of old grain.
Or, desiring a more extensive discipline, he should fetch his daily sustenance every day with a vessel, both morning and evening.

Thereafter, subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses, he should practice; finally, he should resort to water, air, and space. Among these, each successive combination is superior in its result.
Regarding this, they cite two ancient verses: [The verses follow.]

(Ś) The eighty-eight thousand sages who desired offspring took their cremation grounds along the southern path of Aryaman. (Ap2.9.23.4) (Ś) The eighty-eight thousand sages who did not desire offspring attain immortality by following the northern path of Aryaman. (Ap2.9.23.5) Thus ends the praise of those who preserve their vital seed (*ūrdhvaretas*). (Ap2.9.23.6)
Moreover, there are also those whose accomplishments are achieved through mere resolve (*saṃkalpa-siddha*).
For example: the raining of rain, the granting of offspring, vision from afar, speed equal to that of the mind, and whatever else is similarly appropriate.
Therefore, because they are based on sacred revelation (*śruti*) and because their fruits are directly perceptible, some declare these stages of life (*āśrama*) to be superior.

ApDhS 2.9.23.10: For those who are experts in the three Vedas, the final conclusion is that the Vedas are the authoritative source of knowledge. Regarding this, they consider any conduct that contradicts those practices heard in the Vedas—such as the use of rice, barley, animals, clarified butter, milk, potsherds, and the presence of the wife—to be without authority, based on the injunctions that rites must be performed loudly or softly. ApDhS 2.9.23.11: As for what is called the "cremation ground" (*śmaśāna*), this refers to the rite of purification for the person at the end of various life-cycle ceremonies (*saṃskāra*).
ApDhS 2.9.23.12: Beyond that, an eternal fruit is heard of in the Vedas, designated by the term "heaven" (*svarga*).
Moreover, the Veda declares his immortality through progeny: "In thy offspring thou art born again; that, O mortal, is thy immortality.
Furthermore, this very same person is perceived separately as having grown anew, and a similarity is observed, though the physical body is indeed different.

"Those who abide in the duties prescribed for them increase the fame and the heavenly merit of their predecessors in the life hereafter. In this way, each subsequent generation benefits those who came before. Until the dissolution of all beings, they are conquerors of heaven; at the time of re-creation, they become the seeds—so it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa."

Moreover, there is also the word of Prajāpati: "The threefold knowledge, the life of sacred study, progeny, faith, austerity, sacrifice, and the giving of gifts—those who perform these, with them we dwell; becoming dust, we perish, while praising something else."
In that regard, those who have committed evil perish themselves—just as a leaf falls from a tree—but they do not harm others.
In this world, he has no connection with his actions, and likewise in the next world, he has no connection with the fruits of his actions.
This is to be understood by means of this analogy.
ApDhS 2.9.24.12: This is the creation of Prajāpati and the sages.

ApDhS 2.9.24.13: Among them, those who have performed meritorious deeds are perceived to possess supreme, radiant natures. ApDhS 2.9.24.14: However, by means of a portion of their karma or through austerity, someone may—while still embodied—conquer a finite world and attain the fulfillment of their will; yet that does not constitute the superiority of the stages of life (āśramas).
Ap2.9.25.1: The general and specific duties for all social classes have been explained. Now we shall explain those pertaining specifically to the king.
Ap2.9.25.2: He should cause his residence and his city to be laid out with their gates facing the south.
Ap2.9.25.3: His residence shall be within the inner city.

To the east of that [fortress] is the residence; they call that the place of invitation (*āmantraṇa*). To the south of the fortress is the assembly hall (*sabhā*), with doors opening to the south and the north, so that both the interior and the exterior are visible.
In all [these buildings], the sacred fires must be perpetual.

And the daily worship of the sacred fire is to be performed as in the household ritual. He should provide lodging for guests who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and of no lower status than that in his residence. For them, dwellings, bedding, food, and drink should be provided according to their merit.
He should not live at the expense of his teachers or ministers.
And in his territory, no one should perish from hunger, disease, cold, or heat, whether through lack of resources or by intentional neglect.
In the middle of the assembly hall, having raised up a gaming-place and sprinkled it with water, he should cast an even number of Vibhītaka dice according to their purpose.

Noble men should be pure and devoted to truth, and they should be gamblers. The taking up of weapons, dancing, singing, and instrumental music—these should not exist except under the authority of the king.
A king is a provider of security for whom there is no fear of thieves in his realm, whether in the village or in the forest.

ApDhS 2.10.26.1: By giving land and wealth to Brahmins as is appropriate, without causing hardship to his dependents, a king conquers infinite worlds. ApDhS 2.10.26.2: They say that a king who is slain while seeking to recover the property of Brahmins is a sacrifice in which he himself is the sacrificial post and the sacrificial fee is infinite. ApDhS 2.10.26.3: By this, other heroes are also explained—those who, fighting for a righteous cause, lay down their bodies.
In villages and cities, he should appoint noble, pure, and truth-abiding men for the protection of the subjects.
Their attendants should likewise possess those same qualities.
A city extending for one *yojana* in every direction must be protected from thieves.
A *krośa* is the distance from the villages.
Whatever is stolen there, that must be made good by those [villagers]. He shall cause the lawful toll to be paid.
An *akāra* is [the *praṇava*] of a *śrotriya*;
women are [the *praṇava*] of all castes;
and boys [are the *praṇava*] prior to the appearance of their secondary sexual characteristics.
And those who dwell for the sake of learning;
those ascetics who are devoted to dharma;
and the Śūdra who is the water-carrier for washing the feet.
And those who are blind, mute, deaf, afflicted by disease, or possessed by spirits;

and those who are rendered useless by their acquisition of wealth; and one who, without prior intent, enters another's house while adorned as a youth, or approaches another's wife or a maiden, shall be restrained by a verbal reprimand.
But if it is done intentionally, one who has a wicked disposition shall be punished.
(ApDhS 2.10.26.19) When [intercourse] has occurred, the penis shall be cut off along with the testicles.
(ApDhS 2.10.26.20) But in the case of a maiden, he shall be banished after taking his own property. (ApDhS 2.10.26.21)
Now, regarding a servant [who has committed an offense], [the king shall act];
and from this point forward, [he shall act] regarding one who is to be protected from sexual intercourse. However, when a means of atonement has been accepted, he should release him to his masters.
Ap2.10.27.1: When he has behaved as before, the relationship [to his former kin] arises from dharma.
Ap2.10.27.2: He should not point out to others a woman who stands in the place of a *sagotra* relative. Ap2.10.27.3: For they teach that a woman is given away for the sake of the family.
That [conflict] arose from the weakness of the senses.
For the superiority of the hand is indeed no different [from that of the foot].
Indeed, upon the transgression of that [rule], both shall go to hell.

For the prosperity resulting from the undertaking of religious observances (*niyama*) is greater than that resulting from offspring born of such an undertaking. An Ārya man shall not procreate upon a Śūdra woman;
a Śūdra man shall be put to death for procreating upon an Ārya woman.
And he should cause his wife to fast.
They teach that if one has sexual intercourse once with a woman of the same caste who has previously been married to another, one quarter (pāda) of the penance falls upon him;
likewise, for each repetition, a quarter falls.
ApDhS 2.10.27.13: In the fourth case, everything [is prescribed].
ApDhS 2.10.27.14: For a Śūdra who reviles an Ārya who is righteous, the tongue shall be cut out.
ApDhS 2.10.27.15: For one who behaves as an equal [to a superior] regarding speech, the path, the bed, or the seat, there shall be a flogging with a rod.
In cases of killing a human, theft, or seizing land, one who has taken these for himself shall be put to death.
However, in these cases, the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa is the blinding of his eyes.
Or, he may be bound in secret for violating a rule or for other such offenses.
Until the completion [of the offense]; if it is not completed, he is not to be killed.
A teacher, an officiating priest, a bath-graduate (snātaka), and a king—these may provide protection, except in the case of one deserving death.
Ap2.11.28.1: If, after having taken possession of a field, there is no harvest due to a lack of effort, that person who is wealthy shall be made to pay for it.
Ap2.11.28.2–3: For a dependent laborer (*kīnāśa*) who abandons his work, the punishment is flogging; the same applies to a cattle-herder. Ap2.11.28.4:
And he shall be confined along with his livestock.
Having released them from the pen, he should not emaciate the cattle nor cause them to perish. (K 5+6) If he has enclosed the cattle and they die or are lost, he should restore them to the owners.
(K 7) If he sees cattle that have been let loose in the forest through negligence, he should bring them back to the village and restore them to the owners. (K 8)
Furthermore, in the case of negligence, having once restrained [the offender], he should not thereafter neglect [the matter] again.

(ApDhS 2.11.28.8–9) If one who does not know that it belongs to another takes fuel, water, roots, flowers, fruits, fragrances, food, or vegetables, he should be rebuked with the words: "This is another's property.
(ApDhS 2.11.28.10) But for one who knows, there shall be the seizure of his garment. (ApDhS 2.11.28.11)
Ap2.11.28.12: One who takes food when his life is in danger, even if he acts out of desire, is not to be punished. (K 13) Ap2.11.28.13:
When the occasion has arisen, if the king fails to inflict punishment, the sin touches the king himself.
(K 14) Ap2.11.29.1: The instigator, the one who conceives the plan, and the doer—these are the sharers in the fruits of actions leading to heaven or hell.

Ap2.11.29.2: He who undertakes more [of the work] receives a special share of the fruit. Ap2.11.29.3: The two householders are the masters of the wealth. Ap2.11.29.4: With their permission, others also may apply themselves to tasks beneficial to them.
In a dispute, those who are endowed with learning and noble birth, who are aged, wise, and unerring in matters of dharma, should deliberate.
In case of doubt, they should determine the truth through physical signs or by means of divine ordeal.

On an auspicious day, in the morning, when the fire has been kindled at the edge of water in the presence of the king, having had the matter fully declared to both parties with the consent of all, the chief witness shall answer the question of truth.
In the case of falsehood, the king should inflict punishment;
furthermore, there is hell for him in the life hereafter.
In the case of truth, there is heaven and the praise of all beings.
That which exists among women and Śūdras is the ultimate limit of knowledge;
they teach that this is the remnant of the Atharvaveda.
The completion of Dharma is declared to be difficult to achieve, yet it is accomplished through the performance of the prescribed ritual acts as handed down in tradition.

In this regard, the defining characteristic is as follows: in all inhabited regions, one should adopt a conduct similar to that of the noble ones who are exclusively composed, well-disciplined, aged, self-controlled, free from greed, and devoid of hypocrisy. By doing so, one conquers both worlds.
Some say that one should learn the remaining points of dharma from women and from members of all social classes—so say some.
And thus this *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra* is completed.

Now begins the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
Dharma has been taught separately for each Veda.
We shall now explain its [the ritual] procedure in accordance with that.
The second [initiation] is based on the Smṛti.
The third is the tradition of the learned (śiṣṭāgama).
The learned indeed are free from envy, devoid of egoism, possessing only as much grain as fits in a jar, lacking greed, and liberated from hypocrisy, pride, avarice, delusion, and anger.

"Those whose Veda, along with its supplements, has been acquired through righteous means, who are learned in the inference of that [Veda], and for whom the Śruti is a matter of direct perception—they are the cultured (śiṣṭas). [Baudhāyana 1.1.1.6ab–cd] "In their absence, an assembly (pariṣad) of at least ten [members]. [Baudhāyana 1.1.1.7]
Now they also cite: "One learned in the four Vedas, one who can interpret alternatives, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), one who recites the Dharma,
and three Brahmins established in their respective stages of life (*āśrama*)— this assembly (*parṣad*) consists of at least ten members."
"There may be five, or three, or even one who is blameless;
for he alone is a respondent regarding dharma, and not others, however many they may be."
Just as an elephant made of wood, just as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied; these three are merely bearers of names.
Whatever those who are deluded by darkness, fools who do not know the Dharma, say—
that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon the speakers.
The path of Dharma has many doors, and its course is subtle and difficult to follow;
therefore, when a doubt arises, it should not be declared by even one who is highly learned.
The twice-born who have mounted the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wield the sword of the Vedas— whatever they may say, even in jest, that is remembered as the supreme Dharma.
Just as water situated upon a stone may be destroyed by wind and sun,
so too whatever sin exists in the agent dissolves completely like water.
Having carefully considered the body, strength, lifespan, age, time, and the nature of the act, one who knows the Dharma should prescribe the penances with his intellect.

"Among those who lack vows, who do not know the mantras, and who subsist merely by their caste—even if they have gathered in their thousands—the status of an assembly (*pariṣad*) does not exist. Thus [it is said].
There are five different traditions regarding the ritual practice on the south side, as well as on the north side.
We shall now explain those [rites] which are performed on the south side.

For example: eating with one who has not been initiated; eating with a woman; eating food that has been kept overnight; and sexual intercourse with the daughter of one's maternal uncle or paternal aunt.
Then, to the north, there is the sale of wool, the drinking of *sīdhu* liquor, trade with people who have teeth on both jaws, the profession of arms, and sea-voyaging.
If one performs the one rite in the place of the other, he commits an error; if he performs the other in the place of the one, he likewise commits an error.
In each such case, the authority of local custom alone shall prevail.
"This is false," says Gautama.
And one should not respect both [the Vedic injunction and the Smṛti], because a contradiction with the Smṛti of the learned (śiṣṭa) is observed.
That region which lies east of Ādarśa, west of Kanakhala (or Kālakavana), south of the Himavat, and north of the Pāriyātra mountains is Āryāvarta; whatever custom prevails therein is authoritative.
Some say it is the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers.
Now, moreover, regarding this matter, the followers of the Bhāllavi school cite a verse:
"To the west is the Sindhu, the divider; before it is the rising of the sun.
As long as the dark [waters] flow, so long indeed is there spiritual luster."
The Avantyas, Aṅgas, Magadhas, Surāṣṭras, Dakṣiṇāpathas,
Upāvṛts, Sindhus, and Sauvīras— these are of mixed origin.
Having gone to the Āraṭṭas, Kāraskaras, Puṇḍras, Sauvīras, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Prānūnas, one should perform the Punastoma sacrifice or the Sarvapṛṣṭhā sacrifice.
Now they also cite this:
"He who enters the Kaliṅgas commits a sin with his feet;
the seers have declared that the expiation for him is the Vaiśvānara oblation."
Regarding the determination of faults among even many faults that have been committed, they praise the Pavitra-iṣṭi, for it is the supreme purifier.
Now they also cite:
"By performing the Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitra-iṣṭi in every season, one is liberated from sins— one is liberated from sins."
The traditional Vedic studentship lasts for forty-eight years.
Twenty-four or twelve [verses] for each Veda.
Or, he may perform it for each section (kaṇḍa) at intervals of one year.
Or rather, it may end with the taking [of the vow], because life itself is unstable.
"One whose hair is black should establish the sacred fires"—such is the Vedic revelation.
"No one restricts his ritual duties at all until the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;
for he is equal to a Śūdra in his conduct as long as he is not born through the Veda. Thus it is said.
The count of years begins from conception; one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in his eighth year from that point.
If there are more than three [sacrificers], he should initiate a Rājanya.
Therefore, when there is one additional [verse], it is for a Vaiśya.
Spring, summer, and autumn are the seasons according to the sequence of their colors.
[He should recite] with Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī verses, respectively.
Up to the sixteenth, up to the twenty-second, and up to the twenty-fourth year—this is the sequence for these [initiations] before they have passed their time.
The girdles are made of muñja grass, a bowstring, or hempen thread.
The skins of the black antelope, the ruru deer, and the goat are the [prescribed] skins.

The staffs of one who is officiating at a sacrifice are of the length of the distance from the crown of the head to the forehead, or from the crown of the head to the tip of the nose, made from a tree suitable for sacrificial purposes.

He should go for alms with the word "bhavat" at the beginning, "madhya" in the middle, and ending with the word "yācñā"; this alms-round consists of seven syllables, and he should neither increase nor decrease the words "kṣām" and "hiṃ."
A Brāhmaṇa should beg with the word "bhavat" at the beginning, a Rājanya with "bhavat" in the middle, and a Vaiśya with "bhavat" at the end; this applies to all social classes.
These, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, remain established in their own respective duties.
Having always fetched fuel-sticks from the forest, he should place them on the fire.
He should be truthful in speech, modest, and free from egoism.
He should be the first to rise and the last to go to bed.
In all matters, his teacher’s word is unimpeded for him, except in the case of a mortal sin.
He may converse with women only as much as is necessary for a specific purpose.
He shall avoid dancing, singing, instrumental music, perfumes, garlands, the wearing of shoes and umbrellas, and the application of collyrium and ointments.
He should clasp the right [foot] with his right hand and the left [foot] with his left hand.
Desiring long life and heaven, he may, with the permission of his teacher, give [the remainder] at will to another person of virtuous conduct.
"O [Name]!"—saying this while touching the ears, for the purpose of concentrating the mind.
Below the knees, as far as the feet.
He should not [teach] while sitting to one who is not sitting, nor while lying down to one who is not lying down, nor to one who is not self-restrained, nor to one who is not self-restrained.
Within one's capacity, one should not remain impure for even a moment.
One who carries fuel, a water-pot, flowers, or food in his hand should not offer a salutation; nor should he do so with anything else that is similarly held.
One should not offer a formal salutation when in close physical proximity with another.
One who has emitted semen [commits an offense] against the wives of his brothers, against young women, and against the wives of his teachers.
In a boat, on a stone slab, on a wooden plank, on an elephant, on a palace, on a mat, and in vehicles that turn like a wheel, sitting together with [a woman] is not a fault.
Grooming, massaging, bathing, and eating the leftovers [of food] belong to the teacher.
The avoidance of the remnants [of food] applies to his son or to one who has studied the Vedas (anūcāna).
And she, his wife, is likewise exempt from grooming, rubbing with unguents, and bathing.
If he is running, one should run after him; if he is walking, one should walk after him; if he is standing, one should stand after him.
One should not bathe in water while boasting.
He should float like a staff.
In times of distress, one may study under a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher.
Service and following [the teacher] shall continue as long as the study lasts.
For those two, the purification is exactly that same one.
And the same applies to brothers, sons, and pupils.
But one must rise and greet officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger than oneself.
Kātya maintains that this refers to the formal return greeting (*pratyabhivāda*).
[The word "śiśu" refers to] the descendant of Aṅgiras, because it is so seen [in the Vedic texts].
Where neither spiritual merit nor material wealth is found, nor even the corresponding service,
one should rather die with one's learning than sow it upon barren soil.
Like fire consuming dry grass, sacred knowledge destroys one who treats it with disrespect when questioned.
"Therefore, one should certainly not speak [the Veda] to those who do not show honor to the Brahman. Thus it is said.
In this very manner, they announce the speech to him.

Brahman indeed delivered the creatures to Death. He did not deliver the *brahmacārin* to him. Death said, "Let there also be a share for me in this. [Brahman replied], "On whichever night he does not bring fuel."

Therefore, on whatever night a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) does not bring fuel, he dwells having cut away a portion of his own life-span. Therefore, a student of sacred knowledge should bring fuel, thinking: "May I not dwell having cut away a portion of my life-span."

He who undertakes the vow of studentship (*brahmacarya*) indeed enters upon a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*). The fuel-stick (*samidh*) which he places when entering [the vow] is the introductory offering (*prāyaṇīyā*); that which he places when about to bathe is the concluding offering (*udayanīyā*); and those which he places in between are his regular session-offerings (*sattryās*).

When a Brāhmaṇa, entering upon the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*), enters the beings divided into four parts: one foot in the fire, one foot in death, and one foot in the teacher; his fourth foot remains within himself.
When he places a fuel-stick (*samidh*) in the fire, he thereby ransoms that foot of his which is in the fire; having consecrated it, he takes it into himself, and it enters him.

Now, when he makes himself poor, becomes shameless, begs for alms, and practices celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he thereby ransoms that foot of his which is in Death; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him.
Then, when he obeys the word of the teacher (*ācārya*), he thereby ransoms that foot of his which is in the teacher; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him.

Now, as for the fact that he studies his private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*): by that, he ransoms that very portion which is within his own self; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters into him.
Having bathed, he should certainly not beg. Indeed, even after bathing, he may go about begging, even from his kinsmen, even from his ancestors, rather than from other ritual activities.
If he should not find anyone else from whom to beg, he may even beg from his teacher’s wife, or even from his own mother.

No seventh [day] should pass for him without having begged for alms. There is a fault in not going out for alms and in not kindling the sacred fire; having failed to perform this for seven nights, one should observe the vow of an *avakīrṇin*.
All the Vedas enter that very person who knows thus and conducts himself thus.

"Just as a fire, when well-kindled, shines forth, even so does he shine who, knowing this, practices the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) after having bathed"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Thus ends the Brāhmaṇa.
Now follows the ritual for the *snātaka*.
The inner garment and the upper garment.
He should carry a staff made of bamboo.
And he [carries] a water-pot containing water.
Wearing the sacrificial cord over both shoulders.
A turban, a deerskin upper garment, sandals, an umbrella, and the maintenance of the sacred fire along with the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
And on the days of the lunar changes (parvan), there shall be the shaving of the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails.
The procedure for that is as follows.
One should seek raw meat from among Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, Vaiśyas, and Rathakāras.
Or he may subsist on alms.
He should remain silent.
And he should perform all his rites connected with the gods and the ancestors, as well as the auspicious ceremonies belonging to the categories of *pākayajña*.
"By this procedure, the supreme sages of Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin attain the highest goal," so says Baudhāyana.
Now, they teach the practice regarding the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
The purifying fire is declared to reside in the right ear of a goat, in the right hand of a Brahmin,
in water, and likewise in a clump of *kuśa* grass.

Therefore, having performed purification, one should wipe [the vessel] with the hand; this is beneficial as a circumambulation by fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*). By reciting "Shine forth, O Jātavedas," it is superior to burning again.
If, even there, one should perceive anything touched by mind—whether by *kuśa* grass or by ordinary grass—one should kindle it and perform a circumambulation while burning it clockwise.
From this point forward, they teach that for substances defiled by dogs, crows, and the like, the fire-colored [removal] is prescribed.
Baudhāyana 1.4.6.5: The discarding of those [objects] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth.
If the water-pot is broken, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Vyāhṛtis, or recite them.
"Earth has gone to earth; mother has gone unto mother. May we prosper with sons and cattle; may he who hates us be split asunder.
Having gathered the potsherds and thrown them into the water, and having performed the *Sāvitrī* [oblation] at least ten times, he should take up another [pot] once again.
Having taken refuge in Varuṇa, one should meditate on the syllable "Om" while reciting: "This is for you, O Varuṇa; may you lead me back again."
One should take one hundred [cows] from a Śūdra, fifty are prescribed from a Vaiśya,
twenty-five from a Kṣatriya, and ten are declared from a Brāhmaṇa.
When the sun has set, the exponents of the Veda deliberate whether one should take water or not.
"One should take"—this is another [view].
As long as he would take water, for that long he should restrain his breath.
For Agni indeed takes up the water.

Having sprinkled his hands and feet with water from a water-pot, he remains impure to others only as long as they are wet; he purifies himself alone. It is known from tradition that he should not perform any other ritual action [during that time].
Alternatively, Baudhāyana says that one is pure up to the wrists after each individual purification.
Now, they also cite this example:
The water-pot was ordained of old by Brahmā and the foremost sages for the purification of the twice-born; therefore, one should always carry it.
Therefore, purification, drinking [water],
and the performance of the twilight devotions must be carried out without hesitation if one desires one's own welfare.

The wise one should act with a pure mind and should not defile his consciousness; since he was born together with the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) as a self-existent being, he should therefore move about carrying a water-pot.
When voiding urine or excrement, he holds [the water vessel] in his right hand and uses his left hand for sipping; this is established as the practice of the virtuous.
