Just as a cup is called pure because of its connection with Soma,
so too the water-pot is eternally pure because of its connection with water.
Therefore, one should avoid him during rites for the ancestors, the gods, and the sacred fires.
Therefore, one should not travel on a road, nor go from house to house across the boundary, without a water-pot.
"One should not even step [beyond] a foot [from the mark], nor even the length of an arrow, according to some."
Baudhāyana says that if one should desire the continuity of Dharma, [one should perform it].
"By the rule of the Ṛgveda," thus speaks Vāc; "by the rule of the Ṛgveda," thus speaks Vāc.
Now, therefore, follows the foundation of purification.
"The limbs are purified by water; the intellect is purified by knowledge;
the elemental self (*bhūtātman*) is purified by non-violence; and the mind is purified by truth. Thus [it is said].
Purity of mind is internal purity.
We shall now explain the purification of external parts.
The sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) shall be made of kuśa grass or sūtra, and it shall be triple-stranded in three layers.
Up to the navel.
Having raised the right arm and lowered the left, he should place it upon his head.
For the ancestors, it is the reverse.
When it is suspended around the neck, it is the *nivīta*.
That which is suspended below and covered from below is the *adhovīta*.
Seated facing either the east or the north, one should undertake purification in a clean place, having placed the right arm between the knees and having washed both feet and hands up to the wrists.
One should not sip water for ritual purification using the remnants of the water used for washing the feet.
If he should sip water, he should first pour it out onto the ground and then sip it.
One should sip water using the Brāhma-tīrtha.
The base of the thumb is the Brāhma tīrtha.
The tip of the thumb is for the ancestors (pitrya), the tips of the fingers are for the gods (daiva), and the base of the fingers is for the seers (ārṣa).

Not with water that is poured from the fingers, nor with water containing bubbles, nor with water containing foam, nor with water that is hot, nor with water that is alkaline, nor with water that is salty, nor with water that is turbid, nor with water that is discolored, nor with water that has a foul odor or taste.

He should not recite while laughing, nor while talking, nor while standing, nor while looking around, nor while stooping, nor while bowing down, nor with his topknot untied, nor with his neck wrapped, nor with his head covered, nor in haste, nor without the sacred thread, nor with his feet stretched out, nor with his girdle tied, nor with his knees exposed, nor making any sound.
He should drink water that reaches the heart three times.
He should wipe it around three times.
Some say it should be recited twice.
For a Śūdra and for a woman, both [rites] are performed only once.
Now they also quote:
"A Brahmin becomes pure by water reaching the heart; a Kṣatriya, being pure, by water reaching the throat;
a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and women and Śūdras by merely touching [the water] at the end."
Regarding food stuck between the teeth: it is like the teeth themselves;
because they are held by the teeth, when they have fallen out, one need not rinse the mouth, for they are pure like the flow of saliva.
Now they also cite this:
"Regarding food stuck between the teeth like a tooth, and whatever else may be inside the mouth, it remains as a remnant for one who has sipped water; by swallowing it, one becomes pure."
Having touched the cavities with water, he should touch his feet, his navel, his head, and finally his left hand.
If he becomes impure while holding something made of metal, he should discard it, sip water for purification, and, before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water.
Now, if he should become defiled by food, he should discard that [food], sip water, and, when about to take it up again, sprinkle it with water.
Now, if he should become defiled by water, he should discard it, sip water for purification, and, when about to take it up again, sprinkle it with water.
This very same [procedure] is reversed in the case of a vessel.
Regarding the wooden vessel, there is an option.
For metallic objects defiled by food remnants, purification is achieved by scrubbing them with cow dung, earth, or ashes, or with any one of these.
Copper, silver, and gold [are purified] with acidic substances.
The burning of the vessels.
The carving of wooden objects.
[The fuel] of bamboo is [anointed] with cow dung.
For those made of fruit, [the tying is done] with a rope of cow-hair.
With black antelope skins and wood-apple grains.
For those who wear woolen cloths, [the offering] is with *ariṣṭa* fruits.
Those made of wool [are offered] with the verse addressed to Āditya.
Those made of linen [are purified] with a paste of white mustard seeds.
And for the cloth-strainers, [the purification] is with clay.
The rule regarding garments applies to skins as well.
The procedure for stones and gems is like that for metallic objects.
The bones are treated like wood.
The rules for conch shells, horn, mother-of-pearl, and ivory are the same as those for linen.
Or with milk.

If one touches urine, feces, blood, semen, or a corpse—any of the aforementioned substances that are contrary to the sight or smell—one should wipe [the hand] twenty-one times as previously described.
In this manner, there is the discarding of non-metallic objects that have become thus defiled.
In the sacrifice, the cups (camasapātra) are used because of a specific scriptural injunction.
"There is no impurity from Soma," so says the Śruti.
Time, fire, purity of mind, smearing with water and other substances, and that which is unknown to living beings—this is said to be the sixfold purification. (Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra 1.5.8.52)
Now, they also cite this:

"Having understood the time, the place, as well as himself, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the occasion, and the state, one who knows purification, being skillful and desiring righteousness, should practice purification."
"The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale;
alms received by a religious student are always pure—such is the Vedic revelation."
A calf is pure when it causes milk to flow; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall;
women are pure in sexual union; and a dog is pure when catching game.
All mines are pure, with the exception of a distillery for *surā* liquor;
likewise, continuous streams and dust raised by the wind are not defiling.
And in the case of trees grown in impure places that have reached the state of bearing flowers and fruit—
even for those, neither the flowers nor the fruits are defiled.
Having touched a sacred tree, a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, a Caṇḍāla, or a seller of the Vedas,
a Brāhmaṇa shall enter the water along with his clothes.
One's own bed, seat, clothing, wife, offspring, and water-pot—
these are pure for oneself, but impure for others.
A seat, a bed, a vehicle, boats, and grass on the road— these,
when touched by a Caṇḍāla or an outcaste, are purified by the wind alone.

Whatever grain is found in threshing floors or fields, whatever water is in wells or ponds, and whatever milk is found in a cow-pen— even if these come from one whose food is otherwise unfit to be eaten, they are fit for consumption.
The gods ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is praised by speech.
Water that has reached the earth is a purifier, provided that it causes the satisfaction of cows and is not pervaded by impurity, while still possessing its natural fragrance, color, and taste.
But for the ground, purification is achieved through sweeping, sprinkling, smearing, spreading [grass], and scraping, according to the specific location and the particular nature of the defect.
Now, they also quote:

"A spot on the ground the size of a cow-hide, from which no drop of water falls [when touched], becomes pure, whether the impurity has been swept away or not, provided that no impurity is perceived there. Thus [it is said].
When the food has been placed on the fire out of sight, one should illuminate it and then sprinkle water over it.
Likewise, [the same applies] to foods that are purchased in the market.
"For the gods are loathsome and desire purity; they do not enjoy the oblation of one who lacks faith."
Having deliberated upon both— the impure person who lacks faith and the pure person who possesses faith— the gods ordained that food is equal for both.
But Prajāpati said to them: "That is not equal; for it is unequal.
That which is offered by one lacking faith is destroyed, while that which is purified by faith is superior. Thus [it is said].
Now they also cite:
"Lack of faith is the supreme evil; for faith is the supreme austerity. Therefore, the deities do not consume an oblation given without faith."
Even after sacrificing or giving gifts, a fool does not go to heaven.
"One whose conduct is ruined by doubt, who follows his own whims, and who transgresses the scriptures is considered a fool because he obstructs the system of Dharma. Thus [it is said].
But for vegetables, flowers, fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs, there shall be washing.
Having set aside dry grass, wood unfit for sacrifice, or a clod of earth, one should void urine or excrement by day or by night, facing north or south respectively, having bent forward the head.
In the case of urine, there is cleansing with earth and water.
Three times from the hand.
The same applies to the loose earth (*purīṣa*).
In each turn, he wipes the left hand and the right hand three times each.
The same [penance] applies as for urine in the case of the emission of semen.
Having loosened the *nīvī* and put on [the garment], he should touch water.
One should touch moist grass, cow dung, or the earth.
One engaged in ritual action should avoid touching anything below the navel.
"Above the navel of a person is pure, while below it is impure," so says the Śruti.
For Śūdras who are supervised by Āryas, there is shaving every half-month or month, and the ritual for sipping water (ācamana) is to be performed according to the Ārya custom.
A Vaiśya may subsist by means of usury.
However, it should indeed consist of twenty-five [grains], weighing five māṣas each.
Now they also cite:
"He who, having borrowed a loan at a low price, should employ it at a high price—
he is indeed called a usurer, and is censured in all religious duties."
"Vṛddhi and the killing of an embryo he weighed on a scale; the killer of an embryo remained steady at the tip [of the beam], while the usurer trembled. Thus it is said.
One should treat Brahmins who are cattle-herders, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers as one would a Śūdra.
However, they may at will give the two former [vessels] to one who has neglected his duties, who is miserly, an atheist, or a wicked person.
Through failure to perform sacrifices, through not marrying, through the neglect of the Veda,
and through the transgression against Brahmins, families fall into the state of being non-families.
There is no transgression against a Brāhmaṇa who is foolish and devoid of sacred knowledge;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes after having cast aside a blazing fire.
Through cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to kings,
families that are deficient in sacred mantras fall from their noble status to that of commoners.
But those families that are prosperous through the sacred mantras, even if they possess little wealth,
are counted among the great lineages and attain immense fame.
Vedic study leads to the ruin of agriculture, and agriculture leads to the ruin of Vedic study.
One who is capable should practice both; however, one who is incapable should abandon agriculture.
"Indeed, the gods do not partake [of offerings] from one who is corpulent, lacks self-restraint, and bellows loudly like a bull;
rather, those who are emaciated—moving with agility, impetuous, and speaking purposefully—it is they who go there as the subtle ones."

Whatever one performs in youth through delusion— whether it be good or evil, of whatever kind or at whatever time— if one behaves virtuously in later life, that alone belongs to him, and not the other deeds.
One should constantly feel remorse in one's mind, reflecting upon one's evil deeds;
by being ascetic and vigilant, one is then liberated from that sin.

"If drops [of water] touch the feet of one who is making others sip water, there is no state of being *ucchiṣṭa* (ritually impure) due to them; they are equal to those that fall upon the ground. Thus [it is said].
Regarding birth and death, they declare that for sapindas there is impurity lasting ten days, with the exception of officiating priests, those initiated for sacrifice, and celibate students.
Sapiṇḍa-relationship, however, extends among sapindas as far as the seventh degree.
Until the seventh month, or until the eruption of teeth, there is the ritual touching of water (for purification).
The rites of offering rice-balls and water are not prescribed for one who has died under the age of three;
nor should cremation be performed until the eruption of teeth.
And [the same applies] when the girls have not yet been given away in marriage.
Some, it is said, perform [the rites] when the [sacrificial vessels] have been handed over.
For women are considered to be without mantras for the purpose of maintaining the world.
"In the case of women who have not yet been married, the kinsmen become pure after three days;
and the uterine relatives become pure according to the very rule already stated."

Moreover, the great-grandfather, the grandfather, the father, oneself, uterine brothers, the son of a woman of the same caste, the son’s son, and the son’s grandson—excluding their own sons—and the sons and grandsons of these, as long as the inheritance has not been divided, are called *sapiṇḍas*.
They also call those who have divided their inheritance "sakulyas" (agnates).
For when others are absent, the property goes to that [specific person].
In the absence of a *sapiṇḍa*, a *sakulya* [shall perform the rites].
In his absence, the father, the teacher, the pupil, or the officiating priest shall take it.
In its absence, the king shall bestow that property upon those who are learned in the three Vedas and advanced in age.
But under no circumstances whatsoever should a king himself take the property of a Brāhmaṇa.
Now they also cite:
"The property of a Brahmin destroys sons and grandsons; it carries away the solitary man like poison.
They say that poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison."
Therefore, a king should not take the property of a Brāhmaṇa; for the property of a Brāhmaṇa is indeed the most potent poison.
In the case of the coincidence of birth and death, the period of impurity is the same ten nights for both.
Now, if ten-day periods of impurity should coincide, the impurity pertaining to the first ten-day period lasts until the ninth day.
Regarding birth, there is first a ten-day period of impurity for both the mother and the father.
According to some, [the term] "of the mother" [is used] because of the avoidance of that [impurity].
Others say [the child belongs] to the father, because of the predominance of the semen.
For even sons not born from a womb are indeed heard of in the sacred tradition.
But it belongs to the mother and father alone, because of the commonality of their connection [to the child].

In the event of a death, however, having placed the youngest child at the front, having arranged the sacred threads over the right shoulder (apasavya), having descended to a bathing place, having immersed themselves once, three times, and emerged, having ascended and sipped water, having poured out water with the intention directed toward the deceased, having ascended from that very spot and sipped water again, and having touched charcoal and water at the door of the house, they shall sit upon mats for ten days, consuming food that is neither pungent nor salty.
The Śrāddha rite is performed on either the eleventh or the twelfth day.
In the performance of the remaining rites, one must conform to worldly custom.
In this case as well, among those who are not *sapiṇḍas*, one should observe [impurity] for three nights, a day and night, or one day, according to the degree of proximity.
In the case of the death of a teacher, a sub-teacher, or their sons, the impurity lasts for three nights.
And [the same applies] to the officiating priests.
Toward one's disciples, fellow students, and co-residents in the Veda, one should observe [the penance] for three nights, one day and night, or one day respectively.
In the case of a miscarriage, women must observe impurity for a number of nights equal to the months of gestation of the fetus.
If one unintentionally touches a corpse, one becomes pure immediately by touching water while still wearing one's clothes.
If it was done intentionally, the penance lasts for three nights.
And [one should not study] when a woman is in her menses.
He who is born from that is "one accused"; his observances have already been explained.
Having touched one who has sold the Veda, a sacrificial post, a funeral mound,
or even a Caṇḍāla, one should perform a bath.
If a worm should arise from the wound of a Brāhmaṇa when pus and blood have formed there, what expiation (prāyaścitta) should be performed?
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—
one who has been bitten by a worm becomes pure after bathing and drinking these for three days.
One who has been bitten by a dog shall immerse himself in water along with his clothes.
Having washed that spot, touched it with fire, washed it again, and having washed his feet and sipped water, he becomes pure.
Now they also cite this:

"A Brahmin who has been bitten by a dog, having gone to a river that flows to the ocean and having performed a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), becomes purified by consuming clarified butter."
"Or, having bathed with water from the horns of cows mixed with gold and silver, or with water from nine new jars, one becomes pure immediately. Thus it is said.
Domestic animals are not to be eaten.
Carnivorous birds as well.
Likewise, [the meat of] the cock and the pig.
Except for goats and sheep.
The porcupine, the monitor lizard, the hare, the hedgehog, the tortoise, and the rhinoceros—these five five-toed animals are edible, with the exception of the rhinoceros.
Likewise, the five cloven-hoofed animals—the ṛśya, hariṇa, pṛṣata, mahiṣa, and varāha, excluding the kuluṅga—[are permitted].

Baudhāyana 1.5.12.7: Birds—excluding the partridge (*tittiri*), the dove (*kapota*), the grey partridge (*kapiñjala*), the vārdhrāṇasa crane, the peacock (*mayūra*), and the vāraṇāvāraṇa—are the five *viṣkira* (scattering) birds.
The fish are the Sahasradaṃṣṭra, Cilicima, Varmi, Bṛhacchiras, Maśakari, Rohita, and Rājīva.
The milk of a cow that has not yet passed ten days since calving, nor of one in heat, is unfit for drinking.
And [the same applies] to two cows, one whose calf has died and another whose calf is living elsewhere.
Wool from sheep, wool from camels, and the milk of one-hoofed animals are not to be drunk.
For drinking forbidden liquids, the Kṛcchra penance is required, except in the case of cow's milk.
In the case of cow products, however, there is a fast for three nights,
with the exception of stale vegetables, vegetable broth, meat, clarified butter, parched grain boiled in milk, molasses, curd, honey, and flour-meal.
Sour substances and molasses that have turned sour are likewise unfit for use.
Having commenced the term on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Āṣāḍha, they should conclude it on the full moon day of Taiṣya or Māgha. They should conclude it.
The gods enjoy the pure sacrifice.
For the gods desire purity and they themselves are pure.
Regarding this, he recites this verse:

"O Maruts, pure are your oblations; for you who are pure, I prepare the pure sacrifice for the pure ones. By the cosmic order (*ṛta*), those who observe the cosmic order have come—the pure-born, the pure, the purifiers. (Ṛgveda 7.56.12)
A garment that has not been worn is pure;
therefore, whatever is connected with the sacrifice, all of that one should perform using unworn garments.
The wife, the sacrificer, and the officiating priests shall put on unwashed, unbleached garments that have been washed and aired.
In this same manner, after the first step (prakrama).
The same applies to long *soma* sacrifices and to sacrificial sessions (*sattra*).
And according to the traditional recitation.

As for this: at the *iṣṭi*, animal, and *soma* sacrifices performed for malevolent purposes (*abhicaraṇīya*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should proceed wearing red turbans and red garments; and at the *Vṛṣākapi* sacrifice, they should wear variegated garments and variegated upper-vests (*āsaṅga*).
At the establishment of the sacred fires, linen garments are used; in their absence, cotton or woolen garments are used.
For those things defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, purification is by means of earth and water.
The rules for garments made of *tārpya* and *valkala* are the same as those for ordinary clothing.
The same applies to black antelope skins as it does to bark garments.
One should not wear a garment that has been put on, climbed into, and not yet washed, as an upper covering.
One should not employ for the gods water that has been stirred up or that is associated with humans.
The preparation of hard ground consists of striking it and smearing it.
The drawing out of the perforated [ladle].
Having taken a pure portion from the moist [portion], it serves as a covering.
The earth is purified by four means: by treading upon it with cows, by digging, by burning, and by being rained upon.
And from the fifth smearing up to the sixth time-period.
The washing away of grass blades placed upon unprepared ground.
For items that have been struck by something unseen, there is the sprinkling with water.
In this same manner, [the procedure for] the small fuel-sticks is performed.
If large pieces of wood are damaged, they should be washed and then dried.
But for many [items], there is sprinkling.
Wooden vessels that have come into contact with food remnants are to be scraped clean.
The scraping away of those parts defiled by contact with food-leavings or stains.
The discarding of items defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, is prescribed.
This is so except where there is a specific instruction to the contrary.

Just as in these cases—the Agnihotra, the remnant of the Gharma, the Dadhigharma, the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, the Utsarginām Ayana, the Dākṣāyaṇayajña, the Iḍādadha, the Catuścakra, and the Brahmaudanas—in all of these, the cleansing is performed with water using Darbha grass.
In all cases of consuming Soma, the rinsing is performed with water alone at the Mārjālīya shed.
The disposal of objects defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, is as follows.
The overturning of earthen vessels that have come into contact with food remnants is performed while they are held together.
Baudhāyana 1.6.14.2: Items defiled by contact with food remnants or stains are to be burned again.
The discarding of objects defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, is prescribed.
The cleansing of the metallic vessels, having been wiped as before, is performed [as follows].
The materials for wiping are cow dung, earth, and ashes.
Baudhāyana 1.6.14.6: Vessels defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and the like, must be remade.
Or he may remain immersed in cow urine for seven nights, or likewise in a great river.
In the same way, [the procedure applies] to those made of stone.
The wiping of gourds, bilva fruits, and vināḍā vessels is performed with cow-hair.
For mats woven from reeds, bamboo, *śara* grass, or *kuśa* grass, the cleansing is performed with cow-dung and water.
If rice grains are damaged, they should be washed and then dried.
But for many [objects], there is sprinkling.
The discarding of the rice grains.
Thus for the prepared oblations.

In the case of large objects defiled by dogs, crows, or similar creatures, one should remove the portion of the site occupied by human food and perform a sprinkling with this Anuvāka beginning with "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ."
In the case of honey and water, as well as in the case of products derived from milk, there is no requirement for purification when transferring them from one vessel to another.
In this same manner, having poured oil and clarified butter into water that has been touched by food-leavings while being held in contact with the body, one should employ them.
In the event of placing [fuel] on the fire that has become impure, one should consign the fire into it, churn out a new fire, and perform the Pavamāneṣṭi.

In the case of differences regarding purification, place, mantra, repetition, purpose, substance, preparation, and time, each preceding factor possesses greater importance than the one following it; each preceding factor possesses greater importance.
The sacrificial ground is arranged with the ritual movements proceeding from the north.
And likewise, there is completion.
In the rites for the ancestors, the order is reversed.
One should wash what has been stepped upon by the foot.
Having touched a limb or the fringe of his garment, he should touch water.

In this same manner [the rites are performed] for cutting, splitting, digging, throwing out, and for those acts pertaining to the ancestors (pitrya), the Rākṣasas, the Nairṛtas, the Raudras, and for malevolent magic (abhicaraṇīya).
One should not pass oneself around a sacrificial implement accompanied by a mantra.
The sacrificial implements are the internal parts of the sacrifice.
The external officiating priests.
The wife and the sacrificer are the two most closely related to the officiating priests.

From the auxiliary parts of the sacrifice comes the clarified butter; from the clarified butter, the oblations; from the oblations, the animal victim; from the animal victim, Soma; and from Soma, the fires.
The officiating priests should not turn back from the sacrificial ground until the ritual action is completed.
If he is facing east, he should turn around toward his right shoulder.
Facing west, he [places] the left [hand].
The space between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara* is the gateway of the sacrifice.
The Āhavanīya fire and the rubbish-heap (utkara) are located at the edge of the pit (cātvāla).
Then the performers—the sacrificer and his wife—should enter.
When the sacrifice has not been completed.
And when the sacrifice has been completed, the movement [of the priests] takes place from the location of the *utkara* heap.
One should not place a piece of wood or a fuel-stick that has not been sprinkled with water, that has not been brought forward, or that is damp.
The Brahman and the sacrificer enter by the front of the Āhavanīya fire.
Some say [it should be] behind the Āhavanīya fire.
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire is the seat of the Brahman priest; behind that is the seat of the sacrificer.
To the north of the northern hip [of the altar], he places [the seat] for the Hotṛ.
The *utkara* is the [specific] place for the *āgnīdhra*.
Behind the Gārhapatya fire is the place for the wife.
At each respective time, he strews darbha grass upon them.
And for each person, a water-pot should be kept ready for the purpose of sipping water.
One who has entered upon the vow shall be consecrated.
One should not speak of another's sin, nor become angry, nor weep; one should not look at urine or feces.
Upon seeing something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of lights. O Consecration, do not abandon me!"
Now, if it rains upon him, he should recite: "O flowing waters, bestow strength; bestow vigor; bestow strength; do not destroy my consecration (*dīkṣā*) nor my austerity (*tapas*).
The four social classes (*varṇas*) are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.
Among them, according to the sequence of the castes, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives.
There are three for a Kṣatriya.
There are two for a Vaiśya.
A Śūdra has one [tooth].
Among those wives, sons born of women of the same caste or of the next lower caste are of the same caste as their fathers.
From women one degree or two degrees lower [than the father], the Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, and Niṣāda are born.
From women in the inverse order [of castes], there are born the Āyogava, Māgadha, Vaideha, Kṣattṛ, Pulkasa, Kukkuṭa, Vaidehaka, and Caṇḍāla.
From an Ambaṣṭha man and a woman of the first caste, a Śvapāka is born.
From the Ugra, on the second day, the Vaiṇa chant.
From a Niṣāda and a woman of the third [caste], a Pulkasa is born.
In the opposite case, it is a cock.
One born from a Niṣāda father and a Niṣādī mother up to the fifth generation destroys the status of a Śūdra.
One should initiate him; one should cause him to sacrifice in the sixth year.

The seventh is the *avikṛtabīja*; "equal seed" (*samabīja*) and "equal" (*sama*)—these are their designations in sequence. Those whom one may beget through non-vow (*avrata*) due to similarity among the three castes, the wise call them *vrātyas*, fallen from the *Sāvitrī*.
The wise call them *vrātyas*.
They include the *rathakāra*, *ambaṣṭha*, *sūta*, *ugra*, *māgadha*, *āyogava*, *vaiṇa*, *kṣattṛ*, *pulkasa*, *kukkuṭa*, *vaidehaka*, *caṇḍāla*, *śvapāka*, and others.
Among these, those born from women of the same caste as their fathers are of the same caste (*savarṇa*).
From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother, a son is born who is a Brāhmaṇa; from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya mother, an Ambaṣṭha; and from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother, a Niṣāda.
Some say he is a *pāraśava*.
From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother, a Kṣatriya is born; from a Śūdra mother, an Ugra is born.
From a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman is born a Rathakāra.
From a Śūdra, on a Vaiśya woman, a Māgadha is born; on a Kṣatriya woman, a Kṣattṛ; and on a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Caṇḍāla.
From a Vaiśya on a Kṣatriya woman is born an Āyogava; on a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Vaidehaka. From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta.
In that regard, when there is a union between an Ambaṣṭha man and an Ugrā woman, [the offspring] is an Anuloma.
The offspring of a Kṣattṛ and a Vaidehaka are born in the reverse order of castes (pratiloma).
Born from an Ugra man on a Kṣatriya woman, he is a Śvapāka.
From a Vaidehaka father and an Ambaṣṭha mother is born a Vaiṇa.
From a Niṣāda by a Śūdra woman is born a Pulkasa.
From a Śūdra, on a Niṣādī woman, a cock is born.
The wise call those born from the intermixture of castes *vrātyas*—the wise call them *vrātyas*.
The king, who receives a sixth part [of the produce], shall protect the subjects.
Brahman indeed placed his own majesty within the Brāhmaṇas—endowed with study, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving, and receiving—for the protection of the Vedas.
In the Kṣatriya, strength is joined with study, sacrificing, giving, weapons, the treasury, and the protection of beings; this is for the prosperity of the Kṣatriya.
The Vaiśya's [duty] consists of the study of the Vedas, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing, joined with actions for the increase of his livelihood.
Among Śūdras, [the duty] consists of service to those mentioned previously.
"For they were created from the vessel," so it is said.
He should appoint a domestic priest who is capable of bearing the burden in every respect.
One should abide by his instruction.
In battle, he shall not turn back.
One should not strike with weapons that have holes, nor with those smeared with poison.
One should not fight with those who are terrified, intoxicated, insane, distracted, unarmored, women, children, the elderly, or Brahmins.
Except in the case of an assassin.
Now they also cite this:
"If one kills an assailant (*ātatāyin*) born in a family of teachers, he does not become a slayer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*); it is fury that meets fury."
The maritime toll consists of one-tenth of the value of the goods, with an additional fine of one hundred paṇas.
In the case of others as well, he should determine a righteous portion in accordance with their respective capacities, provided it does not cause them harm.
After having guarded for one year property whose owner has disappeared, the king shall take it from a non-Brāhmaṇa.
A Brāhmaṇa is indeed not to be killed for any offenses whatsoever.

In the case of a Brāhmaṇa who has committed the murder of a Brāhmaṇa, sexual intercourse with the Guru’s wife, theft of gold, or the drinking of liquor, he shall be branded on the forehead with red-hot iron with the marks of a Kusindhaka, a Bhaga, a jackal, or a tavern-sign, and then banished from the realm.
In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa, the punishment for Kṣatriyas and others is death and the confiscation of all their property.
In the case of killing those very same persons when they are of equal or inferior status, one should prescribe punishments proportionate to their respective strength.
Upon the killing of a Kṣatriya, one should release a thousand cows with an additional bull to the king for the purpose of avenging the enmity.
For a Vaiśya it is one hundred, for a Śūdra ten; and in this case, a bull is additionally required.
The killing of a woman and the killing of a cow are explained by the [penance for] the killing of a Śūdra, except in the case of killing an Ātreyī woman, or a milch-cow, or a bull.
In the case of killing a milch cow or a bull, one should perform a Cāndrāyaṇa penance at the end [of the period].
The killing of an Ātreyī woman is explained by the [rules for] the killing of a Kṣatriya.

For the killing of a swan, a vulture, a peacock, a ruddy goose, a heron, a crow, an owl, a frog, a *ḍiḍḍika*, a *ḍerikā*, a dog, a brown mongoose, a *nakula*, and so forth, the penance is the same as for a Śūdra.
For the sake of maintaining social order, a witness shall declare his testimony exactly as it was seen or heard.
"One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator; one quarter goes to the witness;
one quarter falls upon all the members of the court; and one quarter reaches the king."
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the court are also released; the guilt goes to the perpetrator where the one deserving of blame is indeed blamed.
And having thus designated a witness, the discerning judge should question him with diligence.
"On the night you were born and on the night you shall die—
whatever good deed you have performed between these two, all that shall go to the King from you who speak untruth."
A witness who speaks falsely in testimony kills three fathers and three grandfathers— seven in all, both those already born and those yet unborn.
In the case of a falsehood regarding gold, one destroys three generations of ancestors;
in the case of a falsehood regarding livestock, one destroys five; in the case of a falsehood regarding cattle, one destroys ten.
A witness who speaks falsely regarding a horse kills a hundred; he kills a thousand for false testimony concerning a man; by speaking falsely regarding land, a witness kills everything.

Members of the four castes who have sons may serve as witnesses, except for those who are Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), members of the royal caste (*rājanya*), renunciants (*pravrajita*), and those deficient in human qualities.
In the Smṛti, the disposal is considered primary.
If one acts otherwise than this, it results in the state of being a cart-breaker.
"One should drink boiled milk for twelve nights, or one should offer oblations with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* verses; or one should offer oblations with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* verses."
There are eight forms of marriage.
Having ascertained [the recipient's] learning and character, that which is given to a seeker who is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) is the *brāhma* [gift].
"Having clothed her and adorned her, [he says]: 'Let her perform the practice of dharma together with you'—this is the formula for the Prājāpatya rite."
Having offered the first oblation of parched grain (*lājāhuti*), the rite accompanied by a pair of cows is the *ārṣa* [form].
When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are being led forward, the rite performed within the altar (*antarvedi*) for the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is the *daiva* [form].
The Āsura form consists of winning her over with wealth.
The Gāndharva form is the mutual union of one who desires her with her who desires him. The Rākṣasa form results from abduction by force.
One should approach a woman who is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged; this is the Paiśāca form of marriage.
Of these, four are for a Brāhmaṇa; among them, each preceding one is superior to the next.
Among the subsequent ones, each succeeding one is more wicked than the preceding.
In this case as well, the sixth and seventh [verses] follow the duties of a Kṣatriya, because they are based on that [status] of a Kṣatriya.
The fifth and eighth [stomas] are for the Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
For the wives of Vaiśyas and Śūdras are indeed unrestrained.
Because he is authorized to perform the service of plowing.
Some also praise the Gāndharva marriage, because it is accompanied by mutual affection in all cases.
"It is known that as the marriage is joined, so the offspring becomes joined."—Baudhāyana 1.11.21.1.

Now they also cite this: "The son of a Brāhmaṇī wife sanctifies ten ancestors through the Ṛṣi-lineage, ten descendants through the Deity-lineage, ten descendants through the Prajāpati-lineage, ten ancestors and ten descendants, as well as himself; thus it is known. Furthermore, the capacity to master the Vedas belongs only to such sons.
A woman who has been purchased with wealth is not ordained as a wife.
She is neither for the rites of the gods nor for the rites of the ancestors; Kāśyapa declared her to be a slave-girl.
Those who, deluded by greed, bestow their own daughter for a bride-price are sellers of themselves; they are sinful and perpetrators of a great crime.
They fall into a terrible hell and destroy their lineage down to the seventh generation;
furthermore, all matters concerning going and coming are regulated by the toll.

There is a suspension of study for one day and night on the full moon, the eighth day, the new moon, during a fire-omen, an earthquake, when visiting a cemetery, upon the arrival of the local ruler or a learned Brahmin, and when traveling to the same sacred bathing-place.
In the case of wind, a putrid odor, mist, or the sounds of dancing, singing, instrumental music, weeping, or Sāman chants, [the suspension lasts] for that duration of time.
When there is a simultaneous occurrence of thunder, rain, and lightning, there shall be a suspension of study for three days, except during the rainy season.
Even during the rainy season, one should perform it except for the time of rain; and during the day and night, it should be performed at that specific time.
And on the day of receiving a gift from or eating at a funeral rite for ancestors, one should remain restrained for the remainder of that day.
In the case of food offerings, [the recitation continues] until the food is digested.
For the Brāhmaṇa has his hands as his mouth.
Now, they also cite [the following]:
"That which is eaten and that which is accepted as a gift are indistinguishable," so says the Śruti.
When the father has passed away, [the period of impurity lasts] for three nights.

There are indeed two kinds of seed for a learned *baudhāyana* who is well-versed in the Vedas: one is above the navel, and the other is below the navel. That which is above the navel—by means of it he procreates when he initiates *brahmins*, when he teaches them, when he performs sacrifices for them, and when he does what is good; all this constitutes his offspring. Then, that which is below the navel—by means of it his own biological offspring (*aurasī*) is produced.
Therefore, they do not say of a learned man who is well-versed in the Vedas, "You are childless."
Therefore, the Brahmin is said to have two names, two faces, two seed-sources, and two births.
And for as long as the sound or sight of a Śūdra’s discarded vessel is heard or seen, [one must remain silent].
One should not study at night when jackals howl, nor until the end of sleep.
And one should not study during the day and night, at the two twilights, or on the days of the lunar festivals (parvan).
One should not eat meat, nor should one approach a woman.
"For it is known that on the days of the lunar changes (*parvan*), *rakṣas* and *piśāca* demons become prone to transgression."
On account of other portents and calamities as well, there shall be no study for a day and a night, except when one's mind is otherwise engaged.
Baudhāyana 1.11.21: Even in the case of mental [birth or death], there is a suspension of Vedic study upon both birth and death.
Now they also cite:
"The eighth day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
the fifteenth day destroys knowledge. Therefore, one should avoid [studying] on the festival days."
Therefore, one should avoid [these acts] on the day of the full moon or new moon.
Baudhāyana 2.1.1.1: Now, therefore, the expiations.
A killer of an embryo [must perform penance] for twelve years.

Bearing a skull, carrying a staff with a skull-topped end, clothed in a donkey skin, and making his dwelling in the forest, he should construct a hut in a cremation ground using a corpse's head as a banner; there he should reside. Wandering for alms at seven houses while proclaiming his own deed, he should sustain his life by that means; if he does not obtain anything, he should fast.
He should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Gosava, or the Agniṣṭut.
Or he may purify himself at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Now they also cite this:
"By killing a Brāhmaṇa unintentionally, one becomes defiled according to dharma;
the seers declare an expiation for that act when it was not preceded by deliberate intent."
For one who kills intentionally, no atonement is found.
"Having threatened [to strike], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance;
for actually striking, the Atikṛcchra; and for the flowing of blood, both the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Therefore, one should never threaten nor cause blood to flow."
For a Kṣatriya, it is nine years.
For a Vaiśya, there are three.
For a Śūdra, [the period of impurity lasts] one year.
And [the same applies] to a woman.
The ritual for the Ātreyī is performed as prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa woman.
One who has violated the teacher's bed shall lie upon a heated iron bed.
Or he should embrace a glowing iron image.
Alternatively, having cut off the male organ together with the testicles and placed it in his joined palms, he should walk between the southern and western directions until he falls down.
A thief, having disheveled his hair and taken a mallet made of *sairīka* wood, should go to the king with it upon his shoulder, saying, "Slay me with this! He shall then strike him with it.
Now they also cite this:
"Taking a pestle upon his shoulder, a thief should approach the king, saying:
'O King, remembering the duty of a Kṣatriya, punish me with this.'"
"Whether by punishing or by releasing him, the thief is freed from his guilt;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. Thus it is said.
Having drunk *surā*, one should burn the body with hot [liquor].
If one drinks [Soma] unintentionally, one should perform a quarter of the Kṛcchra penance for a year and undergo re-initiation.
And there is no omission of the shaving, the vows, or the restrictive observances, because they have already been performed previously.
Now they also cite this:
"Having unintentionally drunk the liquor of Varuṇa, or having consumed urine or feces,
a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya deserves to undergo the rite of re-consecration."
If one drinks water that has stood overnight in a vessel used for storing *surā* liquor,
he should subsist for six days on milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
If one who has been commissioned by his teacher should die, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
This very same [procedure applies] when it has not been consecrated.
For a religious student (brahmacārin), the suspension of his vows occurs through the performance of funeral rites for anyone other than his mother, father, or teacher.
If he should fall ill, he may, at his will, consume all the remnants of his teacher's food for the purpose of medicine.
With whatever [means] he desires, with that he should treat [the patient].
When he is ill, having risen, he should worship the sun with this [verse]: "The swan dwelling in purity... and so forth.
Having emitted semen during the day, one should drink water that reaches the heart three times with the *retasyā* verses.
A student of sacred knowledge who approaches a woman is an *avakīrṇin*.
He should sacrifice a donkey as the animal victim.
The animal victim and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) are dedicated to Nirṛti; their presiding deities are either the Rakṣas or Yama.
"It is known from tradition that they proceed with the portions [of the sacrifice] in the waters, taking the *prāśitra* from the penis."

Alternatively, on the night of the new moon, having established the fire and performed the ritual attendances pertaining to wood-offerings (*dārvihoma*), he offers two oblations of clarified butter with the formulas: "O Kāma, I have spilled my seed; I have spilled my seed, O Kāma! To Kāma, svāhā! O Kāma, I have been deceived; I have been deceived, O Kāma! To Kāma, svāhā!"

Having offered the oblation, with hands joined in reverence, he should address the fire from a slightly oblique position: "May the Maruts sprinkle me; may Indra sprinkle me; may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me; may this Agni sprinkle me with long life and strength; make me long-lived."

Then, his kinsmen should pour out a vessel of water for him in the assembly, saying, "I am so-and-so, having become such-and-such. Having performed the ritual acts involving water, milk, ghee, honey, and salt, the Brāhmaṇas should say to him as he undertakes them, "Have you performed [the penance]? He replies, "Yes. They should then perform for him the *savanīya* sacrifice which effects the completion of the penance.
If one should unintentionally approach a woman of the same gotra, he should support her like a mother.

If [the cow] has given birth, having performed a quarter of a Kṛcchra penance for a year, one should offer oblations with these two [verses]: "Whatever deficiency of mine has occurred" and "Agni has given sight again."
The one who is superseded, the one who supersedes, and she whom he marries—
all these go to hell, with the giver and the officiating priest as the fifth.

The one who has been superseded by a younger brother, the one who supersedes him, the giver [of the bride], and also the officiating priest—these are purified by a twelve-night Kṛcchra penance; a woman is purified in three nights. Thus it is said.
Now, the acts leading to loss of caste (patanīya).
Baudhāyana 2.1.2.2: A voyage upon the ocean.
2.1.2.3. The misappropriation of a deposit belonging to a Brāhmaṇa.
Falsehood regarding land.
Dealing in all kinds of merchandise.
Serving a Śūdra.
Baudhāyana 2.1.2.7: Birth from a Śūdra woman.
And [the status of] being their offspring [is also established].
Having performed one of these [rites].
Eating measured portions at the fourth meal-time, they should descend into the water according to the ritual procedure for the *savana*s;
by alternating between standing and sitting, they destroy that evil within three years.

Whatever sin a Brāhmaṇa incurs by associating with one of black complexion for a single night, he destroys that sin in three years by eating only at the fourth meal-time and subsisting on water. Thus it is said.
Now, the minor offenses (upapātaka).

Having had sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached—such as the wife of a teacher, the female friend of a teacher, the female friend of a preceptor, one who has lost caste, or an outcast; having practiced medicine, officiated at sacrifices for a village, subsisted on the stage, been a teacher of acting, tended cattle or buffalo, or whatever else is of a similar nature, such as defiling a maiden.
But their mode of subsistence shall be that of an outcast for two years.
Now, the things that cause impurity.

Gambling, sorcery, living by gleaning for one who has not established the sacred fires, the practice of begging for food after returning home from studentship, his continued residence in the teacher's house beyond four months, teaching him [the Vedas], and the pointing out of constellations—these are [grounds for loss of caste].

The performance of these [penances] consists of twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of six days, twelve periods of three days, twelve days, six days, three days, one day and night, and one day, according to the repetition of the act.

Now, those who have fallen [from their caste], having come together, should practice their duties as mutual sacrificers, mutual teachers, and marrying among themselves. Having produced sons, they should say: "Depart from us; in this way you will attain the status of Āryas."
Moreover, even one who possesses his sense organs does not fall [from his caste].
This is to be understood by means of this: even one who is deficient in a limb may produce a child who possesses all limbs.
Hārīta says that this is false.
Women should share the same status as a vessel for curd. For when one churns impure milk that has been curdled in a vessel for curd, the learned do not employ it for religious rites.
In this way, when impure semen is discharged, there is no sexual union with it.
For those born from impure semen, if they so desire, there is an expiation.
For those who have committed acts leading to loss of caste, the woman's share shall be one-third of that portion.
Now they also cite this:
"Whatever one does with sesame seeds other than eating them, anointing oneself, or giving them away,
one becomes a worm in a dog's excrement and sinks down along with one's ancestors."
He who sells sesame seeds sells his ancestors; he who sells rice grains sells his vital breaths; and he who, for the sake of profit, gives away his daughter in marriage sells his portions of merit.
Grass and wood that are unaltered may be sold.
Now they also cite this:
"Animals with only one row of teeth, a stone extracted from salt-earth,
and a thread not yet dyed— these, O Brāhmaṇa, are your wares."

Alternatively, excluding those for mortal sins (*pātaka*), one should pour clarified butter over a brownish-pink, hairy cow, scatter black sesame seeds upon it, and give her to a learned man (*anūcāna*).
Or, one may perform the *kūśmāṇḍa* rites for twelve days.
"By this, he is released from whatever sin prior to the killing of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*)."
If one falsely accuses another of a mortal sin (pātaka), the penance is a Kṛcchra.
That year belongs to the one who utters the curse.
One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or sexual union, but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.
For consuming impure substances, the penance is the Naiṣpurīṣya rite; that is accomplished within seven nights.
Water, milk, ghee, and fasting for three days each—these, when performed with hot substances, constitute the *sataptakṛcchra*.

Eating only in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening for three days, eating only what is unasked for for three days, and fasting for the final three days—this is the Parāka Kṛcchra penance.
Eating only what is not solicited in the morning and evening constitutes the *parāka* penance; these three four-night periods constitute the *kṛcchra* for women, children, and the elderly.
One should eat as much as one can take in a single mouthful; this is the Atikṛcchra penance, as described previously.
The third [type] consists of subsisting on water; that is the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra.
In the Kṛcchra penance, there is the ritual touching of water at the three sessions of the day.
Sleeping on the ground.
Wearing a single garment, and the shaving of the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails.
This same [rite] applies to a woman, with the exception of shaving the hair; with the exception of shaving the hair.

One who constantly uses water for purification, constantly wears the sacred thread, constantly engages in Vedic study, avoids the food of a *vṛṣala*, approaches his wife only during her season, and offers oblations according to the rule— such a Brāhmaṇa does not fall from the world of Brahman.
"The sacred tradition states: 'Manu divided his inheritance among his sons.'"
It is to be shared equally among all, because there is no distinction made.
Or the eldest may set aside a choice portion or a specific form [of the inheritance].
"Therefore, they exclude the eldest son from his share of the wealth"—so says the Śruti.
Or the eldest [son] may set aside one from among ten [shares].
The others shall divide it equally.
The division of the inheritance takes place with the father's consent while the father is still living.
Among the four castes, cows, horses, goats, and sheep constitute the senior share.
In the case of a gathering of sons born of women of different castes, one should divide the inheritance into ten shares and distribute them in order: four, three, two, and one.
But when a legitimate son of the body (aurasa) has been born, those of the same caste (savarṇāḥ) shall receive a third share.
Between the son of a wife of equal caste and the son of a wife of the next lower caste, if the son of the next lower caste is virtuous, he shall take the share of the eldest.
For one who possesses virtues is indeed the supporter of his dependents.
One should know that the son begotten by oneself upon a wife of equal caste who has undergone the sacraments is the *aurasa* (legitimate) son.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"From limb after limb you arise; from the heart you are born."
"Thou art indeed the self named son; live for a hundred autumns! [Thus he says].
Regarding a daughter born of a marriage by agreement, the son of such a daughter is called *putrikā-putra*, while any other daughter's son is called *dauhitra*.
Now they also cite [this]:
"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-suta) should designate his mother at the first rice-ball (piṇḍa), her father at the second, and her grandfather at the third. Thus [it is said].
He who is begotten on a wife by another man with her consent—whether the husband is dead, impotent, or diseased—is a *kṣetraja* (son of the soil).
This man, having two fathers and two gotras, becomes an heir to the *svadhā* and the inheritance of both.
Now they also cite:
"In the case of one who has two fathers, there should be the offering of rice balls for both; on each rice ball, the names of both should be mentioned.
Thus, three rice balls are offered for six [ancestors]; by acting in this way, one does not go astray."
One who is given by both parents or by either one of them and is accepted for the sake of offspring is a *datta* (given) son.
One whom he himself makes his own, being similar [to him] and desirous [of the union], is the *kṛtrima* (artificial son).
One born secretly in the house and discovered at the end is a *gūḍhaja* (secret-born son).
One who, having been abandoned by both his mother and father, or by either one of them, is taken up for the sake of offspring, is an *apaviddha*.
He who is born of a woman whom one has approached without having consecrated her and without having given her leave is a *kānīna*.
If a woman who is pregnant is consecrated—whether her condition is known or unknown—the son born of her is a *sahoḍha*.
One who is purchased from the hands of his mother and father, or from either one of them, and is taken for the sake of offspring, is a "purchased" (krīta) son.
If a woman, having abandoned a eunuch or an outcast, finds another husband, the son born of her as a remarried woman (*paunarbhavī*) is called *paunarbhava*.
One who, being destitute of mother and father, gives himself away is a self-given son (*svayaṃdatta*).
One born from a Śūdra woman by a man of the twice-born castes through a *pravara* (ancestral lineage) is a Niṣāda.
The Pāraśava is born from lust; these are the sons.
Now they also cite: "The son of the body,
the son of an appointed daughter, the son born of the wife, the son given, the son made,
the son born in secret, and the son cast off— these are declared to be the sharers of the inheritance."

The son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son received with a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), the purchased son (*krīta*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the self-given son (*svayaṃdatta*), and the *niṣāda*— these they declare to be sharers of the lineage (*gotrabhāj*).
"Aupajaṅghani says that it is only the first of them."
"O Janaka, I am not envious of women now as I was before,
since they have declared in the abode of Yama that one belongs to the begetter of the son."
"The progenitor of the seed leads the son away after death to the abode of Yama;
therefore, fearing the seed of another, they protect their own wives."
"Guard this thread with vigilance; let no one sow another's seed in your field.
In the life hereafter, the son belongs to the progenitor; he who sows the seed makes this thread of his own in vain. Thus it is said.
Until they reach the age of legal capacity, their shares, along with the increments [of interest], shall be kept well-guarded by them [the guardians].
They shall support those whose legal affairs have passed away with food and clothing.
And also those who are blind, mentally deficient, eunuchs, addicted to vices, diseased, and so forth.
Those who do not perform the ritual acts.
With the exception of those who have fallen from their caste and those born of such persons.
There is no social interaction with those who have fallen from their caste.
But even if his mother has fallen [from her caste], he should support her without speaking to her.
The daughters shall receive their mother’s personal ornaments, as well as the traditional inheritance, or whatever else [is left].
A woman possesses no independence.
Now they also cite:
"The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth; the son protects her in old age. A woman does not deserve independence. Thus it is said.
"For women are considered to be devoid of sensory power and without inheritance," so says the Śruti.
Striving for the welfare of their husband, they shall win the heavenly world.
In the event of a transgression, the penance is a *kṛcchra*.
And for a Śūdra, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
In the case of those born in the inverse order among Vaiśyas and the other castes, one should perform the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, and other such penances.
For males, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, the period of studentship (brahmacarya) shall last for one year.
One should burn a Śūdra with a fire from a mat.
Now, they also cite this:
For a non-Brāhmaṇa, corporal punishment shall be the penalty for adultery.
For all social classes alike, one's wife is more worthy of protection than wealth.
But there shall be no execution for women who are performers, nor for those on a stage;
for they cause these men to mingle with one another and even lead them astray when they are well-guarded.
Women are an incomparable means of purification; they are never defiled.
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their sins.
Soma gave them purity; Gandharva, eloquent speech; and Agni, the capacity to consume all things. Therefore, women are free from blemish.

One should abandon a wife who bears no offspring in the tenth year, one whose offspring are all female in the twelfth year, one whose offspring die in the fifteenth year, but one who speaks unpleasantly immediately.
For one year, the wife of the deceased shall avoid honey, meat, liquor, and salt, and she shall sleep on the ground.
"For six months," says Maudgalya.
From this point forward, with the permission of her elders, a sonless woman may procreate a son through her husband's younger brother.
Now they also cite this:
"A barren cow, one that has already given birth, one that is without menses, and one whose offspring have passed away—
such a cow should not be employed against her will if no fruit is to be obtained from her."
A maternal uncle’s sister, a paternal aunt, a sister, a daughter, a daughter-in-law, a maternal aunt, and a female friend’s wife—these are women who must not be approached for sexual intercourse.
For approaching women who should not be approached, the expiation consists of the Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
By this, sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is explained.
Now they also cite this:

"A Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Caṇḍālī woman, or has eaten [with her], or has accepted a gift from her—such a Vipra falls from his status through ignorance; but through knowledge, he would attain equality [with her]."
"By unintentionally approaching the wife of one's father, teacher, or king, one becomes a violator of the Guru’s bed; the atonement for this has been previously stated. Thus [it is said].
If he is unable [to subsist] by teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts, he may live according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, because that is the next in order.
"No," says Gautama; for the duty of a Kṣatriya is exceedingly fierce toward a Brāhmaṇa.
Now, they also cite this:
"For the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, or even in the case of a confusion of castes,
a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya may take up arms out of regard for dharma."
The livelihood of a Vaiśya should be followed because it is immediately adjacent [to the Kṣatriya's].
Before the morning meal, he should be one who practices self-restraint.
[He should sacrifice] with two [testicles] whose noses have not been pierced, together with the testicles, without piercing them with a needle, repeatedly encouraging [the sacrificer].
The fire begins with the wife; in that [fire], the performance of ritual acts takes place prior to the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya).

Baudhāyana 2.2.4.23: From the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) onwards, these [rites] are perpetual (*ajasra*). They are as follows: the *agnyādheya*, the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *āgrayaṇa* at the solstices (*udagayana* and *dakṣiṇāyana*), the animal sacrifice, the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices at the beginning of the seasons, the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* offering, and the *jyotiṣṭoma* in spring; in this manner, one reaches security (*kṣema*).
Now they also cite this:
"Neither by one habituated to sleeping during the day, nor by one who eats all kinds of food,
nor even by one who has fallen from a high station, can it be possible to go to heaven at will."
One should avoid wretchedness, deceit, and crookedness.
Now, they also cite here a verse from the dialogue between Uśanas and Vṛṣaparvan’s two daughters:
“You are indeed the daughter of one who praises, who begs, and who accepts;
but I am the son of one who is praised, who gives, and who does not accept.”
"For one who gives but does not accept."
The ascetic practice consists of immersing oneself in water.
Having satiated the deities, [he performs] the libation for the ancestors.
Along the bank, he pours out water with the verse: "Carrying strength... (RV 10.30.12).
Now they also quote:
"In flowing waters that are not obstructed, members of the three twice-born castes,
having risen in the morning, should perform the libations to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors."
When the waters are obstructed, they shall not perform [the ritual]; in that case, the builder of the embankment is entitled to a share.
Therefore, one should avoid embankments and wells made by others.
Now, they also cite this:
"Or, having extracted three lumps [of earth], one should perform [the rite] in times of distress, but not always;
however, when [water] is obstructed, one should likewise take three lumps of clay from a well and three jars of water."

Having accepted what should not be accepted or having accepted much that should be accepted, or having officiated at a sacrifice for one for whom one should not officiate, or having eaten the food of one whose food should not be eaten, one should mutter the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
Now, they also cite this:
"Those who mix with their teacher's [wives] and those who mix with their pupils,
and those who confuse food and mantras, dwell for a long time in darkness."
Now, the observances of one who has completed his Vedic studies (snātaka).

In the evening and in the morning, having offered the Vaiśvadeva bali with whatever food is fit for consumption, he should honor Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have arrived as guests according to his ability.
If he is unable [to give] to many, he should give to one who possesses good qualities.
Or rather, he who arrives first.
If a Śūdra has arrived, one should employ him in the ritual work.
Or he should give the first portion to one learned in the Vedas.
A distribution of shares has been prescribed for those who are permanent dependents, provided that it does not cause hardship to those who are entitled to the primary shares.
But one should never eat without having first given [to others].
Now, they also cite two verses regarding food in this regard:
"Whoever, out of delusion, eats prepared food without first giving it to the ancestors, the deities, servants, guests, and friends—that person eats poison; I devour him, for I am his death."
Having offered the Agnihotra and performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, he who— having honored his guests and provided for his dependents—
eats what remains with contentment, purity, and faith, for him I become nectar, and he enjoys me.

A distribution of property according to one's ability should be made to those who are not of the Brahmin caste but are learned in the Vedas and have mastered them, to those seeking funds for their teacher, for medicine, for maintaining a livelihood, for those whose resources are exhausted, for those about to perform a sacrifice, for those engaged in Vedic study, for those traveling on a journey, and for those competing in the Vaiśvajita rite—provided they are begging outside the sacrificial altar.
In the case of the others, [the offering] consists of prepared food.

Having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, sipped water for purification, and taken the food brought to him in a clean, enclosed place, he should—having cast away desire, anger, malice, greed, and delusion—consume it with all his fingers, making no sound.
One should not discard the remainder of the rice balls into the vessel.
If one has consumed food mixed with meat, fish, or sesame seeds, one should touch water and then touch the fire.
And the bath [is performed] after the sun has set.
One should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa*.
One should not eat food from one's lap.
One should not eat while seated on a chair.
He should carry a staff made of bamboo, as well as a golden ornament and earrings.
One should avoid washing one's feet with the foot itself and standing upon it.
One should not wear a garland outside [the sacrificial ground].
One should not look at the sun at either sunrise or sunset.
One should not announce "The rainbow! to another person.
If he should say, "The jewel-bow," he should simply say, "The jewel-bow."
One should not pass between the Indra-pillar and the crossbar at the city gate.
One should not walk between the two *pleṅkha* (swing-frames).
And one should not walk over the rope to which the calf is tied.
One should not step upon ashes, bones, hair, chaff, potsherds, or the water used for ritual bathing.
One should not tell another person that a cow is suckling her calf.
One should not say, "The non-cow is a cow."
If he should say, "A cow that is about to give milk," he should simply say, "A cow that is about to give milk."
One should not speak words that are bitter, harsh, or rough.
One should not travel along a road alone.
Not with outcasts, nor with a woman, nor with a Śūdra.
One should not go out again at evening.
One should not bathe naked.
One should not bathe at night.
One should not cross a river by swimming with one's arms.
One should not look down into a well.
One should not look into a pit.
He should not sit down there where someone else might make him rise.
A path must be yielded to a Brāhmaṇa, to a cow, to a king, to one who is sightless,
to an elderly person, to one oppressed by a heavy burden, to a pregnant woman, and to one who is weak.

A righteous person should strive to dwell in a village that has abundant fuel, water, barley, grass, firewood, and *kuśa* grass; where garlands are available; which is accessible for going out; which is crowded with wealthy people; which is prosperous through industry; which abounds in noble persons; and which is not entered by robbers.
In a village where the water is drawn from a single well, a Brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a Śūdra woman,
having lived there for twelve years, attains the same status as a Śūdra.
With his body covered in the dust of the city, his eyes and face completely filled with it,
and dwelling in the city with his self well-restrained, he will attain perfection— this is not so.
The dust of chariots, horses, elephants, grain, and cows is auspicious;
however, that of a broom, dogs, goats, sheep, donkeys, and clothes is not recommended.
One should honor those worthy of honor.
A seer, one who knows the Vedas, an excellent king, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, and an officiating priest—
these are declared by the scriptures to be worthy of the *arghya* offering according to the division of time.

Sages, learned men, and kings who have arrived at the commencement of a rite are to be honored as excellent officiating priests; likewise, a maternal uncle and a father-in-law are to be honored when they arrive after the lapse of a year. Thus it is said.
In the fire-sanctuary, in the midst of cows, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic study, and while eating, one should raise the right arm.
A new upper garment must be worn during these five activities:
the private recitation of the Veda, the formal conclusion of that recitation, the giving of gifts, as well as eating and sipping water for purification.
Offering oblations, eating, giving, presenting offerings, and receiving gifts—these should not be performed with the hands outside the knees; the same rule is prescribed for sipping water (ācamana).
"All beings are supported by food; food is life," so says the Śruti.
Therefore, food must be given, for food is indeed the supreme oblation.
"Sin is pacified by the oblation; the oblation is pacified by food;
food attains peace through the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Such is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
"It attains [peace]"—this is our revealed tradition.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana).

Having gone to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), whether he is unpurified but has bathed, or purified but has not bathed, he washes his feet and hands, sips water (*ācamana*), and by sprinkling himself with water using fragrant substances, with mantras addressed to Varuṇa, with those concerning gold, with the *pāvamānī* verses, with the *vyāhṛtis*, and with other purificatory formulas, he becomes pure.
Now they also cite [the following]:
"Immersion in water—this immersion in water—is prescribed as a bath for all social classes;
however, for the twice-born, sprinkling with mantras is distinguished as superior."
And at the commencement of all ritual acts, prior to the time for the twilight worship, one becomes pure by sprinkling oneself with this very collection of purifiers.
Now they also cite this: "Seated upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, with his hand containing water, facing westward, he should repeat the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times."
Or else, one who has purified himself by breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) may do so a hundred times.
Or he may recite it ten times mentally, with the syllable *praṇava* at both ends and accompanied by the seven *vyāhṛtis*.
And when exhausted by three breath-restraints, he [should worship] with the Brahmahṛdaya.
With two verses addressed to Varuṇa—namely, "imaṃ me varuṇa" and "tat tvā yāmi"—he worships the night.
In the same manner, in the morning, standing facing the east; thus [he offers].
He worships the day with two verses addressed to Mitra: "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people... and "Mitra impels the people..."—with these two.
Even if one begins the *pūrvā* [lunar day] when it is already well-advanced, one should complete it once the sun has risen.
Having commenced before sunset, one may even perform the western [oblation] well after [sunset].
And at the two twilights, for the sake of the continuity of day and night, there is the attainment of union.
Moreover, there are two verses sung by Prajāpati on this subject:
"Those Brahmins who do not worship the morning twilight that has not yet arrived, nor the evening twilight that has not yet passed— how can they be considered true Brahmins?"
"Those Brahmins who do not constantly perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) in the evening and the morning—a righteous king may, at his will, employ them in the labor of Śūdras. Thus [it is said].
In that regard, if there is an omission at evening, there is fasting for the night; if there is an omission at dawn, there is fasting for the day.
One obtains the fruit of standing and sitting.
Now they also cite this:
"Whatever sin has been committed by the lap, or whatever has been done by the feet;
whatever has been done by the arms, or even by the mind, or by speech."
Having performed the evening twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*), one is thereby liberated from that [debt].
And he is joined with the night; moreover, Varuṇa does not seize him.
In this very same way, having performed the morning worship, one is released from the evil committed during the night.
He is united with the day, Mitra protects him, and Āditya leads him up to the heavenly world.

It is known: "In this very manner, worshipping day by day at the junctions of day and night, purified by the Veda, become one with the Veda, a Brahmin who follows the scripture conquers the world of Brahman; he conquers the world of Brahman. It is known: "He conquers the world of Brahman."
Then, having washed his hands and taken hold of his water-pot and a lump of clay, he goes to the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) and washes his feet three times and himself three times.
Now, some indeed say: "A cemetery, water, a temple, a cow-pen, and wherever there are Brahmins—one must not enter these places without having washed one's feet."
Then he approaches the waters, saying:
"I take refuge in Varuṇa of the golden horns; grant me a ford when I am entreated.
Whatever has been eaten by me of the unrighteous, and whatever acceptance of gifts from the wicked [I have made]."
"Whatever evil deed has been committed by me through mind, speech, or action—
may Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ purify that for me again and again."
Then, with his joined palms, he scoops up water, saying: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us."
He sprinkles water toward that direction in which he has someone whom he hates, saying: "May ill-fated enemies befall him who hates us and whom we hate."
Then, having touched water, he turns the water three times clockwise, saying: "Whatever in the waters is cruel, whatever is impure, whatever is unpeaceful—let that depart!"
Having immersed himself in the waters and emerged.
For one who is in water, there is no rinsing, nor washing of clothes, nor ritual sipping.
If they should be besieged, he worships with this: "Homage to Agni accompanied by the waters; homage to Indra; homage to Varuṇa; homage to Vāruṇī; homage to the waters."
Having emerged from the water and sipped water, once he has performed the *ācamana* rite, he should sip water again with the mantra:
"May the waters purify the earth; may the purified earth purify me. May Brahmanaspati purify [me]; may the purified Veda purify me."

"Whatever remains as leavings that is unfit for consumption, or whatever evil deed I have committed—may the waters purify all of that in me, and [purify] the acceptance of gifts from the wicked; svāhā!"

Having prepared the two strainers (*pavitre*), he purifies himself with water using the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, and the verse *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*.

Having purified himself with this section (*anuvāka*), having gone into the water, having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, and having emerged, he wrings out his garment, puts on unwashed clothes that have been washed and aired, sips water, and [sits] upon *darbha* grass.
Sitting down, holding darbha grass, and facing the east, one should repeat the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times, a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times, with ten as the minimum.
Then he worships the sun with the verses: "Up from the darkness we [have risen]," "Up that one," "The bright," "That eye, established by the gods," and "He who has risen."
Now they also cite: "The syllable *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*—these five constitute the Brahmayajñas; performed day after day, they purify the Brāhmaṇa from sin."
Purified by the five Brahma-sacrifices, he then satiates the deities with the subsequent [libations].

Om. I satiate Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Bṛhaspati, and the Sarpas—these deities of the eastern doors, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. Om, I satiate the Vasus.

Om. I satisfy these deities of the southern door—Pitṛs, Aryaman, Bhaga, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra, and Agni—together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas; Om, I satisfy the Rudras as well.

Om. Mitra, Indra, the Great Ancestors, the Waters, the Viśvedevas, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—these deities of the western doors, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas, I satiate. Om, and the Ādityas I satiate.

Om. I satiate the Vasus, Varuṇa, Aja Ekapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Yama—these deities of the northern doors, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. Om, I satiate the Viśvedevas. Om, I satiate the Sādhyas.

Om, I satiate Brahmā; Om, I satiate Prajāpati; Om, I satiate the Four-faced One; Om, I satiate Parameṣṭhin; Om, I satiate Hiraṇyagarbha; Om, I satiate Svayaṃbhū; Om, I satiate the male attendants of Brahmā;
Om, I satiate the female attendants of Brahmā; Om.

[Oṃ] I satiate Agni. [Oṃ] I satiate Vāyu. [Oṃ] I satiate Varuṇa. [Oṃ] I satiate Sūrya. [Oṃ] I satiate Candramas. [Oṃ] I satiate the Nakṣatras. [Oṃ] I satiate the Jyotiṣas. [Oṃ] I satiate Sadyojāta. [Oṃ] I satiate Bhūḥ-puruṣa. [Oṃ] I satiate Bhuvaḥ-puruṣa. [Oṃ] I satiate Suvaḥ-puruṣa.
