(I satisfy / Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa / Oṃ bhūs, I satisfy / Oṃ bhuvas, I satisfy / Oṃ suvas, I satisfy / Oṃ mahas, I satisfy / Oṃ janas, I satisfy / Oṃ tapas, I satisfy / Oṃ satyam, I satisfy).

Om, I satiate the god Bhava; Om, I satiate the god Śarva; Om, I satiate the god Īśāna; Om, I satiate the god Paśupati; Om, I satiate the god Rudra; Om, I satiate the god Ugra; Om, I satiate the god Bhīma; Om, I satiate the god Mahān.

Om, I satiate the wife of the god Bhava; Om, I satiate the wife of the god Śarva; Om, I satiate the wife of the god Īśāna; Om, I satiate the wife of the god Paśupati; Om, I satiate the wife of the god Rudra; Om, I satiate the wife of the god Ugra; Om, I satiate the wife of the god Bhīma; Om, I satiate the wife of the god Mahat.

Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Bhava; Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Śarva; Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Īśāna; Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Paśupati; Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Rudra; Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Ugra; Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Bhīma; Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Mahat; Oṃ, I satiate the Rudras. Oṃ... [he omits].
Oṃ, I satiate the attendants of Rudra; Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Rudra as well.

Oṃ, I satiate Vighna; Oṃ, I satiate Vināyaka; Oṃ, I satiate Vīra; Oṃ, I satiate Sthūla; Oṃ, I satiate Varada; Oṃ, I satiate Hastimukha; Oṃ, I satiate Vakratuṇḍa; Oṃ, I satiate Ekadanta; Oṃ, I satiate Lambodara.
I satiate Gaṇapati. Oṃ, I satiate the male attendants of Vighna. Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Vighna as well.

Om, I satiate Sanatkumāra; Om, I satiate Skanda; Om, I satiate Indra; Om, I satiate Ṣaṣṭhī; Om, I satiate Ṣaṇmukha; Om, I satiate Jayanta; Om, I satiate Viśākha; Om, I satiate Mahāsena; Om, I satiate Subrahmaṇya.
Oṃ, I satiate the attendants of Skanda; Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Skanda as well.
Om, I satiate Āditya; Om, I satiate Soma; Om, I satiate Aṅgāraka; Om, I satiate Budha; Om, I satiate Bṛhaspati; Om, I satiate Śukra; Om, I satiate Śanaiścara; Om, I satiate Rāhu; Om, I satiate Ketu.
Oṃ, I satiate Keśava. Oṃ, I satiate Nārāyaṇa. Oṃ, I satiate Mādhava. Oṃ, I satiate Govinda. Oṃ, I satiate Viṣṇu. Oṃ, I satiate Madhusūdana. Oṃ, I satiate Trivikrama. Oṃ, I satiate Vāmana.
Oṃ, I satiate Śrīdhara. Oṃ... [K omits].
Oṃ, I satiate Hṛṣīkeśa; Oṃ, I satiate Padmanābha; Oṃ, I satiate Dāmodara; Oṃ, I satiate the goddess Śrī; Oṃ, I satiate the goddess Sarasvatī; Oṃ, I satiate Puṣṭi; Oṃ, I satiate Tuṣṭi;
Oṃ, I satiate Garuḍa.
Oṃ, I satiate the attendants of Viṣṇu; Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Viṣṇu as well.

Om, I satiate Yama; Om, I satiate Yamarāja; Om, I satiate Dharma; Om, I satiate Dharmarāja; Om, I satiate Kāla; Om, I satiate Nīla; Om, I satiate Mṛtyu; Om, I satiate Vaivasvata; Om, I satiate Citra; Om, I satiate... [K omits].
Oṃ, I satiate Citragupta; Oṃ, I satiate Audumbara; Oṃ, I satiate Vaivasvata; Oṃ, I satiate the attendants of Vaivasvata; Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Vaivasvata.
Om, I satiate the deities of the earth; Om, I satiate Kaśyapa; Om, I satiate the intermediate space; Om, I satiate knowledge; Om, I satiate Dhanvantari;
Om, I satiate the attendants of Dhanvantari.
(I offer libations: Oṃ, I offer libations to the attendants of Dhanvantari.)
Then, wearing the sacred thread around the neck (nivītin).

Om, I satiate the Ṛṣis; Om, I satiate the Mahārṣis; Om, I satiate the Paramarṣis; Om, I satiate the Brahmarṣis; Om, I satiate the Devarṣis; Om, I satiate the Rājarṣis; Om, I satiate the Śrutarṣis; Om, I satiate the Janarṣis; Om... [text continues].

Oṃ, I satiate the *tapas* seers; Oṃ, I satiate the *satya* seers; Oṃ, I satiate the *sapta* seers; Oṃ, I satiate the *kāṇḍa* seers; Oṃ, I satiate the female seers (*ṛṣikāḥ*); Oṃ, I satiate the wives of the seers (*ṛṣipatnyaḥ*); Oṃ, I satiate the sons of the seers (*ṛṣiputrāḥ*); Oṃ, I satiate the grandsons of the seers (*ṛṣipautrāḥ*).

Om, I satiate Kāṇva Baudhāyana. Om, I satiate Āpastamba, the author of the Sūtra. Om, I satiate Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin. Om, I satiate Yājñavalkya, the Vājasaneyin. Om, I satiate Āśvalāyana Śaunaka. Om, I satiate Vyāsa. Om, I satiate Vasiṣṭha.

Om, I satiate the Praṇava; Om, I satiate the Vyāhṛtis; Om, I satiate Sāvitrī; Om, I satiate Gāyatrī; Om, I satiate the Metres; Om, I satiate the Ṛgveda; Om, I satiate the Yajurveda; Om, I satiate the Sāmaveda;
Om, I satiate the Atharvaveda.
Oṃ, I satiate the Atharvāṅgirases; Oṃ, I satiate the Itihāsas and Purāṇas; Oṃ, I satiate all the Vedas; Oṃ, I satiate all the divine beings; Oṃ, I satiate all living beings. Thus.

Baudh2.5.10.1. Now, these are the five great sacrifices; they indeed are the great sacrificial sessions (*mahāsattras*): the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to Brahman.
Day after day, he should offer with "svāhā" until the fuel is exhausted; in this way, he completes this sacrifice to the gods.
Day by day, he should offer the *svadhā* oblation up to the water-vessel; in this way, he completes this Pitṛyajña.
Day by day he should offer salutations up to the flowers; in this way, he completes this sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*).
Day after day, one should give food to Brahmins, including roots, fruits, and vegetables; in this way, one completes this sacrifice to men (*manuṣyayajña*).
Day by day, one should perform the private recitation of the Veda up to the syllable *praṇava*; in this way, one completes this sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*).

The private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is indeed the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). Of this very sacrifice to Brahman, speech is the *juhū* ladle, the mind is the *upabhṛt*, the eye is the *dhruvā*, wisdom is the *sruva* spoon, truth is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and the heavenly world is the conclusion.

"Those who perform these [rites], with them we are; having become dust, we shall perish while praising something else.
Thus [it is said]: "perishing while praising something else."
Now we shall explain the oblations to the vital breaths for the Śālīnas and Yāyāvaras who sacrifice in themselves.

At the conclusion of all necessary duties, having sat down facing east in a place that has been swept and smeared with cow-dung, and having offered reverence with the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar om" as that [food] is being brought, he should restrain his speech.

Having sprinkled water clockwise around the placed food with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, while not releasing the water from his left hand, he says, "Thou art the spreading of ambrosia. Having first drunk water, he offers five oblations of food to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with the formula: "Seated in the out-breath (*prāṇa*), I offer ambrosia; may it enter me auspiciously for the sake of non-burning. Svāhā to the out-breath! Seated in the in-breath (*apāna*), I offer ambrosia; may it enter me auspiciously for the sake of non-burning. Svāhā to the in-breath! Seated in the diffused breath (*vyāna*), I offer ambrosia..."

"May the auspicious one enter me for the sake of non-burning; svāhā to the vyāna! Seated in the udāna, I offer the nectar; may the auspicious one enter me for the sake of non-burning; svāhā to the udāna! Seated in the samāna, I offer the nectar; may the auspicious one enter me for the sake of non-burning; svāhā to the samāna! Having offered these five oblations of breath with food, he should further observe the vow in silence, meditating on Prajāpati in his mind, and must not release speech in the interval.
If he should release his speech in the interval, having murmured "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar om," he should eat again.

Having seen skin, hair, nails, insects, or mouse-droppings [in the sacrificial ground], one should remove that spot, sprinkle it with water, scatter ashes over it, sprinkle it again with water, and then use it after it has been verbally consecrated as pure.
Now, they also cite this:

"Sitting down, facing the east, with speech restrained and not disparaging the food, one should eat without letting it fall and with a focused mind; having eaten, one should touch fire and perform the ritual sipping of water."
One should not bite with the teeth any edible food, cakes, bulbs, roots, fruits, or meats.
One should not eat to the point of excessive satiety.

With the mantra, "Thou art the covering of immortality," having drunk water from above and sipped it, he touches the region of his heart with the mantra: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; enter me as Rudra, the end-maker; through this food, may I swell."
Having sipped water again, he pours [the remainder] over his right big toe with both hands:
"A person the size of a thumb dwells within the thumb;
the Lord of the entire world, the Master, the consumer of all, is pleased."

With hands raised, he should perform the consecration of the oblation (*huta-anumantraṇa*): "Entering into faith (*śraddhā*) and the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the immortal oblation has been offered; cause the out-breath to swell with food. Entering into faith and the in-breath (*apāna*), the immortal oblation has been offered; cause the out-breath to swell with food. Entering into faith and the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the immortal oblation has been offered; cause the out-breath to swell with food. Entering into faith and the upward breath (*udāna*), the immortal oblation has been offered; cause the out-breath to swell with food. Entering into faith and the pervasive breath (*samāna*), the immortal..."
"Homage! Satisfy my breath with food"—with these five [verses].
"May my self be in Brahman for the sake of immortality"—[with this verse he offers] himself.
And one should unite oneself with the syllable.
Among those who perform all sacrifices, the self-sacrificer is distinguished.
Now they also quote:
For just as a tuft of reed-wool, when cast into a fire, is consumed by flame,
even so are all the sins of one who sacrifices to the Self burnt away.
"He who eats alone becomes one whose merit is consumed by others; the foolish man gains food in vain" (RV 10.117.6).
In this very manner, he should offer oblations every day, both evening and morning.
Or with water at evening.
Now they also cite [the following]:
"First, one should feed the guests; immediately thereafter, those who are pregnant; likewise the children, the elderly, the destitute, and especially the sick."
But he who eats before giving to these [deities] according to the rule—eating while remaining unaware—he does not truly eat; rather, he is eaten.
"Restraining his speech, he should eat the remains of the food after [satisfying] the ancestors, the deities, his dependents, as well as his mother, father, and teacher; thus is the dharma ordained."
Now they also cite:
"An ascetic (*muni*) should consume eight morsels, a forest-dweller sixteen,
a householder thirty-two, and for a student (*brahmacārin*), there is no limit."
"One who has established the sacred fires, an ox, and a student of sacred knowledge—these three succeed only while eating;
there is no success for them if they do not eat."
Whether he be a householder or a student, if one practices austerity while fasting,
he becomes an *avakīrṇin* through the omission of the *prāṇāgnihotra*.
Except in the case of a penance; in the case of a penance, that same rule applies.
Now they also cite this:
"He who never eats anything between his morning meal and his evening meal is, in that very way, always fasting."
One should recite the mantras of the Prāṇāgnihotra when food is withheld;
and one should recite the mantras of the Tretāgnihotra when sacrificial materials are unavailable. Thus it is said.
Practicing in this manner, one is fit for becoming Brahman; one is fit for becoming Brahman.
It pertains to the ancestors, bestows long life, leads to heaven, brings fame, and is a rite for prosperity.

One who knows the *trimadhu*, one who knows the *triṇāciketa*, one who knows the *trisuparṇa*, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, one who knows the *śīrṣaka*, one who chants the *jyeṣṭhasāman*, and a *snātaka*—these are the purifiers of an assembly (*paṅktipāvanas*).
In his absence, one who knows the secret [teachings].
The greatness of the Śrāddha consists of the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants; therefore, one should feed even a relative who knows this.

One should cause [the deceased] to hear, while laying them down gently, the *Sāmans* that slay Rākṣasas, the *Yajus* formulas containing the word *svadhā*, the *Ṛks* concerning honey, and the purificatory verses.

Having invited on the previous day, or indeed in the morning itself, men who are of good conduct, learned in the Vedas, not related by birth, lineage, or mantra, pure, conversant with the sacred texts, at least three in number, and an odd number, he causes them to sit facing either east or north upon seats prepared with Darbha grass.

Then, having caused them to accept water mixed with sesame seeds and having adorned them with perfumes and garlands, he says, "I shall perform the offering in the fire. Being permitted, he kindles the fire, strews grass around it, and having performed the rites up to the *agnimukha*, he offers three oblations of food—[according to K: of clarified butter]—into the fire, saying: "To Soma, drunk by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā!* To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*!
Adoration! *Svāhā!* To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, *svadhā*!
Adoration! *Svāhā!*!"
Having sprinkled the food with the remainder of that [ghee], he should offer these same three oblations of the food.
One should give a ball of food to the birds.
"For the ancestors move about in the likeness of birds," so it is known from scripture.
Then he touches the other [parts] with his hand together with the thumb.

"Of thee who art equal to the earth, Agni is the overseer; the Ṛg-verses are thy greatness, for the non-neglect of what has been given. "That which is given without the thumb, that which is accepted [without the thumb], and he who sips water while standing—by none of these is he made prosperous. Thus it is said.

"His fathers are in front, his grandfathers on the left, his great-grandfathers on the right, and the scrapers for the rice-balls behind. Thus it is said.

having been released from them, the self-possessed man becomes liberated from doubt regarding dharma.
Having honored the seers through the private study of the Vedas, Indra through the Soma sacrifice,
and his ancestors through progeny, he becomes free from debt and rejoices in heaven.
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a grandson, one ascends to the very heavens. Thus it is said.

And it is known from scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born with three debts—to the sages through studentship, to the gods through sacrifice, and to the ancestors through progeny. Thus the Veda demonstrates this connection with debt. (Cf.
BaudhŚS 2.6.11.33) By procreating a virtuous son, one delivers oneself.
One who obtains a virtuous son delivers seven descendants, seven ancestors, six others, and himself as the seventh—from sin and from fear.
Therefore, by producing offspring, one obtains the fruit.
Therefore, one should diligently procreate offspring.
By means of the connection with the mantra for the vegetable oblation.
