Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he prepares [the following items].
The sacrificial staffs, the sling, the water-strainer, the water-pot, and the vessel.

Having taken this [mixture]—clarified butter, milk, and curd—at the edge of the village, at the boundary of the village, or in the fire-hall, he should consume it as a threefold fast-food and then observe the fast.
Or water.

"Oṃ bhūḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *tat savitur vareṇyam*. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *bhargo devasya dhīmahi*. Oṃ suvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*. Thus [he recites] by quarters (*pacchaḥ*), by half-verses (*ardharcaśaḥ*), and then with the whole verse both separately and combined.
It is known from tradition that by leading oneself from one stage of life (*āśrama*) to another, one becomes purified by Brahman.
Now they also cite this:

"Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations and conquered his senses, and being exhausted by begging for alms and making offerings, he finally becomes a mendicant. Thus it is said.
This very mendicant leads to infinity.

Before the setting of the sun, having added fuel to the *gārhapatya* fire, having brought the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and having drawn out the flaming *āhavanīya* fire, he melts clarified butter over the *gārhapatya*, purifies it, takes four spoonfuls into the *sruc* ladle, and offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* which has a fuel-stick placed upon it, saying: "Oṃ svāhā!"
"This is known as the Brahmānvādhāna."

Then, after the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, having strewn grass to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, having placed the vessels upon it in pairs with their openings facing downwards, and having strewn *darbha* grass in the seat of the *brahmán* to the south of the *āhavanīya* fire and spread a black antelope skin over them, he remains awake for this night.
A Brahmin who, knowing this, fasts through the Brahma-rātri, consigns his sacred fires, and dies, overcomes all evil; he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin.
Then, having risen during the *brāhma* muhūrta, he performs the morning *agnihotra* at the very proper time.
Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. That well-known sacrifice is completed.
He throws the Agnihotra vessels—those not made of clay and not made of stone—into the Āhavanīya fire.
At the Gārhapatya fire, he places the two kindling woods [with the mantra]: "May you two be of one mind toward us."
He deposits the fires within himself. With the verse, "That body of yours, O Agni, which is fit for sacrifice," he smells each fire three times.
Then, standing within the altar-ground, having recited three times in a low voice—"Om bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, renounced by me, renounced by me, renounced by me"—he recites it three times aloud.
"For the gods are indeed threefold in truth," so it is known.
And with the words, "Fearlessness to all beings from me," he pours out a full handful of water.
Now they also cite this:
"The sage who wanders about after having granted fearlessness to all beings—no fear arises for him from any being in this world. Thus it is said.
He remains restrained in speech.
"O friend, protect me," he says, as he takes up the staff.
With the words, "That which is beyond this region," he takes up the sling.
With the verse, "By that purifier with which the gods... he takes the water-purifier.
With the mantra, "By that light with which the gods rose upwards," he takes up the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
With the seven vyāhṛtis, he takes up the vessel.

Having taken up the staff, the sling, the water-strainer, the water-pot, and the bowl, he goes to where there is water. Having bathed, sipped water, and purified himself with the *surabhimatī*, the *abliṅga*, the *vāruṇī*, the *hiraṇyavarṇā*, and the *pāvamānī* verses, he enters the water and performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Emerging from the water, wringing out his garment, and putting on another clean garment, he sips water and says:
"Oṃ bhūḥ."

Saying "Bhuvaḥ Suvar," and taking up the water-strainer (*jala-pavitra*), he performs the libation (*tarpaṇa*): "Oṃ Bhuḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ Bhuvaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ Suvaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ Mahas, I satisfy; Oṃ Janas, I satisfy; Oṃ Tapas, I satisfy; Oṃ Satyam, I satisfy."
Having offered a handful of water to the ancestors as he did for the gods, [he says]: "Oṃ bhūḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhuvaḥ svadhā; Oṃ suvaḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar mahar namaḥ."
Then, with the two verses "Upwards that [sun]" and "The bright," he worships the Āditya.

"Om"—this is Brahman. Indeed, he who shines yonder is the light, he is the Veda; he who shines yonder is the light, he is the Veda. That which shines yonder is indeed that which is to be known (*vedya*). In this very way, he satisfies himself; he pays homage to the Self. The Self is Brahman, the Self is the light.
One should repeat the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or one hundred times, or an unlimited number of times.
Saying "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," he takes the water-purifier and draws up the water.
From this point forward, one should not sip water that has not been drawn out, nor that which is unstrained, nor that which is unpurified.
And from this point forward, he shall not wear a white garment.
He may carry either a single staff or three staffs.
Now, these are the observances: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, the avoidance of sexual intercourse, and renunciation—thus indeed.
There are exactly five minor observances (*upavrata*): freedom from anger, service to the teacher, vigilance, purity, and purity of food.
Now follows the practice of begging for alms: he should seek alms from Brāhmaṇas who are householders or wandering mendicants, after the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has been completed.
One should cause [the cow] to move forward with the word "bhavati" at the beginning.
He should wait for the duration of milking a cow.

Then, having returned from the practice of begging for alms, having washed his hands and feet in a clean place, he should offer [the food] first to the Sun with the hymns "ud u tyam" and "citram. He offers it to the Brahman with the hymn "brahma jajñānam."

It is known from scripture: "From the time of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) onwards, the fires belong to the sacrificer himself. His out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the Gārhapatya; his in-breath (*apāna*) is the Anvāhāryapacana; his diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the Āhavanīya; his up-breath (*udāna*) and equalizing breath (*samāna*) are the Sabhya and Āvasathya. These five fires are established within the self; he offers oblations into the self alone."
This very sacrifice of the self, centered on the self and established in the self, leads the self to security; so it is known.
Having first shown compassion toward all living beings, he should distribute [the food] among them; then, having touched the remainder with water, he should eat it like medicine.

Having consumed [the remainder] and sipped water, he worships the sun with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse, "Out of darkness we have risen... (*ud vayaṃ tamasas pari*). Having murmured, "May speech be in my mouth; may breath be in my nostrils" (*vāṅ ma āsan nasoḥ prāṇaḥ*), [he continues].
"Unasked for, unprepared, obtained by chance—let him eat only such food as is sufficient for sustenance, solely for the maintenance of life. Thus [it is said].
Now they also cite:
"An ascetic should eat eight morsels, a forest-dweller sixteen,
a householder thirty-two, and for a student there is no limit."
"Or he may beg for alms from members of all castes, or [receive] food from a single meal among the twice-born;
or again, he may beg from members of all castes, provided it is not from a single meal among the twice-born. Thus it is said.
Now, regarding that which the teachers declare as the Upaniṣad, they cite this:

for one who is engaged in the vow at the fourth, sixth, and eighth periods of the day—consisting of standing, silence, the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*), touching water at the *savana* libations—the observance consists of eating only grains, oil-cake, barley-gruel, curd, and milk.

In that regard, one who is engaged in silence should, with his teeth joined to his teeth, speak only as much as necessary while facing inward, even when addressed by teachers, sages, elders learned in the three Vedas, or others belonging to the various stages of life who are deeply versed in scripture; he should not speak with women, nor where the loss of silence would occur—so it is traditionally taught.
One should practice by employing any one of these: standing, silence, or the hero's posture; one should not combine all three.
It is traditionally taught that wherever one has gone, one should observe the vow for as long as it takes, so that there is no omission of the vow even in times of distress.

For one who is engaged in the vow consisting of standing, silence, the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*), ritual ablutions at the three daily libations (*savana*), and eating at the fourth, sixth, or eighth meal-time: there are eight things that do not break the vow—water, roots, ghee, milk, sacrificial food (*havis*), what is desired by a Brahmin, the word of a teacher, and medicine.
One should mutter the mantras of the evening and morning Agnihotra.
Having performed the evening twilight worship with the Vāruṇī verses and the morning twilight worship with the Maitrī verses.

"Without fire, without a dwelling, without shelter, and without refuge, the sage should seek the village only for the sake of alms; otherwise, he should let his speech flow toward the private recitation of the Veda."

And it is known: "The *ṛc*s are indeed limited, the *sāmans* are limited, and the *yajus* formulas are limited; but there is no end to this which is the *brahman*. One should explain that to the one who responds; that is the *pratigara*."
In this very manner, until the liberation from the body, he who has renounced the Vedas remains a root-dweller at the foot of a tree.
The Veda is a tree; its root is the *praṇava*. The Veda has the *praṇava* as its essence.
"Meditating upon the *praṇava*, one who possesses the *praṇava* becomes fit for becoming Brahman," so indeed said Prajāpati.
One should wash the vessel for the Brahman with the seven vyāhṛtis. (Thus it is said. One should wash it. (Thus it is said.)
Now, regarding those who desire to follow the dharma of the *śālīna*, *yāyāvara*, and *cakracara* [householders], and who subsist by means of nine modes of livelihood:
Their livelihood is said to consist of following that [prescribed] course of conduct.
Because it takes its refuge in the hall (śālā), it is called "shālīna" (modest).
Because he proceeds by means of a chosen mode of livelihood, he is called a Yāyāvara.
Because they move in succession, they are called "wheel-movers" (*cakracara*).
We shall explain them in detail.

The six types of cultivation are: *ṣaṇṇivartanī*, *kauddālī*, *dhruvā*, *saṃprakṣālanī*, *samūhā*, and *phālanī*; and the three types of gathering are: *śiloñchā*, *kāpotā*, and *siddhecchā*—these are the nine.
Or rather, there is yet another tenth occurrence (or increase) of those very same [verses].
Until the completion of nine turns.
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he prepares [the following items].
A black antelope skin, a water-pot, a staff, a shoulder-pack, and a woolen blanket.
Having performed the Traidhātavīya sacrifice, he shall set forth, or [he shall do so] with the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice.

Then, in the morning when the sun has risen, having kindled the fires according to the sūtra, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, having purified it, having heated and wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons, and having taken four portions of butter into the *sruk*, he offers the Vāstoṣpatīya oblation in the Āhavanīya fire.

Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), "O Lord of the Dwelling (*vāstoṣpati*), recognize us," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "O Lord of the Dwelling, with your auspicious assembly..."
Some say that everyone indeed is one who has established the sacred fires.
According to some, he is a Yāyāvara.
Having gone out, he stays at the edge of the village or at the boundary of the village; there he either constructs a hut or a monastery, or enters one already built.

Regarding the black antelope skin and other items that have been prepared, one should employ each for its specific purpose and according to its intended function, in whatever manner is required for that particular object.

The attendance upon the fires is well known; the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is well known; the practice of the five great sacrifices is well known; and the threshing of the produced grains is seen [to be established].
Having prepared them—either with the formula "I pour out what is pleasing to the Viśve Devas" or silently—he cooks them.
For him, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and accepting gifts [are suspended], as are other sacrificial rites.
And it is seen that the sacrificial food intended for the undertaking of the vow is [to be used].
That is to say: mixed with clarified butter, mixed with curd, free from alkaline substances and salt, without meat, and not stale.
He observes celibacy, or he approaches his wife during her season.
At every change of the moon (parvan), one should shave the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails, and perform the rules for purification.
Now they also cite this:
"It is heard that purity is of two kinds, which has been practiced by the learned:
external purity, which is free from stains and odors; and internal purity, which is non-violent."
"The limbs are purified by water; the intellect is purified by knowledge;
the self of living beings is purified by non-violence; and the mind is purified by truth. Thus it is said.
As for this [sacrifice] called the Ṣaṇnivartanī.
He makes exactly six undamaged turns; he either leaves the share for the owner or takes it with the owner's permission.
Before the morning meal, he should plow while his nose is unsewn and his testicles are unretracted, not scratching with a goad but repeatedly encouraging the animal.
By this procedure, he performs six turns; thus it is called the *ṣaṇṇivartanī* (six-turn rite).

Regarding the *kauddālī* [method]: near a body of water, one digs with a spade, a plowshare, or a sharp piece of wood; one sows seeds and produces bulbs, roots, fruits, vegetables, and medicinal herbs.
The Kauddālī [sacrifice] is so called because it is performed with a spade (*kuddāla*).

While proceeding with the *dhruvā* vessel, he wraps his head with a white cloth, saying: "For prosperity, I wrap your head. He takes a black antelope skin, saying: "You are spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); for spiritual luster, you! He takes the strainer with verses addressed to the waters (*ap-liṅga*). He takes a water-pot, saying: "You are strength; for strength, you! He takes a shoulder-yoke, saying: "You are grain; for nourishment, you! He takes a staff, saying: "O friend, protect me!"
Then, having gone out and muttered the *vyāhṛtis*, he mutters the consecration of the quarters:
"May the Earth, the intermediate space, the Sky, the stars, and the quarters;
may Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya—may these deities protect me on the path. Thus.

Having recited the *mānastokīya* hymn and entered the village, he is called "the one who is visible" (*saṃdarśinī*) because he makes himself visible at every house door along with his carrying-pole (*vīvadha*).

Because it is used again and again until no further use remains, and because the ritual proceeds with that very same [ladle] as its constant basis, it is proclaimed as the "dhruvā" (the constant one).

Regarding the term *saṃprakṣālanī*: it refers to the throwing away of herbs that have already grown; there is no setting them aside or piling them up. Having thoroughly washed the vessels, one turns them face down; thus it is called *saṃprakṣālanī*.

"Baudh3.2.12: 'The Samūha' [means]: wherever herbs are found—in unobstructed places, on paths, in fields, or in open spaces—having gathered them by means of the *samūhana* method, one subsists with them; thus it is called *samūha*."

"Phālanī" means "non-harming"; this is what is being said. She desires husked rice grains or seeds from virtuous people; because she protects (*phālayati*) them, she is called *phālanī* (or *pālanī*).

*Śiloñchā*: This refers to subsisting by means of *śila* and *uñcha*. In places where grain is not prohibited—whether on paths, in fields, or in open spaces where there is no obstruction—one gathers a single ear of grain (*kaṇiśa*) wherever herbs are found; thus, maintaining oneself from time to time by means of such ears is called *śiloñchā*.

Regarding the *kāpotā* (pigeon-like) mode of subsistence: in unobstructed places, on paths, in fields, or wherever there is open space where herbs are found, one gathers a single herb at each spot by pinching it between the fingers; because this is done like a pigeon (*kapota*) through such "pinching" (*saṃdaṃśana*), it is called *kāpotā*.

"Siddhecchā" means one who desires prepared food. It refers to one who, being exhausted by various occupations, or due to old age or the depletion of bodily constituents (*dhātu*), desires food that has already been prepared by others. This is "siddhecchā."

The internal depositing of that [fire] within oneself occurs as it does for one who has renounced the world (saṃnyāsin), with the exception of the ritual strainer (pavitra) and the saffron-colored garment.

Or else, she subsists on forest-grown items—namely, trees, creepers, climbing plants, and herbs, including grasses and wild grains such as *śyāmāka* and *jartila*; thus, because she subsists by means of forest-grown things, she is called "Vānyā."
Now they also cite [this]: "Moving about with wild animals, dwelling together with them,
and behaving in a manner similar to them— this is the manifest characteristic of heaven."
"The characteristic of heaven is perceptible. [Baudh3.2.19 = Baudh3.3.22] Now, there is a twofold division of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). [K: of the forest-dweller] Baudh3.3.1.
"Those who cook and those who do not cook."

In that regard, there are five kinds of those who cook for themselves: those who live entirely in the forest, those who remove the husks from grain, those who eat roots and tubers, those who eat fruits, and those who eat vegetables.

In that regard, those known as the Sarvāraṇyakas are of two kinds; they resort to two types of wilderness: those who are "sprinkled by Indra" (indrāvasikta) and those who are "sprinkled with semen" (retovasikta).

In that regard, having brought the plants known as *indrāvasiktā*—consisting of creepers, shrubs, climbing plants, and trees—and having cooked them, one should offer the evening and morning *agnihotra* oblations, give portions to guests and those observing vows, and then consume the remaining portions.

Regarding the meat called *retovasikta*—that which has been killed by a tiger, a wolf, a hawk, or any other such creature—one should bring it, cook it, offer the morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations, give portions to the ascetics, guests, and those observing vows, and then the rest is for the consumption of the leftovers.

The *vaituṣikas*, however, having brought rice grains—excluding those with husks—and having cooked them, having offered the evening and morning *agnihotra* oblations, and having given [portions] to the ascetics, guests, and those observing vows, they then consume the remaining portions.
The same applies even for those who subsist on bulbs, roots, fruits, and vegetables.

There are exactly five types of those who subsist by emerging from water: those who eat what is already offered, those who take food with their mouths, those who do not take it with their hands, those who subsist on water, and those who subsist on air.
In that regard, those called "emergers" (unmajjakas) are exempt from the labor involving metal and stone.
Taking it with the hand, they consume it while moving forward.
Those who take with their mouths take from the mouth.
Baudhāyana 3.3.13: "Subsisting on water" means subsisting solely on water.
They subsist on air and remain without food.
Thus, according to the Vaikhānasas, ten initiation rites (dīkṣās) are prescribed.
He who, having undertaken his own teaching, [maintains] punishment, silence, and vigilance;
The Vaikhānasas are purified by fasting, it is said.
The acceptance of the Śāstra applies to all Brahmins and Vaikhānasas.
One should not harm gadflies or mosquitoes; such a person becomes like the Himalaya, a true ascetic.
Established in the forest, contented, and fond of rags, skins, and water, he is a forest-dweller.
One should first honor guests who have arrived at one's hermitage at the proper time;
likewise, the ascetic should be devoted to the gods, Brahmins, the sacred fires, and austerity.
On that day, he should adopt a difficult mode of life that cannot be maintained by others, one shared with wild animals and birds,
involving provisions gathered from people and consisting of astringent and bitter foods.
Having adopted this auspicious way of life, which is avoided by the wicked,
and having resorted to dwelling in the forest, a Brāhmaṇa does not come to grief.
Moving together with wild animals, dwelling with them alone, and conducting one's life in a manner identical to theirs— this is the manifest characteristic of heaven.
"The characteristic of heaven is directly perceived.

[BaudhŚS 3.3.22 = BaudhŚS 3.2.19] BaudhŚS 3.4.1: Now, if a religious student (*brahmacārin*) should act as if contrary to his vow—whether he should eat meat, or approach a woman, or [be afflicted] by any kind of calamity whatsoever—[he must perform the following].

Baudh3.4.2: Having established the fire within the inner chamber, having strewn grass around it, and having performed the rites up to the *āgnimukha* (cf. Baudh2.8.14.7), he then offers oblations of clarified butter: "That which was done by desire, desire performs; for desire alone is all this. To him who makes me do it, svāhā! That which was done by the mind, the mind performs; for the mind alone is all this. To him who makes me do it, svāhā!
That which was done by passion (*rajas*), passion performs; for passion alone is all this. To him who makes me do it..."

Svāhā! Darkness created by darkness [creates darkness]; to him who makes me do this—this entire [darkness] belonging to darkness—svāhā! Evil created by evil [creates evil]; to him who makes me do this—this entire [evil] belonging to evil—svāhā! Wrath created by wrath [creates wrath]; to him who makes me do this—this entire [wrath] belonging to wrath—svāhā! Thus.
The ritual from the *jaya* offerings onwards is established up to the giving of the choice cow (*dhenu-vara*).
To the west of the fire, having covered himself with a black antelope skin with its neck pointing eastward and the hairy side upward, he remains there.

When it has dawned, having drawn himself away from the rear half [of the sacrificial ground], having gone to a bathing place, bathed according to the established rite, and while standing within the water, having performed sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, and having performed the established worship of the sun (*ādityopasthāna*), he goes to the house of his teacher.
One should understand this to be exactly like the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Aghamarṣaṇa, which is the purifier of purifiers.

Having gone to a sacred bathing place, bathed, and dressed in clean garments, he should, at the edge of the water, clear a sacrificial mound and, with a garment moistened once and his hand filled once, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa as a private Vedic study while facing the sun.
One hundred [cows] in the morning, one hundred at midday, one hundred in the afternoon, or an unlimited number.
When the stars have risen, he should consume a handful of barley-gruel.

One is released from minor offenses committed intentionally or unintentionally after seven nights, except for the killing of an embryo, violating the teacher's bed, stealing gold, and drinking liquor, which require twelve nights.
After the twenty-one-night rite, he crosses over those [obstacles] as well; he conquers them as well.

"He crosses over everything, he conquers everything, he obtains the fruit of all sacrifices; he becomes as one who has bathed in all sacred fords, one who has fulfilled his vows in all the Vedas, and one known by all the gods; he purifies his lineage back to the eye of sight, and his ritual acts are perfected," so says Baudhāyana.
Now, if one should regard oneself as a guru due to the religious acts performed by oneself, one should cook a *prasṛti* measure of barley-gruel for one's own sake when the stars have risen.
He should not offer [an oblation] into the fire from that [ladle].
And there is no offering of oblations (bali-karman) here.
He should consecrate with the mantra the uncooked, the being-cooked, and the cooked [oblation].
"You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey.
You are the cleanser of all sins, declared by the seers to be a means of purification."
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, and barley is water, the nectar of immortality;
purify all my evil, whatever misdeed has been committed by me.
The action performed by speech, the evil thought conceived by the mind—
O barley grains, purify all that for me, including misfortune and Kālakarṇī.
O barley grains, purify for me all that which has been trodden upon by dogs or pigs, that which is defiled by the leavings of crows, and the failure to serve one’s mother and father.
O barley grains, purify me from all heinous crimes involving mortal sins, from terrible offenses against the king, from the misconduct of children and the aged, and from every unrighteousness.
Stealing gold, violating one's vows, officiating at the sacrifice of one for whom it is forbidden, and reviling Brahmins— O barley grains, purify all of these for me!

"The food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a funeral rite or a period of birth-impurity, the food of a thief, and food from a recent funeral—purify all these, O ye who drink Soma! Thus it is said.

While the oblation is being cooked, he should perform the protection rite (*rakṣā*) with the following: "Homage to Rudra, the lord of beings! The sky is pacified! with this *anuvāka* beginning "Make wide your stride like a net" (*kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitiṃ na pṛthvīm*); with the five sections beginning "The gods who dwell in the east, led by Agni, slayers of the Rakṣas"; with "Do not harm us in our offspring" (*mā nas toke*); and with the two verses beginning "The Brahman among the gods" (*brahmā devānām*).
Having poured it into a vessel, he should eat the cooked food while it is still warm, being pure and restrained.

"O gods who are born of the mind, yoked by the mind, highly skillful, sons of Dakṣa—may they protect us, may they favor us; homage to them, svāhā to them!"—with these words, he should offer the oblation into himself.
One who desires sacrificial food (medhas) should perform this for three nights.
Having drunk [the mixture] for six nights, even a doer of evil becomes pure.
Having drunk [the mixture] for seven nights, one purifies oneself from killing a learned Brāhmaṇa (*bhrūṇahatyā*), violating the teacher's bed, stealing gold, and drinking liquor.
By drinking [the soma] for eleven nights, one casts off even the sin committed by one's ancestors.

"Or else, having drunk barley-gruel from grains that have emerged from cows for twenty-one nights, one sees the Gaṇas, one sees the leader of the Gaṇas, one sees Knowledge, and one sees the Lord of Knowledge—so said the venerable Baudhāyana."
One who considers himself as if unpurified should offer oblations with the *kūśmāṇḍa* verses.
As a thief, as a killer of an embryo—even so does he become who sheds semen in a place that is not the womb.
"By this, one is released from whatever sin prior to the killing of an embryo."
Having emitted semen in a non-vaginal place, except during sleep or when it is unintentional, one who desires purification [should perform this].
On either the new moon day or the full moon day, having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he undertakes the vow according to the rule for a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
For a year, a month, twenty-four days, twelve nights, six, or three [nights].
He shall not eat meat, he shall not approach a woman, he shall not sit on elevated ground, and he shall loathe untruth.
"Subsisting on milk" is the first rule; or, consuming barley-gruel, he should either perform the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance or beg for alms.
In those cases prescribed for that [offering], a Rājanya should offer gruel (yavāgū) and a Vaiśya should offer curd-mixture (āmikṣā).

In the forenoon, having established the fire according to the ritual rules for the *pākayajña* and having strewn grass around it, and having performed the rites up to the *agnimukha*, he then offers oblations of clarified butter with these three sections: "O gods, whatever offense against the gods... and "Whatever debt I incurred while not gambling... and "Bestowing life upon you from every side."
He should offer portions of clarified butter with each verse (having offered them).

Having offered four spoonfuls with the verses, "In the lion, in the tiger, or in the viper," and having offered the four "returning" oblations with the verses, "O Agni, thou who returnest," "O Agni Aṅgiras," "With strength again," and "Together with wealth," the sacrificer, standing in the world of men with fuel-sticks in hand, worships with the twelve-verse hymn beginning, "We announce [this] unto Vaiśvānara."

"Whatever sin has ever been committed by me through mind or speech—from all that, O Adorable One, deliver me; for you indeed know things as they truly are, svāhā! Having offered a piece of fuel-wood with this, he gives a boon.
The ritual from the *jaya* oblations onwards is established up to the giving of the choice cow (*dhenu-vara*).
There shall be only one attendant at the fire.

Now, regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*): with the verses, "Whatever offense against the gods," "When not gambling, I incurred a debt," and "Bestowing upon you life from every side," he offers full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Having offered the Agnihotra and being about to commence it, he offers with the Daśahotr formula; having offered the New and Full Moon sacrifices and being about to commence them, he offers with the Caturhotr formula; having offered the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and being about to commence them, he offers with the Pañcahotr formula; having offered at the animal sacrifice, he offers with the Ṣaḍḍhotr formula; having offered at the Soma sacrifice, he offers with the Saptahotr formula.
And it is known from scripture: "One should offer with these at the beginning of rituals; being purified, one attains the worlds of the gods"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should fast on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight.
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved—or at least his beard—he should, wearing an unwashed garment and speaking the truth, enter the place of residence.
In that [fire], his fire is either once-carried forward or produced by churning from the two kindling woods.
A student or a friend should be prepared to give the directions for the rite.
And the sacrificial food fit for consumption is that which is to be taken up as the vow-food.
Having kindled the fire, having strewn grass around it, and having performed the rites up to the offering to Agni, he makes an offering from the cooked food.

Baudhāyana 3.8.8: For Agni, whatever lunar day it may be; for the Nakṣatra together with its presiding deity; here he says, "They agreed upon the cow"—thus for the fifth [lunar day] belonging to the Moon; for Heaven and Earth the sixth; for Day and Night the seventh; for Rudra the eighth; for Sūrya the ninth; for Varuṇa the tenth; for Indra the eleventh; and for the Viśvedevas the twelfth.
Then they recite other [verses]: "And from the quarters together with their deities; for the broad intermediate space together with its deity."

Having offered the oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the verse, "He becomes ever new as he is born," he then draws out the remnants of this sacrificial food into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, pours over it non-sacrificial seasonings, and eats fifteen morsels in their natural state.

With "For breath, thee," he offers the first; with "For out-breath, thee," the second; with "For diffused breath, thee," the third; with "For up-breath, thee," the fourth; and with "For equalizing breath, thee," the fifth. When there are four [oblations], he offers the first two with two [formulas] each. When there are three, he offers the first two with two [formulas] each. When there are two, he offers the first with two [formulas] and the latter with three. One [oblation] is offered with all [the formulas].

"Ye are the *nigrābhyā* waters," he says. Having drunk the water, he then offers oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*), saying: "May my out-breath (*prāṇa*), in-breath (*apāna*), diffused breath (*vyāna*), up-breath (*udāna*), and middle breath (*samāna*) be purified. May I become light, free from passion (*virajas*), and free from evil, *svāhā*! May my speech and mind; my head, hands, skin, hide, and flesh; sound, touch, and form; earth, water, and fire;

and my self consisting of food (*annamaya*), the self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), the self consisting of mind (*manomaya*), the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), and the self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—may these be purified. Light..."
"May I be free from passion and free from evil, svāhā!"—with these seven sections, beginning with "consisting of food" and "consisting of vital breath."
The ritual from the *jaya* offerings onwards is established up until the giving of the cow and the choice of a boon.
He worships the Sun with verses addressed to Sūrya and the Moon with verses addressed to Candra.
"O Agni, do thou watch well," he mutters as he lies down.
"O Agni, you are the guardian of vows," [he says] upon waking.
One should not converse with women or Śūdras, nor should one look at urine or excrement.

Upon seeing something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; Sūrya is the best of lights; O consecration, do not abandon me. [K adds: Now, if it rains upon him, he says: "Wetting [the earth], bestow strength.
On the first day of the latter fortnight, there are fourteen mouthfuls.
In this manner, by omitting one [offering] at a time, [the sequence continues] until the new moon day.
On the new moon day, there is no morsel [of food].
Now, on the first day of the waxing fortnight there is one [offering], and two on the second.
In this manner, with an increase of one [offering] each day, it continues until the full moon.
On the full moon day, he offers of the *sthālīpāka* to Agni, to whichever lunar day (*tithi*) it may be, and to the constellations (*nakṣatra*) together with their presiding deities.
Having offered oblations to the six deities before the constellation Śroṇā and Abhijit, he should give a cow to the Brāhmaṇas.

This same Cāndrāyaṇa, when performed with the middle [day] being the shortest like an ant (*pipīlikā-madhya*), is the "ant-shaped" one; when performed in the reverse order, it is the "barley-shaped" (*yava-madhya*) one.
Having performed either one of these, the evildoer becomes purified from all sins.
"For every desire, this is to be brought forth," so they say.
Whatever desire one may have, that one attains by means of this [rite].

By this very means, the sages of old purified themselves and performed their rites. This [rite] is auspicious, meritorious, conducive to having sons and grandsons, beneficial for cattle, bestowing long life, leading to heaven, bringing fame, and fulfilling all desires.
He attains the splendor of the stars and union with, as well as residence in the same world as, the sun and the moon—whoever studies this, whoever studies this.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the recitation of the entire Veda while fasting.
He should wear clean garments, or else garments made of bark.
One should desire sacrificial food, water, or fruits.

Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of an ox-hide with cow-dung, having sprinkled it with water, having drawn the lines, and having sprinkled it again with water, he should kindle the fire, strew grass around it, and offer oblations to these deities: *Svāhā* to Agni; *Svāhā* to Prajāpati;
*Svāhā* to Soma; *Svāhā* to the Viśvedevas; *Svāhā* to Svayambhū; *Svāhā* to the Ṛg-verses; *Svāhā* to the Yajus-formulas.

He should recite [the Vedic hymns] for the Sāmans, the Atharvans, Faith, Wisdom, Intelligence, Prosperity, Modesty, Savitṛ, Sāvitrī, the Lord of the Assembly, and Anumati; and he should not pause in the middle.
BaudhŚS 3.9.5: Having offered the oblation, he should begin at the beginning of the Veda and recite it continuously.
BaudhŚS 3.9.6: He must not speak in between, nor should he pause in between. BaudhŚS 3.9.7:
If he should speak in between or pause in between, he shall restrain his breath three times and begin again from the very point where he left off.

In the event of a lack of inspiration, he should study that [text] for as long as it takes him not to know it; when he comes to know it—whether from the perspective of the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, or the Sāmaveda.
One should study that Brāhmaṇa, that Vedic text, and that pertaining to the deity.

One should study the twelve Vedic collections (*veda-saṃhitā*). Whatever one has studied during times unfit for study, whatever teachers have been provoked to anger, and whatever improper acts one has committed—one purifies oneself through these. His sacred knowledge (*brahman*) becomes pure and sanctified.
From this point forward, there is the accumulation [of the fires].
Having studied another twelve Vedic collections (*veda-saṃhitā*), one attains through them the world of Uśanas.
Having studied another twelve Vedic collections (*veda-saṃhitā*), one attains the world of Bṛhaspati by means of them.
Having studied another twelve Vedic collections (*veda-saṃhitā*), one attains the world of Prajāpati through them.
Without eating, he should study the *Saṃhitā* a thousand times; having become Brahman, free from passion, he becomes Brahman.
By practicing begging for alms for one year, he obtains divine vision.

For six months he subsists on barley-gruel; for four months he subsists on water and barley-meal; for two months he subsists on fruits; for one month he subsists on water; or, not eating at all for twelve nights, he quickly becomes purified. He purifies seven descendants, seven ancestors, and himself as the fifteenth; he also purifies the line of guests at his meal.
They call this very thing the "divine ladder" (*devaniśrayaṇī*).
By means of this, indeed, the gods attained godhood and the seers attained seerhood.
Indeed, for this very sacrifice, there are exactly three times for its commencement: at the morning pressing, at the midday pressing, or during the latter part of the night in the Brāhma pavamāna.
Prajāpati indeed taught this to the Seven Seers; the Seven Seers to Mahājajñu; and Mahājajñu to the Brāhmaṇas—yes, to the Brāhmaṇas.
The duty of the social classes and the duty of the stages of life have been explained.

Now, indeed, this person acts wrongly through an act that merely requires expiation, or he officiates at a sacrifice for one for whom one should not officiate, or he accepts a gift from one from whom gifts should not be accepted, or he eats the food of one whose food should not be eaten, or he behaves in a manner that should not be practiced.
Regarding this, they deliberate: "Should one perform an expiation, or should one not?"
"For action is never exhausted."
"One should indeed perform it."
It is known from tradition: "Having sacrificed with the Punastoma, they return to the Soma-pressing."
Now, they also cite this: "He who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha overcomes all evil; he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin."
"One who is being falsely accused should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut," so it is said.
Its means of expiation are: silent recitation, austerity, burnt offerings, fasting, and giving gifts.

The Upaniṣads, the beginnings of the Vedas, the Vedāntas, the Saṃhitās among all the meters, the Madhu-hymns, the Aghamarṣaṇa, the Atharvaśiras, the Rudras, the Puruṣasūkta, the Rājana and Rauhiṇa Sāmans, the Bṛhat and Rathantara, the Puruṣagati, the Mahānāmnīs, the Mahāvairāja, the Mahādivākīrtya, any one of the Jyeṣṭhasāmans, the Bahiṣpavamāna, the Kūśmāṇḍas, the Pāvamānīs, and the Sāvitrī—these are the purificatory texts.

According to the principle of the *upasad* rites, the following are purifying (*medhya*) practices: subsisting on milk, eating vegetables, eating fruits, eating roots, consuming a handful of barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), the consumption of gold, the consumption of clarified butter, and the drinking of *soma*.
All mountain peaks, all flowing rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords, the dwellings of seers, and cow-pens, fields, and sanctuaries—these are the regions.

Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, bathing at the three daily libations, service to the teacher, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, wearing a single garment, and fasting—these are the austerities.
Gold, a cow, a garment, a horse, land, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and food—these are the things to be given.
The time periods are: a year, six months, four, three, two, or one month; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, a day and night, and a single day.
These [rites] should be performed when there is no specific instruction.
In cases of heavy sins, the penances are heavy; in cases of light sins, they are light.
The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitti). This is the universal expiation.
We shall explain the expiations for various purposes, each separately,
according to their respective faults— both the heavy and the light.
For if something were appropriate here, he would have pointed it out right there;
likewise, among the more serious [offenses], they are repeated again and again, while for the lighter ones, they are fewer.
One should perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Whatever sin has been committed by the sexual organ, or that which has been committed by the feet,
by the arms, by the mind, by speech, or by the ear, skin, nose, and eyes— [all that is purified].
Alternatively, in the event of transgressions involving the eye, ear, skin, nose, or mind, one is purified by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).

In the case of eating the food of a Śūdra, sexual intercourse with a woman [of forbidden class], or eating [forbidden food] alone—each of these separately—one should perform seven breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) for seven days each.

In the case of consuming what is unfit to be eaten, drunk, licked, or chewed, as well as in the sale of forbidden goods—with the exception of honey, meat, ghee, oil, alkali, salt, and inferior food—and in whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) for each day of a twelve-day penance.

In cases other than the mortal sins (*pātaka*), the sins causing loss of caste (*patanīya*), and the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), as well as whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) for each half-month.

In cases other than those involving mortal sins (*pātaka*) or sins causing loss of caste (*patanīya*), and whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve *prāṇāyāmas* for each of the twelve days.
In cases other than mortal sins (*pātaka*), and for whatever else is similarly constituted, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) each for twelve half-months.
Now, regarding mortal sins (pātaka), one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for each year.
One should give a maiden who is still a *nagnikā* to a virtuous man who is a celibate student;
or, even to one lacking in virtues, but one should not let her remain until she reaches her menses.
He who does not give away a maiden who has reached puberty within three years undoubtedly incurs a guilt equal to that of killing an embryo.
If he does not beg [for alms], this is so; but if he begs, Manu has declared that there is a fault, a sin, in each and every season.
A woman who has reached puberty should wait for her father’s command for three years;
then, in the fourth year, she should find a suitable husband. If no suitable man is available, she may resort even to one lacking good qualities.

If a maiden has been carried off by force, provided she has not been consecrated with the sacred mantras, she may be given to another according to the prescribed rule; for such a girl remains exactly as a maiden.
If her husband dies after she has been given away in marriage, or even after the oblation has been offered,
provided she remains a virgin and returns from her [the husband's] home,
she deserves to undergo the sacramental rite again according to the ritual for a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*).
He who does not approach his wife when she is in her season for three years undoubtedly incurs a fault equal to that of killing an embryo.
But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him—
his ancestors lie within that menstrual flow for that entire month.
"He who does not approach his wife during her season, and he who approaches her outside her season— they both incur an equal fault, as does he who discharges semen into a place that is not the womb."
If a wife, by staying with her husband's [new] residence, should cause the loss of her menstrual period,
she shall be proclaimed as a "slayer of the embryo" in the midst of the village and driven out from the house.
If one does not approach a wife who has bathed after her menses— provided she is self-restrained and observes the dharma—
it is traditionally taught that for such a transgression of the rule, one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) must be performed.

Seated with purifying grass (*pavitra*) in his hand, one should practice the daily Veda (*brahma nityaka*), consisting of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), purificatory formulas (*pavitra*), the *vyāhṛtis*, and likewise the *praṇava*.
Always disciplined, one should repeatedly perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) again and again;
from the tips of the hair to the ends of the nails, one performs the highest austerity.
From suppression, wind is born; from wind, fire is born;
from heat, water is produced; thus, it is purified internally by these three.
Through yoga, knowledge is attained; yoga is the defining characteristic of dharma.
All virtues have their root in yoga; therefore, one should always be disciplined in yoga.
The three Vedas begin with the syllable *praṇava* and are established within the *praṇava*;
the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis* are indeed the eternal, primeval Brahman.
For one who is constantly engaged with the *praṇava*, the seven *vyāhṛtis*,
and the three-footed *gāyatrī*, no fear exists anywhere.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while holding the breath;
that is called prāṇāyāma.
Sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*,
purify even the slayer of a learned Brahmin within a month, provided they are performed day after day.
This is the foremost austerity; this is the defining characteristic of dharma. For the sake of destroying all defects, this alone is distinguished as supreme.
This very same [procedure] is distinguished [as follows].
We shall explain the expiations for various purposes, each separately,
according to their respective faults— both those that are heavy and those that are light.
For if something were appropriate here, he would have pointed it out right there;
likewise, among the more serious [offenses] he mentions them repeatedly, while among the lighter ones he mentions fewer.
One should prescribe the penances according to the procedure seen in the scriptures.
But one who is about to receive [a gift], or likewise one who has already received it,
should recite the four *taratsamandī* verses.
But for eating the food of any of those whose food is not to be eaten,
purification from the sin is performed by sprinkling with the *taratsamandī* verses.
But the rule for killing an embryo is different; I shall explain it hereafter, by which procedure people are liberated from even all sins whatsoever.
Restraining his breath, he should recite the purifiers, the vyāhṛtis, and likewise the praṇava;
being disciplined, he should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn with milk for twelve nights.
Or, for three nights, he may subsist on air alone, wearing wet clothes or remaining immersed in water, thereby becoming pure.
"Having repeatedly practiced even those behaviors that are forbidden, one is released from all sins by performing worship with the Vāruṇī verses. Thus [it is said].

Now, having established the fire at night on the new moon day, the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) performs the ritual service pertaining to wood-offerings (*dārvihomika*) and offers two oblations of clarified butter with the formulas: "O Kāma, I have been scattered; I have been scattered, O Kāma! To Kāma, svāhā! O Kāma, I have been deceived; I have been deceived, O Kāma! To Kāma, svāhā! [cf. Baudh2.1.1.34]

Having offered the oblation, with hands joined in reverence, he should worship the fire from the side with the formula: "May the Maruts sprinkle me; may Indra sprinkle me; may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me; may this Agni sprinkle me with long life and with strength; make me long-lived. Indeed, the Maruts bestow vital breaths upon him, Indra bestows strength, Bṛhaspati bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and Agni bestows everything else.
Having become whole in body, he becomes everything.
One should recite [the mantra] "Āyur" three times over [the water]; for it is known that "the gods are indeed true to their word thrice."
He who might consider himself as if unpurified by minor offenses (upapātaka),
having offered oblations according to this rule, is liberated from all sin.

Alternatively, after consuming food that is unfit to be eaten or drunk, or eating what is forbidden, or performing a blameworthy act—whether intentionally or unintentionally—or after discharging semen into a Śūdra woman or into a non-vaginal opening, one becomes pure by sipping water while reciting the *ābliṅgā* and *vāruṇī* verses.
Now, they also cite this: "In the case of eating what is unfit for consumption, drinking what is forbidden, consuming prohibited food, or performing actions contrary to dharma—
even when such acts are committed intentionally— one is purified from those sins that resemble mortal transgressions (*pātaka*), as well as from all other sins."
Or, fasting for three nights and entering the water three times a day,
restraining his vital breaths within himself, he should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times;
Manu has declared that this is equal to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
And it is known from scripture:
"The ancient, wide-spread, purifying foot, by which one who is purified crosses over evil deeds—
by that pure, purifying [foot], being cleansed, may we cross over sin and hostility."
We shall explain the expiations for those who are concentrated and disciplined, specifically regarding those not previously mentioned, as to how they should be applied in cases of negligence.
Baudhāyana 4.3.2: One should sip water for purification from all sins with all the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ*.
When he sips water for the first time, by that he gratifies the Ṛgveda; when the second time, by that the Yajurveda; when the third time, by that the Sāmaveda.
That which he wipes first, by that [he purifies] the Atharvaveda; that which he wipes second, by that [he purifies] the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

When he sprinkles his left hand, and touches his feet, head, heart, nostrils, eyes, ears, and navel, by that he gratifies the plants, the trees, and all the deities. Therefore, from that very act of sipping water (ācamana), he is liberated from all evil.

Or he should offer eight fuel-sticks: "Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods; svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against men; svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the ancestors; svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against oneself; svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed by day and by night, thou art its expiation; svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed while sleeping or while waking, thou art its expiation; svāhā! For whatever [we have done] knowing..."
"And we, being ignorant, have committed sin; you are the expiation for that, svāhā! You are the expiation for every sin, svāhā! Thus [he says].
Having offered these eight oblations, one is liberated from all evil.
Now they also cite [the following]:
"The *aghamarṣaṇa*, the *devakṛta*, the *śuddhavatī*s,
the *taratsamandī*s, the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses, the *pāvamānī*s, the *virajā*s, and the *mṛtyulāṅgala*."
The Durgā verses, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Rudras are the destroyers of great evils.
"The destroyers of great faults."
We shall explain the expiations that have not been specifically mentioned in detail:
how should it be for those who are composed and disciplined when they commit lapses?
"Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca..."—by reciting this Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Reciting this verse—"This spotted cow has stepped forth"—three times while within the water, one is liberated from all evil.
Reciting this verse, "As if released from a wooden post," three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all evil.
Reciting this verse, "The swan seated in purity," three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Alternatively, by reciting the Sāvitrī verse—first quarter by quarter, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole verse—three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Alternatively, by reciting the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all evil.
Alternatively, by reciting the syllable Om (praṇava) three times while submerged within the water, one is liberated from all sin.
This treatise on Dharma should not be given to one who has no son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has not resided [as a student] for a year.
The sacrificial fee consists of a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh, or it may be the favor of the teacher; or it may be the favor of the teacher.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the rites by which one quickly attains the desires residing in the mind through the Sāman, Ṛc, Yajus, and Atharvan [Vedas].
Having purified one's own body through recitation, burnt offerings, sacrifices, yantras, and so forth, one should accomplish all rites; otherwise, one does not attain success.
A twice-born man, intending to perform recitations, burnt offerings, sacrifices, or mechanical rites,
should first have his hair and beard shaved on days of the bright fortnight, on auspicious days, and under favorable lunar mansions.
He should bathe at the three daily libations; he should protect himself from anger and falsehood;
he should not converse with women or Śūdras; thus does the student, observing the vow of the sacrificial oblation, remain chaste.
One should pay homage to cows, Brahmins, ancestors, and gods while not sleeping during the day;
remaining engaged in recitation, burnt offerings, sacrifices, and ritual diagrams, one should stand during the day and sit at night.

The Prājāpatya penance consists of eating only what is obtained by begging during the day for three days, and during the night for three days; then, for three days each, one subsists on food obtained in order [from the houses of the four castes] and finally on air, for twelve days in total, with each stage lasting three days.
One day [of eating], likewise one night, and subsisting on air for one day—
this threefold cycle, when repeated, is called the Kṛcchra penance for children.
One should eat a single morsel each day for three days each, as previously described;
then for another three days one should subsist on air alone—this is called the *atikṛcchra* penance.
Subsisting on water for these three days, and thereafter subsisting on air, this third penance is known as the *Atikṛcchra*; it is exceedingly purifying.
For three days each, one should drink hot milk, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass;
for another three days, one should subsist on air alone—this is called the *taptakṛcchra*.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with fasting for one night, is known as the *sāṃtapana-kṛcchra*.
Having taken cow’s urine with the *gāyatrī* verse, he takes cow dung with the verse "O you who have fragrance as your door" (*gandhadvārā*);

milk with the verse "May you swell" (*ā pyāyasva*); curd with the verse "O Dadhikrāvan" (*dadhikrāvṇas*); clarified butter with the verse "You are the bright, you are the light" (*śukram asi jyotiḥ*); and *kuśa*-water with the verse "By the impulse of the god" (*devasya tvā*).
One part of cow’s urine, half as much of dung, three parts of milk,
two parts of curd, one part of ghee, and one part of *kuśa* water—
this is the *sāṃtapana* penance, which purifies even a dog-eater.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter—
by subsisting on these five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for five nights, one is purified.
When one who is vigilant abstains from food for twelve days,
this penance called Parāka destroys all sins.
The exponents of the Veda declare that practicing each of these [penances] twenty-one times with cow urine and the other substances constitutes the Mahāsāṃtapana Kṛcchra.
"In the bright fortnight, one increases the morsels by one each day, and in the dark fortnight, one decreases them by one;
then there are two fast days at the end of the two fortnights—this is indeed remembered as the Cāndrāyaṇa."
A Brahmin, being composed, should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set; this is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
Restraining his self, he should perform the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* penance by eating eight morsels of sacrificial food at midday for each month.
By eating two hundred and eighty morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever over the course of a month, a twice-born man attains the same world as the Moon.
Just as the rising moon dispels the world's fear of darkness,
so too does the twice-born who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa penance destroy the fear of sin.
Eating grains, oil-cakes, and buttermilk, or subsisting on barley-water and water,
and fasting for one, three, five, and seven days respectively— this is the Tulāpuruṣa penance, which destroys sin.
Barley-gruel consumed for seven nights destroys the sins of embodied beings; alternatively, fasting for seven nights is likewise observed by the wise.
In the months of Pauṣa, Bhādrapada, and Jyeṣṭha, by taking refuge under the Ārdrā constellation, the open sky, or the sun’s heat,
a twice-born man is freed from the three types of white sins, except for those that cause loss of caste.

Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass, combined with barley and sipping-water (*ācamana*), constitute the *brahmakūrca*, which is supremely purifying.
Fasting on the new moon day and eating only sesame seeds on the full moon day,
one is liberated from the sins committed during the bright and dark fortnights by means of these seasonal observances throughout the year.

One who subsists on alms is purified from the food of those who maintain the sacred fires in one month; from that of those who follow the *yāyāvara* mode of life or those dwelling in the forest, one is purified in ten or five days.
One who possesses the wealth of a single-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) is purified by one day’s food;
one who subsists on the *kāpotavṛtti* mode of life is purified by drinking water for three days.
By reciting the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Sāmaveda*, or any one of the Vedas three times through to completion while fasting, he becomes supremely purifying.
Now, if one who subsists on air during the day hastens to perform [the penance],
and remains standing in water at night until dawn, that is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
Having performed the recitation of the Gāyatrī eight thousand times when the sun has risen,
one is liberated from all sins, provided that he is not a killer of an embryo.
He who gives food, speaks the truth, and abides in compassion toward all beings surpasses all those previously mentioned as purified by the *yantras*.
The Rudra hymn together with the Ādityahṛdaya, the Gāyatrī accompanied by the Praṇava,
and the seven Vyāhṛtis— these should be recited as they destroy all sin.
The Mṛgāreṣṭi, the Pavitreṣṭi, the Trihaviṣ, and also the Pāvamānī— these sacrifices,
when combined with the Vaiśvānarī, are destroyers of sin.
And listen now to this other secret being declared:
one is liberated from all sins, except for the greatest of transgressions.
Performing the purification with strainers while reciting the Rudra-ekādaśinī,
offering the strainers with clarified butter, and bestowing gold, cows, and sesame seeds.
He who eats cooked barley-gruel with cow urine,
dung-water, curd, milk, and clarified butter, is instantly liberated from that sin.
He who has procreated on a Śūdra woman, and he by whom an unapproachable woman has been violated—
both of them are liberated from that sin after seven nights by means of this rite.
In the case of consuming semen, urine, or feces; eating the food of one whose food should not be eaten;

or in the rites of re-consecrating the sacred fires and performing a sacrifice for one who has lost his consecrated fires—this is the remedy. And it is the remedy for the elder brother whose younger brother marries before him.
"Even after having committed very many acts that cause one to fall,
one is released from all sins"— this is the statement of the virtuous.
The ritual procedure, for which the authority of the mantras and the path is proclaimed,
is that by which Bharadvāja and others attained identity with Brahman.
A Brahmin whose heart is serene, through the performance of this rite,
attains whatever various desires reside within his heart.
"Whatever desires reside in the heart," so [it is said].
For that Brahmin who has turned away from evil deeds and is engaged in meritorious deeds,
his ritual actions succeed even without [the use of] yantras.
Therefore, Brāhmaṇas are upright; whatever they desire in their hearts, that very thing they quickly attain, being purified by their straightforward deeds.
Thus,
a wise person should perform these restraints for as long as it takes for the body to attain purity of the self.
Having purified his soul by these restraints and having fasted for three nights,
he should then undertake that rite by which he desires to attain prosperity.
The *kṣmāpavitra*, the *sahasrākṣa*, the *mṛgāra*, the two *aṃhomuc* groups,
the *pāvamānya* verses, the *kūśmāṇḍya* verses, and those verses addressed to Vaiśvānara.
Offering oblations of ghee and boiled rice at the three daily pressings for seven days, he should observe a vow of silence, eat only sacrificial food, and restrain the activities of his senses.
Having looked into a vessel full of water at a crossroads while reciting "siṃhe me," one is released from all sins, even from a great mortal transgression.
Whatever accumulation of sin has been committed in old age, youth, or childhood,
and even that which was done in previous births through ignorance— from all that he is liberated.
Having fed the twice-born at the conclusion with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter, and having bestowed cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold upon those who have eaten;
The Brahmin becomes one whose self is purified, with the fuel of his sins utterly consumed;
he thus becomes fit for rites performed for specific desires as well as for rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires.
He who performs this rite out of excessive greed or through negligence becomes possessed by sin and perishes like one who has swallowed poison.
Performing this rite for his teacher, his father, his mother, and himself, the Brahmin shines like the sun; therefore, this rite must be performed for them.
Who by means of this thousand-eyed purifier made Agni, Vāyu, Ravi, Soma, Yama, and the other lords of the gods pure?
Whatever is renowned here as a meritorious name throughout the three worlds, that belongs to the Brahmins and others; by whom has it been made so through this purifying rite?
This secret *prājāpatya* rite, which destroys evil, arose first;
thereafter, thousands of purifiers (*pavitra*) emerged from it.
He who offers these eight groups of oblations for a year, a half-year, a season, a fortnight, or a day,
purifies ten ancestors and ten descendants of his own lineage.
"And it is known by the immortals dwelling in heaven that he who stands upon earth is a performer of meritorious deeds;
moreover, as a doer of merit, he rejoices like a god in the heavenly world.
"If a twice-born man is unable to offer these eight groups [of oblations]," 4.8.7–8ab.
Even if he offers only one [oblation] with that [mixture], his impurity is thereby destroyed.
He whose sons or disciples offer these eight groups [of oblations] is also liberated from sin, even if they have been hired for the purpose of teaching.
Even by means of wealth purchased [as substitutes], one who desires to destroy his own sin must certainly offer oblations;
for the bearer of the body (the sacrificer) must not be allowed to despair when he is incapable [of performing the rites himself].
The relinquishing of wealth—even for the sake of meritorious deeds—is performed; and at times, the liberation of a man from sin is accomplished when he is free from debt.
One who is liberated from this ocean of all debts of sin by this prescribed method considers himself pure and capable of accomplishing ritual acts.
But whatever rites a person whose soul is liberated from all debts to sin undertakes,
those reach fulfillment without effort for that one of purified body.
This meritorious *prājāpatya* rite was proclaimed by the seer. One who constantly teaches this, retains it in memory, or even hears it,
is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One who desires to master those mantras [should recite them] for twelve days;

having consumed clarified butter, milk, and curd, he should eat boiled rice once at night. Likewise, there is an oblation with clarified butter ten times during each of the three pressings of the Soma sacrifice, for the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and also the Atharvāṅgirasa.
This preliminary service (pūrva-sevā) for these mantras serves as the means for accomplishing the ritual action.

"The purpose of the mantras is the accomplishment of ritual action. [This occurs] through excessive greed or through negligence. Having desisted from evil deeds, the Rudras are well-composed by means of the Vedic meters. Now, therefore, I shall fully declare; we shall proclaim the expiations (*prāyaścittāni*). We shall proclaim the expiations. We shall proclaim the expiations. We shall proclaim the expiations. Thus ends the fourth book (*praśna*). Thus the *Baudhāyana-dharmasūtra* is completed.

[GAUTAMA DHARMASŪTRA 1.1] GAUTAMA 1.1.1: The Veda is the root of Dharma. GAUTAMA 1.1.2: And the tradition and conduct of those who know it.
Gautama 1.3: A transgression of dharma and great acts of violence are seen [even] among the great; [this is so] because the purpose is not seen [to be fulfilled by such means].
Gautama 1.4: Because of the weakness of those who follow later.
Gautama Sūtra 1.4: When there is a conflict between two rules of equal authority, there is an option.

Gautama Sūtra 1.1.11: And because of the recitation of the Veda. Gautama Sūtra 1.1.12: For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, [the periods are] the eleventh and twelfth [years respectively].

For a Kṣatriya, there are twenty-two [years];
for a Vaiśya, two more than that.
The girdles are made of muñja grass, a bowstring, and wool, respectively.
Gautama Dharmasūtra 1.16: The skins of the black antelope, the ruru deer, and the goat [are prescribed].

Gautama 1.1.19: Some [say] even the saffron-colored garment [is appropriate]. Gautama 1.1.20a: A tree-bark garment for a Brāhmaṇa.
Gautama 1.1.20b: Madder-red and turmeric-yellow for the other two [castes].
Gautama Sūtra 1.22: The staffs for a Brāhmaṇa are made of *bilva* or *pālāśa* wood.
Gautama Sūtra 1.23: For the other [castes], they are made of *aśvattha* or *pīlu* wood.

24. They should be unblemished, curved like a sacrificial post (yūpa), and possessed of bark. 25. They should be measured by the height of the head, the forehead, or the tip of the nose.
26. And they may have their hair shaved off, or worn in braids, or with a single tuft (śikhā) left in braided form.
Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.27: One who has something in hand and becomes impure shall rinse his mouth without setting that object down.
Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.28: The purification of objects consists of wiping, heating, scraping, and washing, respectively for metallic items, earthenware, wooden items, and woven textiles.
Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.29: Stones, gems, shells, and pearls are to be purified like metallic items.
[The purification] of bones and ground is like that of wood;
and [the purification] of the earth is by means of sowing.
Gautama 1.1.32: [The purification] of cloth, rope, split bamboo, and leather is like that of clothing.
Gautama 1.1.33: Or there is the discarding of those items that are excessively defiled. Gautama 1.1.34: One should begin the act of purification facing either the east or the north.

Gautama-Dharmasūtra 1.35–36: Sitting in a clean place, having placed his right arm between his knees, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, having washed his hands up to the wrists, and remaining silent, he should sip water three or four times, touching his heart.
He should wipe his mouth twice.
(Variant reading: *parimṛjyāt*).
Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.1.37: And he should sprinkle his feet with water. Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.1.38: And he should touch the cavities of the head.
Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.1.39: And he should place [water] upon his head.

Gautama 1.1.42 / Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.39: Some say this applies until the particle falls out.

Gautama-Dharmasūtra 1.43: One should know that when [semen] is discharged, it is pure even while being swallowed, just like urine. Gautama-Dharmasūtra 1.46: Drops from the mouth do not cause one to become impure, provided they do not fall upon a limb.
Gautama-Dharmasūtra 1.45: Purification from an impure substance consists in the removal of its stain and odor.
Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.46: That [cleansing] is first performed with water and with earth.

Gautama 1.48: And where the sacred tradition (āmnāya) prescribes [a rule].

The touching of the vital breath with *darbha* grass. Gautama 1.48: The touching of the vital breath with *darbha* grass.
Gautama Sūtra 1.49: There are three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), each consisting of fifteen measures (mātrās).
Gautama Sūtra 1.50: And the sitting posture is upon grass blades pointing eastward.
(Variant reading: -tūleṣu)
Gautama-Dharmasūtra 1.1.52: Oṃ; the five preceding *vyāhṛtis* end with *satya*.
Gautama-Dharmasūtra 1.1.53: In the morning, there is the clasping of the teacher’s feet. Gautama-Dharmasūtra 1.1.54: And at the beginning and the end of the recitation of the *brahman* [Veda].
Gautama 1.1.55: Having been permitted, the pupil should sit to the south, facing east, or facing north.
Gautama 1.1.56: And the recitation of the Sāvitrī [is to be performed].
Gautama 1.1.57: At the beginning, when taking up the Veda.
Gautama Sūtra 1.58: The syllable *oṃ* [is used] even elsewhere.
Gautama Sūtra 1.59: Upon going inside [the teacher's presence], there is a renewed formal approach (*upasadana*).
Gautama Dharmasūtra 1.59: For killing a dog, a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a cat, there shall be a fast for three days and staying away from one's home.
Gautama Dharmasūtra 1.60: For other [animals], there are breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) and the consumption of clarified butter.
Gautama Dharmasūtra 1.61: And the same applies to studying [the Veda] while standing near a cremation ground.

Gautama Sūtra 1.2.1: Before initiation, there is freedom of action, freedom of speech, and freedom of eating.

Gautama 1.2.3: He is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*).
Gautama 1.2.4: His discharge of urine and feces is performed as prescribed.

Gautama Dharmasūtra 1.2.25b / Gautama Sūtra 2.20: A Brāhmaṇa must always abstain from intoxicants. Gautama 3.10.4: But upon partition, there is an increase in the share for the eldest. Gautama 3.10.5: The twentieth part [of the estate] belongs to the eldest; [he shall also receive] a pair [of animals], a chariot yoked with animals on both sides, and a bull.
Gautama 3.10.6: If there are several [animals], those that are one-eyed, lame, hornless, or tailless belong to the middlemost son.
If there are many [sons],
a sheep, an iron [implement], a house, a vehicle, and a quadruped— each one [of these] belongs to the youngest.
Gautama 3.10.8: If it is equal, everything else [is shared] equally. Gautama 3.10.9: Or the first-born may receive two shares.
Gautama Sūtra 28.10: For the others, one [gift] each.
Gautama Sūtra 28.11: Or, for those desiring specific rewards, each obtains one form of wealth, starting with the first.
Ten [animals] for domestic animals;
not [ten] for single-hoofed or two-footed creatures.
Gautama 3.10.12: An extra bull is for the eldest son.
Gautama 3.10.13: Sixteen bulls are for the son born of the eldest wife (*jyaiṣṭhineya*).
Gautama 3.10.14: The younger brothers share equally with the son born of the eldest wife.

Gautama 3.10.15: Or, according to their respective mothers, there shall be a specific distinction of shares within their own group. Gautama 3.10.16: A man who has no offspring may, after performing sacrifices to Agni and Prajāpati, designate a daughter as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) by declaring, "This child [shall be] for my sake."
According to some, she becomes a *putrikā* by mere agreement (*abhisaṃdhimātrāt*). Because of the uncertainty regarding that [status], one should not marry a girl who has no brother.
Gautama 3.10.19: Those related by funeral cakes (piṇḍa), lineage (gotra), or sages (ṛṣi) shall divide the inheritance of a woman who has no offspring—or of one who has no offspring at all.
Gautama 3.10.20: Or she may seek to obtain seed [from a kinsman].

Gautama 3.10.21: A son born of a woman other than the wife of the same caste has no share [in the paternal estate]. Gautama 3.10.22: The property of a woman belongs to her daughters who are unmarried and not established in life.
Gautama 3.10.23: The bride-price of a sister belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother's death.
Gautama 3.10.24: And some [teachers] hold that it should be done first.
Gautama 3.10.25: The division of the estate of those who have died without reunited property belongs to the eldest son.
Gautama 3.10.26: When one who has reunited property dies, the reunited kinsman is the heir to the inheritance.
Gautama 3.10.27: A son born after partition inherits only from the father.
Gautama 3.10.28: A learned man may, at his discretion, refuse to give to those who are unlearned property that he has acquired by himself.
Gautama 3.10.29: Those who are unlearned shall divide it equally.

Gautama 3.10.30: The legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the adopted son (*dattaka*), the son made (*kṛtrima*), the son secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*), and the son cast off (*apaviddha*) are the heirs to the estate.

Gautama 3.10.31: The son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son received with the bride (*sahoḍha*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), the son given himself (*svayaṃdatta*), and the son bought (*krīta*) are entitled to a share of the lineage (*gotra*).
Gautama 3.10.32: In the absence of the sons beginning with the legitimate son of the body, these [latter six] receive a fourth part of the inheritance.

Gautama 3.10.33 / Gautama-Dharmasūtra 28.35: The eldest son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya wife, if endowed with good qualities, is entitled to an equal share. Gautama 3.10.34 / Gautama-Dharmasūtra 28.36: The other [shares] are reduced by the portion due to the eldest.
Gautama 3.10.35 / Gautama-Dharmasūtra 28.37: In the case of a combination of sons by a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya wife, it is the same as in the case of a son by a Brāhmaṇa wife.
If [the son] is from a Kṣatriya woman... (Gautama 3.10.36).
If he is from a Śūdra woman, even a son of a Śūdra may, if he is obedient, obtain the means of subsistence according to the rule for a pupil, provided the [father] is childless. (Gautama 3.10.37–38).
[He] shall obtain it. (Variant reading: *labheta*).
Gautama 3.10.38: According to some, even the son of a wife of equal caste does not receive [the inheritance] if he has behaved improperly.
Gautama 3.10.39: The Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) shall divide the estate of a childless Brāhmaṇa. Gautama 3.10.40: In the case of others, the king [shall take it].
The idiot and the eunuch are to be maintained.
The offspring of an idiot is entitled to a share. Those born of women in the inverse order of castes are treated like the son of a Śūdra woman.
Gautama 3.10.44: There is no division of water, of what is acquired for common security, or of prepared food.
Gautama 3.10.45: And the same applies to women who are united [in marriage].

Gautama 3.10.46: When the matter is unknown, an act should be performed as recommended by at least ten learned men who are experts in *ūha* (logical reasoning), free from greed, and of good character.

Gautama 3.10.47 / Gautama Dharmasūtra 28.49: Four who have mastered the four Vedas, three members of the [first] three stages of life (āśrama) prior to the last one, and three who know the Dharma separately— these ten at minimum, they call an assembly (pariṣad).

Gautama Sūtra 3.10.48–50: But in the absence of these [previously mentioned authorities], a Śrotriya who is a knower of the Veda and distinguished in case of conflicting opinions—whatsoever he says; for he is incapable of harming or favoring living beings. Especially among those possessing dharma, the knower of dharma attains the heavenly world through his knowledge and resolute application.
"Thus, this is dharma, this is dharma.
