Accompanied by the commentary of Maskari,
having prostrated with devotion before the primordial deity Vāsudeva,
[this work] is a compendium of all the Smṛtis under the guise of the Gautamīya.
Today, a commentary is being composed by me, the son of Vāmana.
What is the connection? This is stated: there are fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), namely:

the six auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive system of Logic (*nyāyavistara*), the Purāṇa, and the Treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*); these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Thus [it is said].
The connection [of the sentence] is that this *Dharmaśāstra*, which is enumerated among those [sciences], is now commenced.

Alternatively, *saṃsāra* is the continuous succession of birth, old age, and death, consisting of the conjunction with and disjunction from the body, senses, and objects for the sake of a person’s experience of pleasure and pain;
and that [succession] has its cause in *dharma* and *adharma*, and not in any other cause.
Furthermore, because these two—dharma and adharma—are the causes for the experience of desired and undesired results, they are objects to be either adopted or avoided.
Since neither of these is possible without full comprehension, Gautama composed this treatise for the purpose of understanding the true nature of dharma and adharma.
Moreover, this alone is its practical purpose, as the adoption of dharma and the avoidance of adharma constitute the ultimate goal of human endeavor.

The subject matter [of this work] consists of the *aṣṭakā* rites and others; just as the *agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*) are necessarily to be performed, so too are the *aṣṭakā* rites and others.
Since it is observed that all actions proceed from a cause, he first states the following in order to establish the specific cause:
"The Veda is the root of Dharma" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.1).

Now, an objection may be raised: since a treatise consists of injunctions and prohibitions, one should have stated only such things as "the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa occurs in the eighth year," and so forth; it should not have been stated that "the Veda is the root of Dharma" and so on, because a mere restatement (anuvāda) is purposeless. Furthermore, the authority of the Veda is not established by this [statement], for its authority is self-evident (*svataḥ-siddha*). Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), wherein the authority of that which establishes the authority [of the Veda] would require another, and that yet another, and so on.
It is said: This restatement that the Veda is the root of Dharma is for the purpose of establishing that Smṛti and Śīla are also roots of Dharma by means of it.

If one asks how so, it is replied: That understanding which arises without doubt regarding a specific meaning from the uttered words of the Veda for those who know the meaning of its terms—and which does not undergo reversal at another time, in another place, in another person, or in another state—that is the root of Dharma.
And when a cognition arises that is free from doubt and non-erroneous, its validity can be determined.
Furthermore, the falsity of the conviction produced by the Veda cannot be attributed to defects in its cause, because an author is not admitted [for it].
For it is a defect residing in an author that brings about the falsity of a cognition produced by words.
Thus, this is a restatement for the sake of what follows.
Now the Sūtra is explained: therein, the Veda is a collection of texts known as Mantra and Brāhmaṇa.
[The root] *vid* means "to know"; it is called the Veda because by means of it the nature of Dharma and other such things is known.
Although the Smṛtis and other such works possess an equality with this [Veda], [they are not the Veda].
Nevertheless, there is no fault, because [the term] is used by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), as in the case of "wandering mendicants" (*parivrājaka*) and others.
And so it is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"The *Śruti* is to be understood as the Veda, while the *Smṛti* is indeed the *Dharmaśāstra*."
Thus.
And that [dharma] is divided according to the distinctions of the Ṛgveda and so forth;
the singular number is used with reference to the genus.
Its meaning is "duty," "action," or "conduct," or else it refers to that which is called *apūrva*.

The word "root" (*mūla*) means the cause, the indicator, that is, the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that in this context the Veda, consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*), alone attains the status of making known *dharma* and so forth, and not that which takes the form of mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), it is replied: since even the explanatory passages and the rest are auxiliary by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with the injunctions, their status as the root of *dharma* through an indirect lineage is not contradictory. To begin with, the explanatory passage attains the nature of an injunction or prohibition by way of praise or blame; the mantra, however, [attains it] because it serves to remind one of the enjoined matter at the time of performance.
Therefore, the Veda in its entirety is the root of Dharma.

Some, however, maintain that it is rooted solely in mantras and arthavādas, as in the case of [the passage] "O thou who art like a watering-place in the desert," where it is concluded that a watering-place must be constructed, and so forth.

Others, however, say that the accomplishment of dharma results from mere study alone, as it is said: "Even he who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability, performs the highest austerity even unto the tips of his fingernails."
Thus [it is said].

Therefore, [the claim] that the mere recitation [of the Veda] alone is the root of *dharma* is incorrect; for it would result in the absurdity of the scriptural teachings on the fruits of ritual action being purposeless, and because the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the fruit of study is not the attainment of the truth (*tattva*).
Alternatively, the word "Veda" refers to the action expressed by the Veda, and that [action] is the root of *dharma*.

If it is argued that [the principle] does not apply to the hawk-sacrifice and similar rites, it is replied: even there, dharma certainly exists by way of protecting one's life, wealth, children, wife, and so forth, through the slaying of an enemy.
From this it is understood that whatever is seen, such as children, cattle, and villages, and whatever is unseen, such as the beginning of creation—all of that has dharma as its cause.

Dharma is of five kinds: the dharma of caste (*varṇadharma*), the dharma of stage of life (*āśramadharma*), the dharma of quality (*guṇadharma*), the dharma of both caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), and the dharma of occasion (*nimittadharma*). The dharma of caste consists of study and so forth; the dharma of stage of life consists of the placing of fuel on the fire and so forth; the dharma of quality consists of the protection and other duties of one endowed with qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*); the dharma of both caste and stage of life consists of the palāśa staff for a Brāhmaṇa and so forth; and the dharma of occasion consists of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth. "Root" means the primary cause.
And so it has been said: "For dharma shone forth from the Veda.
Furthermore, the purpose for commencing this Sūtra is to show that just as the Veda is the root of dharma, so too are tradition (smṛti) and conduct (śīla).
The Veda alone is not the sole root of Dharma; rather, it is also the tradition and conduct of those who know it. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.2)

And those [traditions] of the knowers of the Veda which consist of memory (smṛti) and conduct (śīla), they too have their root in the Dharma; furthermore, they must not contradict the Veda, because of the phrase "of those who know that" (*tadvidām*). And since the word "root" (*mūla*) is connected with both [the Veda and the traditions], it should be understood as having a dual ending.
By the word "that" (*tat*), the Veda along with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is indicated.

*Smṛti* consists of that which has been composed by Manu, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Vyāsa, Śātātapa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Hārīta, Bodhāyana, Yājñavalkya, Pracetas, and others.

*Śīla* is uncodified customary practice (*samācāra*), such as auspicious rites for joy (*kautuka-maṅgala*) and the like; it is not codified because of its great variety and because it differs according to each region.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of including what has not been mentioned.
As Manu said:
"The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it."
And the conduct of the virtuous, as well as self-satisfaction.
Thus [it is said].

Performing three circumambulations and so forth at the time of the conclusion of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyopāsanā) is the practice of the learned (śiṣṭācāra). That conviction which arises from those who know the Vedas and are devoted to the performance of all duties, being free from fault, is "satisfaction of the self" (ātmatuṣṭi). As he will say: "And that which the wise elders... and so forth.

Some describe [the matter] as follows: just like the *aṣṭakā* rites and others, there is no formal injunction for these auspicious ceremonies (*kautuka-maṅgala*) and so forth, because there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in their non-performance.
Furthermore, both "custom" (*ācāra*) and "self-satisfaction" (*ātmatuṣṭi*) are included within "virtue" (*śīla*) itself, and thus are not mentioned separately.
The word "and" (*ca*) also serves the purpose of a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*) of what has already been stated.
Now the opponent raises an objection: the conduct of those who know the Veda is not the root of Dharma, because a transgression of Dharma is observed [among them]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.3)
The ellipsis is "it does not attain the status of being rooted in Dharma.
For example: Prajāpati’s desire for his own daughter; Indra’s illicit approach to Ahalyā and so forth; and the failure of Vyāsa, Bhīṣma, and others to abide within the stages of life (āśrama).
Moreover:
"And the transgression of the great ones [is grave]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.4)
In this case as well, the implication is that [the act] does not have its root in *dharma*, because of the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*). By the word "force" (*sahaḥ*), strength is meant;
as Nārada says: "Force is here called strength."
Therefore, that which is done without regard for the treatises and worldly convention is recklessness (*sāhasa*). This refers to the deeds of those renowned in the world as great men;
for example, Rāma’s slaying of women such as Tāṭakā.
There is the severing of the head of Jamadagnya’s mother and the drowning of Vasiṣṭha in water, and so forth;
therefore, it is incorrect to claim that moral conduct is the root of dharma.

Furthermore, what is the distinction between the transgression of dharma and rashness? That which is performed improperly out of desire for sense objects is the transgression of dharma; that which is done under the sway of anger and so forth is rashness.
To this, he states the following reply:
"But not so in the case of a visible purpose, because of the weakness of the unseen. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.5)
The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the alternative position.
That which has a visible object—that is, a visible purpose—in that case where there is a visible purpose, ethical conduct (*śīla*) is not the root of the Dharma.
And so it is said:

Vasiṣṭha says: "Dharma is that whose cause is not perceived. This is not a statement regarding the transgression of dharma and acts of violence for a visible purpose; for if that were perceived, then since the designation *pragṛhya* would apply by the rule "īdūt-ed-ot," the reading would have to be "dṛṣṭārthe 'varadaurbalyāt."

"Due to the weakness of the inferior": the "inferior" (*avara*) means one who is base, overcome by hatred and other passions, and lacks knowledge of the ultimate truth—this is the meaning. "Due to his weakness" means due to his incapacity for the full discernment of dharma and adharma. By this, it is made known that even among the great ones who possess such [knowledge], there may occasionally be an overcoming [by passion]; for since pleasure and pain are inevitable for those possessing a body, as long as these [great ones] are overcome by defects such as attachment, their conduct (*ācāra*) must not be accepted.
And so Vasiṣṭha says: "But the disciplined man is one whose nature is free from desire.
Alternatively, by the word *avara* (inferior), those men of the present Kali age are meant; [the practice is not for them] because of their weakness, that is, their lack of capacity.

Having thus stated the authority of tradition (smṛti), he now says—addressing the question of what should be done when there is a mutual contradiction between statements that apply to the same subject matter:
"In the case of a conflict between [authorities] of equal strength, there is an option. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.6)
An object established by an equal means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) possesses equal force.

When there is mutual contradiction between these two, an option (vikalpa) is to be understood, such as "either this or that. There is no abandonment of both, because both have been established by valid cognition.
There is no acceptance of either alternative, for if one were accepted, it would result in the second being rendered meaningless.
What is the illustration? First, in the Śruti: "The oblation should be offered after sunrise," "The oblation should be offered before sunrise," and so forth.
Also in the Smṛti, Gautama says: "That which is contaminated by hair or insects is always unfit to be eaten."
Food that has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, stepped over, sneezed upon,
or defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth over it.
Thus says Manu.
Now, one might object: since the alternative options are already established here by the very force of the context, this sūtra is redundant; for a combination of times is simply not possible here.

Indeed, it is not possible to offer after sunset and then offer again at sunrise, because it is improper for the primary act—the oblation—to be repeated on account of its subordinate attribute, namely time.
For subordinate factors (guṇas) must follow the dictates of the primary factor (pradhāna), but the primary factor does not follow the dictates of the subordinate factor.
Furthermore, it is not possible for a cause to be non-obstructed at both times;
likewise, in the case of memory as well, a conjunction of purity and abandonment is not possible because they are mutually contradictory.
And it has already been stated that the abandonment of both is not tenable.
Therefore, in this case, it follows that there is only conceptual construction; thus, this [scriptural passage] has no purpose.
In that case, this is a restatement of what is established by logic for the sake of specifying a particular point.

What is the specification? It is that an option (*vikalpa*) occurs only when there is a conflict between two things of equal strength, whereas when they are of unequal strength, there is simply sublation (*bādha*).
Therefore, in a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, the Smṛti alone is sublated.
For in the case of the Śruti, the word is directly perceived, whereas in the case of the Smṛti, it is inferential.
And an inference does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge when it contradicts direct perception.

Likewise, in the case of a conflict between Smṛti and custom (ācāra), customs such as marrying the daughter of one's maternal uncle are sublated; for in that instance, the inference of a Smṛti rule is derived from the custom.

Because there is an option when there is a contradiction; however, when there is no contradiction, there is a combination of those things enjoined by equal authorities, as in the case of sipping water (ācamana) and so forth during Vedic rituals.

But surely, if it is only by accepting that the Smṛti originates from the indicative marks (liṅga) of the Veda that its inequality of strength with respect to Śruti is established, then those indicative marks found in Mantra and Arthavāda passages—which, though intended for another purpose, serve as weak supports for Smārta duties, such as "The boys are like arrows"—would necessarily be weaker when they contradict an explicit Vedic statement, because their inferential capacity would be blocked by that contradictory statement.

However, when it is accepted that there are Smṛtis whose original Vedic branches have been lost—as Āpastamba stated: "The injunctions declared in the Brāhmaṇas have their textual readings lost; they are inferred from their practical application"—then, since both are Vedic in origin, they necessarily possess equal authority.

For there is no distinction in strength between an inferred Vedic sentence and one directly perceived, just as there is none between fire determined through perception and fire determined through inference.

It might be argued: "In cases where a Smṛti statement contradicts the Veda, it cannot be inferred as being based on a Vedic text; rather, it must originate from error and the like. This is not tenable, because if one were to admit that the author of the Dharmaśāstra is untrustworthy, it would lead to a total lack of confidence [in his work]. Furthermore, even when a Smṛti is accepted as having come down through an uninterrupted tradition just like the Veda, the argument that they possess equal authority still does not hold.

As for that custom which was proposed, such as marrying the daughter of one’s maternal uncle and so forth, because it occurs when one is overcome by desire and the like, it is a corrupt practice and cannot possibly be considered the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).

However, that which is practiced without dissent by the learned who possess the aforementioned characteristics, since there is no difference in its being rooted in the Veda, it necessarily attains equal authority with the Smṛti.
Furthermore, a different purpose has been taught for those practices that have a basis and those that lack a basis.

Furthermore, the relative strength or weakness of a traditional practice (samācāra) based on its proximity to the inference of a Vedic statement—wherein the form [of that Vedic statement] is mediated by another Smṛti passage—is not established.
To this it is replied: First of all, the inequality of strength between the Vedas and the others is understood from the very force (*sāmarthya*) of the commencement of this Sūtra.

For if these were of equal strength, then in the event of a conflict, an option (*vikalpa*) would be established by that same force; what then would be the purpose of this Sūtra? Furthermore, the mention of "equal strength" would be rendered meaningless.
Moreover, even in this context, the greater weakness of the Smṛti compared to the Vedas and so forth is logically established.
In that regard, it has been stated that its arising from a mark (liṅga) is logical;
therefore, this very position concerning the entity is correct.

The independent position has been stated; however, since that position—namely, "and the tradition and conduct of those who know it"—is difficult to establish, it follows that the view that the Smṛtis originate solely from the Veda is far more faultless.

But even so, this is not tenable, because in some cases we observe that Śruti is sublated by Smṛti; for example, the eligibility for Vedic rites, which applies generally, is restricted by Smṛti to specific individuals such as those who have undergone initiation (upanīta).

Likewise, since a specific result is declared when there is a connection with a quality of the self even through a single part of the *saṃskāras*, so too, although the slaughter of a cow is enjoined by the Vedic text "One should sacrifice a cow," it is not performed because the prohibition found in the *Smṛti* is more authoritative. Similarly, rites such as the *agnihotra*, which are enjoined as means of livelihood and accomplished through material substances, are not performed by first acquiring those substances through theft and the like, even though such acquisition is prohibited by the *Smṛti*.
Therefore, the statement that "the *Smṛti* is sublated by the *Śruti*" is incorrect.
It is said: The consideration of the relative strength and weakness of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is appropriate only when there is a contradiction;
however, where no contradiction exists, even that which is weak is not sublated at all.

To begin with, the entitlement to ritual action for one who has been initiated is not contradicted by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), because initiation is for the purpose of learning the Vedas, and that [learning] is for the purpose of ritual action; furthermore, the accomplishment of the primary rite does not occur without a connection to the transcendental result (*apūrva*).

As for what was said—that even though enjoined by Śruti, the *govardheya* sacrifice is not performed—that too is not based on Smṛti alone, but also from the wording of a mantra: "Do not let the cows perish; let the horses perish," and so forth.
Therefore, Śruti is never sublated by Smṛti.
Some say that Smṛti is preceded by a lost (*utsanna*) Śākhā.
That is incorrect.
In this regard, it is examined: did the branches perish prior to the recollection, or at a later time?
If they perished prior [to the recollection], then recollection would not be possible there, because they have already perished, and because memory is similar to its preceding cognition.
If [the text] were of a later period, then it would not be appropriate to say that it is preceded by lost branches, because it is being perceived at that very time.

This is also the intended meaning of what was stated by Āpastamba: "They are lost in some places, but not everywhere. An explanation must also be provided for the statement: "Their lost readings are inferred from usage."
Thus, this definition of the means of knowing dharma has been stated. Now, in order to state that which is measured by memory, he says:
"The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa [should take place] in the eighth [year]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.7)
*Upanayana* is the leading near [the child] to the Veda, to the fire, to the teacher, or to the restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*).
This occurs in the eighth year, because the calculation of years is based on the beginning of the year.
This time for *upanayana* is obligatory (*nitya*), since the optional (*kāmya*) and emergency (*āpaddharma*) times are mentioned only after this.

Since [the status of] the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya has been declared above, and because the Śūdra possesses only a single birth (*ekajāti*), this undertaking is for the purpose of establishing that the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa"—even though its meaning is already established—is based on the specific caste (*jāti*).
Furthermore, Brāhmaṇahood is not something produced like the state of being twice-born (*dvijatva*).

And thus, injunctions prescribed with reference to a Brāhmaṇa, such as "They should pour hot [liquor] upon the Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor" (*surāpasya brāhmaṇasyoṣṇām āsiñceyuḥ*), apply even to one who has not undergone initiation (*anupanīta*).

Alternatively, were it not for the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," this [rite] would be obligatory for all three [classes]; however, the optional rite would apply to the Brāhmaṇa in the ninth or fifth year, while for the other two, it would apply in the eleventh or twelfth years, because they are mentioned immediately after the optional rite.

Furthermore, even in the absence of previous sacraments, one is entitled [to the rites] through initiation (*upanayana*), but not by means of these subsequent rites without it; thus, without mentioning *garbhādhāna* and the others, the commencement here is specifically that of initiation.
The optional [rite] is performed on the ninth or the fifth day.

"Kāmya" means that which is beneficial for desire, being capable of producing it. Although one might have said "in the fifth or the ninth," the deviation in the order [of the months] is intended to include the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas in the period for optional conception between these two [the third and the eighth].
And so Manu says:
For a king seeking power, [the period] is on the sixth day; for a Vaiśya seeking wealth, it is on the eighth.
The irregularity of the months is for the purpose of indicating the different desires [of the candidate].
Thus, another Smṛti states: "In the ninth month for one desiring long life; in the fifth for one desiring spiritual luster.
The word "vā" (or) signifies an option.
He is to be seen according to one's wish.
The number of years begins from conception. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.9)

The ten months accompanied by the embryo are called "the womb" (*garbha*); the calculation of years should begin from that point, not from birth. Consequently, in such passages as "the initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa," one should apply the phrase "in the eighth [year] from conception" (*garbhāṣṭame*), and so forth.
That is his second birth. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.10)
That initiation (upanayana) is the second birth;
the meaning is that one who is consecrated by it becomes a twice-born (dvija).
The designation "twice-born" is established for the sake of conventional usage in such expressions as "the study [of the Veda] belongs to the twice-born."
The inclusion of the word "that" (tat) is for the purpose of encompassing both the obligatory and the optional initiations.
For that reason, he is called the teacher (ācārya). (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.11)
The inclusion of the word "that" (tat) is for the purpose of including both the obligatory and optional initiations (*upanayana*).
This is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) made for the sake of conventional usage in such passages as "The teacher (*ācārya*) is the best among gurus."
And because of the recitation of the Vedas. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.12)
"Vedānuvacana" means the recitation of the entire Veda;
it is for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), as the teacher [performs it] by teaching even a single portion.
And so says Manu:
One should recognize as a teacher even that person who benefits one with their learning, whether it be little or much, by means of that very assistance through sacred knowledge.
Thus it is said.
If the purpose has been seen, he is an *upādhyāya*;
and thus Vasiṣṭha says: "But he who [teaches] one part is an *upādhyāya*. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the expounder of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) is also included.

And thus says Yāska: "An *ācārya* gathers (*ācinoti*) conducts, he gathers meanings, or [he gathers] intelligence. Some explain the word *ca* (and) as having the sense of conjunction with the preceding sūtra; by that, one is an *ācārya* precisely because of performing both functions.
And so Manu says:
"That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil,
teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the Rahasyas, him they call an Ācārya."
Thus it is said.
The eleventh and twelfth [days] are for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, respectively. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.13)
This time is eternal, because it is mentioned after the sections on optional rites and those performed for specific purposes.
But when there is an omission of either the obligatory or the optional [rites] due to some cause such as famine, he then states the rule for times of distress:
"The *sāvitrī* of a Brāhmaṇa does not fall away until the sixteenth year. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.14)

The prefix *āṅ* has the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*), as in "along with the sixteenth year"; this is indicated by the grammatical mark (*liṅga*) in the word "of two more" (*dvyadhikāyāḥ*) and by the observation of another Smṛti text stating, "In the sixteenth [year], one may desire all things.
"Not fallen" means not having lost [the right].
By the word *sāvitrī*, its means—the initiation (*upanayana*)—is expressed; the meaning is that one becomes eligible for initiation.
And thus, even in the case of those such as a father who have not been initiated, one becomes eligible for initiation through the performance of an expiatory rite (prāyaścitta).
Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "He whose father... grandfather... great-grandfather... and so forth.
For a member of the royal caste (rājanya), two parts from twenty. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.15)
Here too, the particle "ā" (inclusive) is understood, as is the phrase "together with the years.
The use of the word *rājanya* is for the purpose of establishing his status as a king; thus, the right to rule belongs only to one who has been initiated (*upanīta*).
For a Vaiśya, it is two years more. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.16)
The twenty-two that are accompanied by two additional [factors] are "dvyadhikāḥ" (those increased by two); this means "of twenty-four.

Although it should have been stated as "caturviṃśateḥ" (of twenty-four), the expression was formulated in this way in order to indicate that the prefix *aṅ* [in the preceding rule] has the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*).
The time for initiation has been stated. Now, with the intention of describing its requirements, he says:
"The girdles are made of muñja grass, a bowstring, or hempen thread, respectively. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.17)
The word *mauñjī* is a derivative of *muñja*;
*mūrvā* is well known, and *maurvī* is a derivative of that.
The compound *jyāmaurvī* is a descriptive determinative (*karmadhāraya*) compound, meaning "that which is both a bowstring and made of *mūrvā*."
Then, having removed [the string] from the bow, it should be taken up. The cord is made of hemp; the bowstring is single-ply, while the other two are triple-stranded.
As Manu has said:
"The girdle of a Brahmin should be made of muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of mūrvā fiber; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads."
Thus [it is said].
The mention of "in order" (*krama*) is for the purpose of excluding the possibility of two [simultaneous] bowstrings.
Some describe it as having an optional sense regarding non-existence.
And so says Manu:
In the absence of muñja grass, however, it should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balbaja grass;
it should have three strands and be bound with one, three, or five knots.
Since the sequence is established by logic, the mention of "sequence" serves another purpose.
The skins of the black antelope, the ruru deer, and the goat.
The word *ajina* (deer-skin) is connected with each [term].
*Kṛṣṇa* is the black antelope; *ruru* is the spotted deer; *basta* is well known [as the goat].
These are, respectively, the upper garments.
And likewise, another Smṛti states: "They should wear only a deerskin as an upper garment."
The garments of all [ascetics] are made of hemp, linen, bark, or blankets of goat's hair.
The section on *śāṇa*:
*śāṇa* [is derived from] *kṣumā*, which is *atasī* (linseed); its derivative product is *kṣauma*.
*Cīra* is that which is completely finished from *darbha* grass and similar materials.
*Kutapa* is made from the wool of mountain-dwelling goats;
these are the lower garments (*adhovāsana*).

Since it is already established that all [the items] are of uneven number, the mention of "all" in another Smṛti—"linen cloth for a Brāhmaṇa"—is intended either to preclude the application of that rule by correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) or to serve as a general heading (*adhikāra*).
And cotton that has not been processed. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.20)
The words "of all" and "clothing" carry over [from the previous context].
"Unaltered" means not connected with passion;
the meaning is that it is naturally white.
And the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of indicating that the preceding [elements] are also unmodified.
Some [say] even the saffron robe [is forbidden]. (Gautama 1.21)
Some also maintain that there is a connection with passion;
the word "also" (api) is used for the sake of censure.
Therefore, it should be understood as referring to the absence of the aforementioned [causes].
Now, in order to provide a restrictive rule regarding the side of the ochre robe, he says:
"The garment of a Brāhmaṇa shall be made of tree-bark. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.22)
Or a garment made from the decoction of vṛṣaka, or one made of bark, is the dress for a Brāhmaṇa.
Māñjiṣṭha and hāridra for the other two.
That which is dyed with madder is for a Kṣatriya;
that which is dyed with turmeric is for a Vaiśya.
The staves of a Brāhmaṇa are made of *bailva* or *pālāśa* wood. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.24)
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Bilva or Palāśa wood.

Although they are mentioned here in a dual compound, nevertheless, because of the singular reference in the rule "or one fit for sacrifice for all," and because of the observation of another Smṛti text stating "having taken the desired staff," it is proper that only one staff be carried.
In the remaining cases, [the staff] shall be made of *aśvattha* or *pīlu* wood. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.25)
The *aśvattha* is well known; the *pīlu* is the *kalki*; as for the remainder, it concerns the *kṣatriya* and the *vaiśya*.
Even there, the *aśvattha* is for the *kṣatriya*, and the *pailava* is for the *vaiśya*.
Or rather, all [the castes] are fit for sacrifice. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.26)
The meaning is that it should be a specific type of tree suitable for sacrifice, one that is free from the *vibhītaka*, *bilvaka*, *yāvaka*, and so forth.
The word "or" (*vā*) signifies an alternative in the absence [of the primary option]; thus, it applies when the preceding [options] are unavailable.
Otherwise, the word "or" would be purposeless.
The inclusion of "all" is intended so that it should not apply only to the two immediately preceding ones.
Now he states the qualities of the staff:
"It should not be gnarled, it should not be curved like a sacrificial post, and it should have bark. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.27)
"Unoppressed" means not damaged by things such as vines, creeping insects, fire, and so forth;
"curved like a sacrificial post" (yūpavakra) means having tips bent like a sacrificial post; "with bark" (saśalka) means possessing their outer skin.
Without forming a compound, all [the qualities] are thus described, but not according to their respective order. Thus Manu said:
"They should all be straight, without blemishes, and pleasing to behold."
The skins of animals that do not cause alarm to humans, which have their hair intact, and which have not been defiled by fire [are fit for use].
Thus it is said.
The [measures] for the crown of the head, the forehead, and the tip of the nose are equal. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.28)
The word "measure" (pramāṇa) is connected with each [term]:
the height of a Brāhmaṇa is measured to the top of the head, that of a Kṣatriya to the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya to the tip of the nose.
And so Manu says:
"The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made according to the measurement reaching to the hairline;
that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the tip of the nose."
Thus it is said.
Now he describes the dress of the religious student (brahmacārī):
"Those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, and those with topknots of matted hair" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.29).
A *muṇḍa* is one whose head has been shaven;
a *jaṭila* is one who still has hair;
one for whom the topknot itself constitutes matted locks is a *śikhājaṭa*.

Thus, by the word *muṇḍa*, complete tonsure is expressed. The particle *vā* has the sense of "or" and is connected to each term individually—as one who is tonsured, or one with matted hair, or one with a topknot of matted hair.
The plural number is used with reference to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Or rather, it was not stated [in that way] for the sake of avoiding a sequential application.
And thus Manu says:
"He may be shaven-headed, or he may wear matted hair, or he may have a single lock of matted hair on the crown."
Thus [it is said].
Now, since the qualification for study depends upon purity, the purification of substances is first described for the sake of that purity:
"One who is impure while holding a substance should set it down and perform ācamana. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.30)

When one who has food in hand has begun to feed Brāhmaṇas or perform other such rites, and having previously been free from ritual impurity, becomes impure through contact with something defiled for some reason, then he should place that object on the ground and perform ācamana (ritual sipping of water).
Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "If, while engaged in serving food, one should touch something defiled..."
Having placed that substance on the ground and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should proceed once again.
Thus it is said.
If the intention were to describe the purification of the person, the mention of "taking hold of the object with the hand" would be redundant;
therefore, purification of the object occurs merely by setting it down, while the person is purified by sipping water (ācamana).

As for the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the object mentioned in another Smṛti—"An object becomes pure by being set on the ground and then sprinkled"—that should be understood as referring specifically to edible cooked substances.

But how is a distinction understood in a sūtra that is otherwise identical—namely, that one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) after setting [the object] down, and not without setting it down? It is said in reply: if the intention were simply to sip water without setting [the object] down, then only this much would need to be stated: "One who has something other than a substance in hand should sip water while being impure"; for what purpose would the mention of "setting down" serve? Therefore, because of this addition in the sūtra, it is understood that the position requiring the setting down is indeed intended.
As for that which was stated by Manu:
If one who holds a substance in his hand should somehow be touched by something defiled by food remnants,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that substance down.
Thus it is said.
This should be understood as referring to substances that are not fit for consumption.
Thus, in the case of edible substances such as unripe plantains and the like, purification occurs merely by setting them aside;
whereas in the case of those that have been ripened, purification occurs by placing them on the ground and sprinkling them with water.
For substances that cannot be consumed, such as clothing and the like, purification is achieved by not setting them down and performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Now he states the purification of substances: GautDhS 1.31: "The purification of metallic, earthen, wooden, and woven-fiber vessels consists of scrubbing, burning, scraping, and washing."
The purification of substances such as those made of metal is achieved through methods such as scrubbing, performed in their proper sequence.
Once their status as substances is established, the specific mention of them as "substances" is for the purpose of indicating their capacity to accomplish their own respective functions;
consequently, broken vessels and the like do not undergo purification.
Those things which are made from fire as their material cause are "fiery" (*taijasa*), such as gold and the like.
Regarding those fiery objects that are smeared with food-leavings:
why is this so? Because for objects defiled by urine and the like, another method of purification is prescribed in other Smṛtis.

Likewise, the *Uśanasa-smṛti* states: "For metallic objects defiled by urine, feces, semen, or a corpse, there shall be scrubbing, scraping, and wiping twenty-one times with ashes; for non-metallic objects defiled in this manner, there shall be discarding. Similarly, regarding an object defiled by the impurities of another's body, the *Kaṇva-smṛti* begins its statement: "For objects defiled by phlegm and the like, purification is achieved through twenty-one wipes."

Accordingly, the statement of Auśanasa is appropriately introduced regarding those defiled by untouchables or by food-leavings: "For things defiled by *anuloma* Śūdras, dogs, or crows, there is scraping; for those defiled by touchables among the *pratilomas*, there is wiping twenty-one times; for those defiled by untouchables, there is overturning.

Likewise, the statement of Śaṅkha is introduced regarding things defiled by meat or blood: "Substances for purification include earth, bricks, the paste of *iṅguda*, *bilva*, and mustard seeds, cow's urine, cow dung, and so forth."

Likewise, there is the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "In the case of vessels defiled by a menstruating woman or other impurities, purification occurs by immersing them in *pañcagavya* for one day and scrubbing them twenty-one times.
Similarly, other methods of purification have been prescribed in other Smṛtis for metallic objects defiled by various types of impurities.
Therefore, it is logical to conclude that in this context, the rule applies specifically to those [metallic vessels] smeared with food-leavings.

The wiping of those [utensils] smeared with food-remnants should be done all around, on every side, with ashes. This applies to earthenware—that is, objects made of clay—which have been defiled by contact with the untouchable.
Why? Because a specific rule is seen in another Smṛti text.
Likewise, there is the statement of Uśanas: "For earthen vessels smeared with food-leavings, there is wiping; for those touched by leavings, there is sprinkling.
Similarly, there is the statement of Vasiṣṭha:
"By wine, urine, and feces, and by phlegm, pus, tears, and blood..."
An earthen vessel that has been touched [by an impure substance] cannot be purified by baking it again.
Thus, the abandonment of items defiled by liquor and the like has been stated;
however, in this context, it is more logical to apply this rule only to those things contaminated by Caṇḍālas and others.
"Pradāha" means burning thoroughly—that is, the restoration of the original nature [of the object].

For wooden items such as seats, beds, and the like, which have been defiled by impure substances (aṇehya) and so forth, purification consists of planing or thinning them down to the extent that they were affected.
For those touched by the untouchable (aspṛśya), purification is by sprinkling (prokṣaṇa). Why? Because of the statement of Manu: "Sprinkling is for solid objects."

For those things that can be washed, washing is prescribed—namely, for woven items made of threads, such as products of cotton and the like, when defiled by contact with the untouchable. Regarding defilement by impurity (*mala*), another Smṛti text should be consulted: "Washing, cutting out that specific part, or discarding [the item]."

The statement of Paiṭhīnasi is: "Of garments and the like that have been defiled by impurities (mala) and so forth. Likewise, one should observe the rules stated by Manu, such as: "Of silk cloths [one should use] wood-apples (śrīphala). Regarding many garments defiled by those who are untouchable (aspṛśya), there is sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), because Manu has prescribed purification for many grains and clothes by means of sprinkling alone: "Of many grains and clothes... Therefore, for a small number [of garments] defiled by the untouchable, there is washing (nirṇejana).
Like fire, [the perception of] stones, gems, conch shells, and mother-of-pearl [occurs]. (Gautama Sūtra 1.32)
The purification of stones and the like is like that of metallic objects;
this extension [of the rule] is for the purpose of referring to the purification mentioned in other Smṛtis.
Regarding stones and gems, it is heard [in scripture]:
An unblemished golden vessel is purified by water alone,
as are those made of lotus-fiber, stone, and silver, provided they have not been chemically treated.
And for conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and gems, purification is by means of cow urine or water.
Thus says the statement of Manu;
"By means of milk, [the purity] of conch-shells and mother-of-pearl," thus says the statement of Paiṭhīnasi.
In the case of bone and earth, [the purification is] like that of wood. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.33)
Bone refers to substances fit for common use, such as ivory and the like.

By stating that "land, houses, and so forth are like wood"—thereby applying an extension (*atideśa*) based on the material substance—he makes this known: that whatever impurity (*śauca*) is prescribed for a derivative product (*vikāra*), that same [impurity] applies to its constituent material substance (*prakṛtidravya*) as well. Otherwise, he would have had to say "like wooden objects" (*dāravavat*).
The extension [of the rule] to the cases of bones and the earth has the purpose of referring to what is taught in another Smṛti;
and thus the extension refers to what is taught in another Smṛti.
Accordingly, there is another Smṛti—the statement of Kaṇva: "The purification of bones and the earth that have been touched by those who are untouchable is achieved through sprinkling."
And the sowing of seeds upon the ground. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.34)
The mention of "ground" (bhūmi) is for the purpose of excluding bones.
From the *Cakora*, those [rules] mentioned in other Smṛtis should also be understood.
Thus it was said by Vasiṣṭha:
The earth is purified by four means: by digging, by burning, by plowing with cattle, and also by smearing; and by a fifth, by plastering.
Thus it is said;
and likewise Manu states:
"By sweeping, by sprinkling, by burning, and by scraping..."
And the ground is purified by the five methods, including the dwelling of cows.
Thus,
purification should be performed according to the nature of the stain, either by means of an alternative or by a combination of methods.
[The purification] of cloth, ropes, split bamboo, and leather [is by sprinkling]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.35)
A rope is made from *darbha* grass and the like;

a wicker-work (*vidala*) is made from bamboo, peacock feathers, and so forth; and leather is tiger-skin and the like. Regarding these when touched by those who are untouchable, purification is the same as for cloth—that is, as for garments.
By the word "leather" (*carman*), through the inclusion of the material source, its derivatives are also included.
There is an extension of this rule even to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of ropes and the like for the purpose of their admission [into the ritual].
Therefore, even the sprinkling of those things touched by the untouchable (*aspṛśya*) must be performed.
And so says Paiṭhīnasi: "The purification of ropes, split bamboo, and leather that have been touched by the untouchable is achieved through sprinkling."
Or there is the discarding of those that are utterly defiled.
Or there may be the relinquishing of ropes and so forth;
this is a conventional distinction.
Therefore, there is the relinquishing of those that are utterly ruined.
This is the purification for others.
Now, since it has been stated, "One who has something in hand or is impure from eating should set it down and perform ācamana," he speaks with the intention of prescribing that rite of sipping water:
"One should begin the purification facing either the east or the north. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.37)
"Facing east or north" is an option according to one's preference.
Now, an objection may be raised: "The mention of 'purity' (śauca) is redundant, because the author will state later, 'having performed the ācamana,' and by that alone the purpose is accomplished.
It is replied: This is stated so that one should perform other ancillaries of purity (*śaucāṅga*) while facing this very direction as well.

And thus, one should perform even such acts as the washing of the feet while facing that very direction. The word "should begin" is intended to convey the state of being composed; therefore, until the completion of the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana), one should remain with an undistracted mind for that entire duration.

Seated in a clean place, having placed his right arm between his knees, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, having washed his hands up to the wrists, and remaining silent, he should sip water three or four times so that it touches his heart. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.38)
"In a clean place" means in a spot that is not defiled;
and thus, the washing of the feet is also established by implication, lest the place itself become impure through contact with the impure feet.
And so says Vasiṣṭha: "Having washed both feet and the hands up to the wrists";
[he should do this] while sitting only, not in any other posture.
And so says Vasiṣṭha: "One should not sip water while walking, standing, lying down, or bowing."
Having placed the right arm between the knees;
"yajñopavītī" means that even if one happens to be sitting without the sacred thread, one must nevertheless necessarily be wearing the sacred thread during the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

And likewise Āpastamba says: "In the service of gurus, elders, and guests; during the fire-oblation, the rite of recitation, eating, sipping water, and Vedic study, one should wear the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder.
This is either for the purpose of making the *yajñopavīta* a constituent part of the act of sipping water (*ācamana*), or for the purpose of producing another sacrificial thread.
And so says Vasiṣṭha:
For those who have completed their studies (snātakas), there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper garment;
two sacred threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water.
Thus it is said.

The place where the jewel (maṇi) is bound is the "wrist" (maṇibandha). Having washed his hands from that wrist down, he should, with speech restrained and silently, touch his heart—that is, apply water reaching to the heart.
This is for the purpose of defining the quantity of water.
They should be of such a quantity as to submerge a bean;
thus Uśanas says: "They should reach the heart, being of the measure that submerges a bean.
Regarding the option of "three times or four times," the rule is established as follows: when one sips water after reciting the mantra beginning with "May the waters purify," then it is four times.

"Except for the three [substances]" means that the mention of water is for the purpose of excluding cow-urine and the like; otherwise, because they share the common quality of being causes of purification, they might be included.
Alternatively, it is for the purpose of excluding hot water, bubbles, foam, decoctions, and so forth.
Where one might have simply said "he should drink" (*pibet*), the teacher has composed the sūtra as "he should sip water" (*ācāmet*) in order to include other related injunctions.

Regarding this, Uśanas says: "Having placed the palm of the right hand in the shape of a cow's ear, he should drink silently through the *brāhma* *tīrtha*, meditating upon the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas."
One should wipe [the mouth] twice. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.39)
The lips are the natural [tīrtha], because it is not mentioned here and because it is seen in other Smṛtis; this is by means of the Brāhma-tīrtha alone.
The prefix *pari* is intended to include other related rules.
Regarding this, Kaṇva has stated: "While meditating upon the Atharvaveda, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas, one should wipe the hairy part of the lips with the Brāhma-tīrtha."
And he should sprinkle water on his feet. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.40)
By the use of the word "ca" (and), the mouth is also included.
The prefix "abhi" is intended to include other alternative rules.
Regarding this, Bhārgava says: "Then one should wipe the lips and the mouth."
One should wipe the fire, then meditate on Agni; thereafter, one should sprinkle water on the feet while meditating on Viṣṇu.
And one should touch the cavities of the head. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.41)
The apertures in the head are the eyes, nose, and ears;
by the word "and" (ca), the heart is also included.
And so Manu says:
One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should touch the cavities with water, as well as the self, the heart, and the head.
Thus [it is said].

The prefix *upa-* is for the purpose of including other methods. Thus, having meditated on the sun and moon as the two eyes while touching them with the thumb and the ring finger, and having touched [the face] thereafter; having meditated on the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) as the two nostrils while touching them with the index finger and the thumb, and having touched [the face] thereafter; having meditated on the quarters of space as the two ears while touching them with the little finger and the thumb, and having touched [the face] thereafter; one should touch the heart with the thumb alone, meditating upon the Self (*ātman*). Thus it is said.
And one should place it upon the head. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.42)
If it were intended that [the water] should be placed on the head, the inclusion of the word "should give" (dadyāt) would be for the purpose of including all the fingers;
thus another Smṛti says: "Having meditated on Śrī with all the fingers, one should cast [the water] upon the head.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is also [to be done] on the left hand.
And so Vasiṣṭha says: "And one should place [the water] on the head and in the left hand.

Since no specific exception is mentioned for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, this same method of sipping applies to them as well. Furthermore, because another Smṛti states, "Women and Śūdras [should sip] once each," it should be understood that for women and Śūdras, purification is achieved by drinking once and touching the lips once, even though this is not explicitly stated here.
Rinsing the mouth is not required solely upon contact with food remnants; he now states other occasions for rinsing the mouth:
"After sleeping, after eating, and after sneezing. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.43)

The repetition [of the word "again"] is for the purpose of indicating that one should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) both at the beginning and at the end; by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is also implied after bathing and weeping.
Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Having slept, eaten, sneezed, bathed, drunk, or wept, one who has already sipped water should sip water again."
If it is argued that because the time of hunger is uncertain, sipping water (ācamana) is impossible at the outset, even in that case the undertaking [of the rule] is for the sake of constant purity.
As Āpastamba has said: "One should not remain impure even for a moment, provided one is capable.
For even one who is already pure must perform sipping water after sleep and so forth, by virtue of the force of the initial undertaking [of the rule].

Therefore, one should perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) both at the beginning and at the end of that meal; regarding this meal, some authorities maintain that one should perform *ācamana* twice even at the very beginning.
Thus says Āpastamba: "One who is about to eat, being pure, should sip water twice.
Others, however, maintain that one should perform *ācamana* twice only at the end, as Hośanā states:

"Having slept, eaten, sneezed, bathed, drunk, or wept, one who has sipped water (ācānta) should sip water again twice. Thus, it is established as the settled conclusion that there are two sippings of water at the beginning and end of a meal; one at the beginning and two at the end of sleep and so forth; and for one who has sneezed, because it is not fixed [in timing], there are two only at the end.
Now, since impurity would otherwise result from contact with food remnants, he says: "Regarding what clings to the teeth, it is like the teeth themselves, except when touched by the tongue."
The meaning is that when parts of food— whether solid or soft— are caught between the teeth, one does not become "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa),
provided they are not touched by the tongue.
Regarding this as well, some say: "prior to falling away" (Gautama Sūtra 1.44).
Some maintain that even when there is contact with the tongue, one remains pure as long as [the substances] do not fall from their place.
One should know that when [insects] have fallen [into food], it is like [the case of] the outflows; one becomes pure simply by swallowing it. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.46)
Just as water that has fallen into the mouth from an impure source becomes pure upon being swallowed,
so too there is no suspicion of needing to perform ritual rinsing (*ācamana*). This is the meaning.
In this way, even while swallowing saliva, one remains pure;
for why else would it be stated that "one is pure when swallowing what has fallen [from the teeth]," beginning with the rule "one should know it to be like saliva"?
Gautama, however, maintains that one becomes impure when there is contact with the tongue of particles stuck between the teeth.
"But according to another opinion, it is prior to death.
This is a settled alternative: for one authorized to perform ritual acts, there is sipping of water (ācamana), but not for anyone else.

Just as a fragment of food residue that has fallen outside renders one impure, so too would it follow for secretions; therefore, he says: "Droplets that do not fall upon the body do not, in their primary sense, make one impure. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.47)

The term *mukhya* means "belonging to the mouth"; these refer to the droplets (*vipruṣ*) which are constituent parts of the nasal discharge. When they issue forth from one who is reciting a mantra, they do not cause a state of ritual impurity (*aprāyatya*) provided they do not fall upon a limb such as the breast or the belly.

The word *ni* signifies certainty; therefore, it is certain that if they fall upon a limb, they cause impurity at that very moment, and not merely by the possibility [of their falling]. Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is this: a constituent part of the discharge causes impurity wherever it may fall, whereas the discharge itself [causes impurity] only when it falls upon a limb.
Now this is stated for the sake of all forms of purification: "Purification consists in the removal of stains and odors from that which is smeared with impurities. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.48)
When the removal of stains and odors has been accomplished, that which was smeared with impurity or connected with impurity becomes pure;
by the word "impurity" (amedhya), the twelve types of impurities are meant.
As Manu said: "Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, nasal mucus, earwax, excrement, phlegm, tears, and rheum— these twelve are the impurities of human beings."
The mention of "smearing" (*lepa*) is because phlegm and other such substances, whose odors are not manifest, are seen merely as smears.
The mention of "odor" (*gandha*) is because urine and other such substances do not have smears perceived, but their odor alone is perceived.

Furthermore, the repetition of the word "purity" (*śauca*) in the section on purification is for the purpose of indicating that even metallic objects and the like attain purity only through the removal of both smears and odors.
To the question "By what means should that be done?", he says:
"That [is done] with water, and first with earth. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.49)
That purification is first with water, then with earth;
by the use of "and" (ca), it is then with both.
The mention of "that" (tat) is for the purpose of removing even the remnants of food (annalepa) with powder and the like.

Although it could have been stated simply as "with that [water] and with clay," the inclusion of the word "prior" (pūrva) is for the purpose of indicating that where no significant residue is observed, purification is by water alone; as Manu says:
"A gold vessel free from residue is purified by water alone, as are those made of stone, silver, and unadorned [vessels]."
Thus it is said.
Alternatively, this is for the purpose of establishing that wherever purification is prescribed, there purification must first be performed with water alone.

Just as [the rule] "with earth and water" implies a conjunction, so too the use of the non-compound (visamāsa) here implies a conjunction with ashes and other substances as well, since those materials such as *taijasa* (metallic) have already been mentioned. This purification should be understood to apply to a part of the body smeared with impure matter (*amedhya*).
And in the presence of urine, feces, semen, exudations, and the act of eating; Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.50.
The word *ca* (and) serves to draw in [the rule for] sipping water (*ācamana*).
*Visraṃsana* means casting out; it is connected individually with urine, feces, and oily substances.
*Abhyavahārasaṃyoga* is the consumption of edible substances.

Because that [food] is impure, this statement is intended for the purpose of removing stains and odors; since the requirement for sipping water (*ācamana*) is already established by the rule "having slept or having eaten," one should effect the removal of stains and odors by washing with earth and water.
And thus, what was stated in the verse "first with water" regarding the removal of food-stains by means of powder and the like should be understood as impossible in this case.
Alternatively, even the mention of contact with food is introduced solely for the purpose of [indicating when] sipping water is required.

The phrase "having slept or eaten" is restated as already established for the sake of indicating the sequence. How so? By the mention of that [washing], the removal of food-stains is indicated; the purpose is that one should rinse the mouth (*ācamet*) only after first performing that removal. Otherwise, there would be doubt. Thus says Āpastamba: "Having voided urine or feces, having washed away the stains of urine and feces, the stains of food, the stains of food-leavings, and whatever stains of semen there may be, and having washed his feet and rinsed his mouth, he becomes pure."
Urine and feces are well known.
"Sneha" refers to semen.

The mention of urine and the other substances is for the purpose of [prescribing] sipping water (ācamana), since the removal of stains and odors is already established by the rule: "Purity consists in the removal of stains and odors."
And where the sacred tradition (āmnāya) may enjoin [a practice]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.51)
In that context, the remainder of the sense is "that very thing remains as it is.

*Āmnāya* means the Veda; where, in the domain of sacrifice, it prescribes purification by the mere washing of the wooden sword (*sphya*) and other implements, there that very [prescription] applies, and not [purification] such as carving based on the commonality of being wood. If it is argued that this is already established because of their unequal strength, [the answer is: this statement is made for the purpose of ensuring that what is declared in the Śruti does not intrude into the worldly domain. Just as in the case of the sacrificial ladle (*darvī*), purification by washing is prescribed by Śruti in the context of sacrifice, so too, even when that [rule] is operative in the worldly sphere...
This introduction is for the purpose that one should not perform what is prescribed by the Śruti merely because it is common to all mendicants (darvī), but rather what is prescribed by the Smṛti;
or else, by the word "Āmnāya," Manu is meant—
wherever he may prescribe purification, that alone [should be followed], as in the passage beginning, "But for ascetics, fourfold [the usual amount]," and so forth.
If it is argued that there is no doubt precisely because it has been so stated, we reply: regarding a subject on which nothing is said, the rule from another Smṛti applies;

however, where something such as the removal of stains and odors is mentioned, a suspicion arises that there may be an option (vikalpa) with another Smṛti. To dispel that, it is stated: "And where the Veda prescribes [a rule]. Thus, even when the removal of stains and odors has been performed, one must still resort to rules such as "the penance for a student is double."
Now, he states the rule for approaching the teacher for the purpose of study by the student who has performed his purification:
"Having grasped the left hand [of the teacher] except for the thumb, he should address the teacher, saying: 'Recite, sir! (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.52).
Having grasped with his right hand the left hand of the teacher—the instructor—excluding the thumb, he should request the teacher, saying, "Recite, sir!
The mention of the hand is for the purpose of excluding the feet;
since the context concerns the hand, it is understood that "the left [hand]" refers specifically to the left hand.
The grasping is understood to be at the region of the fingers, because it has been stated that the thumb is not included.
Furthermore, in that regard, the eye is the mind. (Gautama Sūtra 1.53)
The meaning is that one should fix the eyes and the mind upon the guru there.
Furthermore:
the touching of the vital breaths [is performed] with *darbha* grass. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.54)
The word "kāryam" (should be done) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Since direct contact with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is impossible, the term "prāṇa" here refers to the sense organs located in the head, such as the eyes and so forth.
One should touch them with *darbha* grass, following the sequence prescribed for the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*).
Furthermore:
"The three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) consist of fifteen measures (mātrās). (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.55)

The word "should be performed" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the restraint of the breath, remaining without inhalation; these three should be performed, each consisting of fifteen *mātrās*.
What is called a *mātrā* is well-known in the world by the term "middle finger and thumb."
Furthermore:
"And the seat should have its blades pointing eastward. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.56)
On seats with their tips pointing eastward—by implication, on *darbha* grass—the act of sitting, that is, taking one's seat, is to be performed; this is the remainder [of the sentence].
By the word "and" (*ca*), the use of *darbha* strainers for the breaths is also included.
Furthermore:
"The five Vyāhṛtis preceded by Oṃ and ending with Satya. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.57)
The word "should be cited" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Each [of these] begins with the *praṇava* (OM), consists of the three worlds starting with *bhūḥ*, has *puruṣa* in the middle, and ends with *satya*.
Thus it is well known in the *Jābāli-śruti*.
Furthermore:
"In the morning, one should perform the clasping of the teacher's feet. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.58)
The word "kāryam" (should be done) is understood as the ellipsis.
Although one might have said "upasaṅgrahaṇam" (clasping), the use of the term "pāda" (feet) is for the purpose of including the rules taught in other Smṛtis.
As Manu says:
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.
Thus it is said.
Rising day after day at dawn,
one should perform the touching of the vital breaths (prāṇopasparśana) for oneself before the formal reception of the teacher, lest it be performed in his presence.
Furthermore:
"And at the beginning and end of the recitation of the Veda, [one should perform the *brahmayajña*]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.59)
"At the beginning and end of the Vedic recitation" means at its commencement and conclusion;
the word "ca" (and) serves to include the clasping of the feet.
Furthermore:
Having been permitted, he should sit facing east; the disciple should sit to his right, facing either north or east. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.60)

Instructed by the teacher, he should sit to the south of him, facing either east or north; the option depends on what is possible. The meaning is that he should sit facing either east or north in such a way that he is turned toward the teacher while the teacher is seated.
How so? Because it has been stated, "there, with a fourfold mind.
The mention of the "disciple" (śiṣya) is for the purpose of making known that this same rule applies to anyone else who has approached [the teacher].

The phrase "permitted [to sit] on the right" is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (niyama), meaning that one should not sit down without being permitted, nor [sit] anywhere other than on the right.
Furthermore:
"And the Sāvitrī is to be recited at the beginning when undertaking the Veda. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.61)
The Sāvitrī begins with "tat savituḥ" and so forth; by the word "and" (ca), the Vyāhṛtis preceded by the syllable Oṃ are also included.
And thus says Manu:
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable Oṃ,
together with the three-footed Gāyatrī, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
Thus [it is said].
The recitation is to be studied.
"At the taking up of the Veda" means at the commencement of the Veda, that is, at the time of beginning its study;
"from the beginning" means previously.
Furthermore:
"The syllable Oṃ [is used] elsewhere as well. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.62)
After the recitation, the syllable *oṃ* should also be uttered elsewhere. Herein is the sequence:

having risen in the morning, one should perform the clasping of the teacher's feet; being called by him, one should sit upon *darbha* grass. Then, there is the touching of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with *darbha* blades. After performing the breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and reciting the five Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), one should address the teacher with joined palms, saying, "Recite, sir! Having then recited the Utterances preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and the *Sāvitrī*, one should study the text preceded by the *praṇava*.

Why is this rule [stated] specifically in the first chapter? Because, although one could have simply said, "Having taught the Sāvitrī, he should thereafter study," the text begins with "the taking up of the Veda from the beginning.
Furthermore, it is stated that every day one should utter only the syllable *oṃ*;
why? Because it has been stated elsewhere that the syllable *oṃ* [is used for other purposes].
"Except for the first chapter"—
the word "also" (api) indicates that the insertion of the *praṇava* applies even in the first chapter.
Some, by the phrase "even elsewhere," maintain that the *praṇava* should be used at the beginning of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and so forth.
Furthermore, if one has sexual intercourse in between, there must be a renewed initiation.

If someone should pass between those who are studying, then for the sake of expiation, one must again perform the entire procedure beginning with the clasping of the feet and ending with the utterance of the *praṇava*.

Although this occurs outside of the formal context (*aprakaraṇe*), the expiation is prescribed so that the study may continue without interruption. This rule applies to humans; for others, it is mentioned subsequently.
Since there is no mention of a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) here, one should study immediately after the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
The repetition [of the term] refers to the initial commencement of study, because in other cases there is no formal sitting down (*upasadana*).
Therefore, in other instances, the sitting down must be performed solely for the purpose of expiation, and study should be undertaken immediately thereafter.
Likewise, Āpastamba says: "Having said, 'Recite, sir,' one should either study or teach."
Furthermore:
For dogs, mongooses, snakes, frogs, and cats, there shall be a fast for three days and a period of staying away from home. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.64)
These are well-known.

For each of these, such as dogs and so forth, the penance is the abandonment of food for three days. "Separation from the teacher" (vipravāsa) refers to remaining in the absence of the teacher for one day;
and thus, by the very instruction regarding separation from the teacher, the suspension of study (anadhyāya) for one day is established.

If it is asked, "Why is there learning for only one day? [the answer is: because of the irregularity. Otherwise, he would have stated that there is fasting and staying away for three days. Therefore, the suspension of study lasts for only one day.

And so Manu says: "In the case of passing between [the teacher and pupil] when cattle, frogs, cats, dogs, snakes, or mongooses are present, one should know that there is no study for a day and a night."
Thus it is said.

Thus, here too, the mention of the dog is an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*) for four-footed animals (*catuṣpada-paśu*), since the cat is included within the category of four-footed animals. However, the cat is mentioned again for the purpose of prescribing a more severe penance (*prāyaścitta-gaurava*).
As Uśanas says: "If one approaches a female cat, one should consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*) for three days and fast."
The particle *ca* serves the purpose of drawing in the act of approaching [the teacher].
Therefore, having performed that [approaching] at the time of study, one should study.
Some say that fasting and the abandonment of study [are required].
Whether that is logical or illogical must be investigated.
Furthermore:
"For others, there are breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and the consumption of clarified butter. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.65)
For others, such as crows and the like, there are three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), because of the hearing of the plural number.
The consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*) consists merely of bathing the body.
The word "and" (*ca*) has the purpose of drawing in [the requirement of] approaching the teacher (*upasadana*).

Then, having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), consumed clarified butter, and performed the formal sitting (upasadana), he should study, since no specific days of non-study (anadhyāya) have been mentioned.
And likewise regarding study near a cremation ground, and likewise regarding study near a cremation ground. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.66)
Āpastamba has stated that one should not study within the range of a *śamyā*-throw from any side;
therefore, studying in its vicinity constitutes "studying at a cremation ground.
The prefix *abhi-* is intended to indicate that this is done intentionally.
Therefore, in a case where [the act] was unintentional, another expiation that is lighter should be observed.
Thus Uśanas says: "If one studies in a cremation ground without prior intention, he should study after saying, 'Recite, sir!

By the word *ca* ("and"), there is the application of everything previously mentioned, such as the *praṇāyāma*; by the word *evam* ("thus"), the application of only the *upasadana* (approaching) mentioned immediately before is effected.
If it is argued that, in that case, only the word *evaṃ* (thus) should be stated, we say no; for this meaning is obtained from both words together.
How so? When either the word *evaṃ* or the word *ca* (and) ought to be stated, it is logical to assume a different purpose for the recitation of both, rather than for only one.
Therefore, the act of approaching (*upasadana*) must indeed be performed.

And so another Smṛti states: "Having studied near a cremation ground, one should restrain the breath, perform the ritual touching of the vital breaths (prāṇopasparśana), offer salutation, and recite the Sāvitrī," and so forth.
The repetition [of the concluding statement] is for the purpose of marking the end of the chapter.
All this expiation (prāyaścitta) mentioned above applies only to the student, because the study and other such acts are for his sake.

Furthermore, in all cases, the expiation consists precisely in approaching [the teacher]; "approaching," however, refers to salutation and so forth, and such salutation is not possible toward one's own teacher.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Maskarīya Gautama-bhāṣya.
The second chapter:
The initiation ceremony for the twice-born has been described.

Since it is maintained by some that even prior to initiation (*upanayana*), these [members of the first three classes] possess entitlement to certain duties of their respective castes (*varṇadharma*), he says the following for that purpose:
"Prior to initiation, one may act, speak, and eat according to one's desire" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.1).
But surely this should have been stated even before initiation; in that case, it would not be necessary to say "prior to initiation."
It is said: This is true;
however, the purpose for stating the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) at the beginning has already been explained.
It is not enjoined by this [text], because it is already established by the sense of the matter.

Nor is it a restrictive injunction (*niyama*), because there is no obligation that must necessarily be performed; for it will be stated later that "the rule begins with initiation (*upanayana*"), and because [the action] is not merely optional (*pākṣika*).

Nor is it an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*), because there is nothing to be excluded; for [in this case], conduct such as acting according to one's own desire has not been previously established [as a possibility].
Therefore, this sūtra is explanatory (anuvādaka), intended to make known the absence of both expiation and royal punishment, since those two have been taught in a general sense.
But surely, royal punishments and penances are prescribed for the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is forbidden;
yet this [person] has no entitlement (adhikāra) under either injunctions or prohibitions. Nor does he have an entitlement under injunctions or prohibitions.
Furthermore, neither an injunction nor a prohibition for this [act] is heard in scripture;

nor is it the case that its being unoffered and so forth will be enjoined or prohibited such that both [results] would follow upon its transgression, because of the instruction regarding the ancestors and others.
Therefore, this sūtra is purposeless.

To this it is replied: whatever expiation has been prescribed for the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is forbidden, or whatever royal punishment [is ordained], both of these certainly apply to him as well.

Even though no specific injunction or prohibition is heard with reference to him alone, nevertheless, that which is stated in general terms—such as "non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing"—applies to him too because it constitutes the duty of his caste (varṇadharma).
Upon its transgression, both royal punishment and expiation occur.
Therefore, in order to remove that [misconception], the sūtra has been commenced in the form of a restatement (anuvāda).

By this sūtra, "The rule begins with the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*)," it will be stated that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies only to the transgression of those injunctions prescribed starting from the initiation ceremony, and not to the transgression of others.

By that very principle, it can be understood that there is an absence of expiation for the transgression of the duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*), as well as an absence of royal punishment.
