Nevertheless, this Sūtra has been commenced for the following purposes: first, for one who has passed the time for the regular initiation (*upanayana*) and possesses a distinct intellect but remains capable, so that he may enter into half of the penance (*prāyaścitta*) after the eleventh year and before the sixteenth; second, for the sake of the father and others entering into the penance after five years and before that [sixteenth]; and third, to demonstrate the absence of fault in cases prior to that.
Thus, it is stated in the Bhārgavīya:
"He whose years are eighty, or a boy less than sixteen..."
Women and those who are afflicted by disease deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
For one who is less than eleven years of age but more than five years old,
a friend or a teacher should perform the penance for the sake of purification.
Therefore, there is no offense whatsoever for one who is even more ignorant than that;
consequently, neither royal punishment nor penance is prescribed for him.
Thus it is said.

And thus, although it is generally appropriate for one to act according to one's own will prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), nevertheless, absolute freedom of action exists only until the age of five; thereafter, the child must be directed toward the duties of his social class (*varṇadharma*) by his father and others, because scriptural authority is heard regarding the penance required for the parents and others if they fail in this duty while the child is still young.
Enough of this digression.

Now the Sūtra is being explained: prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), there is freedom of action (*kāmacāra*) and movement according to one's will. Therefore, regarding the touching of a *caṇḍāla* and so forth, he will state that "mere sprinkling" (*prokṣaṇa*) is required—as in the phrase "from [the age of] sprinklings"—and it has been stated that even this applies only before the fifth year.
Beyond that, upon touching a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, one must be bathed.
From the eleventh year onwards, one should bathe by oneself.
Thus it is in all cases:
one who speaks according to desire speaks even what is vulgar and the like;
one who sides with desire eats even what is stale and the like.
After five years, [the boy] should be made to perform those duties that do not conflict with the dharma of his caste (*varṇadharma*).
The phrase "prior to initiation" (*upanayanāt prāk*) includes even the initiation performed in times of distress (*āpadkalpa-upanayana*).
Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) [in the text], namely the term *brahmacārī*.

Since it is already established that no deviation from celibacy is possible prior to the period of lifelong studenthood (*nityakāla*), the instruction to protect celibacy would be purposeless. He himself will provide an example of unrestrained conduct later, stating: "He becomes one who voids urine and excrement wherever he happens to be. Therefore, even during the state of extreme childhood, one must strive to prevent him from committing such acts as the killing of a Brahmin.

In matters of speech such as false accusation and the like, and regarding the consumption of food such as drinking *surā* liquor and so forth, one must strive to restrain [the child] even during the state of extreme childhood; for although this is already established by the phrase "acting according to desire" (*kāmacāra*), the repetition of "speech" and "eating" is for emphasis.

While it would have been sufficient to say "from initiation" (*upanayanāt*), the inclusion of the word "prior" (*prāk*) is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that [the state of] acting according to desire and so forth applies only prior to initiation.

If this restriction were not present, then by the rule "and this is not inconsistent with the subsequent [stages]," the prohibition of eating the remnants of oblations and other such rules would apply even to ascetics (*yatins*).
Now he states an exception regarding the consumption of food obtained through begging:
"A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) [may eat] from what has not been offered as a sacrificial oblation. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.2)

The term *hutam* refers to what has been offered, such as the *caru*, *puroḍāśa*, and so forth, which remains after the offering; it does not refer to the remnants of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, because that is intended for all purposes.
Thus Āpastamba says: "One should make all [deities] sharers in the *vaiśvadeva*.
The phrase "it should be done from the *ahuta*" implies that the remainder is to be used.
This prohibition regarding one who has attained wealth is an instruction for fathers and others, because a child lacks discernment;
it is stated that from the age of eleven years onwards, the authority belongs to the child himself.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī). // Gautama 2.3 //
One must practice the preservation of celibacy.
Now he states an illustration of acting according to one's own will: "He passes urine and excrement wherever it may happen. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.4)
The meaning is that just as urine and feces are produced even when one is being dragged along with one's head wrapped up, or while standing, so too one should do it right there.
Furthermore, no rule for sipping water (ācamana) applies to him. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.5)

From the age of five until before the eleventh year, the rule for *ācamana*—the ritual procedure for sipping water—is not prescribed. Because of this prohibition regarding the specific rules (*kalpa*), it is understood that there is merely the act of sipping water itself.

In this regard, since another *smṛti* states, "Indeed, he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born through the Veda," and because his duties are heard to be identical to those of a Śūdra, his *ācamana* should be observed as being like that of a Śūdra.

Why is it said "of one less than eleven years"? Because the text begins with the word "his" (*asya*); because it is heard that there is no fault prior to five years; and because from the eleventh year onwards, he is entitled to the duties of his caste (*varṇadharma*).
It is understood, therefore, that even the ritual procedure for sipping water (*ācamana*) exists for him from the eleventh year onwards.
Now, regarding the very young child, he says:
"Except for wiping, rubbing, and sprinkling. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.6)
The phrase "is not found for him" continues [from the previous context].
The meaning is that for this child under five years of age, no other method of purification exists apart from wiping and so forth.
"Wiping" (*apamārjana*) refers to the removal of food remnants from the mouth with the hand moistened with water.
Washing (*prakṣālana*) refers to cleansing after urination, defecation, and so forth;

sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) refers to the ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) upon touching a *caṇḍāla* or similar person. Since such contact does not occur [in his case], "the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*) does not exist for him."

If it is argued that the non-performance of these two prohibitions—namely, "except for wiping, washing, and sprinkling"—would follow [as a consequence], this is not a fault. By the rule "the procedure for sipping water (ācamana) is not prescribed for him," the procedure for sipping water is enjoined for one under sixteen years of age by way of prohibition;
whereas by the rule "except for wiping, washing, and sprinkling," the wiping and so forth are enjoined for one under five years of age by way of prohibiting other methods of purification.
Furthermore:
"There is no impurity resulting from touching that [corpse]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.7)
By the mention of "that," one who has not yet performed purification is meant.
Through the touch of such a person who has not performed purification, or through being touched by him, impurity does not arise [in the object]. This rule applies specifically to very young children.

In that case, the prescription for purification would be useless; why? Because only two purposes for the prescription of purification are observed: to make one fit for contact with others and for the performance of religious rites.
However, this [wind] does not serve the purpose of making one fit for contact with others, because even one who has not performed purification is fit for contact, according to the statement:
"There is no impurity from touching it."
And it does not exist for the sake of practice, because there is an absence of its practice.
It is not purposeless, because the injunction for purification is for the sake of protection;
likewise, another Smṛti states: "One should perform purification for the protection of a child until the fifth year."
The use of the prefix *upa-* is intended to indicate the absence of fault when touching this very person while he has not yet performed purification;
thus, in the case of touching others who have become impure by food remnants, urine, or feces, one must perform ritual sipping (*ācamana*).
There is no fault in touching that [corpse], because it is enumerated among those touched by a corpse in the *Śavaspṛṣṭi-sūtra*.
Likewise, another *Smṛti* states:
"He who touches one who is impure is indeed defiled alone."
Having touched it, another shall not be defiled; this is the rule regarding all objects.
Thus it is said.

Regarding the touching of a Caṇḍāla, however, he will state in the *Śavaspṛṣṭi-sūtra*: "One should touch him"; yet, where it ought to have been said that "there is no impurity from touching him," the author of the Sūtra composed the rule "not [from] touching him" for the purpose of setting aside even the restriction that applies prior to initiation (*upanayana*).
Consequently, even after initiation, one must perform sipping of water (*ācamana*) upon touching those things rendered impure by food remnants, or urine and feces.
Furthermore:
"But one should not employ him for the Agnihotra sacrifice or for the offering of bali. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.8)
The word "this" (*enam*) is used for the purpose of including everyone who has not yet been initiated (*anupanīta*).

That which is performed in the fire, such as the *agnihotra* oblation and so forth, is the "fire-oblation" (*agnihavana*). That sacrificial food (*bali*) which is offered to the deities of the directions after the *vaiśvadeva* rite is the "offering of bali" (*baliharaṇa*).

The word *tu* expresses a distinction: one should not employ [the mantra] even for the washing of the feet of Brahmins at the Aṣṭakā and other rites, much less specifically for the fire-oblation (*agnihavana*) and the food-offering (*baliharaṇa*).

The word *eva* is used for this purpose: lest one, having learned the mantra anywhere at random due to acting according to one's own will, should proceed to perform the Agnihotra and other rites on one's own initiative; in that case, even the one who authorized it would not be considered its approver.
This statement is intended to enjoin the initiated person (*upanīta*), because there is no possibility of its application elsewhere, and thus it serves as a specific prohibition.

And thus, although according to the Vedic injunction "one who knows [the ritual] should offer the Agnihotra," only one who has heard much (bahuśruta) is qualified, nevertheless, in the absence of such a person, one should employ even one of little learning who has been initiated.
Likewise, Manu says:
"Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool [should perform it]."
One who is neither afflicted by illness nor lacking in sacramental rites should be the performer of the Agnihotra.
Thus it is said.

In that context, since the prohibition [of uninitiated persons] is already established by the very prohibition of those with little learning (*alpavidya*), it has been explained that the specific prohibition "not one who is unrefined" (*nāsaṃskṛta*) is intended to permit even a refined person of little learning, in the absence of any other learned person.
As for what was stated previously regarding "before initiation" (*prāgupanayanāt*) and so forth, that should be understood to apply to women as well, until marriage.
Why? Because another Smṛti text is observed which states: "The rite of marriage is declared to be the initiatory rite (*aupanāyanika*) for women."
In this way, the prohibition of *niyoga* (the practice of levirate) for a maiden is also established regarding the performance of the *agnihotra* and the offering of the *bali*.
Therefore, *niyoga* must be performed after marriage.

In that regard, since it is prohibited for a woman by the Vedic injunction "A woman shall not offer the oblation" (*na strī juhuyāt*) in the case of the *agnihotra*, it should be understood as applying to the *aupāsana* fire and other such rites.
And so another Smṛti states: "One should offer oblations into the *aupāsana* fire and perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice," and so forth.
Furthermore, the prohibition against a "young woman" (*yuvati*) is not a fault, as it refers specifically to the wives of others.
Furthermore:
"One should not utter the word 'brahman' except when offering the *svadhā* libation. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.9)
The word "thus" (evam) is understood to carry over.
By the word "brahman," the Vedas are meant;
therefore, one should not teach him [the Veda].

Since the study of the Veda is enjoined for one who has been initiated by the rule, "After the *upākaraṇa* ceremony, he should study the *chandas*," the prohibition of the uninitiated is already established; therefore, the repeated prohibition of the Veda is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the Veda alone must not be taught. Consequently, there is no fault in teaching the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*).
Furthermore, because of the principle of acting according to one's own will (*kāmacāritva*), one should not even utter a mantra acquired by any other means.
Why? Because of the statement "he should cause [him] to teach," which implies that one should not utter [the mantra] except when specifically commenced [for that purpose].
"Except for the offering of the *svadhā*," meaning excluding the offering of the *svadhā*.
Having said, "The *svadhā* for such-and-such," that which is given to the deceased, such as the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and water, is the "offering of the *svadhā*.
This also serves as an indicative term for the entire ritual performed for the deceased.
And so Vasiṣṭha says: "Except for water-rites, the svadhā-offering, and those connected with the ancestors.

Thus, even when a son exists though he be uninitiated, the funeral rites (pretakriyā) must not be performed by the sapindas and others, lest there be the contingency of the scriptural injunction becoming meaningless.
Having stated [the rules] for one who has not been initiated, he now states those for one who has been initiated:
"The restrictive rule begins with the initiation ceremony. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.10)
The rule that has been stated beginning from the initiation ceremony (upanayana) is designated as a "niyama" (observance).

Thus, in the event of its non-performance, there is an expiation (prāyaścitta), but not for the preceding [acts]. Therefore, starting from this point, the "niyama"—which will be described as the observance of vows (vratadhāraṇa) such as the kindling of the sacred fire (agnīndhana) and so forth—is to be performed beginning with the initiation ceremony.
Furthermore, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been described. (Gautama 2.11)
The inclusion of the word "stated" (ukta) indicates that this [prohibition] is indeed a restrictive rule (*niyama*) prior to initiation (*upanayana*).

Consequently, in the event of a transgression of that rule, even for one who has not been initiated, it should be understood that his eligibility [for Vedic study] is restored solely through the penance for an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken the vow of celibacy).

Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "One who has become corrupted should be initiated after he has been purified by the vow of an *avakīrṇin*, provided he is under seventeen years of age; beyond that age, he must undergo both the *brātya* and *avakīrṇin* vows."

If it is argued that [the prohibition of looking at women and so forth] is already established by implication for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) because of the specific prohibitions against such acts, we say no; for such acts are possible even in the case of animals and the like.
Furthermore:
[The study of] fire, fuel, and the practice of begging for alms. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.12)
The kindling of the fire, the fuel, and the oblation—
these and the other [items] are well known.
These are to be performed every day.
The simultaneous mention [of these acts] is for the purpose of ensuring their immediate performance;
and so Manu says:
"Having accepted the desired staff and having attended upon the sun..."
Having circumambulated the fire from left to right, he should go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.
Thus it is said.

In that regard, it has been stated that by the phrase "having circumambulated the fire from left to right," the offering with fuel-sticks (*samid-āhuti*) is prescribed. Since it is heard in the scriptures that "one should eat food twice—morning and evening—honored and without finding fault," the kindling of the fire must also be understood to occur twice, in the evening and in the morning.
And so another Smṛti states:
"Having fetched fuel-sticks from afar, he should place them in the open air;
evening and morning, he should offer oblations with them into the fire without sloth."
Thus it is said;
some, however, desire that the offering of fuel-sticks be performed only in the evening.
Furthermore—truthful speech. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.13)
The verb "should perform" (kartavyā) is to be supplied everywhere.
The explicit mention of the word "speech" (vacana) is for the sake of removing doubt; otherwise, there might be the doubt that "the touching of water" (upaspṛśanam) itself constitutes the truth.
The separate mention [of speech] is for the purpose of ensuring its performance even by one who is ill.
And therefore, that [is not the case] for the two preceding [stages].
Likewise, Manu says:
"Without having gone for alms and without having kindled the sacred fire..."
If he is not ill, he shall perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin* for seven nights.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore—touching water. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.14)
The mention of "ashes" (*ab*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for ashes and other such substances.
Thus says Bhṛgu:
"Five meritorious baths have been proclaimed by the great seers."
The fire-born, the water-born, the Brahman-born, the wind-born, and likewise the celestial.

The fire-related bath is performed with ashes; the water-related bath is immersion; the brahminical bath is performed with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; and the wind-related bath is known to be the dust raised by cows.
That which consists of a divine year of heat is called the "divine bath.
If one is unable to perform the Varuṇa bath, one should perform the Āgneya and other baths instead.
Thus it is said.
Although one should have said simply "bathing" (*snānam*), this specific expression is used for the purpose of including the rules for bathing mentioned in other *smṛtis*.
And thus, that which is stated in other *smṛtis* should be observed.
The prefix *upa-* is intended to exclude water that is not clearly recognized as such.

The separate mention of "tending the fire" and "wandering for alms" is for the purpose of prohibiting the daily bath after one has eaten, but not the occasional (naimittika) bath; therefore, the occasional bath must be performed.
The separate mention of "speaking the truth" is for the purpose of prohibiting even the occasional bath for one who is ill.
Some say that the prefix *upa-* is intended to prohibit bathing at midnight.
Whatever has been stated here has also been stated by Manu:
"One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor during the great night."
Nor should one do so constantly with clothes on, nor in an unknown body of water.
Thus [it is said].
Some say it consists of the gift of a cow and so forth. (Gautama 2.15)
The Godāna, known as the second vow for the Chandogas, should be observed by others as well in the sixteenth year;
some desire that even they observe the Godāna in the sixteenth year. From that point onward, some desire the ceremonial bath (snāna).
Prior to the gift of a cow (godāna), one should not perform the daily bath (nityasnāna); rather, only the occasional bath (naimittika) should be performed.
Some teachers maintain that from that point onward, even the daily bath is required;
however, because of the use of the word "some" (eka), Gautama does not hold this view.
And [the state of] being outside the twilight periods. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.16)
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of carrying forward the mention of "some" [teachers].
Some desire that the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) be performed outside the village;
however, Gautama does not.
But not so, according to Gautama.

This is what is meant: the view of some is that the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) must be performed only outside the village; whereas the opinion of Gautama is that it should be performed anywhere—in either an outdoor or an indoor location—provided it is a pure place.
Now, as an incidental discussion, since it must be determined when and how that twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) is to be performed, he says:
"One should stand during the morning [twilight] and sit during the evening [twilight], remaining silent, as long as the light [of the sun or stars] is visible. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.17)
The term "vāgyataḥ" (with speech restrained) is connected to both "standing" and "sitting.
That time at which the sun rises is the morning twilight (*pūrvā saṃdhyā*);
the word *saṃdhyā* is carried over from the preceding portion of the sūtra.

That time at which the sun sets is the later twilight (*uttarā saṃdhyā*). Here, standing and sitting are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), while the act of worship (*upāsana*) is the primary ritual action (*pradhāna karma*).
Therefore, although it is stated that "he should stand," it should nevertheless be understood as "standing he should meditate" and "seated he should meditate.
And so says Manu:
"By reciting [the prayers] while standing during the morning twilight, one destroys the sin committed at night."
But sitting facing the west, one destroys the impurity created during the day.
Thus:

"The time is 'with light' (sajyotis)"; that is, when the light of the stars is present in the east. That period of time which exists together with the light of the stars is called "with light" (sajyotis); the commencement [of the rite] should be performed during that "with-light" time.

In the other [direction], it is likewise the light of the sun. "Until the sight of the light" means until the sight of the sun in the former [direction] and until the sight of the stars in the latter. Although one should have said "until the light," the inclusion of the word "sight" (darśana) is for the purpose of completeness.
And so Manu says: "By virtue of their long practice of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), the sages obtained long life,
as well as wisdom, fame, renown, and spiritual luster."
Thus it is said.

But is it not the case that by the rule, "And for those in the northern regions, this is not contradictory," this [practice] is not obtained for a *snātaka* who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimān*), because his time is already occupied by the fire-oblation (*agnihavana*)? It is said in reply: As for the domestic oblation (*homa*) prescribed by the *Smṛti* to be performed in the evening and morning, there is indeed no contradiction due to the difference in time.

How so? By the word "evening" (*sāyam*), night is meant, and by the word "morning" (*prātaḥ*), the day is meant. Since there is no such thing here as the injunction for an oblation at sunrise (*uditahoma*) and so forth, the oblation must enter into the ritual immediately after the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*).

Moreover, even though for some it is stated that the *homa* (fire-oblation) should be performed at the very time of twilight (*sandhyākāla*), since the "long twilight" (*dīrghasandhyatva*) is desired there as well, there is still room for the performance of the *sandhyopāsana* (twilight worship) after the *homa*.
Thus, there is no contradiction even regarding the Vedic rules concerning the *uditahoma* (oblation after sunrise) and so forth.

Although it should have been stated as "one should perform the morning twilight devotion standing and the evening one sitting," this specific formulation is intended to include the injunctions mentioned in other Smṛtis as well.

Likewise, Uśanas says: "Having gone to water in the evening and morning, having become pure and having cleansed oneself with a purifier, one should [recite] the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the *abliṅga* verses, and the *vāmadevya* hymn. Then, sitting on *darbha* grass in a clean place, holding *darbha* blades, facing west, with speech restrained and meditating upon the Self, one should then perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*)—namely *sarecaka*, *sūrakaka*, and *kumbhaka*—and [recite] the *Sāvitrī* beginning with *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ* a thousand times, preceded by meditation upon the seers, the meters, and the deity."

One should recite it a hundred times, or at least ten times, while rising; having offered salutations to Agni, Yama, and Brahmā in the west, south, and north respectively, and having circumambulated three times clockwise, one should again offer salutation to the western direction.
In the same manner, standing in the morning facing east, one should offer salutations to Mitra and the other deities.
Thus it is said.
One should not look at the sun.

If this prohibition were intended only for the two twilight periods (*sandhyā*), then a single sūtra would have been composed as follows: "One should stand during the former [twilight] and sit during the latter; [one should remain] until the stars appear, or until the light [of the sun] is seen; restrained in speech, one should not look at the sun.
If, on the other hand, it were intended to apply at all times, then in such passages as "One should avoid honey and meat," he would have also mentioned the looking at the sun.

It can be understood that this was stated with another intention, because it is not performed in both ways; and that intention should be seen as stated in another Smṛti, just as Uśanas says: "One should not look at the sun when it has reached the twilight, when it is at midday, when it is eclipsed by Rāhu, or when it is reflected in water."

He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, speaking, playing musical instruments, bathing, cleaning the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.19)
The word "should avoid" is connected to each [item].

Honey refers to that produced by bees; there is no fault in consuming it unintentionally, as seen in another Smṛti: "Honey that comes unexpectedly does not cause impurity, according to the Vājasaneyaka.
As for meat, although it is not prohibited for a householder, [it should still be avoided].

Even in that case, there is no fault in eating meat that is the leavings of a guru for the sake of medicine when one is ill; for another Smṛti states: "If he should become ill, he may at will eat everything that is the leavings of his guru for the purpose of medicine.
Thus, it must be avoided even at a Śrāddha by one who is not ill.
And so says Manu:
At a rite for the gods, one may eat at will when invited, as if observing a vow, for the sake of the pleasure of the ritual; likewise at a rite for the ṛṣis, his vow is not violated.
And so forth. "Fragrance" refers to sandalwood and the like;

this prohibition applies even to that which is for the sake of pleasure, but not to that which is consecrated by a deity, because another Smṛti text is seen to state: "A religious student should accept only that which is consecrated by a deity."
The same applies to wearing a garland.
Day-sleeping means indulging in sleep during the day; that too is not a fault for one who is ill. Applying collyrium to the eyes [is likewise permitted].
Here too, the prohibition concerns that which is for the purpose of enjoyment, not that which is for medicinal purposes.
"Anointing" (*abhyañjana*) refers to the rubbing of the limbs with oil;
some say this is a prohibition specifically against scented oil.
In that case, there is no fault regarding the other [term].

If it is argued that this negation is already established by the negation of odor itself, we say no; because it is based specifically on what is well-known in the world, there is no apprehension of the general category of odor [in that context].
"Vehicle" refers to a palanquin and the like.
That too applies only to one who is not ill;
shoes and umbrellas are well-known [as permitted],
and there is no fault in those made of peacock feathers.
Desire (*kāma*) is the longing for enjoyment directed toward women;
anger (*krodha*) is the thinking of harm toward another;
greed (*lobha*) is the seizing of another's property and so forth by unjust means.
Delusion is ignorance; idle chatter is excessive prattle;
playing instruments refers to the beating of drums and the like.
Bathing refers to bathing the head and so forth, by means of which there is enjoyment, since the other [types of bathing] are prescribed [for other occasions]. Cleaning the teeth is well known.
That [cleaning] should not be done even with a betel leaf, because another Smṛti text states: "One observing a vow should have teeth as if covered in mud."

Joy (*harṣa*) is indeed delight (*prīti*); thus, the prohibition of watching plays and the like—which are the causes thereof—is established, because it is impossible to prevent the arising of delight upon seeing them.
*Nṛtta* is the movement of the limbs;
*gīta* is the utterance of words related to music (*gāndharva*).
Slander is the proclaiming of another's faults.
Fear is the terrifying of another, because it cannot be avoided by the other person.
Furthermore:
when in the presence of one's teacher, one must not cover the neck, sit with the knees bound by a cloth (avasakthika), lean against a support, or stretch out the feet. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.20)
"Guru" refers to the preceptor (ācārya) and others.
Why? Because if only the preceptor were intended to be included, then one would have to say "seeing the preceptor" (ācāryadarśana).
The inclusion of the term "guru" is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of all those who occupy the position of a guru.
And so another Smṛti states: "He should remain with his limbs contracted in the presence of all those who are superior. Wrapping the neck (*kaṇṭhaprāvaraṇam*) means throwing a cloth around the neck.
Crossing the legs (*avasakthikām*) means binding the knees together by placing one leg over the other.
The rest is well known.
Since these [actions] are performed under the influence of others, they are prohibited.
Furthermore:
spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the knuckles. (Gautama Sūtra 2.21)
It is mentioned separately for the purpose of avoiding it both in the presence of the guru and in the presence of others.
Spitting is well known [as improper]. Even when under the influence of another, laughter must be restrained with effort.
And likewise Āpastamba says: "One should not smile; if one should smile, one should smile after covering [the mouth]," according to the Brāhmaṇa.
Yawning is well known.
Snapping the joints is the making of a sound while releasing a joint.
Furthermore:
"Upon seeing or obtaining a woman, there arises the suspicion of sexual intercourse. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.22)
The word "should avoid" (varjayet) carries over from the previous context.

"Gazing" (prekṣaṇa) means looking intently, that is, the detailed examination of the individual parts; it does not mean merely seeing the form, because it is impossible to prevent the blinking of the eyes.
"Touching" (ālambana) means physical contact.
Although it should have been stated simply as "in touching," the expression used here is for the purpose of excluding intentional touching;
thus, there is no fault if it occurs through negligence.
However, if done intentionally, one must not touch [the object] even in darkness and similar conditions.
One should not perform either of those two acts with a woman;
only with her regarding whom others might suspect sexual intercourse, and not with any other.
Gambling, service to the low-born, taking what is not given, and violence. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.23)
"He should avoid" means exactly that.
"Gambling" refers to playing with dice and the like.
"Service to the lowly" refers to service such as cleaning away urine and excrement.
And thus, even toward a guru, service that is inappropriate should not be performed.
Taking what is not given means taking even that which has been discarded without permission.
Violence means the killing of living beings or the harming of living beings.
One should neither cause [a ritual] to be performed on an inauspicious lunar day, nor even give one's approval for it.
Furthermore:
[One should avoid uttering] the names of one's teacher, his son, a woman, and an initiated person. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.24)
The subject at hand is "one should avoid.
One should not utter the names of the teacher, his son, his wife, or one who has been initiated, as given by the father or others.
Furthermore:
"Acid words. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.25)
One should avoid all those who are harsh, cruel, and who cause agitation to others.
A Brahmin must always abstain from intoxicants. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.26)
"One should avoid" is the subject under discussion.
A Brāhmaṇa should always avoid liquor—whether it is made from molasses, honey, or flour, or any other intoxicant—even prior to initiation (*upanayana*).

Likewise, for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, there is no prohibition against *surā* (liquor) other than that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*), both before initiation and after [initiation] until the period of studenthood (*brahmacarya*) ends, as seen in other Smṛti texts.
As Manu has said:
"Sura is to be known as threefold—distilled from molasses (gauḍī), from honey (mādhvī), and from flour (paiṣṭī).
Just as one is so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born."
Thus [it is said].
Now, for the purpose of explaining what ought to be done, he says:
"He should sleep on a low bed or seat, rise before [others], and go to rest after [them]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.27)
In relation to the guru, one should use a lower bed and seat;
one should rise before him and go to rest after him.
As Manu has said:
His bed and seat should always be lower than those of his teacher;
he should rise before him and go to rest after him.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore:
"He is restrained in speech, arms, and belly. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.28)
The word "syāt" (should be) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
One who is restrained in speech is one who has desisted from idle chatter.
One who is restrained in the arms is one who avoids crushing clods of earth and similar acts.
"Restrained in the stomach" means eating what is wholesome and moderate.

Some read it as "restrained in the actions of speech, arms, and stomach"; however, since restraint of the arms is already implied by the sense [of general self-restraint], one must consider whether that reading is appropriate or not.
Furthermore:
One should mention the name and lineage of the teacher with respect. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.29)
The mention of "the guru" is an elliptical expression that includes the preceptor and others as well.
"From [him] equally" means from one who is properly bowed to, that is, one who is humble;
the meaning is: having meditated upon him and having performed a salutation.

And thus, even in that context, the mention of "the teacher and his son" (*ācāryatatputra*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the preceptor and others as well, because the utterance of their names is likewise prohibited.
Accordingly, another Smṛti states:
"The teacher, his son, his wife, the initiated one, and the guru..."
As well as his father, paternal uncle, mother, and maternal uncle.
A wise man should not mention by name his father-in-law or husband, even if they are well-wishers and learned; likewise, he should not mention the name of his mother’s sister.
But if he should speak, one should meditate upon him, pay homage, and then address him.
Thus [it is said].
And likewise, when one honors those who are superior. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.30)
The meaning is that he is one who is honored, venerable, and learned;
he should be understood as being superior, a well-wisher, and advanced in age.
Since this [superiority] is already established by the word "and" (ca), the word "thus" (evam) is intended for the purpose of extending [the rules] to the entire [set].
And therefore, whatever [actions] such as salutation are prescribed upon seeing the Guru, those should be understood to apply here as well.
Having left behind his bed, seat, and dwelling place, he should respond [to the call]. 2.31.
When the Guru gives the command, then "bed" refers to a couch and the like;
"seat" refers to a wooden plank and the like;
and "place" refers to where one is situated.
The meaning is that, having set aside and abandoned these [objections], one should give a response, that is, a reply.
One should approach [the teacher] when summoned by one who is invisible. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.32)
The meaning is that when an instruction is being given by an invisible teacher, one should perform an approach, which is to say, go toward him.
One should rise upon seeing one's teacher when he is standing below, seated, or moving horizontally, or when one is sitting in a lower position. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.33)
When the teacher stands or sits below or at a lower level, there is the service of facing away (tiryagvātasevā) and the voiding of urine and feces;
upon seeing the teacher in that situation, one should rise,
and according to the word "and" (ca), one should turn one's face away.
And so another Smṛti says:
"Upon seeing his teacher standing in a well or likewise standing on the bank of a pond,
the disciple and the servant alike should stand with their faces turned away."
Thus [it is said].
Alternatively, by the word "and" (ca), departure is also expressed.

In that case, the meaning of the Sūtra should be understood as follows: "In the event of [the presence of] one standing below, sitting, or [the blowing of] crosswinds, he should rise and depart in due order. Here, the sequence is: upon seeing someone standing below or sitting, he should rise; and in the event of [the presence of] crosswinds, he should depart.
One should follow after him as he walks. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.34)
"Seeing him going, one should follow after him.
The word "and" (ca) carries over [from the previous rule];
by it, even what is not explicitly stated is included: seeing him seated, one should rise; seeing him lying down, one should sit.
And so another Smṛti says: "One should follow him when he goes, stand up when he sits, and sit near him when he lies down."
Having made known one's action, [one should confess it]. (Gautama 2.35)

Having informed the teacher, "I shall perform whatever task is to be done by him," and having performed it, he should stand by after announcing, "It is done. Because the sentence is incomplete, the word "having performed" (*kṛtvā*) must be supplied after "having informed" (*vijñāpya*); likewise, the verb "should stand" (*tiṣṭhet*) is to be supplied after "having announced" (*ākhyāya*), as in the expression "Enter and eat the cake" (*praviśa piṇḍīm*).
He should study when summoned. // Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.36 //
The meaning is that he should study only when summoned by the teacher; he should not, however, urge him [to study].
He should be intent upon what is pleasant and beneficial. // Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.37 //
The word "syāt" (might be) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the verb]. "Devoted to that" means intent upon both the pleasant and the beneficial in combination.

Because that which is beneficial but unpleasant should not be done; "pleasant" means causing immediate delight, while "beneficial" means enduring for the future. The meaning is that one should do only that which is both pleasant and enduring for the future.
And the same applies to his wife's sons. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.38)
He should also be intent upon the welfare and benefit of those two who are his own kindred—his wife and son—who resemble him;
the word "and" (ca) implies that he should also provide for his neck-clothing and other such necessities.
If it is asked why only those of the same caste are mentioned, it is because the plural number is used for the sake of honor.
Now he states the exceptions to that rule:
"There shall be no eating of leftovers, bathing [him], adorning [him], washing his feet, massaging him, or clasping his feet. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.39)
One should not perform these [rites] for his wife or son;
although they would otherwise be required because of their being dear and beneficial, they are here prohibited.
Since these two alone are prohibited, it follows that these rites must certainly be performed for the teacher.

Likewise, Āpastamba states: "One who has gone abroad should eat after having offered alms-food into the fire; alms-food is praised as being equivalent to sacrificial oblation (*havis*). In that regard, the teacher serves as the deity and the *āhavanīya* fire; having fed him, one eats what remains as leavings, for that is indeed the leavings of the sacrificial oblation," and so forth. Similarly, Vasiṣṭha also says: "The leavings of one who is not one's guru are not to be eaten," and so on.
*Prasādhana* means ornamentation.
The remainder is well known.
Now he states the exception regarding the act of clasping the feet:
"After returning from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the wives of one's teachers. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.40)
Upon returning from a journey abroad, one should perform the salutation by grasping the feet of the wives of one's teachers;
not at any other time,
nor toward the wives of others.
But even in that case, he should not [accept food] from young women who have attained the age of marriage. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.41)
The meaning is: "by one who is capable of legal transactions and has reached the full age of sixteen years.
Some maintain that for young women—that is, for maidens—even after returning from travel, [the marriage] should not be performed; however, Gautama does not hold this view.
It should be understood in relation to what is to be suspected and what is not to be suspected.
It has been stated: "Regarding fire, fuel, and the practice of begging.
In that context, since fire and fuel are obtained individually from householders alone, he now states the rule for the practice of begging:
"The practice of begging is to be performed among all castes, with the exception of those who are accused of crimes and those who have fallen [from their status]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.42)

For what purpose is this sūtra commenced? First of all, the practice of wandering for alms is not enjoined by this [sūtra], because it has already been enjoined by the rule: "kindling the fire and wandering for alms. Furthermore, the avoidance of those accused of crimes has already been stated by the rule: "of those who are praiseworthy in their own duties."
Regarding this, some say: "This undertaking is for the purpose of including the Śūdra, because [the Śūdra] was not included by the rule, 'of those who are praiseworthy in their own duties'.
However, this is not correct, because the permission for a Śūdra in times of distress is already established by the rule, "if there is no means of livelihood other than from a Śūdra.
Nor is it proper to assume that this [text] permits a student (brahmacārin) to accept [gifts] from a Śūdra even when not in distress, since in another Smṛti such a thing is absolutely prohibited.
One whose limbs are nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food does not attain the highest state, even if he studies constantly, offers oblations, or recites prayers.
Thus it is said.

Therefore, this undertaking is intended for the sake of excluding a religious student (*brahmacārin*) from [the status of] an unpraiseworthy twice-born (*dvijāti*), even in the absence of an emergency; for when there is a general application of the term "unpraiseworthy" without distinction, the prohibition—"excepting those who are accused or outcasts"—is indeed appropriate.

Otherwise, if the case of a Śūdra were already included [by general rules], there would be no possibility of reaching those such as the "accused" (abhiśasta) and so forth, and thus their prohibition would be illogical; nor can it be argued that this exception applies only to the subject of Śūdras, for where the twice-born (dvijāti) are prescribed as the qualified subjects, the Śūdra is likewise considered qualified there, and thus there is no occasion at all for the other [prohibition].

Therefore, it is established that in the first kalpa, a religious student (brahmacārin) should practice begging for alms from those who are praiseworthy; in their absence, from those who are not praiseworthy; in their absence, from his teacher (ācārya) and others; and in the absence of all these, in times of distress, even from a Śūdra.
"Sārvavarṇika" means belonging to all castes (*sarvavarṇa*); the meaning is that it pertains to everyone.

The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of including the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; otherwise, since the right to receive gifts belongs only to the Brāhmaṇa, it would apply to him alone. The inclusion of the word "caste" (*varṇa*) is for the purpose of including the Śūdra as well; for if the word "caste" were not used, the term "all" would apply only to those two [the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya]. It is for this reason that the word "caste" has been employed.
Therefore, since the [rule] does not apply to a Śūdra, the mention of "caste" (varṇa) is for the purpose of extending it to him.
Consequently, there is no fault in a Śūdra who is destitute of a livelihood practicing mendicancy;
"bhaikṣa" is a collection of alms, and thus it must be gathered from many houses.
One who is "accused" (abhiśasta) is understood as one accused of a minor offense (upapātaka), because one accused of a major sin (pātaka) is already covered by the term "outcast" (patita).
Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a sin causing loss of caste (patanīya) or a sin not causing loss of caste (upapatanīya)."
Some analyze the term as *sārvavarṇika*, meaning "belonging to all castes" (*sarveṣu varṇeṣu bhavam*). For them, we do not see the purpose of the word "all" (*sarva*).
If it is intended to include those of inferior twice-born status, that cannot be so, because that very purpose is already covered by the commencement of the Sūtra itself.
If its purpose is to include Śūdras, the refutation has already been stated. Therefore, this matter should be investigated by learned Brahmins.
The word "existence" (bhava) should be employed at the beginning, middle, and end [of the instruction], according to the sequence of the syllables.

In the request expressed by the words "Give alms to a biped," since the word *dehi* (give) is also obtained through the force of the imperative suffix, the word *bhavat* (sir/your honor) must first be employed by a Brāhmaṇa, in the middle by a Kṣatriya, and at the end by a Vaiśya.

Because *bhavat* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and cannot be used in its isolated form, it should be used in the vocative case-ending when addressing women, as in "O lady, give alms" (*bhavati bhikṣāṃ dehi*). When addressing men, it should be used as "Sir, give alms" (*bhavan bhikṣāṃ dehi*).
Following the prefix *pra*, one should also observe what is stated in other Smṛtis;
that too states that the syllables *kṣa* and *hi* should not be pronounced aloud.

As the Gṛhya-smṛti says: "A Brāhmaṇa should beg, saying, 'Lady, give alms' (*bhavati bhikṣāṃ dehi*); a Kṣatriya [should beg] with the word *bhavat* in the middle, saying, 'Lady, give alms' (*bhavati bhikṣāṃ dehi*); a Vaiśya [should beg] with the word *bhavat* at the end, saying, 'Give alms, lady' (*dehi bhavati*). And he should not lengthen the syllables *kṣa* and *hi*."

The mention of "caste" (*varṇa*) is for the purpose of including the Śūdra in the attainment of mantras; consequently, one of the mantras belonging to the three [higher] castes should be understood as applicable, or else another specific composition must be made. Alternatively, it should be understood as that which is prescribed for the Vaiśya, based on the observation of another Smṛti text stating, "The livelihood of the Śūdra is like that of the Vaiśya."
The mantra was not explicitly stated for the purpose of making known that the mode of life is indefinite;
likewise, Vasiṣṭha says: "And the mode of life is indefinite, as are the hair and dress," and so forth.
The mention of the sequence [of stages] is so that there may be no misconception regarding a single [stage].
In the absence of these, one may do so with others, except for the teacher, a kinsman, a guru, or one's own [superior].
The teacher has said:
"kinsman" refers to a sapinda relative; "teacher" refers to a maternal uncle and so forth; and "one's own" refers to what belongs to oneself.
If [alms] cannot be obtained elsewhere, one should request alms from these [categories of people].
The sequence, however, has already been explained.
In this case as well,
one should avoid each preceding one of those [faults].
Whichever among them is mentioned first in each respective case, one should avoid that; however,
if [the desired food] cannot be obtained elsewhere, even after avoiding those mentioned earlier, one should continue to seek alms from among those very same persons.
The mention of these [other sources] is for the purpose of establishing a restriction—that [one should not eat] from the teacher's house alone.
Consequently, it should be understood that when nothing else is available, one may indeed take [food] from the teacher's house.
And so says another Smṛti: "In the absence [of other food], even from the teacher's house."
Having offered [the food] to the teacher and being permitted by him, he should eat. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.46)
Having announced to the teacher, "This is the alms-food," he should eat it when permitted by him with the words, "Eat.
This announcement is for the purpose of consecrating the alms-food, as indicated by the expression "being permitted.
If the teacher should take [some] for himself, then more must be brought.
In his absence, [the gift] goes to his wife, his son, his fellow student, or to virtuous persons.
In the presence of the teacher, an announcement should be made regarding his wife and others as appropriate.

The mention of "his" (tad-) is for the purpose of indicating that the wife and son must be of the same caste. A *sabrahmacārī* is one who studies the same Vedic branch (*caraṇa*); he is a "good" (*san*) person, meaning one endowed with excellent qualities.
Regarding how he should eat, it is said:
"Restraining his speech, being satisfied, and not being greedy, having placed water nearby. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.48)
"Restrained in speech" means silently; "being satisfied" means practicing contentment—the sense being that even if one was previously dissatisfied, one should rejoice at the mere sight of food.
And so another Smṛti says: "Upon seeing it, one should rejoice, become serene, and welcome it in every way."
Thus,
the meaning is that one should avoid overeating, remaining free from greed and abandoning the desire for special delicacies.
And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
Excessive eating is detrimental to longevity, detrimental to health, and detrimental to prosperity.
It is non-meritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
Thus [it is said].
Alternatively, the meaning is "not avoiding the rules for eating.
Accordingly, the rules for eating should be observed in another Smṛti text.
The meaning is that one should sip water after having correctly applied [the mantra].
The prefix *sam-* is intended to include the procedure mentioned in other Smṛtis.
Thus, Uśanas says: "Having sprinkled water with the mantra beginning 'Truth, indeed, by the truth,' one should cause [the person] to sip it with the mantra beginning 'The underlayer of nectar.'"

Alternatively, "water" refers to a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*); having placed that [nearby], it follows that the student (*brahmacārin*) must also carry a water-pot. Likewise, Manu also indicates the carrying of a water-pot by the student, because it is prescribed as a practice together with the girdle (*mekhalā*) and other such items.
Having cast away into the water the girdle, the antelope skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread, and the water-pot when they are worn out, he should take others according to the prescribed mantras.
Thus,
for this reason, the sipping of water (ācamana) must be performed from that very [source], by virtue of the force of the scriptural statement;
there is no fault in touching what has been defiled by food remnants.
Or rather, that which is stated in another Smṛti should be observed.
As Vasiṣṭha says:
"Fire prepared in water, in the hand, or in wood is pure."
Therefore, one should wipe the water-pot with both hands and water.
Thus,
some support this meaning by means of the prefix itself.
Now, if a religious student (brahmacārī) should abide in proper discipline toward his teacher, what then should be done? To this he says:
"The instruction of the pupil is by means of non-corporal punishment. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.49)

"Instruction of the pupil" (śiṣyāśiṣṭiḥ) means the disciplining of the pupil; it should be carried out by means of censure and so forth, excluding physical punishment (avadhena vadhaṃ muktvā). Although this is already established by the context of the section, the explicit mention of "pupil" is for the purpose of making known that this same rule applies to anyone else who must be disciplined, such as a wife or a son.
If unable [to do so], he may use thin strips of rope or split bamboo.
If instruction through reprimand and other such means proves ineffective, one may use either a rope or a split bamboo cane;
since these two are mentioned together as having the same purpose, they are optional alternatives.
Even with that, the pupil should be instructed gently.
If he strikes with something other than that, he should be punished according to the king's command.
One who strikes with anything other than the hand or foot out of anger shall be punished by the king;
the mention of the "king" is for the sake of showing respect.
Now, as to how long he should observe this [vow], he says:
"He should practice the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years for each Veda. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.52)
One who is about to study a single Veda should practice— that is, observe— the student's life (brahmacarya) for twelve years in the manner previously described.
By the term *brahmacarya*, the entire collection of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) is meant, because it has Brahman as its purpose.
Or up to twelve [times]. (Gautama 2.53)
Or he should observe the vow of celibacy for twelve years for each Veda.
Or, in all cases, [the period lasts] until the time of grasping [the next stage].
For as long as it takes to complete the study of all the Vedas, for that same length of time one should observe the life of a religious student (brahmacarya), because that is the purpose of it.
The inclusion of the word "all" is for the sake of indicating whether one studies one, or two, or indeed all of them.
And so says Manu:
Having studied the Vedas—either all four, or two, or even one—in the proper sequence.
Thus,
this is an exception (apavāda) regarding the previously stated limit, whether it be subsequent or prior;
it is a statement of a restrictive rule (niyamokti) to the effect that what is studied according to this rule becomes efficacious (vīryavat).
At the conclusion of his studies, the teacher should be invited with a gift of wealth.

Upon the completion of his studies, but not necessarily upon the completion of his vows, he should invite the teacher—the ācārya—with a purpose or motive, asking, "What may I do for the sake of my guru?"
Then, having performed the bath, he may either do so with permission or without it. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.56)

"Having performed" means having given; that is, the matter instructed by the teacher. Or, for one who has been permitted with the words "Enough with this fee for the teacher," the ritual bath is the *samāvartana* (the return ceremony).
Now, since there may be several gurus such as one's father and others present together, [the text] states which one is to be honored first:
"The teacher is the most excellent among gurus. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.57)
The teacher (ācārya) is defined by the characteristics previously stated; he is the most excellent and the foremost among all gurus, including others such as one's father and so forth.
Consequently, in the rule "in the case of a collision [of authorities], [one follows] the other," it is this very person who is referred to by the word "other" (para).
"Some say 'Mother,' some say 'Mother. (Gautama 2.58)
Some consider the mother to be superior;
others [consider] the father [superior], because of the use of the particle *iti*.
Otherwise, since the form *mātaika* would already be established [by the rule for ordinal numbers], there would be no need for this.
The teacher is more important than the father alone;
thus says Manu:
"That which the mother and father produce for him through their union out of desire..."
One should know that to be his true birth, which occurs when he is born from a womb.
But whatever birth the teacher, who has mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule by means of the Sāvitrī— that birth is real, free from old age, and immortal.
Thus,
if the father himself is the teacher, then the father is distinguished;
[nevertheless], the mother is the most excellent of all.
And so Vasiṣṭha says: "An Ācārya is ten times more venerable than an Upādhyāya, a father is a hundred times more venerable than an Ācārya, and a mother exceeds a father a thousandfold in respect."
In this context, by the word "father" (pitṛ), only that teacher who is actually one's father is intended.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Maskarīya Gautama-bhāṣya.
Chapter Three:
Thus, for one who has established the rules of conduct and perfected their knowledge—
Some state that there is an option regarding his stage of life (āśrama). 3.1.
Of him who has maintained his vow of celibacy without interruption;
and thus Manu says:
"Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda, in due order..."
Having remained inviolate in his celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder.
Thus,
the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) should be understood as applicable to one who has thus fallen away from his duty.
Alternatively, the mention of that [penance] is for the purpose of excluding the Śūdra, so that the description of the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) does not apply to him either.

Or rather, the repetition "of that [and] of that" (tasya tasya) is intended to include the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya. If it is argued that this is already established by the general heading even without mentioning them specifically, we say no; for its purpose is to dispel the suspicion that this might be a mere semblance of another Smṛti. For another Smṛti appears to state: "This fourfold duty has been declared to you for the Brāhmaṇa. In that case, there might arise the doubt that this fourfold duty belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone, while for the other two castes it is of only one kind. Thus, the repetition is necessary.

If it is asked, "How then is that so?", [the answer is: there, the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is for the sake of illustration. If it is asked, "How is that understood? [it is because] we see in another Smṛti that the four stages of life (āśramas) belong to only three of the castes (varṇas).

Likewise, Āpastamba states: "For all [castes], residence in the teacher's family begins from the initiation (upanayana); for all, there is no relinquishment until the completion of learning; having understood the duties, one may undertake whatever one desires."
Some say: because their fruits are equal, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the stages of life (*āśrama*).
For the fruit is twofold—consisting of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and consisting of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)—and it is obtained by means of either one of these.

And so says the Śruti: "There are three branches of dharma: sacrifice, study, and charity—this is the first; austerity alone is the second; and dwelling in the teacher’s family is the third. Having ascended these, one goes to the world of Brahman; he who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality."

The meaning, however, is as follows: there are three bases of dharma. "Sacrifice, study, and charity"—this is the instruction for the householder; "penance alone"—this is the dharma of the forest-dweller and the wandering mendicant; "dwelling in the teacher’s family"—this is for the student. "Having ascended these" means having properly established oneself in the stage of the student, the stage of the householder, the stage of the forest-dweller, or the stage of the wandering mendicant. "Among them, he who is established in Brahman"—that is, one who is devoted to Brahman.
The knower attains immortality; that is, he goes to liberation.
Furthermore, because it is taught that all [of these stages] lead to the attainment of the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), it is stated that their fruits are indeed equal.

Likewise, in the Jābāla Śruti as well, the equality of their fruits is heard: "Having completed the stage of studentship (brahmacarya), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller."
"Having become a forest-dweller, he should go forth;
or otherwise, he may go forth directly from the stage of studentship, or from the house, or from the forest; thus he goes to the world of Brahmā.
Manu also says:
All these, when practiced in succession according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.
Thus [it is said].
Here too, because of the word "api" (also/even), one [additional stage] is also to be understood.
Āpastamba also says: "There are four stages of life: the householder's state, dwelling in the teacher's family, the state of the silent sage, and forest-dwelling."
"By proceeding without distraction among all of these according to the instruction, one attains security";
thus, because they yield an equal result, there is an option (vikalpa).

[Objection: But if [the results] were equal, then since both kinds of fruits would be attained through *brahmacarya* alone, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the injunctions for the other stages of life (*āśrama*) being purposeless. [Reply:
It is said: The injunctions for the other stages of life are intended for one who is capable of practicing that particular stage;
or else, they are for the sake of attaining a desired stage of life through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous births.
The scripture states: "Knowledge and action follow him, as does his prior wisdom.
Furthermore, the scriptural injunction regarding lifelong [performance of rites] is to be understood as applying to a householder who possesses desire and the capacity [for such duties].

When this is accepted, the scriptural passage concerning renunciation also becomes consistent: "Having thus known that Self, they rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lead the life of a mendicant."
Otherwise, the instruction for renunciation—namely, "the practice of begging for alms"—would not be tenable.

Furthermore, by the *jāyamāna-śruti* (the scripture concerning the one being born), the necessity of performing sacrifices and other duties is established for the householder, but not for the newborn alone, because the connection with the three debts is absolutely impossible [for the latter]. This is because such an interpretation would contradict the *śruti*: "One should renounce even from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*)," while it does not contradict such *smṛti* texts as: "From that very stage of studentship he renounces," and "He may dwell in whichever [stage] he desires. Moreover, explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) are subordinate to what is to be performed (*kārya*).
And therefore, the meaning of the passage should be understood as follows: a householder being born enters the state of householdership through his prior latent impressions (*pūrvavāsanā*).
The mention of "Brahmin" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
He becomes bound by three debts: he becomes indebted to the gods through sacrifice; therefore, sacrifice must be performed.
"From this [duty], one should procreate for the sake of the ancestors; therefore, the procreation of offspring must be performed.
From this [duty], one should practice celibacy for the sake of the seers (ṛṣis); therefore, the observance of celibacy must be maintained on the days of the lunar festivals (parvan) and so forth.
When understood in this way, there is no contradiction anywhere between the Śruti and the Smṛti.
Because of the mention of "some" (eke), Gautama is not included; rather, his view is considered to be a cumulative one.

How is this understood? From the fact that the position of opposition—"the teachers [hold] to a single stage of life" (*aikāśramya*)—is presented as the opinion of others (*paramata*), and from the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—"there are three stages of life before the last"—since there would otherwise be no mention of the three stages prior to the final one.
As for Gautama, he maintains the following regarding the position of option (*vikalpa*):
Through sacrifice one attains the gods; through austerity, the realm of Vairāja;
through renunciation, the station of Brahman; and through dispassion, dissolution into Prakṛti.

Thus, because they are taught as having distinct results; because even in the Jābāla Śruti, instead of saying "having ascended any one of these," it says "having ascended these," indicating an intention toward their combination; because the attainment of the world of Brahman is also taught as the result of that combination; and because even in the Jābāla Śruti, the position of combination alone was stated first as being primary—"all [the paths] also, in succession."

In this statement of Manu as well, because the word "api" (also/even) has the sense of conjunction; and in the statement of Āpastamba as well, because of the plural "teṣu sarveṣu" (in all of those), it is said with the intention that [the knowledge] does not reside in only one, but resides in all of them; furthermore, because the scriptural mention of the three debts is established only in its literal sense; and because the scriptural text "and prior wisdom" is also established with the intention of referring to knowledge (*vidyā*); and because the scriptural text regarding lifelong [performance] also applies—[stating]: "If a householder should enter the forest, or if he should desire the household itself, then... [it follows that knowledge is required even in the householder stage].

Because the Jābāla Śruti statement, "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives," shows that it is not mandatory, and because under this view the scriptural injunction regarding withdrawal (*vyutthāna*) is all the more easily justified; and because Manu, by the words "the fourth part of life," has also spoken while relying precisely on the position of combination (*samuccaya*), the position of combination alone is superior.
For this very reason, the positions of option (*vikalpa*) and sublation (*bādha*) have been presented as the views of others.
And thus, it should be understood that statements such as "one may dwell in whichever [stage] he desires" were spoken from the perspective of the teachers who advocate for option.

The meaning is that even though it is already established by implication, it is stated with the intention that one who is incapable of performing the combined practice (*samuccaya*)—due to defects such as blindness or lameness, or due to poverty and the like—must resort to the option of alternation (*vikalpa*).
Alternatively, one who possesses knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātmajñānin*) should resort to the option of alternation, while another should resort to the option of combination.
Why? Because the purpose of the performance [of rituals] is the arising of spiritual realization (*vijñāna*).
When that [knowledge] has arisen, the human goal (puruṣārtha) is accomplished for one staying in any hermitage whatsoever;
the mention of "hermitage" is for the sake of conventional usage, as in such passages as "the castes and the stages of life."
What, then, are those stages of life? To this he says: "The student, the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.2)

One who practices celibacy (*brahmacarya*), or one who moves about without desire for the domain of Brahman itself, is a *brahmacārī*. One who has a house—that is, a wife—and dwells in connection with her is a *gṛhastha*.
One whose nature is to subsist on alms and so forth is a *bhikṣu*.
The scripture proclaimed by Vikhanas is the Vaikhānasa; one who conducts himself according to its rules is a Vaikhānasa.

This irregular compound (visamāsa) is intended to indicate their distinctness, as for example Uśanas says: "There are two types of *brahmacārins*: the *upakurvāṇa* and the *naiṣṭhika*; there are two types of *vaikhānasas*: those with wives and those without wives; there are two types of *saṃnyāsins*: the *bhikṣusaṃnyāsī* and the *vedasaṃnyāsī*; and the householder is of many kinds through distinctions such as the *śālīna*, the *yāyāvara*, and so forth. And so on.

But surely, since in another Smṛti the term *bhikṣu* is mentioned after defining the *vaikhānasa*, for what purpose is there this difference in order here? It is said in reply: the difference in order is intended to exclude the *vaikhānasa* from the rule "the first three among the highest are the stages of life" (*aprāguttamās traya āśramiṇaḥ*).

If it is argued that this is already established simply because of the prohibition against the *vaikhānasa* entering a village, we say no; for it is possible that those seeking [alms] might go to the forest as well. And so says another Smṛti:
The master of the four Vedas, the dialectician, the etymologist, the reciter of the Dharma, the celibate student, the householder, and the monk— this assembly consists of at least ten members.
Thus it is said.
But some say:
"Having performed the Prajāpatya sacrifice in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having consigned the sacred fires into oneself, a Brāhmaṇa may go forth from his home."
Relying on this other Smṛti text, some describe the difference in sequence as having the purpose that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) must be undertaken from the state of a householder alone;
the learned among the twice-born should investigate whether this has already been established by the preceding Sūtra or not.
Among them, the householder is the source of the others, because they do not produce offspring on their own.
Among all four stages of life (*āśrama*), the householder is the cause, because the others—the student (*brahmacārin*) and so forth—lack progeny.

The statement regarding the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) is for the sake of providing a reason; for the student is already established by the very preservation of his celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and even for the mendicant (*bhikṣu*), the practice of upward-directed semen (*ūrdhvaretas*) is prescribed.
Thus, even in the case of the forest-dweller who maintains a wife, the preservation of celibacy must be observed.

Although [the status of] these [outcastes] is already established by the context itself, the inclusion of the word "of them" (teṣām) is for the purpose of indicating that the entitlement to this dharma belongs only to those born of householders.
And so says Śātātapa:
"Caṇḍālas, those who have fallen from their vows, wandering mendicants, and ascetics..."
Their offspring, once born, one should cause to dwell together with the Caṇḍālas.

Thus, when it is stated that "the householder alone is their source," the word "alone" (eva) already establishes that the others must maintain their state of studenthood (*brahmacarya*); nevertheless, this specific mention is made so that there might not be a return to those [other stages].
If they were to turn back toward the householder’s life (*gārhasthya*), then they become *caṇḍālas*. Why? Because of the cited statement of Śātātapa:
"In that case, they become *caṇḍālas*."

Those wandering mendicants and ascetics who have fallen away from their vows—namely, those perpetual celibates and forest-dwellers—the king should cause the offspring born of them to dwell together with Caṇḍālas, meaning either in a village or elsewhere.

Now, since the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) are to be explained in their proper sequence, and because they apply equally to all stages, [the author] has first described those of the student (upakurvāṇa); he now speaks in order to describe those of the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), which follows in sequence: "In that regard, what was stated for the religious student (brahmacārin) [applies here as well]. (Gautama 3.4)

In this regard, there is an extension (*atideśa*) stating that whatever has been prescribed for the kindling of the fire and so forth by way of the *upanayana* ceremony applies to him as well. Now, one might ask: how is it known that this applies only to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) and not to the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*)? It is said: because the duties of the temporary student have already been described; because the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller will be described later on; therefore, it applies only to the lifelong student.
If it is asked, "Then what is the purpose of mentioning the 'student' (*brahmacārin*)? [the answer is: it is for the sake of that very person who has performed the vows of the temporary student.
This is for the purpose of establishing the qualification for the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*).

Having stated that by way of extension (*atideśa*) the very same vows of the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*) must be performed by the lifelong student as well, he now states the specific rule for the latter: "Dependence upon the teacher until the end" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.5).
Dependence upon the teacher—that is, conforming to his will—must be maintained until death.
Furthermore:
"He should recite [the mantra] with the remainder of the teacher's ritual duties. (Gautama 3.6)
At times other than those spent in service to the guru, one should perform recitation (*japa*).
In this way, recitation alone becomes his preeminent means for accomplishing dharma.
Although "teacher" (*ācārya*) was the subject under discussion, the mention of "guru" is for the purpose of including the service of one's mother and father as well.
Thus says Manu:
"Service to these three is said to be the supreme austerity."
Without being authorized by them, one should not practice any other dharma.
Thus [it is said].
In the absence of the guru, one's conduct [toward him] should be directed toward his offspring.

In the absence of the teacher, service should be rendered to his offspring; in the absence of the instructor, service should be rendered to his offspring—this is for the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). The mention of "teacher" (*guru*) is intended to include an offspring of the same caste. The mention of "offspring" (*apatya*) is intended to exclude the wife.
In his absence, it should be offered to an elder fellow-student or into the fire.

In the absence of that [the teacher], [one should serve] the son of the teacher; in the absence of him, one who is superior in knowledge and so forth; in the absence of him, a fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*) who has practiced the same Vedic course; in the absence of him, the fire.
Service to the fire consists of meditating upon the fire in its form as light.
Furthermore, what is the fruit of this stage of life? To this he says:
"One who conducts himself thus and has conquered his senses attains the world of Brahman. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.9)
Thus, by acting according to the instruction, one attains the world of Brahmā, the abode of Brahmā, provided that one has conquered the senses.

Since the instruction on the protection of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) mentions the organ of generation, this [conquest of the senses] should be understood as referring to the objects of the eyes and the other sense organs.
As Manu says:
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor desponds, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
Thus, this very [practice] is the primary one even for those that follow; it is for this purpose that its prescription occurs at the conclusion of the fruit.
Now he states the common duty for others as well:
"And this is not in conflict with those who follow the higher stages. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.10)
Whatever has been prescribed for the student (brahmacārin) applies also to those who follow, provided it is not contradictory—such as the avoidance of gambling and similar activities.

That which is contradictory is excluded, as for example: fire-sacrifices for the renunciant (pravrajita), residence in the teacher’s house for the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa), and the observance of celibacy for the householder.

The word "ca" (and) indicates that whatever is to be stated hereafter also applies to the preceding stages if it is not contradictory, such as: "One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or the unrighteous," and so forth.
A monk is one who has no accumulation. // Gautama 3.11 //

Now, it might be asked: "The duties of the householder, whose turn has now arrived, ought to be stated; why, then, are they being set aside while those of the mendicant are being described? To this it is replied: The householder has much to be said regarding him. Some of his duties, when being described, are not inconsistent [with those of others]; how then might they be understood by the ancients? It is for that purpose that they are stated out of order.

If it is then asked, "In that case, the duties of the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa) should be stated," there is no fault, as they have already been mentioned according to the sequence of their introduction.
Therefore, regarding the monk first:
by the word "non-accumulation," the relinquishing of material things that are subject to increase is meant, not the relinquishing of permanent items such as the topknot or the sacred thread.
