But surely, the abandonment of that which is permanent alone is logical; for by the word *upavīta*, a specific manner of wearing [the sacred thread] is denoted:
"When the right hand is raised, it is called *upavīta* by the wise."
Thus.
The sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is to be worn according to the prescribed rule;
for him, there is no entitlement to perform sacrifices.
He should not [perform rites] in a pit, nor in water, nor at a confluence, nor on a garment, nor at the *tripuṣkara* site.
He for whom there is no knowledge of liberation has nothing to do with his house, his seat, or his food.
Thus, because of the instruction for the renunciation of the water-pot and other such items;
and because in the Jābāla Śruti it is also instructed that the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) is to be abandoned, as in the passage: "Having cut off his nails, he should cast away the sacred thread."

It is said in reply: First, regarding what was stated—that there is no qualification for sacrifice (*yajña*)—the word *yāga* (sacrifice) also applies to the worship of the gods and the like. However, for this [ascetic], the worship of the Supreme Self through meditation does indeed exist. Why?

"For one who is constant in the forest, who has conquered the senses, who brings about the satisfaction of the Self that pervades all, whose mind is absorbed in the contemplation of the inner self, and who is indifferent [to worldly objects]—for such a one, non-return [to saṃsāra] is certain. (Gītā 5.27)

Because another Smṛti text is seen to show that the qualification belongs specifically to the sacrifice of the self (ātma-yāga), and it is thus heard in the Śruti: "Dharma and adharma are the oblation; the mind is the sacrificial ladle; the vital breath is the Adhvaryu priest; the senses are the Udgātṛ priests; sound and the other objects are the Hotṛ priests; with these as the officiating priests and with that ladle, one should offer that oblation day after day into the fire of the Supreme Self.
Therefore, since there exists the qualification for yoga, there is no fault.

As for what was said—“There is no attachment to the water-pot (kuṇḍikā) nor to water”—even there, the abandonment intended is that of attachment itself, for the purpose of avoiding its various forms, not of the water-pot and such items.
Why? Because it will be stated in that very same context: “wearing the sacred thread, with a water-pot in hand.”

If it is argued that, in that context, the phrase "the most righteous among all bases" (sarvāśrayāṇāṃ dharmiṣṭham), although functioning as a general rule due to its application to all stages of life (āśrama), is set aside by a specific rule—[we reply: no, for if the application to all stages of life is intended there, then within that section, for the sake of constructing the meaning of the sentence, [it must be understood as] "wearing the sacred thread and holding a water-pot in hand."

Thus, he would have stated it by means of positive suffixes (bhāvapratyaya) alone, saying: "The avoidance of backbiting, envy, pride, egoism, dishonesty, self-praise, reviling others, hypocrisy, greed, anger, and delusion is the most righteous duty for all stages of life. Having first spoken thus, the subsequent specification by means of negative suffixes (abhāvapratyaya), namely the injunction "wearing the sacred thread with a water-pot in hand," can be understood as intended to exclude the eligibility of all other stages of life.

Therefore, since there is no authority for all the stages of life (āśrama) in that state, one can certainly understand that the abandonment of attachment alone is enjoined by the words "no attachment to a hut, nor to water," so as to avoid the contingency of contradiction between earlier and later passages.
It is precisely for this purpose that the word "attachment" (saṅga) is also specified.

Therefore, even by that [text], there is no renunciation of the water-pot and other items. As for what was stated—“having clipped the nails and discarded the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)”—even there, at the time of first entering the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), one merely discards the old sacred thread; it is not a prohibition against the one being taken up at that moment.

Why? Because another Smṛti text is heard: “Having clipped the nails and having discarded the old garment, the sacred thread, and the water-pot, and having taken up new ones, one should enter the [renunciatory] stage.
Therefore, there is renunciation of those articles that have reached their end through wear.

Furthermore, if there were a renunciation of permanent possessions, it would follow that a monk could not perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), because the rule begins with "one should sip water while wearing the sacred thread" (*yajñopavītī*); in the absence of that [thread], the sipping of water would also be impossible. If you argue: "In the case of the option 'either shaven-headed or with a topknot' (*muṇḍaśikhī vā*), you yourself accept that sipping water is permissible even for one who has discarded the topknot—which is an auxiliary part of the rite—so we too may do the same," we say no. In that case, there is no fault because of the specific scriptural statement: "shaven-headed or with a topknot.
For you, however, there is indeed a fault, as there is no such scriptural statement permitting the discarding of the sacred thread.

While it should have been said "a monk is one who has no accumulation," the mention of "dharma" at the beginning is for the purpose of including the renunciation of even those things considered eternal, such as the *agnihotra* fire and one's wife.
Thus, he who would go forth from the state of a householder must renounce both the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires, along with the elaborations of wife, sons, sacrifices, and so forth.

For one who would renounce from the state of a Vaiśvānara-sacrificer, even in that case, there must be the abandonment of the wife—who has been obtained according to the rule for having a wife—and of the Śrāmaṇaka fire, as well as the five great sacrifices and so forth.
Some explain that the initial mention [of the recitation] is for the purpose of prescribing that even the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) is not required to maintain the sacred fires;

however, that is incorrect, because it is the recitation (*japa*) itself that is taught as the primary duty in the statement, "He should recite with the remainder of his duties toward the teacher," and by that alone, the absence of the maintenance of the fires and so forth can certainly be understood.
One whose vital energy flows upward. // Gautama 3.12 //

By the statement, "And this is not inconsistent with the subsequent [stages]," since his [the householder's] maintenance of celibacy is already established by what was said regarding the student (*brahmacārin*), the mention of the "one whose semen is drawn up" (*ūrdhvaretas*) is for the purpose of indicating that one should employ means such that the depletion of semen occurs [only gradually].
And the means consists of consuming small amounts of food and so forth.
As the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva has said:
The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food, with the exception of the craving for taste; even that craving for taste ceases for him upon seeing the Supreme.
Thus, with the intention of referring to the consumption of very little food, it is also stated in another Smṛti: "Eight mouthfuls are the meal of a sage," and so forth.
And in this way, there is no fault in a student (brahmacārin) eating a full meal.
And so another Smṛti states:
"The ox, the student, and the one who has maintained the sacred fires—these three achieve success only while eating; for them there is no success through fasting."
Thus:
"One who is firm in his conduct [should remain] during the rainy season. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.13)
Because of the plural form "in the rains" (*varṣāsu*), the meaning is that one should not travel from village to village during the four months [of the rainy season].
The mention of "conduct" (*śīla*) is because even if one dwells in a single place, there might still be the exertion of wandering;
by this very [rule], his state of having no fixed abode (*aniketanatva*) is established.
And so another Smṛti says: "At the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the root of a tree.
By mentioning the adoption of the [ascetic] conduct (śīla), he indicates that it need not necessarily be exactly thus;
therefore, one may go even during times of famine, the collapse of a kingdom, and so forth.
One seeking alms should go to the village. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.14)

"Begging" refers to food because it is obtained by begging, as well as clothing, a water-pot, and so forth; for the sake of these, he should go to the village—by implication, it is established that at all other times he should remain in the forest, in temples, or similar places.
When the time for alms has arrived, the student should say: "I shall go for alms at the lowest [time], without having turned back. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.15)
"Jaghanya" means after the act of eating;
thus says Manu:
"When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle is laid aside, when the embers are extinguished, and when the people have finished their meal..."
When the clatter of the alms-bowl has ceased, the ascetic should always go for alms.
Thus:
the meaning is that one should not enter again on that same day a house where [food] was refused and from which [the mendicant] has not turned away.
The word "should practice" (caret) is for the purpose of including other Smṛti texts.
As Vasiṣṭha said: "When the smoke has ceased and the pestle is laid aside, wearing a single garment or an antelope skin."
One whose desire for gain has ceased. // Gautama 3.16 //
The meaning is that he does not employ benedictions when giving alms, returning greetings, and so forth.

If it is argued that this is already understood by the phrase "one who does not undertake violence or favor," we say no; for favor (*anugraha*) consists in action, whereas a benediction (*āśis*) consists in speech.
He is restrained in speech, sight, and action. // Gautama 3.17 //

Since this is already established by the statement "restrained in speech, arms, and belly" within the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*), the repetition here is for the sake of emphasizing excellence.

Therefore, restraint of speech is silence (*mauna*), except in the cases of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), recitation (*japa*), asking for directions on the road, and inquiries regarding dharma and yoga—namely: "Vedic study, as well as inquiries on dharma and yoga, and likewise inquiries on the road..."
One should not disparage even a mendicant when he speaks the words "give" for the sake of alms.
This is because of the statement in another Smṛti:
"Restraint of the eyes" means that one must not even look at one's own disease;
and likewise Vasiṣṭha says: "One who is indifferent toward all beings."
Restraint of action consists merely in the performance of what is prescribed, so that there may be no engagement in actions performed for the sake of desired rewards.
Now, by the statement "a monk is one who has no accumulation," once all accumulative property has been relinquished, an exception is made:
he may wear a garment for the purpose of covering his private parts. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.18)
"Kaupīna" refers to nakedness;
one should wear only such clothing as serves to cover that.
And thus, there is no fault in accepting only that much from praiseworthy members of the twice-born.
And furthermore:
"But he who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back [from his vow],"
He who always accepts [gifts] destroys both those who have been born and those yet to be born.
Thus, the enumeration of faults found in another Smṛti should be understood as referring to cases other than this one.
Some wash it away once it has been discarded. (Gautama 3.19)

Some think that for the sake of avoiding the fault of accepting [garments], one should wash and then wear what has been discarded on the road or elsewhere; the term "having washed" (*nirṇijya*) is used for the purpose of attaining personal purity.
One should not take a limb from medicinal plants or trees that has not been separated [from the whole].
Plants (*oṣadhayaḥ*) are those that end with the ripening of their fruit;
those that bear fruit without flowers are forest trees (*vanaspatayaḥ*).
By including both categories, all stationary beings (*sthāvarāḥ*) are also encompassed.

If it is argued that the phrase "one who does not undertake [acts of] injury or favor" already establishes that one should not take branches, leaves, and so forth— which are inseparable from and not distinct from those [living beings]—
then there is no fault, because some maintain that in this context "injury" refers specifically to the killing of mobile creatures, and the statement was made with that intention.
Because of the word "upa," the instigator would also not be [the agent].
Since it has been taught that one's conduct must be constant, and since the possibility of acting according to one's own desire might arise outside of the rainy season, he says:
"He may stay in a village for a second night during the non-rainy season. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.21)
By the word *ṛtu*, only the rainy season is meant.
When the rainy season has passed, one should not stay for a second night in a village;
the meaning is that one should not stay in a single village for two days.
By the mention of "village," there is no fault in staying in the forest. By the mention of "non-season," there is no fault even for one who stays during the rains for a second [night];
by the word "rains" (varṣā), the winter and summer seasons are intended.
And consequently, it follows as a matter of course that during that rainy season one should dwell in one place alone and not elsewhere.
He may be either shaven-headed or wear a topknot.
This undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting the wearing of matted hair.
There is an option according to one's preference.
One should avoid the destruction of seeds. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.23)
One should not perform the destruction of seeds, such as rice and other grains, by means of threshing and similar processes.
He is equal toward all living beings. // Gautama 3.24 //
The meaning is that one should be impartial toward all living beings, avoiding the distinction between one's own side and the side of others.
He should not engage in acts of either injury or favor. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.25)
Since this is already established by the word "violence" (*hiṃsām*) in the section on the student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), this repetition is for the sake of emphasizing its gravity.
Consequently, even when the killing of a living being is unintentional, an expiation must be performed every day to avoid that [sin].
Thus Uśanas says: "For the purification of an unintentional killing, one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) during the night and three during the day."
By the word *anugraha*, affection (*sneha*) is meant;
the meaning is that one should not even perform that.
Having spoken concerning the mendicant, he now states the dharma of the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa):
"The forest-dweller, subsisting on roots and fruits in the forest, is devoted to austerity. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.26)
The word *vaikhānasa* is derived from the root *sṛ* (to move).
Its meaning is that one who dwells in the forest should be habituated to eating roots and such things; the sense is that he should not eat prepared food.
He should be habituated to austerity, meaning habituated to the emaciation of the body.

And in this way, he should consume even roots, fruits, and so forth, only in small quantities, because another Smṛti text is seen to state: "For the forest-dweller, sixteen [mouthfuls]" (Vānaprasthasya ṣoḍaśa).
Having established the sacred fire according to the Śrāmaṇaka rite. // Gautama 3.27 //
The *śrāmaṇaka* is the treatise of the *vaikhānasas*.
By means of it, having established the sacred fires and taken them up, one should perform the oblation in the evening and in the morning; this is the remainder [of the sense].
He shall not eat food that is vulgar. 3.28.
One should not eat even wild roots and fruits that have been cultivated in a village.
He should worship the gods, the ancestors, humans, spirits, and sages. // Gautama 3.29 //
The five great sacrifices (*pañca mahāyajñāḥ*) of the householder are accomplished by means of village food.
This [section] is commenced so that, because of the prohibition against non-village food for him, there might not be a cessation of those [sacrifices].
And thus says Manu:
With various pure forest products, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
one should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
He should be hospitable to all guests, with the exception of those who are prohibited.
The meaning is that as long as he goes to his hermitage, everyone there is indeed his guest;
thus, there is no restriction regarding caste (*varṇa*), such as "for a Brāhmaṇa, one who is not a Brāhmaṇa is not a guest," nor is there any restriction regarding number.
This applies with the exception of those who are prohibited, such as thieves and others, as well as those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*).
One may also consume meat from a sacrificial victim. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.31)
The meat of an animal killed by wild beasts such as tigers is *vaiṣka*;
one should consume that.
The word "api" is used here in the sense of censure.
Thereafter, one should employ it only in times of distress.
One should not stand upon ground that has been ploughed by a plow.
The meaning is that even in the forest, one should not step upon a ploughed area, nor should one make a dwelling there.

Although the sense of "should step upon" (*ākrāmet*) is already established, the use of the term "should occupy" (*adhitiṣṭhet*) is intended to indicate that there is no fault in stepping upon such ground through inadvertence.
Although the sense of "ploughed" (*kṛṣṭam*) is already established, the specific mention of "ploughshare" (*phāla*) is for the purpose of prohibiting a dwelling in the immediate vicinity of a field.
And he should not enter a village. (Gautama 3.33)
One should not enter a human habitation even by a path not ploughed by a plow;
by the use of the word "and," [it is implied that one should not enter] even another village.
He has matted hair and wears garments of bark or deerskin.

*Jaṭilaḥ* means one with matted hair (*keśī*). This rule is formulated for the purpose of restriction, so that he must indeed be one with matted hair. *Cīra* is [a garment] made from *darbha* grass and the like.
This is to be seen as the lower garment; the *ajina* is the skin;
this is the upper garment.
And so it is stated in another Smṛti: "Clothed in rags and wearing an antelope skin as an upper garment."
One should not eat food that has been kept for more than a year.
One should not consume even roots and fruits that are more than a year old;
likewise, Manu says: "In the month of Āśvayuja, one should abandon [them]," and so forth.
And thus...
The accumulation for only one year has been accomplished.

Having spoken of the Vaikhānasa, he now says, desiring to state the view of certain authorities regarding the sublation of the stages of life (āśrama), based on the single stage of life: "But the Teacher [Gautama] maintains that there is only one stage of life, because of the direct injunction of the householder's life. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.36)
"Aikāśramya" means existing in a single āśrama;
the word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis;
and the genitive case in "gārhasthyasya" is used in the sense of the object.

The teachers maintain that the householder’s stage alone is intended [as the final one]. Why? Because of its direct injunction; the meaning is: because it is found to be enjoined by revealed scripture (*śruti*).

Even though there is no injunction in the form "one should become a householder," nevertheless, since the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra*—which are to be accomplished by a householder—is enjoined, the injunction for that very stage is to be understood.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
[From] the *Vaikhānasa-dharmasūtra* (1–3), which corresponds to the *Vaikhānasa-smārtasūtra* 8–10;
