http://gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/gretil.htm Vaikh 01.01.(112.1): Now, the duties of the social classes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma).
Vaikh 01.01.(112.1–2): The four social classes (varṇas) were born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet of [the Creator]: the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.
For the Śruti declares: "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth. (Vaikh 01.01.112.2–3).
For the first three [classes], the sacraments beginning with *niṣeka* (impregnation) are prescribed. (Vaikh 01.01.112.3–4).
These twice-born ones possess the entitlement to the Veda. (Vaikh 01.01.112.4).
Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa there are six duties: studying, teaching, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, [the duties] are sacrificing for oneself, studying, and giving gifts.
For the Kṣatriya, [there are additionally] protecting the subjects, punishing the wicked, and fighting.
Vaikh 01.01.(112.7): For a Vaiśya, [the occupations are] cattle-rearing, money-lending, and trade.
Vaikh 01.01.(112.8): For a Śūdra, [the duties are] service to the twice-born and agriculture.
Vaikh 01.01.(112.8–9): There are four stages of life (āśramas) for a Brāhmaṇa, the first three for a Kṣatriya, and only two for a Vaiśya.

Vaikh 01.01. (112.9–10): There are four types of those belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*): the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*).

Vaikh 01.02. (112.11–13): Having been initiated, the student wears a girdle, a sacrificial thread, a deerskin, and carries a staff. Having bathed, he performs the libations (*tarpaṇa*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) both morning and evening, and the oblation of fuel-sticks (*samiddhoma*). Having clasped the feet of his teacher and saluted him daily, he studies the Veda according to his vow.

While the teacher remains seated, [the pupil] should remain seated; when he has risen, having risen before him, he should follow him as he walks. When [the teacher] is sitting or lying down, being so directed, he should perform sitting and lying down in a lower position. Without being told, he does not perform any action whatsoever.
Even without being told, he should perform his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) and his daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*).

Having avoided bathing in warm water, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, ointments, perfumes, flowers, sandals, umbrellas, sleeping during the day, the emission of semen, looking at or touching women, sexual intercourse, lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, violence, and so forth, he should always be intent on serving his teacher and perform deeds that are pleasing and beneficial to him.
Free from malice and agreeable in speech and mind, he speaks what is pleasant and true;
even when distressed, he does not utter what is untrue or unpleasant, nor does he speak slander.

Vaikh 01.02. (113.4–5) Abstaining from eating honey, meat, fish, broth, fermented liquids, and other forbidden foods, he should practice the conduct of begging for alms; having done so, and being permitted by his teacher, he should eat the food obtained as alms.
(113.5–6) He should not utter the names of his teacher, elders, or those initiated for sacrifice.
(113.6–7) In the absence of his teacher, he performs his duties toward the teacher’s son just as he would toward the teacher himself.
Vaikh 01.03 (113.8–9): There are four kinds of *brahmacārins*: the *gāyatra*, the *brāhma*, the *prājāpatya*, and the *naiṣṭhika*.

Vaikh 01.03 (113.9–10): The *gāyatra* [type] is one who, after the initiation (*upanayana*), for three nights eats neither pungent nor salty food; having studied the *Gāyatrī* [verse], he remains a practitioner of the vow until the completion of the *Sāvitra-vrata*.

Vaikh 01.03. (113.10–14): After the *sāvitra-vrata*, one should practice begging for alms in the houses of householders who are neither accused nor fallen, and observe the vows of the Veda; having stayed in the teacher’s family for twelve or twenty years, and having completed the study of the Vedas—either all four, two, or one, together with the *sūtras*—one should enter the state of a householder.

Vaikh 01.03. (113.14–15): The *prājāpatya* [initiation]: Having bathed, being devoted to his daily duties (*nityakarman*) and the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and being intent upon Nārāyaṇa, he reflects upon the meaning of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas and then performs the taking of a wife.
Vaikh 01.03. (113.15–16): Regarding the *prājāpatya*, the sages declare that one should not remain [without marriage] for more than three years.

The lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), having put on a saffron-colored garment, a hide, or a bark-cloth, with matted hair or a top-knot, wearing a girdle, carrying a staff, and bearing the sacred thread and hide, remains chaste, pure, and abstaining from pungent food and salt for as long as he lives; staying in the teacher’s family, he subsists on alms-food that has been announced [to him].

Having taken a wife, the householder—observing the rules and conduct such as ritual bathing and always performing the *aupāsana* fire-sacrifice and the *pākayajñas*—upon the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* oblation, rises to meet and salutes a teacher (*guru*) or a *snātaka* who has arrived at his home; having offered them a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*), and having presented the *madhuparka* mixed with ghee, curd, and milk, he feeds them with various foods according to his ability.

He honors, as is appropriate, mendicants, celibate students, guests who are knowers of the Veda and learned in the Vedas, paternal uncles, teachers, officiating priests, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, and others who have arrived, as well as children, the elderly, the helpless, the afflicted, and those exhausted by travel (Vaikh 01.04, 114.7–10).
Even if he is unable [to provide much], he should eat only after giving the first portion or a morsel of almsfood along with water to them (Vaikh 01.04, 114.10).

Endowed with compassion, truthfulness, purity, and right conduct, he should constantly worship the sages (*ṛṣis*) through Vedic study and libations; the gods through sacrifice, offerings, oblations, water, flowers, and the like; the ancestors through *śrāddha* rites and sons; and all beings through offerings, as well as humans with food and other necessities.

(Vaikh 01.04) Thus, freed from the three debts, he becomes debtless. (Vaikh 01.04) Householders are of four kinds: those who live by agriculture and trade (*vārtā-vṛtti*), the *śālīna*, the *yāyāvara*, and the *ghora-ācārika*. (Vaikh 08.05)

One who subsists by the livelihood of *vārttā*—that is, one who lives by agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade—is a *vārttāvṛtti*. (Gṛhyasūtra 8.5, 114.14–15) One who follows the *śālīna* mode of life is endowed with restrictive observances; having performed the *pākayajñas*, having established the sacred fires, he performs the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices every fortnight, and every four months...

One who sacrifices at the Cāturmāsya festivals, one who performs the Paśubandha sacrifice every six months, and one who sacrifices with Soma every year; one who is a Yāyāvara, performing Havis-sacrifices and Soma-sacrifices, studying and teaching, giving and receiving, devoted to the six duties, constantly tending the sacred fires, and providing food to guests who arrive—such a person is a Ghorācārika who, being bound by observances, sacrifices but does not officiate for others.

He studies but does not teach; he gives but does not accept gifts; he subsists on the practice of gleaning grains. Devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, having offered the morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations, he performs the *asidhārā-vrata* during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Jyeṣṭha, attending to the sacred fire with forest herbs.

Vaikh 01.06. (115.8–11): A householder together with his wife, whether he maintains the five fires (*pañcāgni*) or the three fires (*tretāgni*), when intending to go from the house to the forest hermitage (*vana-āśrama*), should—whether he has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) or not—place the *aupāsana* fire upon the two kindling sticks (*araṇi*) and churn it out in the house. Having established the fire according to the rules for the ascetic’s fire (*śrāmaṇakīya-vidhāna*), having offered the *āghāra* libations, and having taken the ascetic’s fire, he should proceed to the third stage of life. Vaikh 01.06. (115.11–12): As before, he should perform the rites beginning with the sprinkling of the fire-chamber and the scraping of the ground.

Having wiped the third altar as well, and having prepared a grass-mat for spreading (*paristaraṇa-kūrca*)—measuring thirty-six finger-breadths, made of six finger-breadths of *darbha* grass tied beneath with a cord, divided into three parts like a rope, and bound at its base—he spreads it upon the middle altar for the *śrāmaṇaka* rite.

Vaikh 01.06 (115.15–17): Having invoked [the deities] up to "the Śrāmaṇaka sacrifice, the sacrifice-deities, the Viśve Devas," having poured out the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having offered oblations up to "Svāhā to the Śrāmaṇaka, Svāhā to the Śrāmaṇaka sacrifice, Svāhā to the Viśve Devas, the deities of the sacrifice," one should offer the *caru*—this is the specific rule for the establishment of the fire (*ādhāra-viśeṣa*).
Vaikh 01.06 (115.18–116.1): And the altar (*vedi*) for the Śrāmaṇaka fire is thirty-two finger-breadths long, four finger-breadths wide, and four finger-breadths high.
The middle [altar] is surrounded by that [first one], measuring five finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in height.
The third altar is below it, elevated to the same extent as the width of the upper altar.

Having constructed a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) twelve finger-breadths deep in the center, provided with these three altars, the forest-dweller, having established the fire, should daily offer the morning and evening oblations like those of the *aupāsana* fire, and should sacrifice into the *śrāmaṇaka* fire with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.
Vaikh 01.06: One who has a wife may go to the forest without his wives and without the sacred fires.
Vaikh 01.07: Forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) are both those with their wives and those without their wives.
Vaikh 01.07: Those with their wives are of four kinds.
The Audumbara, the Vairiñca, the Vālakhilya, and the Phenapa—these are the types [of forest-dwellers].

The Audumbara, subsisting on uncultivated fruits and herbs that have ripened naturally, or eating roots and fruits, avoids onions, asafoetida, garlic, honey, fish, meat, putrid food, grain, sour substances, contact with others, and the cooking of food by others; he worships the gods, sages, ancestors, and men; he dwells in the forest, staying outside the village; and having performed the morning and evening *agnihotra* as well as the *śrāmaṇaka-agni-homa* and the *vaiśvadeva-homa*, he practices austerity (*tapas*).
Vaikh 01.07. (116.12): Having established only the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, he offers oblations—so say some.

Vaikh 01.07. (116.12–15): He gazes toward the eastern direction; having gone in that direction, and having nourished his own guests with whatever is obtained there, such as *priyaṅgu*, barley, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, and so forth, he becomes one who performs the *agnihotra*, *śrāmaṇaka*, and *vaiśvadeva* offerings, one who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa, and one whose nature is asceticism (*tapas*).

Vaikh 01.07. (116.15–17): A Vālakhilya, wearing matted hair and clothed in rags and bark, having the sun for his fire, shall, on the full moon day of Kārttika, abandon abundant food and thereafter subsist on the remainder for the rest of the months, performing penance.
Vaikh 01.07. (116.18): They declare that for him, the sun itself becomes the fire.

Vaikh 01.07. (116.18–117.2): The foam-drinker (*phenapa*), the one with raised staff (*ud-daṇḍaka*), the madman (*unmattaka*), the one who blocks [the senses] (*nirodhaka*), and the one who subsists on withered and fallen leaves (*śīrṇa-patita-pattra-āhārī*), while performing the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow, sleeping on the ground and meditating upon Nārāyaṇa, seeks only liberation (*mokṣa*).
Vaikh 01.08. (117.3): There are many kinds of those who are without wives (*a-patnīka*).

Vaikh 01.08. (117.3–11): [They are] those who eat at fixed times, those with raised staffs, those who have turned [to asceticism], those who grind with stones, those who possess uplifted fruits, those who use their teeth as a mortar, those who live by gleaning, those who live by sight, those who live like pigeons, those who move like deer, those who take [food] with the hand, those who take [food] from rocks or wooden planks, those who eat what is scorched by the sun, those who eat bilva fruit, those who eat flowers, those who eat fallen leaves, those who eat at intervals of time, those who eat once a day, those who eat four times a day, those who sleep on thorns, those who sleep in the *vīrāsana* posture, and those who sleep in the midst of five fires.

"It is known that there are those of various practices: those who eat smoke, those who sleep on stones, those who plunge into water, those who dwell in water-jars, those who observe silence, those who remain with their heads downward, those who face the sun, those with arms raised, and those standing on one foot. (Vaikh 01.09) "Furthermore, mendicants seeking liberation are of four kinds: the *kuṭīcakas*, the *bahūdakas*, the *haṃsas*, and the *paramahaṃsas*. (Vaikh 01.09)

Among them, the *kuṭīcakas*—who know the reality of the path of yoga and seek only liberation—subsist on eight morsels of food in the hermitages of Gautama, Bhāradvāja, Yājñavalkya, Hārīta, and others.

(Vaikh 01.09, 117.13–15) The *bahūdakas*, who carry the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and garments dyed with ochre (*kāṣāya-dhātu-vastra*), and who assume the appearance of mendicants, seek only liberation by begging for alms at seven houses among the dwellings of Brahmanical seers and other virtuous people, while avoiding meat, salt, and stale food. (Vaikh 01.09, 117.15–118.1)

The *haṃsas* dwell for one night in a village and five nights in a town; not dwelling beyond that, they subsist on cow urine and cow dung, or fast for a month, or observe the perpetual *cāndrāyaṇa* vow, always aspiring only for rising [from their practice]. The *paramahaṃsas*, however, dwell at the foot of a single tree, in an empty house, or in a cremation ground; they are either clothed in a garment or clothed in the directions [naked]. For them, there is no duality such as virtue and vice, truth and falsehood, purity and impurity, and so forth.
Vaikh 01.09. (118.6–7): Being equal toward all and having realized the Self in all, they practice begging for alms among all social classes (*varṇas*), regarding a clod of earth and gold as the same.

Vaikh 01.09. (118.7–8): The fourfold stage of life (*caturāśramya*) is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, the threefold stage of life (*tryāśramya*) for Kṣatriyas, and the twofold stage of life (*dvayāśramya*) for Vaiśyas.
Vaikh 01.09. (118.8–9): For its fruit is of two kinds: that which is accompanied by desire (*sakāma*) and that which is free from desire (*niṣkāma*).

*Sa-kāma* (with desire) refers here in this *saṃsāra* to the longing for the attainment of a son and so forth, having recognized worldly prosperity, or the longing for other fruits such as heaven. *Niṣkāma* (without desire) refers to the performance of prescribed duties without any longing whatsoever. In that regard, *niṣkāma* is of two kinds: *pravṛtti* (active engagement) and *nivṛtti* (renunciation).

*Pravṛtti* is the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Having disregarded the knowledge of the number [of breaths] and having relied upon it, one who is engaged in *prāṇāyāma*, *āsana*, *pratyāhāra*, and *dhāraṇā* achieves mastery over the vital air (*vāyu*) and attains the supernatural powers (*aiśvarya*) beginning with *aṇimā*.
However, because that [attainment] again leads to rebirth due to the exhaustion of merit from austerity and because of the abundance of diseases, the supreme sages do not hold it in high regard.

Vaikh 01.09. (119.1–6): "Renunciation" (*nivṛtti*) means that, having realized the impermanence of the worlds and understanding that there is nothing other than the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), one disregards *saṃsāra*, severs the bond consisting of wife and family, becomes one whose senses are conquered, and leaves the body. Having established the union (*yoga*) between the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Self, it is known as the entry into the supreme light—which is beyond the senses, the seed of the entire universe, devoid of all particularity, eternal bliss, which like drinking the nectar of immortality always brings satisfaction, and is the gateway to liberation.

Vaikh 01.10 (119.7–8): "Due to differences in their conduct regarding cessation (*nivṛtti*), yogins are of three kinds: *sāraṅga*, *ekārtha*, and *visaraga*. Vaikh 01.10 (119.8–9): "The *sāraṅgas* are fourfold: those who do not restrain [the breath], those who restrain it, those who follow the path, and those who follow the wrong path.

Vaikh 01.10 (119.9–10): "The *ekārthas* are fivefold: those who go far, those who do not go far, those who go between the eyebrows, those who are undivided (*asaṃbhakta*), and those who are divided (*saṃbhakta*)."
Vaikh 01.10. (119.10–11): Those who possess number are not *visaragas* (those who have gone forth).

Vaikh 01.10. (119.11–13): Among them, the *sāraṅgas* are so called because they go toward the essence (*sāra*), which is the *kṣetrajña*. Regarding those [who think], "I am Viṣṇu," and move about having meditated thus, for them there are no breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the like.

Vaikh 01.10. (119.13–14): But for those who are suppressors (*nirodhakas*), there exist the sixteen digits (*kalā*), beginning with breath-control, withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
Vaikh 01.10. (119.14–15): For those who follow the path, there are only six [limbs], beginning with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Vaikh 01.10. (119.15–17): For those who follow the divergent paths, they conceive of eight limbs—namely, restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*)—and thus they also conceptualize the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) in a different way. Vaikh 01.11. (120.1): Now, regarding the single seer (*ekārṣya*).
Those who have a single seer as their authority are called *ekārṣya*.
For those among them who travel by the distant path, this is the way:

through the *piṅgalā* channel they enter the solar orb; there, having united with the Person residing there, they proceed to the lunar orb and unite with the Person residing there; from there they go to lightning and unite with the Person residing there; and then, in due order, they attain union (*sāyujya*) with Vaikuṇṭha.
Vaikh 01.11. (120.5): This is the rule for those who do not go far [from their homes].

Vaikh 01.11. (120.5–7): Having brought about the union of the individual self (*kṣetrajña*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) by means of the individual self, and having meditated upon the total dissolution right there, they meditate: "I am pure existence alone, like space."

Vaikh 01.11 (120.7–10): Those who go between the eyebrows perform the drawing [of the breath] from the five locations beginning with the big toe by means of the union of the *kṣetrajña* and the *paramātman*, leading it to the space between the eyebrows through the fire-gate of *sattva*; then they effect its exit through the *piṅgalā* channel until the end of dissolution (*pralaya*) or until the conclusion of the yoga of the *kṣetrajña*.

Vaikh 01.11 (120.10–11): Those called "unassociated" (*asaṃbhakta*) perform meditation (*dhyāna*) with the mind. Vaikh 01.11 (120.11): They hear the scripture that explains that [meditation] with their ears.
With the eye they perceive the deity;
with the nose they experience odor;
with the hand they pay homage to the deity.

Vaikh 01.11 (120.13–14): He is called the "Pervader" (*saṃbhakta*), the Brāhmaṇa, because that Supreme Self, having pervaded everything like space, remains as both the joined (*yukta*) and the unjoined (*ayukta*). Vaikh 01.11 (120.15): Therefore, apart from this Brahman, one does not perceive a self anywhere else.
Vaikh 01.11 (120.16): It has been stated that even for one who has reached the middle of the eyebrows, [all] doubts are indeed without basis.
Therefore, nothing other than Brahman is logically possible.
Because they follow various paths, perceive various views, and travel upon evil ways, they are called *visaraga* (those who wander away).
In ancient times, Prajāpati perceived the faction of those who wander away (*visaraga-pakṣa*) for the purpose of concealing his instruction.
Seeing him, even the sages fell into a state of delusion, let alone ordinary men.
For those who possess the ego-sense and are intent on liberation through the path of renunciation, there is no liberation in this life, but only in future births.
Therefore, the path of renunciation is not to be practiced.

Vaikh 01.11. (121.5–8): Some [attain liberation] through physical mortification; some through the recitation of mantras; some through a particular form of meditation; some through a particular syllable; others through the conquest of the vital breath (*vāyu*); and still others, having united the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), meditate. These [latter] do not desire union with the Supreme Self alone. Vaikh 01.11. (121.8–9): They declare that the Person (*puruṣa*) resides within the heart. Vaikh 01.11. (121.9–10): Some, understanding that yoga is the performance of what has been prescribed—without any meditation at all—desire liberation.

Vaikh 01.11 (121.10–11): For those who follow the path of animal sacrifice (*visaraga-paśu*), there is no liberation in this birth. Vaikh 01.11 (121.11–12): One who desires liberation in this very life must not practice the path of animal sacrifice.

Vaikh 01.11 (121.12–15): It is known that one should first fix the intellect upon Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahman*) and subsequently apply effort by taking refuge in Brahman without attributes (*nirguṇa-brahman*).
Vaikh 02.01.(122.1): Now follows the rule for the *śrāmaṇaka* (the forest-dweller’s life) for one who has retired to the forest.

Vaikh 02.01.(122.1–3): A householder who has performed the *soma* sacrifice, having seen his son and grandson and having established his sons and others in the household, shall shave his head and perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
Vaikh 02.01.(122.3–4): In the spring, during the bright fortnight, at an auspicious place, he shall go to the forest hermitage together with his wife.
Vaikh 02.01. (122.4–5): On the preceding day, having bathed and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he should drink water with *kuśa* grass and observe a fast.
Vaikh 02.01. (122.5–6): Having performed the *aupāsana* oblation, he should consign the fire into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) with the verse, "Thy womb is of fire...

Vaikh 02.01. (122.6–8): Having gathered the *darbha* grass and other materials according to the procedure for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, he prepares—as before—the ritual mats for strewing, the enclosing sticks, the fuel-sticks, the bamboo staff, the sacred thread (*upavīta*), the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the bark garment, and so forth.
Vaikh 02.01. (122.8): One should construct the fire-pit according to the procedure previously described.

Vaikh 02.01. (122.8–10): On the following day, having churned and kindled the fire with the Vaiśvānara-sūkta, and having placed the fire while reciting "O Agni, come hither" (*agna āyāhi*) and "Descend" (*upāvaroha*), one offers the *āghāra* libation to the Śrāmaṇaka fire as before.

Having bowed to the fire and sprinkled it around, and having offered the five expiatory oblations with the mantra "O Agni, you are the expiation" (*agne prāyaścitte tvam*), he should sprinkle himself with water and gold-vessels, and then sacrifice the principal offerings dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the five Varuṇas, ending with the *vyāhṛtis*.

To the west of the fire, having placed two *kuśa* blades with their tips pointing eastward and an upper stone upon them, he should step upon the stone with the tip of his right big toe while reciting, "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ... (*tat savitur vareṇyam*). Having put on a bark garment, an antelope skin, or a hempen cloth, as before, he takes up the three items beginning with the girdle, the sacred thread, and the upper garment, as well as the black antelope skin.
Having sipped water (*ācamya*), saying "May there be well-being for the gods," and having circumambulated the fire and paid obeisance (*pradakṣiṇa-praṇāma*), he should sit down.

Having sprinkled water on his own head with the mantra "May the altars be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no vedīḥ*), and having offered the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations as well as the *vyāhṛtis*, he should consume the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*) while practicing breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having sipped water twice with the mantra "In every union" (*yoge yoge*), and having performed obeisance with "A hundred autumns indeed" (*śatam in nu śaradaḥ*) and circumambulation of the sun with "We have come together with the great one" (*āgantrā samagan mahi*), he should so act.
With the mantra, "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom" (*rāṣṭrabhṛd asi*), he should take hold of a seat of *kūrca* grass with its tips pointing upward.

Having recited the Sāvitrī verse—first part by part (*pacchaḥ*) as "Oṃ bhūs tat savituḥ," "Oṃ bhuvo bhargo devasya," and "Oṃ suvardhiyo yo naḥ"; then half-verse by half-verse (*ardharcaśaḥ*) as "Oṃ bhūr bhuvas tat savituḥ" and "Oṃ suvardhiyo yo naḥ"; and finally the whole verse (*samastā*) as "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvas tat savituḥ"—and having entered the forest hermitage (*vanāśrama*), he should formally resolve upon the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya-vrata*).
And his wife should likewise remain a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacāriṇī*).

Having himself circumambulated the fire from left to right, he offers with clarified butter the oblation to Prajāpati, the *dhātṛ* and other *minda* oblations, the interrupted oblation to Indra, the Vaiśvadeva, the Vaiṣṇava, the outer oblations beginning with *viṣṇo nuka*, the *prājāpatya-sūkta*, and the binding of that vow; having again offered the principal oblations, he binds the *prājāpatya-vrata*.

Having stood [there], with the two mantras "devasya tvā" and "yo me daṇḍaḥ," he takes up the double-staff (*dvidaṇḍa*) belonging to Viṣṇu—provided with five, seven, or nine joints, reaching to the hairline, and straight—with whichever of these measurements is appropriate.
With the mantra "yena devāḥ," he takes up the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and the clay-strainer (*mṛdgrahiṇī*), as well as the sandals and the umbrella, as previously described.

Having kindled the fires, beginning with the Gārhapatya, and having performed the Agnihotra, he offers the Prājāpatya oblation and the Viṣṇu-sūkta into the Āhavanīya fire. Having offered everywhere with the formulas "Svāhā to Agni" and "Svāhā to Soma and Viṣṇu," he consigns the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*).
In the forest, on a mountain, or in a secluded place on a riverbank, having prepared a forest hermitage (*vanāśrama*), he should construct the fire-pits as previously described.

VaikhSmS 02.03 (124.1–2): Taking the sacred fires together with his wife and equipped with the necessary vessels and materials, he enters the forest hermitage (*vanāśrama*). VaikhSmS 02.04 (124.3–4): Having sprinkled water upon the site for the fire-altar, having dug it out, and having drawn six lines, he should place a fragment of gold and grains of rice there and establish the *śrāmaṇaka* fire.

Vaikh 02.04 (124.4–7): He collects wild materials—terrestrial and arboreal—such as *kulīra*, *udghāta*, and *añchaṇa* plants; old *kuśa* and *darbha* grasses; a tuft of wool; the tip of a *plakṣa* tree; fragrant reeds (*tejana*); *guggulu* resin; pieces of gold; and a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*). Vaikh 02.04 (124.7–9): Having chosen forest-dwelling ascetics as his officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and having churned the fire, he establishes the three sacred fires—the *Āhavanīya*, *Gārhapatya*, and *Dakṣiṇāgni*—or the five fires according to the procedure for the formal setting up of the fires (*agnyādheya*). Then, having offered two oblations each, he performs the daily offerings twice a day using only wild materials.

The forest-dwelling sage practices these ten observances (*niyamas*)—namely, bathing, purity, self-study, austerity, charity, sacrifice, fasting, restraint of the sexual organ, vows, and silence—as well as these ten restraints (*yamas*): truthfulness, kindness, straightforwardness, forbearance, self-control, affection, serenity, gentleness, non-violence, and sweetness.

Meditating upon Viṣṇu with devotion, not omitting the two daily offerings of the *agnihotra* and the *śrāmaṇaka* fire-sacrifice, and having abandoned village food, he resolves upon forest herbs, fruits, roots, or vegetables as his constant sustenance. Having fetched [the materials] with the mantra "Tirodhā bhūḥ," he himself, together with his wife, cooks the sacrificial oblation in the afternoon. At the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, after feeding the guests who have arrived, he eats an unlimited amount.
At night, he shall not eat.

Vaikh 02.05. (125.1–2): Having spread *darbha* grass, ordinary grass, or leaves below, the one who is firm in his vow (*su-vrata*) shall lie down alone, without his wife who is likewise firm in her vow. Vaikh 02.05. (125.2–3): She performs service for him; he must not approach her. Vaikh 02.05. (125.3):
Free from desire, with his vital seed drawn up and his senses conquered, he should look upon her as he would upon his mother.

Vaikh 02.05.(125.4-5): He should perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the Nakṣatra-iṣṭi, and the Āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi with wild herbs, in due order as before. Vaikh 02.05.(125.5-7): Sustaining his life with roots, fruits, leaves, or flowers that have ripened in their respective seasons and fallen off naturally, he should practice an ever-increasing application of austerity, distinguished by the excellence of the fruits and other such qualities.

Vaikh 02.05. (125.7–10): Alternatively, one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), having consigned all the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), and having gathered together all the terrestrial and arboreal fires with all the *saṃvāpa* mantras, should produce fire by friction according to this rule and the procedure for the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*). Then, with all the mantras, he should establish the *śrāmaṇaka* fire in the hearth of the *sabhya* fire and maintain it.
Vaikh 02.05. (125.10): They say that the *śrāmaṇaka* fire is a modification of the *sabhya* fire.

Vaikh 02.05. (125.10–13): A man without a wife, having performed an oblation in the fire like a mendicant, having discarded his forest-vessels and other implements, having entrusted his wife to a son, and likewise having internalized the sacred fires within himself, shall take up bark garments, a sacred thread, and so forth, as well as an alms-bowl; then, being without fire and without a wife, he shall go and dwell in the forest.
Vaikh 02.05. (125.13–15): "This is the root of all ascetic practices (*tapas*); therefore, Vikhanas declared this rule and this fire to be 'belonging to the ascetic' (*śrāmaṇaka*)."

Vaikh 02.06. (125.16–17): When one who is seventy years of age or older, childless, or bereft [of family], having reflected upon birth, death, old age, and so forth, becomes desirous of Yoga—that is the time for renunciation.
Or else, having entrusted his wife to his son and having fixed his mind on the Supreme Self, he should go from the forest to renunciation.

Having shaved his head according to the rule and bathed, he should perform the *prājāpatya* penance outside the village; then, having gathered in the forenoon a triple staff, a sling, an ochre robe, a water-purifier, a vessel for taking earth, and an alms-bowl, and having consumed the three-fold [mixture] and observed a fast, he should bathe again in the morning on the following day, offer the *agnihotra* and the *vaiśvadeva*, and perform the offering to Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds.

Vaikh 02.06. Having prepared clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, and having offered two full oblations and the *puruṣasūkta* into the *āhavanīya* fire, he offers [the oblation] with the formula: “To Agni, to Soma, to Dhruva, to Dhruvakaraṇa, to the Supreme Self Nārāyaṇa, svāhā! Vaikh 02.07.
Having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruk* ladle by means of the *sruva* spoon, he should offer it into all the fires with the formula: “Oṃ svāhā!
He discards the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle into the *āhavanīya* fire, and the other vessels made of stone into the *gārhapatya* fire.

Vaikh 02.07. (126.9–10): A householder who has not established the sacred fires, as well as a forest-dweller, having offered the oblation in the *aupāsana* fire or the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, should cast away the ritual vessels.

Vaikh 02.07. (126.10–12): Having recited the *Sāvitrī* verse—first foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, then separately and then as a whole—he enters [the order] with the words, "I enter the stage of mendicancy.

Vaikh 02.07. (126.12–14): Standing within the sacrificial altar (*vedī*), having smelled each of the fires beginning with the *gārhapatya* three times with the mantra, "O Agni, that which is yours, worthy of sacrifice," he should consign them into himself with the words, "May you two be of one mind toward us."

Having uttered the call three times, both in a low voice and aloud, saying, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ; it has been renounced by me," and having drunk water once with his right hand and performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), he should again speak as before and release three handfuls of water.
He should give him a girdle, four sacred threads (*upavīta*) or one sacred thread, a black antelope skin as an upper garment, and so forth, as previously described.

With the three mantras, "Of the god thee," "The staff which is mine," and "My friend, protect me," he should take up the triple-staff (*tri-daṇḍa*); with "That which is on the further shore of the darkness," the sling (*śikya*); with "By which the gods [purify] with the filter," the water-filter (*appavitra*); and with "By which the gods [attain] the light," the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and the clay-receptacle (*mṛd-grahaṇī*).
Having bathed, he should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite with the *aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta*.

Having sipped water (ācamana) and performed sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and having recited the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand or a hundred times, he likewise takes up an alms-bowl made of gourd, wood, or clay.

Having offered libations of water to the gods with the seven vyāhṛtis preceded by the Praṇava, each separately, saying "I satisfy [you]," he should then offer libations to the ancestors with the first four [vyāhṛtis], saying "Svadhā.
He should then worship the sun with the verse beginning "ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ."
Having offered a handful of water, he should grant fearlessness to all beings.

The ascetic, delighting in the supreme self, subsisting on alms, practicing the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), with his senses controlled, perceives the Supreme Self through the yoga of meditation.
This is the righteous conduct of the virtuous.

Vaikh 02.09. (127.9–11): Having placed the sacrificial cord over the right ear so as to wear it around the neck (*nivīta*), sitting in a squatting posture (*utkaṭika*), one should void urine and feces during the day facing north and at night facing south, after having covered the ground with grass.
Vaikh 02.09. (127.11–12): One should not perform this [act] in a river, a cow-pen, on a path, in the shade, on ashes, in water, on *kuśa* grass, or on *darbha* grass.
Vaikh 02.09. (127.12–13): One should do so without looking at cows, Brahmins, water, fire, wind, the sun, the stars, or the moon.

Vaikh 02.09. (127.13–16): Having grasped the penis with the left hand and risen, the student (*brahmacārī*) and likewise the householder (*gṛhastha*), sitting by the side of water, should perform purification with water drawn up [from a vessel] after applying clay: twice on the penis, twice on each of the two hands, and six times on the anus. Vaikh 02.09. (127.16–17): He should wash the left hand ten times and both hands likewise with clay and water.
Vaikh 02.09. (127.17): For the forest-dweller (*vanastha*) and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*), this is doubled.
Vaikh 02.09. (127.17–18): Or at night, half of what has been prescribed.

Vaikh 02.09. (127.18–128.1): Upon the emission of semen, purification should be performed as for urine; some say three times for the semen. Vaikh 02.09. (128.1–3): Wearing the sacred thread, facing either east or north, having sat down elsewhere, and having washed his feet and hands with earth and water as before, he sips water while reciting the mantra.
A Brāhmaṇa should sip water that reaches his heart, a Kṣatriya water that reaches his throat, and a Vaiśya water that reaches his palate (Vaikh 02.10.128.4–5).
Having sprinkled himself with water and released the water toward each sun, he circumambulates the sun (Vaikh 02.10.128.5–6).

Having restrained his breaths on the left side of either the water or the fire, he should mutter three times the Gāyatrī together with the Śiras, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and the seven *vyāhṛtis* for each [repetition]. That is the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*). Having performed three or one such breath-regulations, he becomes purified. (Vaikh 02.10.128.6–8)

Vaikh 02.10. (128.8–10): By performing the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) one hundred, ten, or eight times, both the sin of the night and that of the day are wiped away. Vaikh 02.10. (128.10): A twice-born man who is devoid of the twilight worship becomes equal to a *śūdra*.
Vaikh 02.10. (128.11): A religious student (*brahmacārī*), having announced his own name, should offer salutation saying, "I am so-and-so, O venerable sir" (*ahaṃ bho*).

Having touched his ears and the teacher’s feet—grasping the right foot with his right hand and the left foot with his left hand, alternating them while holding them down to his feet—he salutes with his head bowed.
[The teacher] should address him, saying, “May you be long-lived, O gentle one. One who does not offer such a blessing is not to be saluted.
Vaikh 02.10. (128.14–15): One’s mother, father, teacher, and learned men are to be saluted every day.
Vaikh 02.11. (128.16): Other relatives are to be saluted upon returning from a journey.

Vaikh 02.11. (128.16–18): An elder brother, a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, and a father-in-law are to be honored like a father; a father’s sister, a mother’s sister, an elder wife, and an elder sister are to be honored like a mother.
For all [these], the mother is most excellent, and the teacher is even more excellent. When touching a young woman who is another’s wife, one should salute her while remaining on the ground.
Through saluting those worthy of salutation, longevity, knowledge, strength, health, and auspiciousness arise.
Vaikh 02.11. (129.2): One should not wear a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), a girdle (*mekhalā*), an antelope skin (*ajina*), or a staff (*daṇḍa*) that have been held by another.

Vaikh 02.11. (129.2–4): Having commenced his studies, being free from laziness and pure, he should study the Veda beginning with the *praṇava*. He must not study on the new moon day, the full moon day, the fourteenth days, the first days of the lunar fortnights, or the eighth days.
Vaikh 02.11. (129.4–5): There is no prohibition against study during the daily recitation (*japa*) or the fire-oblation (*homa*).

Vaikh 02.11. (129.5–8): When a cat, mongoose, frog, dog, snake, donkey, boar, or other such animal passes between [the teacher and the student], there shall be a suspension of study for one day and night; likewise during the impurity caused by birth (*sūtaka*) or death (*pretaka*), for that duration. During the three *aṣṭakā* festivals and when the teacher has died, the suspension shall be for three nights. Vaikh 02.12. (129.9–10): Upon the death of his wife, his son, or his own pupil, as well as during a human sacrifice (*manuṣya-yajña*) and while eating at a *śrāddha*, there shall be a suspension of study for one day, provided there is no state of ritual impurity due to misfortune or distress.

Vaikh 02.12. (129.10–14): One who has mounted a tree, a boat, a vehicle, or a bed; one who has extended his feet; during the discharge of urine, feces, or semen; when there is a corpse within a village; while eating food that is not fit to be eaten; upon vomiting; in a cremation ground; during the twilight hours; when there is thunder; during an earthquake; when the quarters of the sky are ablaze; at the fall of lightning or meteors; during a rain of blood, stones, or dust; and during an eclipse of the sun, the moon, or Rāhu—at these respective times, one should not study.
Vaikh 02.12. (129.14–15): The Veda brings about the highest good both here and in the hereafter; therefore, it should be studied.
At the end, having uttered the *praṇava*, he speaks [the following]:
Having offered two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the common fire, the silent practitioner should eat pure alms-food that bestows intelligence.

In the month of Pauṣa or Māgha, outside the village at the water’s edge, having performed the oblation for the conclusion of the vow as before, and having suspended his private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), he should study the Veda during the bright fortnight and the Vedic supplements (*vedāṅga*) during the dark fortnight until the very end. Then, having given the teacher his fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he should perform the return ceremony (*samāvartana*).

At midday, having washed his feet and hands with earth and water in pure water, having sipped water (ācamana), and having purified his limbs, he should immerse himself in the water while reciting, "May the waters purify [me]. (Vaikhānasa-smārtasūtra 2.13)

Having sipped water and bowed to Viṣṇu with the Vaiṣṇava mantras beginning with "Viṣṇu hiraṇyaśṛṅga" and to Varuṇa, and having performed the ritual washing away of sin (*aghamarṣaṇa*) with the *Aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta*, he should bathe while reciting "Idam āpaḥ śivāḥ. The four types of ascetics perform the obligatory bath according to this previously stated rule, as well as the optional and occasional baths.

Having covered himself with a washed garment, having sipped water as before and sprinkled himself, sitting or standing and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he should mutter the *Sāvitrī* and worship the Sun.

Vaikh 02.13 (130.10–14): Having gratified the kings and others with water from the *brāhma* (thumb-root) *tīrtha* of the right hand; Nārāyaṇa and others with the *daiva* (forefinger-root); the wells and other waters with the *ārṣa* (middle-finger-root); Viśvāmitra and others with the *paitṛka* (base-of-the-palm) *tīrtha*; and the ancestors and others with the *paitṛka* [tīrtha], he who intends to perform the *brahmayajña* should recite the *svādhyāya*—the first three *anuvākas* of the *Yajurveda-saṃhitā*—according to his desire, [beginning] with the formulas "For sap, thee" (*amiṣe tvā*) and "For strength, thee" (*ūrje tvā*).
Vaikh 02.13 (130.14–15): Or he may study the occasional [texts], such as the hymns beginning with "Righteousness and Truth" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*), or the mantras beginning with the four Vedas.
The sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) is the beginning of all sacrifices. Therefore, it must be performed by the twice-born starting from the time of their initiation (*upanayana*).
One should perform the ritual bath in a river, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), in a natural pool dug by the gods, in a lake, or in a common reservoir.
In the water of another person, one should bathe after having extracted five lumps of clay.
At a well, one should sprinkle oneself three times with a jar on its bank. One who is impure or naked should not bathe; likewise, one should not sleep [in such a state].
Vaikh 02.14. (131.3): One who is ill should not immerse himself in water.

Vaikh 02.14. (131.3–5): When there is an occasional bath for one who is ill, another person who is not ill should immerse him in the water ten or twelve times, then sip water, and touch him; thereby he becomes purified. Vaikh 02.14. (131.5–7): Twice a day, at the conclusion of the *homa*, having washed his feet and sipped water, he should stand on his seat facing either east or west upon a square, smeared mandala, and place a clean vessel there.
Having placed food therein, he honors it.

Placing two feet or one foot on the ground, he sprinkles [the food] in the evening with the mantra: "I sprinkle thee, the pleasant, with *ṛta* (cosmic order) and *satya* (truth). He sprinkles it in the morning with: "I sprinkle thee, the true, with *ṛta*.

Having drunk the rinsing water (*ādhāva*) with the mantra: "Thou art the under-layer of immortality," and having offered the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇa-āhutis*) according to the rule, he eats the food without disparaging it.
Having eaten, he should drink water with the mantra *amṛtāpidhānam asi*, and having sipped water (*ācamya*), he should rinse his mouth.
(Vaikh 02.14.131.11–12) Wearing a single garment, while lying down, standing, not bathing, reciting prayers, or performing oblations, or when his feet are dry, or facing north, he does not eat.
(Vaikh 02.14.131.13) He should not eat food from a broken vessel, nor food that is stale, nor food placed upon a bed, a seat, or one's lap.
Vaikh 02.14.(131.13-14): One should not drink water with cupped hands (*añjali*).

Vaikh 02.14.(131.14-15): One should not eat food that has been touched by those who are impure due to remnants of food (*ucchiṣṭa*), those who are unclean (*aśuci*), those in a state of ritual impurity (*āśaucin*), outcasts (*patita*), or during the periods of birth or death (*sūtaka-pretaka*).
Vaikh 02.15.(132.1): Sesame flour (*tila-saktu*), curd (*dadhi*), and parched grain (*lāja*) are not to be eaten at night.
Vaikh 02.15.(131.1–2): Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with clarified butter or curd.
Vaikh 02.15.(131.2–3): Food contaminated by worms, hair, or insects, smelled by a cow, or pecked at by birds becomes pure when sprinkled with ashes and water.

Vaikh 02.15.(131.3–5): When a large quantity of food is defiled by a dog, a crow, or similar creatures, one should remove from that very spot only as much as would satisfy a man, discard it, and then sprinkle the remainder with ashes and water while reciting "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," touch it with a firebrand of *darbha* grass, and take it up.

Vaikh 02.15.(132.6–7): During the ten-day period following childbirth, cow’s milk is always [forbidden], as are the milk of one-hoofed animals, camels, and women; likewise, the meat of the *palaṇḍuka*, *vakala*, *śuna*, *gṛñjana*, and *viḍja*—which have not been specifically mentioned—and fish-meat must be avoided.
Vaikh 02.15.(132.8): Meat that remains from a sacrifice may be eaten.
Vaikh 02.15.(132.8–9): One should avoid food touched by a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), or touched by *śūdras* or *anulomas*, as well as their food.
Vaikh 02.15. (132.9–10): One who follows his own dharma may accept raw food from Śūdras and Anulomas when he is hungry.
Vaikh 02.15. (132.10–11): Even when hungry, he should not with effort accept either raw or cooked food from all those born in the inverse order (Pratiloma), the intermediate castes, or Vratyas.
Vaikh 02.15. (132.11–12): He abandons cooked food that has been touched by them or mixed with them.
Vaikh 02.15: Constantly performing the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti through actions of mind, speech, and body, he gradually practices dharma.
Vaikh 03.01: One in the stage of the householder (gṛhasthāśramin) should carry two sacrificial threads (yajñopavīta), a bamboo staff (vaiṇava-daṇḍa), and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Having bathed together with his wife, he should perform the domestic rites (gārhya-karmāṇi) in the domestic fire (gṛhya-agni) and the Śrauta rites in the Śrauta fires.
Vaikh 03.01. (133.3–4): At the conclusion of the evening *homa*, having fed any guests who have arrived and having eaten a moderate amount himself, he should sleep with his wife.
(133.4–5): He should not sleep with wet feet or with his head toward the west or the north. (133.5): During the nights of her season, he should approach his own wife.
Vaikh 03.01 (133.5–6): At the outset, for three nights, he should avoid approaching a woman in her courses, as well as sitting or lying down with her.
Vaikh 03.01 (133.6–7): He should not have sexual intercourse with another man’s wife.
Vaikh 03.01 (133.7): Through intercourse with another man’s wife, one’s lifespan, prosperity, and Vedic luster perish.
Vaikh 03.01.(133.7–8): He does not eat together with his wife.
Vaikh 03.01.(133.8): He should not look at her while she is eating, yawning, or naked.
Vaikh 03.01.(133.9): He avoids speaking untruths.
There is no sin greater than untruth, and no virtue greater than truth.
One should live by non-injury toward all living beings; being pure and possessing wealth, one should possess a granary of grain, a jar of grain, or be one who does not provide for the morrow.
A twice-born man should not touch those who have fallen from their caste or those born of the lowest castes.
At sunrise and at sunset, one should not look at the sun.
One should pass by gods, teachers, Brahmins, clarified butter, milk, curd, earth, water, sacrificial fuel, *darbha* grass, fire, and trees by keeping them to one’s right.
One should yield the way to a *snātaka*, a king, a teacher, an elder, a sick person, a burden-carrier, and a pregnant woman.
The paths are purified by the rays of the sun and the wind.
One should not use the seat or bed of another if they have not been given. If one uses what has not been given, he loses a fourth part of his own merit.
One should not wear clothes, garlands, sandals, or umbrellas that have been used by others.
One should not warm one’s feet over the fire, nor blow upon it with the mouth, nor touch it with the foot. One should not place anything beneath the fire.
One should not throw fire into another fire, nor into a temple, nor into water; nor should one cast urine, feces, pus, blood, semen, phlegm, food remnants, or bodily excretions into the fire.
One should not look at a naked woman, nor at another's wife, nor at feces or urine.
While impure from eating, one should not gaze upon the gods, the sun, the moon, planets, constellations, or stars.
One should not step upon the shadow of a deity, a teacher, a *snātaka*, an initiate, a king, a cow, or an eminent person.
One should not show the rainbow to another, nor speak of it. One should not wake one who is sleeping.
One should not travel alone on a road.
One should not restrain a cow grazing in another's field nor a suckling calf; one should not even report it. One should not wear soiled or tattered clothing.
One should avoid playing with dice, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and exposure to the morning sun.
One should not stand upon hair, body hair, chaff, charcoal, potsherds, bones, feces, urine, pus, blood, semen, phlegm, or the remnants of food.

(Vaikh 03.03.134.7–9) If a limb is smeared with an impure substance, one should purify it with earth and water until the stain, the odor, and the mental suspicion [of impurity] have ceased. (Vaikh 03.03.134.9–10) One should not dwell together with outcasts, those of the lowest castes, fools, unrighteous people, or enemies. (Vaikh 03.03.134.10–11)
Vaikh 03.03. (134.11): Being impure or defiled by food remnants, one should not touch the gods, cows, Brahmins, or fires.

Vaikh 03.03. (134.11–12): One should not show contempt for the gods, the Vedas, kings, teachers, parents, or learned Brahmins; nor should one revile them. Vaikh 03.03. (134.12–13): Both the one who shows contempt and the one who reviles perish.
One should not engage in reviling or striking any living being.
One should not carry out disputes with one's teacher, mother, father, their fathers and so forth, brothers, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, preceptors, officiating priests, and others.
Among all forms of purification for a person, the purification of wealth, the purification of women, and the purification of food are the most excellent.

Regarding objects made of gems, gold, or silver, one purifies them with water or exposes them to fire. Copper, tin, lead, iron, and the like are purified by acidic water; those made of wood or ivory by planing or scrubbing; and sacrificial vessels by wiping or washing with the right hand.
One should sprinkle leather items, woven fabrics, and vegetables, roots, and fruits; small quantities, however, should be washed.
Having purified the substances such as clarified butter and others with a firebrand, one should display them.

Silk and woolen items [should be purified] with saline earth; fine cotton cloths with bilva fruits; conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, and cow-horns with mustard seeds mixed with water; earthenware by burning again; and the ground by sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, digging, filling with other soil, and by the dwelling of cows and so forth, as well as by sweeping and other such means. One should thus purify them.
Water on the ground that satisfies the thirst of a cow is free from defects and well-purified; water approved by word, water cleansed by a stream, and water not seen [to be impure] are pure.
The mouth of a woman and the hand of an artisan with goods displayed for sale are always pure.
Fruit left over by a bird is not to be censured.
(Vaikh 03.04) Things upon which mosquitoes or flies have settled, as well as their droplets, are not defiled.
(Vaikh 03.04) And that which has been touched by wind, fire, or the rays of the sun is pure.

Vaikh 03.04. (135.13–14): When one is ill, when dealing with a child, or in a kitchen, purity need not be scrutinized; it should be maintained according to one's capacity. Vaikh 03.04. (135.14): Water that is abundant is not defiled by feces or urine.

Vaikh 03.04. (135.14–15): When another person is sipping water for purification (*ācamana*), one who is himself sipping water does not become impure by drops of water that have fallen to the ground, risen back up, and touched his feet.

Vaikh 03.05. (136.1–2): A forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) should constantly engage in the private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*). He should gather *kuśa* grass, fuel, and other materials for the sake of the sacred fires, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits grown in a pure place for the sake of his food.
Vaikh 03.05. (136.2–3): He should avoid that which depends on others, that which has been abandoned by others, that which grows in an impure place, and cow’s milk.
Vaikh 03.05. (136.3): He should not accumulate grain or wealth.
He should not wear [unwashed] clothing.
When [the host] says "honey," he takes water; when [the host] says "meat," he takes food made of flour.

Compassionate toward all beings, impartial, patient, pure, free from malice, indifferent to pleasure, speaking auspiciously, and avoiding envy and miserliness—he should avoid fish and other biting creatures, plants grown in ploughed soil, bulbs, roots, fruits, and leafy vegetables; wearing matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails, bathing at the three periods of the day, subsisting on food from the forest, he should offer sacrificial oblations (*caru*) and cakes (*puroḍāśa*) with forest-grown materials alone.
He avoids onions and the like, exudations, white eggplant, *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *śleṣmātaka*, *vrajakali*, *citraka*, drumstick tree (*śigru*), earth, grass, *kovidāra*, and radish.
For a sage, all meat is equal to beef, and fermented grain-liquor (*dhānyāmla*) is equal to *surā* liquor.
He abandons food stored from previous times and his former garments in the month of Āśvayuja.
Vaikh 03.05. (136.13): A practitioner of meditation (*dhyānayogin*) performs austerity (*tapas*) in accordance with the Veda and Vedānta.

Vaikh 03.05. (136.13–137.2): Being without a wife, without sacred fires, without a household, and without a fixed dwelling, he dwells at the foot of a tree or in the hermitages of forest-dwellers, or in the houses of householders; having begged for alms, he eats food sufficient merely for the maintenance of life on a pure leaf by the water’s edge, like a mendicant.
Vaikh 03.05. (137.2): Withering his body, he should perform increasingly intense austerity.

Vaikh 03.06. (137.4): Having bathed daily, the mendicant should satisfy himself with the syllable *praṇava*. (137.4–5): With that same [syllable], he should offer salutation. (137.5–6): Having performed at least six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and having recited the *Sāvitrī* at least one hundred times, he should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*).
Vaikh 03.06. (137.6): He should sip water purified by a water-strainer (*ap-pavitra*).
Vaikh 03.06. (137.6–7): He should practice wearing saffron robes, renouncing everything, abstaining from sexual intercourse, and avoiding theft and other such acts.

Vaikh 03.06. (137.7–10): Without companions, without fire, without a fixed dwelling, free from doubt, equal toward honor and dishonor, and avoiding dispute, anger, greed, delusion, and falsehood, he should dwell outside the village in a secluded place, in a temple, or at the foot of a tree.
Vaikh 03.06. (137.10): Except during the four-month period [of the rains], he shall not dwell in one place for more than a single day.
Vaikh 03.06. (137.10–11): During the rainy season, the autumn, and the four-month period, he may dwell in one place alone.

Vaikh 03.06. (137.11–13): Having attached the triple staff, the ochre-colored garment, the water-purifier, and other items, and wearing them with his left hand around his neck while holding the alms-bowl with his right hand, he shall go for alms at one mealtime to the houses of pure Brahmins at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Having looked at living beings on the ground, he should place his foot while avoiding them. Standing with his face turned downward, he should seek alms.
Having stood for the duration of time it takes to milk a cow, or half that time, he should proceed.

Even when food is not obtained, and even when treated with contempt, he should remain free from despondency; even when food is obtained with honor, he should remain free from satisfaction. He should not walk either too quickly or too slowly.
Except at the time for begging, he should not go to another's house.
Vaikh 03.07. (137.19): He should not go beyond one *krośa* to beg.

(137.19–138.3): Having gone for alms and washed his hands and feet near water, having sipped water (*ācamana*), he should offer the first portion of the alms to the Sun with the verse "ud u tyam," to Viṣṇu with "ato devā," and to Brahmā with "brahma jajñānam"; then he should cast the *bali* offering for all beings with the words "to all beings."

Having resolved upon the sacrifice to the self (*ātmayajña*) according to the procedure for the *agnihotra* with his hand, he should eat either eight mouthfuls or just enough for the maintenance of life; or he may eat at will, or not eat at all.
Having drunk water purified by a cloth and performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), he sips water again.
He should not engage in censure or abuse.
He should abandon kinsmen and relatives;
he should not speak of his lineage, conduct, austerity, or learning.

Having abandoned attachment and being observant of the rules and restraints, speaking what is pleasant and true, non-opposing toward all beings, always equanimous, delighting in the inner self, and a practitioner of meditation-yoga, beholding Nārāyaṇa as the supreme Brahman, he should maintain meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
Vaikh 03.07 (138.8–9): "One attains the imperishable Brahman.
Vaikh 03.07 (138.9): "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman"—thus says the Śruti.

Vaikh 03.08 (138.10–13): When the body of a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) who has not maintained the sacred fires has died, his son or another person, having covered it with grass, shall place it near pure Brāhmaṇas or in a mechanical device, and then dig a pit on the bank of a river flowing toward the ocean or in a sandy place, so that it remains untouched by jackals and other such creatures.

Vaikh 03.08. (138.13–139.1): Having bathed [the image] with the Gāyatrī, and having likewise seated or laid it down there, one should place the triple staff (*tri-daṇḍa*) in the right hand with Vaiṣṇava mantras; the water-strainer (*śikya*) and the water-purifier (*ap-pavitra*) in the left with the verse *yad asya pāre rajasaḥ*; the alms-bowl (*bhikṣā-pātra*) on the belly with the Sāvitrī; and the saffron robe (*kāṣāya*), the clay-receptacle, and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in the private region with the verse *bhūmir bhūmiṃ*. Having placed these, one should close [the eyes]. Vaikh 03.08. (139.1–2): If that [image] is touched by jackals or similar creatures, the one who performs that act becomes more sinful.

For one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), having internalized the fires within himself (*ātmany āropya*) as a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*), one should bathe his deceased body with the *Gāyatrī* mantra, carry it away as previously described, and place it in a pure location. Having then descended the fire into the common (*laukika*) fire with the mantra "Descend [O Fire] into this" (*upāvaroha*), and having poured clarified butter and milk into the mouth with the mantra "Thou art the purifier" (*pavitraṃ te*), one should arrange the triple staff (*tri-daṇḍa*) and other implements as before. Then, one performs the cremation using those very fires and the mantras of the *āhitāgni*, according to either the *Brahmamedha* or the *Pitṛmedha* rites.

For those two [the deceased and the one who dies with them], one should not perform the impurity rites, the water offering (*udaka-bali*), the rice-ball offerings (*piṇḍa-dāna*), the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha, and so forth.
One should instead perform the Nārāyaṇa-bali.
Whether one performs the burial, the covering [of the grave], the cremation, or the Nārāyaṇa-bali, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.

Regarding the *Nārāyaṇabali*: "From Nārāyaṇa alone comes the accomplishment of all goals. [One performs this] for one killed by men led by Brahmā and others, for a self-killer, for one who has died from all manner of sins through ropes, weapons, water, lightning, fanged beasts, serpents, and so forth, for those whose bodies are not to be cremated, for a mendicant, and after eleven days have passed; and for the five great sinners (*mahāpātakin*), after twelve years have passed—at the place where the *Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* would otherwise be performed—for the sake of the deceased, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight or under the asterism Śravaṇa.
On the previous day, he should invite twelve Brāhmaṇas.

On the following day, having prepared a fire-sanctuary (agnyāyatana) beside the temple of Viṣṇu, on a riverbank, or in a house, he should perform the *āghāra* libation. Having strewn grass around the fire, he should place an image made of gold or something of that nature upon darbha grass in the north-western direction of the fire. Meditating upon the Person, he should invoke the god Nārāyaṇa, facing eastward, with the mantra beginning "Oṃ bhūḥ puruṣam," and offer a seat (*āsana*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*).

Having bathed [the deity] with the *Puruṣasūkta*, or with the eight-syllable mantra beginning with "We know Nārāyaṇa" (*nārāyaṇāya vidmahe*), he worships him with a garment, an upper cloth, ornaments, water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), flowers, scents, incense, a lamp, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and further water for sipping.
(Vaikh 03.09) He should offer libations of water with the twelve names beginning with Keśava.

(Vaikh 03.10) Having sprinkled [the oblation], he should offer clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the verses beginning with "Thousand-headed" (*sahasraśīrṣā*) and "Of Viṣṇu... (*viṣṇor nu kaṃ*), as well as with the twelve names. (Vaikh 03.10)

Having offered milk-rice oblation (*pāyasa*) mixed with jaggery, clarified butter, and fruit to the Lord of the Gods (*deva-īśa*) with the *Viṣṇu-gāyatrī*, one should present water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and mouth-freshener (*mukha-vāsa*).

Vaikh 03.10. (140.8–13): Having worshipped on the southern side of the fire upon *darbha* grass with their tips pointing northward, beginning from the south, he offers an oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with the following mantras ending in "to the Sādhyas": "To Nārāyaṇa, the thousand-headed, the thousand-eyed, the thousand-footed, the Supreme Person, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Light, the Supreme Brahman, the Unmanifest, the Cause of All, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Soul of Sacrifice, to all the Gods, to all the deities. Then he offers clarified butter (*ājya*) with these same [mantras].

Having washed the feet of the Brāhmaṇas, having given them new garments, upper cloths, and ornaments, and having worshipped them with flowers and other offerings, he should feed them white food accompanied by side-dishes, ghee, molasses, curds, and fruit, while meditating upon the twelve forms [of Viṣṇu]. He gives gold as a sacrificial fee according to his ability.
Having praised [the deity] with the hymns beginning with "Sahasraśīrṣā" and with the twelve names, he should prostrate himself. He performs the concluding oblation (*anta-homa*).
"Having attained the supreme goal desired by him, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
[The text now describes] the origin, names, and livelihoods of those born from the intermixture of the four varṇas—namely, the *anulomas*, *pratilomas*, *antarālas*, and *vrātyas*.
One born from a man of a higher caste (*ūrdhvajāta*) and a woman of a lower caste (*adhojātā*) is an *anuloma*.
Vaikh 03.11. (141.5): One born from a woman of higher birth by a man of lower birth is a *pratiloma*.

Vaikh 03.11. (141.5–6): One born from an *anuloma* father by an *anuloma* mother is an *antarāla*. Vaikh 03.11. (141.6–7): One born from a *pratiloma* father by a *pratiloma* mother becomes a *vrātya*.

Vaikh 03.11.(141.7-8): From the mouth of Brahmā were born the Brāhmaṇas and Brāhmaṇīs; the Brahmarṣis became their wives. Vaikh 03.11.(141.8-9): A son born from them, when a Brāhmaṇī of a non-identical lineage (asagotra) has been taken according to the prescribed rite with the recitation of mantras, shall be a pure Brāhmaṇa. Vaikh 03.11.(141.10-11): One born by an improper rite from a woman who has had a previous husband, or from a Golakī, is a Kuṇḍa; both these types of Brāhmaṇas are censured.
Therefore, one born according to the rule from a Kṣatriya father and a Kṣatriya mother below the level of the two arms is a pure Kṣatriya.

(Vaikh 03.11.141.12–14) One born to those two [parents] by an illicit union in secret is impure and is called a Bhoja; he is not to be consecrated, yet he performs the binding of the turban for the king’s generalship. (Vaikh 03.11.141.14–15) In the absence of a pure [Kṣatriya], one who has not bound the turban shall protect the people.
His conduct should be like that of a king. From a Vaiśya born below the thighs upon a Vaiśya woman, there is likewise a Vaiśya who is pure.
Excluding the [prescribed] rites, he may be a jeweler—an impure one who pierces gems, pearls, and the like, and fashions conch shells and bracelets.
Now, from a Śūdra born of a Śūdra woman by a Śūdra through the proper method, there is a pure Śūdra.
From a paramour, there is the despised Mālavaka Śūdra, as well as the horse-keeper and the gatherer of grass for horses. These are the members of the four castes.
All those born from the refinement of these very [castes], beginning with the *anuloma* [progeny], are [of the same status].
Among the *anulomas*, one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya maiden is a *Savarṇa* and is the foremost.
His livelihood consists of the rites of the Atharvaveda, the driving and riding of horses, elephants, and chariots, the office of commander-in-chief for the king, and the practice of Āyurveda.
Vaikh 03.12. (142.8): One born in secret is called *abhiniṣakta*.
Vaikh 03.12. (142.9): If he becomes an anointed king, he should study the eight-limbed *Āyurveda* or the *Bhūtatantra*.
Vaikh 03.12. (142.9–11): Following the conduct prescribed therein, endowed with compassion, and speaking the truth, he should act for the welfare of all living beings according to those injunctions.
Or one whose livelihood is excessive, such as the calculation of celestial bodies (*jyotiḥ*) and so forth.

From a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is born an Ambaṣṭha; his occupations are the management of horse-trappings (*kakṣyājīvya*), the worship of the fire (*āgneya*), dancing, the sounding of banners (*dhvajaviśrāvī*), and the treatment of wounds (*śalyacikitsī*).
From old age [he becomes] a potter, following the profession of a wheelwright (*kulālavṛtti*), a barber (*nāpita*), and one who shaves from the navel upwards.

From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother is born the Madgu; having attained preeminence, he is known as Mahānarman and follows the occupation of a Vaiśya, yet does not perform the duties of a Kṣatriya.
From a concealed union (of a Kṣatriya with a Śūdra woman) is born the Āśvika, who is a trader in horses.

From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother is born the Pāraśava, whose livelihood consists of the worship of Bhadrakālī, painting, the science of bodily marks, the sounding of musical instruments, and massage.

A Niṣāda, born from a paramour, is one who commits violence against beasts of prey and other wild animals (Vaikh 03.13.143.2–3). From a Kṣatriya man and a Śūdra woman is born an Ugra, whose duty is to inflict severe punishments (Vaikh 03.13.143.3).
From a paramour is born a Śūlika, whose duty is to carry out tortures such as impalement on a stake (Vaikh 03.13.143.3–4).
From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother is born the Cūcuka, who trades in betel nuts, betel leaves, sugar, and similar goods.

From a secret union [of the same parents] are born the Kaṭakāra and the Kaṭakārī. Furthermore, one born from an Anuloma father and an Anuloma mother is an Anuloma; he shall follow the occupation of either his father or his mother.

Vaikh 03.13 (143.7–9): A son born from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa maiden through the performance of mantras is a Sūta; he is the foremost among those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*). Though initiated with mantras, he is devoid of the duties of the twice-born. Vaikh 03.13 (143.9): His livelihood consists of instructing the king in his duties and preparing his food.

Vaikh 03.13 (143.10–11): One born from an illicit union (*jāra*) without the use of mantras is a Rathakāra; he is excluded from the status of the twice-born, performs the work of a Śūdra, and lives by the service of horses, such as their nourishment and training.

From a Vaiśya by a Brāhmaṇī woman is born a Māgadha. Even among Śūdras, he is not one whose food may be eaten, yet he is not untouchable; he is a servant to all, and his livelihood consists of praising, proclaiming, singing, and running errands.
(Vaikh 03.13) From a secret union, a Cakrin shall be a seller of salt and oil.
(Vaikh 03.14) From a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is born an Āyogava, a weaver who makes cloth, living by means of garments and bell-metal.
From a hidden practice comes the Pulinda, who subsists on the forest and slays wicked beasts and creatures.
From a Śūdra and a Kṣatriya woman is born a Pulkasa, who, having offered *kṛtakā* or *ārkṣā* liquor into the fire, sells cooked food.
From one who lives by thievery comes the Velava, whose occupations are biting, dancing, and singing.

From a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is born a Vaidehaka; he is untouchable even by Śūdras, and his food is not to be eaten by them. He subsists on forest produce, tending goats, buffaloes, and cattle, and sells their products.
If he lives by theft, he becomes a Cakrika, living by means of salt, oil, and oil-cakes.

From a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is born a Caṇḍāla. Wearing ornaments of lead and iron, with a leather strap bound around his neck and a girdle of *kakṣerī* grass, wandering here and there, excluded from all activities, he removes impurities elsewhere and casts them outside the village street in the forenoon.
He shall dwell far outside the village with those of his own kind;
after midday, he does not enter the village. This...
If he enters [the village], he shall be put to death by the king;
otherwise, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā),
as well as the penance for those in the intermediate period of impurity.
From a Brahmin woman, Takṣaka is born; he is untouchable, has a hand-drum in his hand, and is a woodworker, a goldsmith, an iron-smith, or a brazier.
From a Kṣatriya woman, Matsyabandhu is born; he is a fisherman. From a Vaiśya woman, Sāmudra is born; he lives by sea-trade and is a killer of fish. (Vaikh 03.14)
From an Ambaṣṭha father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born a Nāvika, who lives by sea-trade and catching fish, and who causes a boat to cross the ocean.

From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born an Adhonāpita, one who shaves hair only below the navel. From a Madgu father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born a Veṇuka, a player of the flute and the lute.
From a Kṣatriya woman, [the son of a Vaiśya] is a laborer, one who performs manual work.

From a Vaiśya man and a Brāhmaṇa woman, [the son] is a leather-worker, one who lives by leather. From a Vaiśya man and a Kṣatriya woman, he is a tailor, one whose occupation involves piercing with needles.
From an Āyogava by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Tāmra, who lives by working with copper;
by a Kṣatriya woman, a Khanaka, who lives by digging;
and from a Śūdra woman by a Khanaka is born an Udbandhaka, a washerman who is untouchable for Śūdras.
From a Pulkasa and a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Rajaka, a washer of clothes who cleanses away dirt.

From a Caṇḍāla and a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Śvapaca; endowed with the marks of a Caṇḍāla, he is eternally contemptible and excluded from all activities. Dwelling in cremation grounds and the like, he is the remover of filth; he must take discarded vessels and release a corpse that has no relatives.

Having killed those deserving of death, he shall seize their clothes and other possessions, subsist on food dependent on others, eat from a broken vessel, consume dog-meat, and engage in the trade of skins, bamboo, and reeds.
From such a son, who is base and fallen, one is ruined and goes to terrible hells.
A virtuous son, however, protects his ancestors from the hells, purifies them, and leads them to auspicious worlds.
"Therefore, Brāhmaṇas and others should procreate a son according to the rule upon a wife of the same caste"—thus says Vikhanas. End of the text.

Now, therefore, for the sake of the ultimate liberation of man, there is the inquiry into dharma.
And having known [the Dharma], one who practices it is a righteous person.
He becomes the most praiseworthy in the world, and after passing away, he attains the heavenly realm.
Dharma is that which is prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti.
Va.1.5 In the absence of that, the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is the authority.
Furthermore, a cultured person (śiṣṭa) is one whose nature is free from desire.
A phenomenon whose cause is not perceived.
Va.1.8: [The region] of the Āryāvarta is east of the Ādarśa mountains, west of the Kālaka forest, north of the Pāriyātra mountains, and south of the Himavat.
And to the north of the Vindhya mountains.
Whatever dharmas and whatever customs exist in that region, all of them are to be accepted everywhere.
But this does not apply to others who follow the duties of those born in the inverse order.
Some [say] it is also between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Others say that as far as a black antelope wanders, so far extends the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*).
Moreover, the Bhāllavins cite this verse in their Nidāna:
To the west lies the Sindhu-vighāraṇī, and to the east the rising of the sun;
as far as Kṛṣṇa runs, so far indeed extends the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa).

"Whatever those who are learned in the three Vedas and knowers of dharma may declare here as dharma—both that which purifies and that which is to be purified—that is indeed dharma; there is no doubt about this. (VaDh 1.16)
Manu declared that, due to the absence of Vedic revelation, there exist local customs, caste customs, and family customs.
One who has been overtaken by the rising sun (sūryābhyudita) and one who has been overtaken by the setting sun (sūryābhinimrukta)—
these are declared to be the five great sins (pañca mahāpātakāni).
Violating the teacher's bed, drinking liquor, killing an embryo, stealing the gold of a Brahmin, and associating with those who have fallen from their caste.
Either through the sacred thread (brahmanical) lineage or through the marriage (yoni) lineage.
Moreover, they cite this:
"One falls from his status after a year by associating with one who has fallen—
through officiating at sacrifices for him, teaching him, or through marriage— but not by sharing a vehicle, a seat, or gifts."
Va.1.23: One who casts away the sacred fires, one who shows hostility toward his teacher, an atheist, one who lives as an atheist, and one who sells *soma*—these are minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
A Brāhmaṇa may have three wives in the order of the castes; a Rājanya, two; and a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, one each.
Some [teachers] say that even a Śūdra woman may be used in this same manner, with the exception of the recitation of mantras.
One should not act in that manner.
For from this [cause] follows the certain degradation of one's lineage and the loss of heaven after death.
Va.1.28 There are six forms of marriage.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Gāndharva, the Kṣātra, and the Mānuṣa [are the six forms of marriage].
If one should give a maiden who has expressed her own desire, preceded by water, that is the Brāhma marriage.
When the sacrificial ritual has been spread out and the officiating priest is performing his duty, one should give a girl adorned with ornaments; this they call the *daiva* (divine) marriage.
And the Ārṣa [form of marriage] is [contracted] by means of a pair of cattle.
If he approaches a willing woman of equal birth when she desires him, that is the Gāndharva marriage.
That which they seize by force, having violently overwhelmed [the victim], is the *kṣātra* [form].
That which has been purchased with wealth by means of bargaining is "human" (sa mānuṣaḥ).
