Therefore, in the case of one who possesses daughters, "a hundred [cows] plus an extra chariot (adhiratha) should be given"; by this, the purchase-price (*kraya*) is understood here.
"She who, having been purchased by her husband, then behaves [unfaithfully] with others"—thus it is said in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Moreover, they cite this:
"Knowledge that has been lost may return; but upon the destruction of a family, there is total ruin in this world.
For even one who is merely designated by his family name is worthy of honor; therefore, they marry women of noble birth."
The other three castes should conduct themselves according to the instruction of the Brāhmaṇa.
A Brahmin should proclaim the duties.
And the king shall issue his command.
But the king, ruling according to dharma, shall take a sixth part of the wealth.
Except for a Brāhmaṇa.
"But he partakes of a sixth share of his sacrifices and charitable works," so it is said.
The Brāhmaṇa makes the Veda prosperous; the Brāhmaṇa delivers one from calamities; therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is not to be eaten. Soma is his king—so it is said.
"And that which pertains to prosperity after death," so it is taught; "so it is taught."
Va.2.1 There are four castes: Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
The three castes—the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—are the twice-born.
For them,
the first birth is from the mother, and the second is at the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;
here, his mother is said to be the Sāvitrī, while the teacher is called the father.
Because he bestows the Veda, they call the teacher "father."
Nevertheless, they cite this:

"There are indeed two kinds of seed for a Brāhmaṇa: that which is above the navel and that which is below it. That which is above the navel—by means of that he procreates offspring when he initiates Brāhmaṇas, when he teaches them, when he performs sacrifices for them, and when he performs meritorious deeds. But that which is below the navel—by means of that his own biological offspring is born here."
Therefore, they do not say of one who is learned in the Vedas and has studied them thoroughly, "You are childless."
Hārīta also cites:
"Indeed, no ritual action whatsoever exists for him prior to the binding of the girdle of muñja grass;
for as long as he is not born into the Veda, he is equal to a Śūdra in his mode of livelihood."
Except for water-libations and those rites connected with the *svadhā* offering to the ancestors.
Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: "Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak of me to one who is envious, dishonest, or undisciplined, so that I may remain full of power."
O Brahmin, teach me to that person alone who is pure, vigilant, intelligent, endowed with the practice of celibacy,
and who would never deceive you in any way whatsoever, for he shall be my guardian of the treasure.
He who pierces one's ears with what is not false, causing no pain and bestowing immortality—him one should regard as both father and mother; one should never do him harm on any day whatsoever.
Those Brahmins who, having been taught by their teacher, do not respect him in word, thought, or deed—
just as they are not worthy of being fed by their teacher, even so does that sacred learning not nourish them.
Just as fire burns dry grass, so does the Veda burn one who questions it without respect;
one should not explain the Veda to such a person who fails to show honor.
Va.2.13 There are six duties for a Brāhmaṇa.
The study of one's own Vedic recitation, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving, and receiving gifts.
Va.2.15 Three [stomas] for a Kṣatriya.
Va.2.16 Study, sacrifice, and giving.
And the protection of the subjects by means of the sword is his own duty; he should live by that.
These same [rites] belong to the Vaiśya.
Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending.
Service to them is the constant duty of a Śūdra, and this is his prescribed means of livelihood.
Va.2.21 All [the ascetics] shall have their hair and dress regulated, or they may have their hair loose, except for the top-knot.
Va.2.22 Those who do not live by their own dharma should adopt the next lower occupation. They should follow the occupation of one younger than themselves.
But one should never [approach] a woman who is superior [in age].
Having adopted the livelihood of a Vaiśya, for one who lives by trade, there is no offense regarding stones, salt, gems, whetstones, silk, linen, and skins.
And all woven cloth that is dyed red.
Va.2.26 Prepared food, flowers, fruits, roots, perfumes, juices, water, the sap of medicinal herbs, soma, weapons, poison, meat, milk and its derivatives, iron, tin, lac, and lead.
Furthermore, they cite this:
"One falls immediately by [selling] meat, lac, and salt;
a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra in three days by selling milk. Thus it is said.
Among village animals, those with solid hooves and those with manes; all wild animals; birds; and fanged beasts.
Regarding grains, they say that sesame seeds are the foremost.
Moreover, they cite this:
"If one performs any act with sesame seeds other than eating them, anointing oneself with them, or giving them as a gift,
having become a worm, he sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors."
Or rather, they may themselves cultivate sesame seeds by plowing and produce them, and then sell them.
Therefore, from the time he has testicles until they are covered with hair, he should be a tiller of the soil before his morning meal.
In the summer heat, one should offer water.
Va.2.34: "The plough with its iron share, most auspicious, the Soma-presser;
that he sows: the cow, the ewe, the prolific and fat mare, and the wagon for the chariot."

(2.35) The plough is like a spear, possessed of heroes, possessed of good men, and possessed of oxen; it is very auspicious, with a beautiful nose—for its nose is indeed beautiful—by means of the nose it sows and casts away far. It is *somapitsaru*, for Soma reaches it; that is its *sarū* (shaft), and by it it sows. [It bestows] cows and sheep, goats, horses, mules, and camels, as well as a full-thighed, beautiful, auspicious, and excellent young woman.
For how indeed could one raise a plough otherwise than by selling grain?
The essences and non-essences of the Great Element (mahat) are to be distinguished according to whether they are superior or inferior.
But one should certainly not [use] salt with savory juices.
Va.2.39 One should know that sesame, rice, and cooked food are prescribed for exchange with a human woman. Va.2.40 A Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya shall not give out money at usury.
Moreover, they cite this:
"He who, having set aside grain of equal value, offers grain of great value,
is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda."
He weighed the killing of a Brahmin against usury on a scale;
the killer of an embryo remained steady at the end, while the usurer trembled at the tip. Thus it is said.
Or rather, they may at will give [the bowl] to one who is more wicked and whose duties have been neglected.
Gold is [to be repaid] twofold, and grain threefold.
By means of grain itself, the liquids are explained.
And flowers, roots, and fruits [are not to be accepted].
That which is weighed on a scale is worth eight times [the standard].
Furthermore, they cite this:
"One may take interest on money lent according to the order of the castes, at the rate of two, three, four, five,
or a hundred [per month]."
But a king, by means of his death, may cause the destruction of the increase of wealth;
yet again, through royal consecration, the root of wealth increases.
Listen now to the interest declared by the words of Vasiṣṭha regarding usury:
"Five māṣas on twenty [kārṣāpaṇas]—thus the dharma is not violated. (VaDh 2.50)
Va.2.50 One does not fall away (from it).
Those who are not learned in the Vedas, who do not recite the sacred texts, or who do not maintain the sacred fires, become equal in status to Śūdras.
And regarding this, they cite a verse of Manu:
"The twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other matters,
quickly becomes a Śūdra even while living, along with his lineage."
He shall not be a reciter of the Ṛgveda or a Brāhmaṇa-priest, nor a merchant, nor an actor;
he shall not be one who performs service for Śūdras, nor a thief, nor a physician.
That village where twice-born men live as beggars, being devoid of vows and unlearned in the Vedas, the king should punish; for such a place is a provider of sustenance for thieves.
For those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist merely by their birth—
though they may assemble by the thousands— an assembly does not exist among them.
Whatever those fools, deluded by darkness and ignorant of the Dharma, say—
that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon those who speak it.
Whether they be four or even three who have mastered the Vedas, whatever they may declare should be known as Dharma; it is not so for thousands of others.
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors should always be given to one learned in the Vedas;
for what is given to one unlearned in the Vedas reaches neither the ancestors nor the deities.

If one person in a house is ignorant and another is deeply learned, whether he be far away or near, the gift should be given to the deeply learned; there is no transgression in not giving it to the ignorant one.
There is no transgression against a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the Veda;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes after having cast away a blazing fire.
An elephant made of wood, a deer made of leather,
and a Brahmin who has not studied— the three of these are merely bearers of names.
In those kingdoms where the ignorant eat foods fit for the wise,
they encounter drought or a great danger arises.
Va.3.13 If a Brāhmaṇa should find property that is unrecognizable while engaged in the six duties, the king shall not take it.
Va.3.15 Having slain an assassin, they say there is no sin whatsoever for the one who takes the life.
Moreover, they cite this:
"The incendiary, the poisoner, the one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and likewise the one who seizes land or a wife— these six are *ātatāyin*s (assassins)."
One may strike down even one who has mastered the end of the Vedas if he approaches as an assassin intent on killing; by doing so, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin.

"He who kills an assailant (*ātatāyin*) born in a family of Vedic students does not thereby become a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*); rather, it is the anger of the assailant that meets the anger of the slayer. Thus [it is said].

One who has performed the *triṇāciketa* sacrifice, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the *tri-suparṇa*, one who has performed the four *medha* sacrifices, a follower of the *Vājasaneyin* school, one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one whose lineage has been sustained by the gift of Vedic knowledge, a singer of the *Chandoga* hymns, a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, and one who knows both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas—these study the Dharma. Furthermore, those whose maternal and paternal lineages extend ten generations back and are known to be learned *śrotriyas*—these learned men and *snātakas* are purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).
One who is learned in the four Vedas, one who is capable of critical analysis, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), and a reciter of the Dharma—
these three types of persons established in their respective stages of life (*āśrama*) constitute the formal assembly (*parṣad*), provided they number at least ten.
Having initiated him, he should teach him the entire Veda; such a person is an Ācārya.
But he who teaches a single portion [of the Veda] is an upādhyāya.
And he who knows the auxiliary sciences of the Veda (veda-aṅga).
Va.3.24 For the protection of themselves and for the defense of the social classes, a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya may take up arms.
But for a Kṣatriya, that [study] is indeed obligatory, because his duty is the protection [of the people].

Having washed his feet and his hands up to the wrists, sitting facing either east or north, he should sip water three times with the *brāhma-tīrtha*—the line above the root of the thumb—without making any sound.
He should wipe it twice.
Va.3.28 One should touch the bodily apertures with water.
One should pour water on the head and into the left hand.
One should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while walking, standing, lying down, or bowing.
A Brāhmaṇa [should sip] water that reaches the heart, which is free of bubbles and free of foam.
But by those reaching the throat, one becomes a Kṣatriya.
A Vaiśya [becomes pure] by rinsing with water that has been sipped.
And likewise, [one becomes impure] by touching a woman or a Śūdra who have been touched [by an impure person].
Those cows which, even from a small wound, would be capable of providing nourishment;
those that are not corrupted by defects of color, smell, or taste, and whose arrival is auspicious.
Va.3.37 Drops [of saliva] that do not touch the body do not make one impure by causing one to become *ucchiṣṭa*.
Having slept, eaten, sneezed, drunk, wept, or bathed, one should sip water again at the end; likewise, after putting on a garment.
Va.3.39 Where the two lips touch one another and are hairless.
Va.3.40 There is no fault regarding the residue remaining on the beard.
Va.3.41 Regarding food stuck between the teeth, as with the teeth themselves, whatever may be inside the mouth, one becomes pure simply by swallowing it.
Even when one causes others to sip water, those drops that fall upon the feet do not cause one to become impure; they are considered by tradition to be the same as the ground.
Va.3.43 If, while walking or during meals, he should happen to touch something that is impure from food remnants,
he should set that object down on the ground, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then proceed with his activity once more.
Whatever may need to be examined, one should touch it with water.
Wild animals killed by dogs, fruit fallen by birds, that which has been stepped over by children, and that which has been trodden upon by women; [these are forbidden].
And whatever merchandise is displayed, as well as those defects found in the faces of women.
He is not harmed by mosquitoes or flies that have settled upon him.
Prajāpati has declared all water standing on the ground to be pure, provided it is sufficient to satisfy cows. Thus he spoke.
Va.3.48 For the removal of stains and odors, purification of that which is smeared with impure substances is performed with water and clay.
Va.3.49 For objects made of metal, clay, wood, and woven fiber, the methods of purification are respectively: ash, wiping, burning, planing, and washing.
Va.3.50 The same [rule] applies to crystals and gems as it does to fire.
The rules for gems apply likewise to conch-shells and mother-of-pearl.
Va.3.52 Bones [are treated] like wood.
Va.3.53: The purification of ropes, split bamboo, and leather is like that of cloth.
Va.3.54: [The measurement] of fruit[-trees] is by means of cow-hair.
Va.3.55 For those made of linen, [the purification is] with a paste of white mustard seeds.

Va.3.56 But the ground attains purity through sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, scraping, sprinkling, and [the application of] cow-products, according to the specific nature of the defect and its location. {BṣPṣ upalena}{E upalepana} Va.3.57 Now they also cite this: Through digging, burning, trampling, and also by the treading of cows.
The ground is purified by four means, and by the fifth, by smearing.
A woman is purified by her menstrual flow; a river is purified by its current;
bell-metal is purified by ashes; and earthenware is purified by being fired again.
An earthen vessel that has been touched by intoxicating liquors, urine, or feces, or by phlegm, pus, tears, or blood,
is not purified even by re-firing.
"The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the elemental self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom. Thus it is said.
Gold is purified by water alone.
Likewise, silver [is not perceived].
Copper is purified by means of an acid.
At the base of the little finger is the divine *tīrtha*.
Va.3.65: For the sages, [the measure] is one finger-breadth.
On the tips of the fingers, it is human.
Va.3.67 The palm of the hand is sacred to Agni.
Between the forefinger and the thumb is the region of the ancestors (pitrya).
Thinking, "It pleases me," one should praise the evening and morning meals.
Va.3.70 "It is well-eaten," [is said] at a rite for the ancestors.
Va.3.71: The term "accomplished" (*saṃpanna*) is used in reference to *ābhyudayika* (prosperity-related) rites. Va.4.1:
The fourfold caste system is distinguished by its original nature and by specific purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
"The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms;
that which was the Vaiśya was his thighs; from his feet the Śūdra was born. Thus also there is a Vedic citation (nigama).

With the *gāyatrī* he created the Brāhmaṇa, with the *triṣṭubh* the Rājanya, and with the *jagatī* the Vaiśya; but with no *chandas* at all [he created] the Śūdra—thus it is known that he is not to be consecrated (*asaṃskārya*).
For all [these], truthfulness, freedom from anger, generosity, non-violence, and procreation are essential.
"Even in the worship of ancestors, deities, and guests, one should not kill an animal"—this is the teaching of Manu.
"Manu has declared that one may kill an animal only on these occasions: at the honey-mixture offering (*madhuparka*), at a sacrifice, and at rites for the ancestors or the gods; not otherwise."

Meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings; nor does the slaughter of living beings lead to heaven. Therefore, in a sacrifice, what is called "slaughter" is actually no slaughter at all.
Moreover, they cook a large bull or a large goat for a Brahmin or a Kshatriya who has arrived as a guest; in this way, they provide hospitality to him.
And the ritual water-offering and purification shall take place from the second year onwards.
According to some, [the period lasts] until the eruption of the teeth.
Having consigned the body to the fire, they descend into the water without looking back.
Va.4.12 They should perform the water-rites with both hands, using the left hand for the other [hand], on odd-numbered days, facing the south.
Va.4.13 For this direction, the south, indeed belongs to the ancestors.
Having gone to their houses, they should remain for three days on a layer of grass, not eating.
If they are unable [to subsist by their own means], they should live on what has been purchased or produced.
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among the sapinda relatives.
Sapiṇḍa-relationship is understood to extend up to the seventh person.
And for women who have been given away in marriage, the [impurity] is known to extend through three generations.
The others shall perform [the funeral rites] for those who have been given away in marriage, and they [in turn] shall perform them for those [others].
For those who desire a thorough purification, this same [rule] would apply even in the case of birth.
Or [the name] of the mother and father. Va.4.21.
Some say it is because the mother is the cause of that [birth].
Moreover, they also cite this:

"There is no impurity for a man during childbirth if he does not come into contact [with it]. In that case, it is the menstrual flow (*rajas*) that should be known as impure, and that is not found in a man."
If that very same offense should recur, they shall be purified by the remaining penance.
Va.4.25: When the night has passed, [one should recite] two [verses].
At dawn, with three [verses].
A Brahmin [is purified] by ten nights.
A Kṣatriya [should perform] the fifteen-night sacrifice.
A Vaiśya [is purified] by twenty nights.
A Śūdra becomes pure after one month.
Moreover, they cite this:
"He who eats during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, or even during his birth-impurity (sūtaka),
shall go to a terrible hell and be born among the animal species."
Va.4.32 A twice-born man who, having been invited, eats at a funeral meal within ten days of the death, becomes a worm at the end of his body and consumes that very excrement. Thus it is said.
It is traditionally known that one who studies the Saṃhitā while fasting for twelve months or twelve half-months becomes purified.
Va.4.34 When a child dies before reaching two years of age, or in the case of a miscarriage, the period of impurity for the sapinda relatives is three nights.
Gautama says that there is immediate purification.
If one hears that a person residing in another region has died after the ten-day period has passed, the period of impurity lasts for one night.
If one who has maintained the sacred fires should die while traveling abroad, Gautama says that after performing the cremation rites again, the purification is to be conducted as if it were a corpse.

Having touched a sacrificial post, a funeral pyre, a cemetery, a menstruating woman, a woman who has recently given birth, or anything impure, one should enter the water with the head uncovered, saying "Apo! Apo! (O Waters!).
A woman is not independent; she has man as her primary authority.
It is known from tradition that those who do not maintain the sacred fires or those who have reached their menses may [partake of] the *amṛta*.
Moreover, they cite this:
"The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence. Thus it is said.
Va.5.4: Regarding her, the expiation for the husband's malevolent magic has been stated in the secret [sections].
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
A woman in her menses remains impure for three nights.

She should not apply collyrium, nor should she anoint herself; she should not bathe in water, nor sleep on the ground, nor sleep during the day; she should not touch fire, nor let go of her thread, nor brush her teeth, nor eat meat, nor gaze at the planets, nor laugh, nor do anything of this sort; she should not run, but drink from a vessel that is not broken, or drink with her cupped hands, or with a vessel of red iron.

Or rather, this is understood: having killed Tvaṣṭṛ’s three-headed son, Indra was seized by evil and, being bound by great unrighteousness, thought of himself thus: "I am [a sinner]. All beings reviled him, crying out, "Bhrūṇahan! Bhrūṇahan! He ran to women, saying: "Accept a third part of this guilt of killing an embryo for me."

They said, "What might happen to us? He said, "Choose a boon. They said, "May we obtain offspring during the fertile season; may we unite according to our desire until the time of childbirth. "So be it," he replied, and they accepted [this]. That very act of destroying the embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*) manifests month after month. Therefore, one should not eat the food of a woman who is menstruating; she remains there having assumed the very form of the destruction of the embryo.

Regarding this they say: "Cosmetic ointment and salve are not to be accepted from her, for that is the food of women; therefore people feel revulsion toward her and toward that [ointment], thinking, 'She has come near.'"
"Those among whom women remain menstruating, those who are without sacred fires,
and those whose family lacks Vedic learning— all these follow the dharma of Śūdras."
All of them follow the dharma of Śūdras.
It is certain that for all people, conduct is the supreme dharma;
one whose soul is overwhelmed by deficient conduct perishes both in this world and after death.
Neither austerities, nor sacred knowledge, nor the Agnihotra sacrifice,
nor sacrificial fees can in any way rescue one who has fallen away from this [path] due to deficient conduct.
The Vedas, even if studied together with their six auxiliary limbs, do not purify one who is deficient in conduct;
at the time of death, the Vedic hymns abandon him, just as birds with grown wings leave their nest.
But for a Brāhmaṇa who is deficient in conduct, even the Vedas in their entirety, along with the six auxiliary sciences and the sacrifices,
are incapable of producing any joy, just as beautiful wives are to a blind man.
The Vedic meters do not deliver him from evil who is deceitful and lives by guile.
Even when both syllables are correctly recited, that sacred word purifies him, just as rain-clouds purify the earth.
For a man of evil conduct in this world becomes censured;
he is constantly a partaker of suffering, afflicted by disease, and short-lived indeed.
From good conduct dharma bears fruit; from good conduct wealth bears fruit.
Through good conduct one attains prosperity; good conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
Even a man who is devoid of all auspicious marks, if he possesses good conduct,
is faithful, and is free from envy, lives for a hundred years.
One who knows the Dharma should ensure that his intake of food, excretion, and movements are well-restrained;
likewise, his speech, mental activities, ascetic practices, as well as his wealth and lifespan, must be kept strictly guarded.
One should void both urine and feces facing north during the day; at night, however, one should do so facing south. For in this way, one's life-span is not harmed.
Facing the fire, facing the sun, facing a cow, and facing a Brahmin;
facing Soma, water, and the twilight—his wisdom perishes through such urination.
One should not urinate in a river, nor on a path, nor in ashes;
nor in cow dung, nor in a ploughed field, nor in a sown field, nor in the shade of trees that provide livelihood for grass-eating animals.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, O twice-born one,
one may face whichever direction is comfortable, as well as when there is fear of danger to life.
One should perform the ritual action with water that has been drawn out [of the vessel].
Va.6.15 One may bathe even with water that has not been drawn out [of a well or pond].
A Brahmin should fetch clay from a riverbank that contains sand.
The five types of earth— namely, that from within water, from a temple, from an anthill, from a mouse-hole, or what remains after purification— should not be used.
One application of clay is prescribed for the penis, three for each hand—thus two applications of clay are traditionally taught;
five for the anus, ten for one foot, and seven for both feet.
This purification prescribed for householders is twofold for students,
threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
A sage's meal consists of eight mouthfuls, that of a forest-dweller sixteen,
that of a householder thirty-two, and that of a student is unlimited.
The maintainer of the sacred fires, the ox, and the student—these three succeed only while eating;
for them, there is no success if they do not eat.
Regarding vows and observances, as well as the duties of sacrifice and study.
Yoga, austerity, self-control, charity, truthfulness, purity, sacred learning, compassion, knowledge, discernment, and faith— this is the defining characteristic of a Brahmin.
One should know that long-standing enmity, malice, untruthfulness, reviling Brahmins, backbiting, and mercilessness are the characteristics of a Śūdra.

Those Brahmins who are peaceful and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with the sacred scriptures, who have conquered their senses, who have desisted from the slaughter of living beings, and who hold back their outstretched hands from accepting gifts— they alone are capable of delivering others across the ocean of existence.
One vessel consists of the Veda, and another vessel consists of austerity;
yet among all vessels, that one is the true vessel whose stomach does not contain the food of a Śūdra.
If a twice-born man dies while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach,
he shall become a domestic pig or be born into that Śūdra’s family.
For one whose limbs are nourished by the food and essence of a Śūdra, even if he studies constantly,
or performs oblations, or recites prayers, he does not attain the higher goal.
But he who engages in sexual intercourse after having eaten the food of a Śūdra—
his offspring belong to the one whose food it was, and he himself shall not ascend to heaven.
One who has risen through Vedic study, who possesses a noble birth, who is tranquil, established in the maintenance of the sacred fires, fearful of sin, and possessed of great knowledge;
one who is patient toward women, righteous, a refuge for cows, and exhausted by religious observances—such a person they call a worthy recipient.
Just as milk, curd, ghee,
or honey placed in an unbaked clay vessel would perish due to the weakness of the vessel, yet neither the vessel nor those liquids [would remain].
In this way, an ignorant man who accepts cows, gold, clothing, a horse, land, or sesame seeds is reduced to ashes like a piece of wood.
One should not practice scratching the nails with the fingers.
And one should not eat food with the fingernails at the beginning of a meal.
And one should not drink water with cupped hands.
One should not strike the water with the foot or with the hand.
One should not [use] water with water.
One should not cut fruit with bricks.
One fruit does not [arise] from another fruit.
One should not be deceitful nor fraudulent.
One should not learn the language of the Mlecchas.
Moreover, they cite this:
"One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes;
nor should one be fickle with speech or limbs—this is the sphere of activity for the disciplined."

Those Brāhmaṇas whose Veda has come down through an unbroken lineage along with its supplements (paribṛṃhaṇa), and who have direct perception of the revealed scripture (śruti) as their authority, are to be known as the learned (śiṣṭas).
He whom no one knows— whether as existing or non-existing, as unlearned or widely learned, as well-behaved or ill-behaved— that man is a Brāhmaṇa.
"He is a brahmin."
Va.7.1 There are four stages of life (āśramas).
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the wandering mendicant.
Va.7.3. Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas, he who has maintained his vow of studentship without breach may dwell with whomever he desires.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) shall attend upon his teacher until the liberation from the body.
And when the teacher has died, one should tend the sacred fire.
For it is known that Agni is your teacher.
Restrained in speech.
One who eats only at the fourth, sixth, and eighth meal-times.
He should go about for alms.
He is dependent upon his teacher.
He may have matted hair, or his hair may be matted only at the topknot.
One should follow a teacher who is walking; if he is sitting, one should stand; if he is lying down, one should sit near him.
He shall study when called upon.
Having reported everything that has been obtained, one should eat it with their permission.
He shall avoid using a bedstead, sleeping on it, brushing his teeth, washing [his face], applying collyrium, anointing [the body with oil], sandals, and an umbrella.
During the day he should stand; at night he should sit.
Three times a day he should approach water, saying "water," saying "water."

Va.8.1 A householder, having subdued anger and joy and being permitted by his teacher, shall bathe and take a wife who is of a different *ārṣeya* lineage, who has not had sexual intercourse, who is younger than himself, and of equal status.
The fifth [generation] on the mother's side and the seventh on the father's side.
He should kindle the nuptial fire.
One should not turn away a guest who has arrived in the evening.
One should not dwell in his house without eating.
If a Brāhmaṇa seeking clothing comes to one's house and does not eat,
he departs taking away whatever merit that person has accumulated.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is remembered as a guest (*atithi*);
because he stays for a non-permanent period, he is therefore called a guest.
A Brahmin who is not a resident of the same village, as well as a traveling companion,
shall not stay in one's house without eating, whether the proper time has arrived or not.
One who possesses faith and moral conduct, and is free from covetousness, is fully capable of establishing the sacred fires; he should not remain one who has not established the fires.
And one who does not sacrifice with Soma is not fit for the Soma [sacrifice].
He should be devoted to Vedic study, sacrifice, and procreation.
One should honor a guest who has arrived at one's house by rising from one's seat, offering a seat, speaking kind words, and being free from malice.
And one should sustain all beings with food according to one's ability.
The householder alone performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity. Indeed, among the four stages of life, the householder is distinguished as superior.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
so do all those in the various stages of life find their resting place in the householder.
Just as all living beings live by depending on their mother,
so too do all mendicants live by depending on the householder.
One who constantly uses water for purification, always wears the sacrificial thread, is constantly devoted to Vedic study, avoids the food of outcasts,
approaches his wife only during her season, and offers oblations according to the rules— such a Brāhmaṇa does not fall from the world of Brahman.
"From the world of Brahmā," thus [it is said].
Va.9.1 The forest-dweller has matted hair and wears garments of bark or deerskin.
And he should not enter a village.
Va.9.3 One should not stand upon land that has been ploughed.
He should gather roots and fruits from unplowed ground.
Va.9.5 One whose semen flows upwards;
Va.9.6 one whose disposition is patient.
One should honor a guest who has arrived at the hermitage with alms consisting of roots and fruits.
One should indeed give, but one should not accept.
He should touch water three times a day.
Having kindled the fire according to the ascetic rite, one becomes a maintainer of the sacred fires.
Va.9.11 Having the root of a tree as his dwelling, after six months have passed, he shall be without fire and without a fixed abode.
"He who should give to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings would go to the infinite heaven"—thus it is called "the infinite" (ānantya).
The wandering mendicant, having given the gift of fearlessness to all beings, should depart.
Moreover, they cite this:
"The sage who wanders about after having granted fearlessness to all beings—
for him, too, there is never any fear from any being."
But he who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back from his purpose,
kills both those born and those unborn, and seizes their possessions.
One may renounce all ritual actions, but one must not renounce the Veda;
by renouncing the Veda, one becomes a Śūdra; therefore, one must not renounce the Veda.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath-restraint is the supreme austerity.
Alms-gathering is superior to fasting; compassion excels giving. Thus it is said.
Shaven-headed, without a sense of "mine," and without possessions.
One should go for alms to seven houses that have not been previously designated.
When the smoke has subsided and the pestle has been set aside.
Va.10.9 Wearing a single garment.
Or, having spread his body with a deerskin or with grasses cut by a cow's hooves.
Va.10.11 He is one who sleeps on the bare ground.
One should dwell in an impermanent residence.
At the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the foot of a tree.
One who studies knowledge with the mind.
He is one who constantly dwells in the forest.
One should not walk about while looking at domestic animals.

"For one who is constantly dwelling in the forest, whose senses are conquered, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses, whose mind is intent on reflection upon the inner self, and who is equanimous—rebirth is indeed certain no longer to occur. Thus it is said.
One whose outward signs are unmanifest and whose conduct is unmanifest.
One who is not insane but wears the garb of an insane person.
Moreover, they cite this:
"Liberation is not for one who delights in the science of grammar, nor for one who delights in winning over the world;
it is not for one intent on food and clothing, nor for one who is fond of beautiful dwellings."
A mendicant should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks,
nor through instructions or discourses.
In the absence of gain, one should not be despondent; nor indeed should one rejoice upon obtaining it.
One should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, remaining free from attachment to material things.
"He who has no attachment to a hut, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to the triple-bowl;
nor to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food—he indeed is a knower of liberation."
In a brahmin family, he may eat as much as he obtains, both morning and evening, with the exception of honey and meat.
And one should not be satisfied.
Or he may dwell in a village.
He is straightforward, not deceitful, not treacherous, not fickle, and not wavering.
And one should not engage in sensory contact with anyone at all.
Va.10.29 He is indifferent toward all beings by avoiding both injury and favor.

The avoidance of slander, envy, arrogance, egoism, lack of faith, dishonesty, self-praise, disparagement of others, hypocrisy, greed, delusion, anger, and malice is the dharma desired for all stages of life.

A Brahmin who wears the sacrificial thread, carries a water-pot in his hand, remains pure, and avoids the food of a *vṛṣala* does not fall from the world of Brahman—from the world of Brahman. Thus it is said.
There are six who are worthy of the guest-offering (argha).
The officiating priest, the bridegroom, the king, the paternal uncle, the one who has completed his Vedic studies (snātaka), and the maternal uncle [are those who must be honored].
Having prepared the Vaiśvadeva food, one should offer oblations in the domestic fire every morning and evening.
One should offer an oblation to the household deities.
Having given the first portion to a learned Vedic scholar or to a student of sacred knowledge, he should immediately thereafter offer it to the ancestors.
Then he should feed the guest, starting with those who are more distinguished, in successive order.
Among those belonging to one's own household—maidens, children, the elderly, the young, and women who have recently given birth—
Then, he should take up other domestic [fires].
One should scatter [food] on the ground for dogs, caṇḍālas, outcasts, and crows.
One should give to a Śūdra either the remains of one's meal or that which is not the remains.
The husband and wife should eat the remainder.

Va.11.12 If a guest should arrive when the Vaiśvadeva offering has already been set aside, one should have special food prepared for him using all available resources, even if it requires cooking again.
For it is known: "The Vaiśvānara enters the house as a guest Brāhmaṇa; therefore they bring water and food from the rain-clouds, for people know him to be peace."
Having fed him, one should sit near him in attendance.
One should follow [the teacher] as far as the boundary, or until permission is granted.
In the dark fortnight, after the fourth day, one should offer [the śrāddha] to the ancestors.

On the day before, having assembled Brahmins—whether ascetics or householders, virtuous men who are not yet advanced in age, those established in their duties, learned in the Vedas, and neither formal students nor resident pupils.
One should also feed disciples who possess virtuous qualities.
Va.11.19 With the exception of those who are naked, white-skinned, eunuchs, blind, those with black teeth, lepers, and those with deformed nails.
Moreover, they cite this:
"But if one who knows the mantras is disciplined, even if he possesses bodily defects that defile the company, Yama declared him to be undefiled; indeed, he is a purifier of the company."
At a Śrāddha, the remnants of the food must not be removed until the end of the day;
for streams of nectar flow from them, which those who have not yet performed their water-libations drink.
One should not wipe away the remnants [of food] as long as the sun has not set;
from that, streams of milk flow forth, inexhaustible and partaking in the movement [of merit].
It is the established rule that for those of one's own lineage who have died before the performance of the purificatory rites,
Manu has declared both the food-leavings and the remnants of the meal to be their allotted portion.
One should offer the remnants that have fallen on the ground, the scattered food, and the water used for smearing as food for those deceased who are childless and short-lived.
When food has been offered to the ancestors with both hands released,
the evil-minded Asuras watch for that very interval.
Therefore, one should not perform the reception of food with empty hands;
nor, having taken hold of the meal, should one stand over both types of leavings.
Two [should be invited] for the rite for the gods, three for the ancestral rite, or one for each of the two.
Even if one is very wealthy, one should feed [the monks] but should not become attached to a large assembly.
Hospitality, the proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmin—these five things are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should avoid it.
Or alternatively, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, and who is free from all inauspicious marks.
Va.11.30 If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the rite for the gods (daiva) be performed there?
Having set aside a portion of food from all that has been prepared into a vessel—
Having performed [the rite] in a temple of the gods, one should then proceed with the śrāddha;
or else, one should cast that food into the fire or give it to a student observing the vow of celibacy.
As long as the food remains warm, and as long as they eat with speech restrained,
so long do the ancestors eat, provided that the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been mentioned.
The qualities of the sacrificial oblation (havis) should not be mentioned as long as the ancestors have not been satiated;
once the ancestors have been satiated, the oblation may thereafter be described as excellent.
But an ascetic who, when appointed to a *śrāddha* or a rite for the gods, should discard meat,
falls into hell for as many years as there are hairs on that animal.
At a Śrāddha ceremony, three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, kusa grass, and sesame seeds;
and three things they praise therein: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
When the sun has become dim during the eighth part of the day, that time should be known as *ku-yuga*;
what is given to the ancestors at that time becomes inexhaustible.
If one engages in sexual intercourse after having given or eaten at a *śrāddha* feast,
his ancestors become consumers of that semen for the duration of that month.
The embryo that is born from such a person, having given away and having consumed the paternal inheritance,
does not attain knowledge and is born with a diminished lifespan.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
wait upon the newborn son just as birds wait upon the fig tree.
"With honey, meat, vegetables, milk, and milk-rice—
this man will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism."
The ancestors rejoice in a son who increases the lineage, who is diligent in his father’s duties, and who is endowed with devotion to the gods and the Brahmins.
"His ancestors rejoice like farmers with well-plowed fields;
when one staying at Gayā gives food, by that act his ancestors become truly possessed of a son."
One should offer to the ancestors on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa and Āgrahāyaṇī, as well as on the Anvaṣṭakā.
Or, when the materials, the location, and the Brahmins are available, there is no restriction regarding the time.
A Brahmin must necessarily establish the sacred fires.
And he should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi, Cāturmāsya, Paśu, and Soma sacrifices.
For this is both a regular obligation and is commended as a debt.

For it is known: "A Brahmin is born burdened by three debts—by sacrifice to the gods, by progeny to the ancestors, and by the life of a student (brahmacarya) to the seers. He indeed is free from debt who has sacrificed, who has a son, and who has lived as a student.
Va.11.49 One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception. Va.11.50 [One should initiate] a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception.
A Vaiśya [should be initiated] in the twelfth years from conception.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa shall be made of Palāśa wood.
Or, for a Kṣatriya, it may be made of nyagrodha wood.
Or a staff made of udumbara wood for a Vaiśya.
Va.11.55 The sacrificial cord of a Brāhmaṇa should reach as far as his hair.
For a Kṣatriya, it should reach up to the forehead.
The nose-length [staff] is for the Vaiśya.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa shall be made of muñja grass.
Va.11.59 A bowstring is for a Kṣatriya.
The garment made of hemp fibers is for the Vaiśya.
A black antelope skin serves as the upper garment for a Brāhmaṇa.
Va.11.62 For a Kṣatriya, the Raurava [sāman].
For a Vaiśya, it shall be a cowhide or a goat-skin.
A white, unwashed garment is for a Brāhmaṇa.
Va.11.65 A kṣatriya’s [should be] madder-red.
Va.11.66 A Vaiśya’s [upper garment] shall be yellow or made of silk.
Or, alternatively, all [the monks] may have woven cloth that is not dyed.
A Brahmin should ask for alms, placing the word "bhavat" (sir) at the beginning.
A Kṣatriya [is formed] with the word *bhavat* placed in the middle.
A Vaiśya [should address] one who ends with "bhavat".
Up to the sixteenth year is the time for a Brahmin; it has not passed.
For a Kṣatriya, [the period of impurity lasts] up to twenty-two days.
For a Vaiśya, [the period of impurity lasts] up to twenty-four days.
From this point forward, they become those for whom the Sāvitrī has fallen away.
One should not initiate them, nor teach them, nor officiate sacrifices for them, nor should they intermarry with these [persons].
One whose *sāvitrī* has fallen shall perform the *uddālaka-vrata*.

For two months he should subsist on barley-gruel; for one month on milk; for half a month on curdled milk (*āmikṣā*); for eight nights on clarified butter; for six nights on food obtained unasked; for three nights he should subsist on water; and for one day and night he should fast.
One should go to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the horse sacrifice.
Or he should sacrifice with the Vrātyastoma; "or he should sacrifice, or he should sacrifice," [it is said].
Now, therefore, follow the observances for one who has completed his Vedic studies (the Snātaka).
He should not beg from anyone, except for the attendants of the king.
But one who is overcome by hunger may beg for anything at all—be it a field, whether cultivated or uncultivated, a cow, a goat, or a sheep, or finally, gold, grain, or food.
But the instruction is that a Snātaka shall not suffer from hunger.
One should not live together with one who wears soiled clothes.
Not with a woman who is menstruating.
Not with one who is unsuitable.
One who is not a *kulaṃkula* shall not be so.
One should not step over a stretched-out calf-rope.
One should not look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting.
One should not void urine or excrement in water.
One should not spit.

Having covered the ground with sacrificially forbidden grass, one whose head is wrapped [with a cloth] should void urine and feces facing north during the day; at night, facing south. One should sit toward the north during the two twilights. Regarding this, they also cite: "For *snātakas*, there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper garment."
Two sacrificial threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water.
Water, the hand, and wood are declared to be pure when placed in fire;
therefore, one should wipe the water-pot with both water and the hand.
For Manu, Prajāpati, has declared this to be the rite of carrying fire around [the victim].
And having performed the obligatory duties, one should sip water for purification, being most intent on purity.
One should eat food facing the east.
One should swallow the entire morsel silently, including the thumb.
And one should not make a sound.
He should approach his own wife during her fertile period, avoiding the forbidden days.
He should not approach her from the side.
But he who performs sexual intercourse in the mouth of his wedded wife,
his ancestors exist for that month as consumers of semen.
That pleasure which occurs through unchaste conduct is based on unrighteousness.
Moreover, it is known in the *Kāṭhaka*: "May our daughters, when they are about to give birth tomorrow, lie down with their husbands"—this is the boon granted to women by Indra.
One should not climb a tree.
One should not descend into a well.
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth.
One should not pass between the fire and a Brahmin.
Not [the word] "fire" (agni) in the dual.
Nor [should one eat] at the houses of two Brahmins without having obtained their permission.
"One should not eat together with one's wife," so it is known in the Vājasaneyaka, [on the grounds] that "the offspring will be lacking in vigor."
One should not point it out by the name "Indra’s bow."
One should say, "a jeweled bow."
One should avoid a seat made of *palāśa* wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick made of *palāśa*.
One should not eat from one's lap.
One should not eat while seated on a low couch.
He should carry a staff made of bamboo.
And [the theft of] gold ornaments and earrings [is also a grave offense].
One should not wear a garland outside [the house], except for one made of gold.
One should avoid assemblies and gatherings.
Moreover, they cite this:
"The invalidation of the Vedas and the reviling of the sages,
as well as a lack of discipline in all matters— this is the destruction of the self."
One who has not been invited should not go to a sacrifice; if he should go, he must return by walking around it clockwise.
One should not set out upon a path until the sun has risen above the trees.
And one should not board a boat that is in a state of uncertainty.
One should not cross a river with one's arms.
Having risen during the latter part of the night and studied, he should not go back to sleep again.
During the *muhūrta* sacred to Prajāpati, a Brāhmaṇa should observe certain restrictive rules; he should observe them.
Now, therefore, follows the commencement of Vedic study (*svādhyāya-upākarma*), on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or of Prauṣṭhapada.
Having kindled the fire, he offers parched grains.
"To the gods, to the seers, and to the meters."
Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce auspicious blessings and having consumed curd, they should then commence the study of the Vedic sections.
For four and a half months, or five and a half months.
From this point forward, one should study during the bright fortnights.
But the Vedāṅgas may be studied at will.
Va.13.8 These are his occasions for non-study.
Va.13.9 [It is forbidden to study] when there is thunder at twilight.
At the twilights.
In cities where there is a corpse within them or where there is public proclamation during the day.
Va.13.12 It may be done at will on ground that has been smeared with cow-dung or scraped clean.
At the edge of a cemetery.
[The same applies] to one who is lying down.
Va.13.15 [The offense belongs to] the one who performs the *śrāddha* ceremony.
And regarding this, they cite a verse from the *Mānava*:

"Having accepted fruits, water, sesame seeds, food, or whatever else may pertain to a *śrāddha*, even though it is a time when study is forbidden, Brahmins are traditionally said to have their hands for mouths."
For one who runs, [the fault applies] in the case of a foul odor and so forth, or on barren soil.
[The same applies] to one who has climbed a tree. Va.13.18.
And [the same applies] on a boat and in an army.
And having eaten, [one should not study] while the hands are still wet.
Va.13.21 In the sound of an arrow.
On the fourteenth day, on the new moon day, on the eighth day, and during the Aṣṭakā festivals.
And [the same applies] to one who has extended his legs and rests upon his lap.
Va.13.24 In the presence of the teacher.
Va.13.25 In the case of one who has abstained from sexual intercourse.
Va.13.26 With a garment that has been used for sexual intercourse and has not been washed.
Va.13.27 At the edge of a village.
[The same applies to] that which has been vomited.
Va.13.29 [This refers to] one who has urinated or evacuated.
And [there is no offense] when the word "Sāman" is used for the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda.
Va.13.31 When there is indigestion.
Va.13.32 In the case of a thunderclap.
Va.13.33 Regarding an earthquake.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
In the case of cries from the quarters, mountains, and precipices, or during showers of stones, blood, and dust, [the death] occurs before the end of the year.
In the case of the conjunction of a meteor and lightning, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
A meteor, lightning, or anything possessing light.
Va.13.38. Outside the proper season, it is forbidden for a period of one night.
When the teacher has died, [the period of impurity lasts] for three nights.
One may have sexual intercourse with the wives of a teacher’s son or a pupil day and night.
One should rise to greet and address with salutation an officiating priest, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, and a maternal uncle who are not younger than oneself.
And those who are to be saluted by prostration with the feet, as well as the wife of one's teacher, [are also not to be saluted in that manner].
And both mother and father.
He who knows how to greet [another] should say, "I am so-and-so, sir."
And he who does not know [it].

In a response to a greeting (*pratyabhivāda*), when addressed, the final vowel together with the following consonant undergoes elision (*plava*), provided it is a conjunct vowel (*saṃdhyakṣara*) not subject to *pragṛhya* status; furthermore, it undergoes the change to *āy* or *āv*, as in the example: "O, sir! (*bho bhāo*).
A father who has fallen [from his caste] is to be abandoned, but a mother does not fall [from her status] because of her son.
Moreover, they cite this:
"Ten teachers are equal to one sub-teacher; a father is equal to a hundred teachers;
a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in respect."

A wife, sons, and disciples who associate with those of evil deeds should be rebuked and then abandoned; he who abandons one who has fallen [from his status] otherwise [than by these means] [is at fault].
A sacrificing priest and a teacher who do not perform sacrifices or teach should be abandoned; by failing to abandon them, one falls [from his status].
"If one is born from one who has fallen [into sin], he becomes fallen," so they say, except in the case of a woman.
For she is one who goes to another.
One should approach her as one who has no inheritance.
When the teacher's own teacher is present, one is required to behave toward him as toward the teacher;
for the sacred tradition declares that one should behave toward the teacher's son as toward the teacher himself.
A weapon, poison, and liquor are not to be accepted by a Brahmin.
Learning, wealth, age, kinship, and action are grounds for respect.
Each preceding one is more serious than the one following it.

Va.13.58: When an elderly person, a child, one who is ill, a burden-carrier, a woman, or a person in a vehicle meet [on the road], the way must be yielded by each to the other. Va.13.59: When a king and a *snātaka* meet, the way must be yielded by the king to the *snātaka*.
Va.13.60 [The ritual] for the bride being carried away by all [the relatives] together.
Grass, land, fire, water, kind speech, truthfulness, and freedom from malice—these things in the house of the virtuous are never, ever cut off.
Now, therefore, we shall describe what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten.
The food of physicians, hunters, unchaste women, judges, thieves, those accused of crimes, eunuchs, and outcasts is unfit to be eaten.
[The food] of a miser, one initiated for a sacrifice, a prisoner, one who is ill, a seller of Soma, a carpenter, a washerman, a vintner, a slanderer, a usurer, and a leather-cutter [is forbidden].
And [the same applies] for a Śūdra.
And those who bear weapons [are also to be honored].
And he who is a paramour, yet considers himself a husband.
And whoever should set fire to houses.
And he who does not strike those deserving of death.
"Who will eat?"—thus it was proclaimed by voice.
The food of a group and the food of a courtesan.
Moreover, they cite this:
"The gods do not eat the food of one who keeps a dog, nor of the husband of a low-caste woman; they do not eat the food of one conquered by his wife, nor of him in whose house there is a paramour."
One may accept these things: fuel, water, fodder, *kuśa* grass, parched grain, a vehicle offered for one's arrival, a dwelling, a small fish, *priyaṅgu* seeds, a garland, perfume, honey, and meat.
Moreover, they cite this:
"One who wishes to support his wife for the sake of his teacher, or who intends to honor the deities and guests, may accept gifts from anyone; yet he himself must not be satisfied by that alone."
The food of a hunter who wanders with his bow and arrows is not to be avoided.

For it is known that Agastya engaged in hunting during a sacrificial session (*sattra*) lasting a thousand years. His sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) were prepared from the flesh of excellent wild animals and birds at times when no other provisions were available.
Regarding this, they indeed cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"Alms that are offered, brought forth, or presented before one has even requested them..."
Prajāpati considered her fit to be eaten even by one who has committed evil deeds.

One may eat the food of a person who has faith, even if he is a thief, and especially so if he is one who performs many sacrifices or initiates many pupils. But one must never eat the food of such a person.
His ancestors do not eat for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblations, he who treats such a woman with contempt.
"Even if she is offered, she is not to be accepted from a physician, a hunter, a remover of arrows, a sinner, a eunuch, or an unchaste woman. Thus it is said.
Va.14.20 The leavings of one who is not one's teacher are not to be eaten.
One's own leavings, and what has been defiled by the leavings of another.
And that which is defiled by clothing, hair, or insects.
However, one may at will remove hair and insects, sprinkle them with water, scatter ashes over them, and then consume what has been declared pure by word.
For in this regard, they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
The gods ordained three purifiers for the Brāhmaṇas:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is praised by speech.
In a divine trough, at weddings, and at sacrifices that have been commenced,
food touched by crows or dogs should not be discarded. Therefore, having removed that food, the remainder deserves purification.
For liquids, by means of immersion alone; for solids, however, by means of sprinkling.
For that which has been touched by the mouth of a cat shall indeed remain pure.
Food that has been kept overnight, food corrupted by its nature, food containing hair or insects, food that has been re-cooked, raw meat, and cooked meat [are forbidden].
However, one may at will consume it after it has been sprinkled with curd or ghee.
For in this regard, they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"Whether it be ghee or oil, if a Brahmin eats what has fallen from his fingernails,
Yama declares that impurity to be equal to the eating of beef."
But those oily substances, salt, and condiments that have been placed directly into the hand do not reach the giver; the eater incurs the sin.
One should give [the gift], but never with the hand nor with iron.

In the case of eating garlic, onions, leeks, *gṛñjana*, exudations from trees that cause phlegm (*śleṣmāntaka*), red sap, things cut by an axe, what has been licked by a dog or a crow, or the remnants of a Śūdra’s meal, the *atikṛcchra* penance is required.
The milk of a cow in heat and the milk of a cow whose calf has been taken away.
[The same applies to] cows, buffaloes, and goats that have not passed ten days [since giving birth].
Water inside a boat.
One should avoid cakes, parched grain, flour-mash, barley-meal, small cakes, oil, milk-rice, and vegetables that have turned sour.
And other preparations made from milk, barley, and flour.
Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the hedgehog, the rabbit, the tortoise, and the iguana are edible.
And among animals other than camels, those that have teeth only on one side [are not to be eaten].
Or, for fish, [the flesh of] the ceṭa, gavaya, śiśumāra, nakra, and kulīra [is used].
They have deformed shapes and heads like those of serpents.
The gaurī, gavaya, and śarabha.
Likewise, those who have not been formally assigned [a task] are also [not to be approached].
A milch cow and a bull that have not yet cut their teeth [are exempt from the tax].
In the Vājasaneyaka, however, it is known that a milch cow and a bull are fit for consumption as sacrificial food.
But regarding the rhinoceros and the non-domestic boar, there are conflicting opinions.

And among birds: the *viṣuviṣkara*, web-footed birds, the *kalaviṅka*, the *plava*, the swan (*haṃsa*), the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), the *bhāsa*, the crow (*vāyasa*), the turtle-dove (*pārāvata*), the osprey (*kurara*), the *sāraṅga*, the pale pigeon (*pāṇḍu-kapota*), the curlew (*krauñca*), the *krakara*, the heron (*kaṅka*), the vulture (*gṛdhra*), the hawk (*śyena*), the crane (*baka*), the *balāka*, the cormorant (*madgu*), the lapwing (*ṭiṭṭibha*), the *māndhāla*, the night-prowler (*naktañcara*), the woodpecker (*dārvāghāṭa*), the *cakaṭa*, the *railātaka*, the *hārīta*, the wagtail (*khañjarīṭa*), the domestic cock (*grāmya-kukkuṭa*), the parrot (*śuka*), the starling (*śārika*), the cuckoo (*kokila*), and carnivorous birds that frequent villages—these are the village-frequenting birds. And those that frequent villages... [and so on].
A person arises from the union of blood and semen, having the mother and father as its cause.
In the matters of giving, selling, or renouncing it, the mother and father have authority.
But one should neither give nor receive an only son.
For he was indeed for the continuation of his ancestors.
A woman shall neither give away nor receive a son as a gift, except with the permission of her husband.

One who intends to adopt a son should summon his kinsmen, inform the king, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* formulas in the middle of his dwelling, he should adopt a boy who is not too distant in kinship and is closely related to him.
And when doubt has arisen, one should treat him as a distant kinsman or like a Śūdra.
For it is known that by means of one person, many are saved here.
If, after he has been adopted, a legitimate son (aurasa) should be born, the adopted son shall be entitled to a fourth part of the inheritance.
If he were not engaged in rites for prosperity, it would be improper.

Those who corrupt the Vedas and those who officiate at sacrifices for Śūdras are outcasts from the ranks of the highest varṇas; the pouring out of water [from their vessels] constitutes their purification.

Va.15.12 From the mixing of vessels, having taken up an incomplete vessel, a slave, or the son of a woman of a different caste, or a kinsman who is dissimilar or devoid of good qualities, shall spread out *darbha* grass with their tips pointing forward or red flowers with his left foot, and pour out the full vessel for him.
And when he has been led away, his kinsmen, with disheveled hair, shall follow and seize him.
Having placed their sacred threads over the right shoulder, they may enter the houses at will.
From that time forward, they shall not subject him to judicial proceedings.
Those who have that as their nature are those who practice that dharma.
But for those who have fallen [from their status], there is restoration once they have performed the prescribed penance.
Moreover, they cite this:
"For those who first lift [the vessel], it goes as if playing and as if laughing;
for those who later let it fall, it goes as if grieving and as if weeping. Thus it is said.
Those who have killed their teacher, mother, or father may, through his favor or by means of expiation, achieve restoration from those [sins].

Va.15.20 Having filled a golden vessel or one made of clay with water drawn from a sacred pool (*puṇyahrada*), they consecrate him with those waters while reciting the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses [RV 10.9.1]: "O Waters, you are most healing... and so forth. Va.15.21 The ritual reversal (*pratyuddhāra*) for one who has been consecrated is explained by the birth of a son; it is explained, it is explained.
Now, the legal procedures (vyavahāra).
The king or the minister shall carry out the affairs of the assembly.
When two people are disputing, one should not take the side of either.
Just as there is an offense regarding the seat, so too is there an offense for one who has gone beyond the limit.
One should behave toward all beings as toward one's own seat; for the first two castes, there is no offense until the completion of their education.
And once it has been accomplished, he should protect it.
Va.16.7 The property of kings and children.
[This applies] to those who have not attained legal capacity.
But when the time has arrived, that which is appropriate [should be done].
"Written evidence, witnesses, and possession are declared to be the three kinds of proof.
The owner who first takes possession of the property shall recover that wealth. Thus it is said.
The release [of water] from the fields along the paths, as well as its diversion; in the case of young houses and other such matters, [the fine shall be] three-quarters of a pāda.
In a dispute over a house or a field, the testimony of the neighbors is decisive.
In the case of a dispute with a neighbor, a written document is the means of proof.
In case of a contradiction with a counter-document, the evidence of the village elders, city elders, and guilds shall be authoritative.
Moreover, they cite this:

"That which is inherited from the father, that which is purchased, that which is received as a gift, that which is obtained through a subsequent marriage, that which is acquired by inheritance, that which is received as a dowry, and likewise that which comes from a sacrifice—these are the eight kinds of property. Thus it is said.
In that case, the period is ten years for both enjoyed and unenjoyed [property].
Moreover, they cite another [verse]:
"A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the wealth of a *śrotriya* are not lost through [long] possession."
Property that has been abandoned becomes the property of the king.
Therefore, otherwise, the king should carry out his affairs together with his ministers and the citizens.
Or rather, a king who is a creator of order would be superior if he were to have a retinue of vultures.
Or rather, a king with a retinue of vultures is superior.
A vulture may have a retinue of vultures, but a vulture does not have a retinue that is not vultures.
For indeed, faults arise from association.
And the stealing, carrying away, and destruction [of property].
Therefore, one should first ask about the retinue.
Now, concerning witnesses.
Witnesses shall be those who are learned in the Vedas, handsome, virtuous, meritorious, and truthful.
In all [cases], either all [the factors] indeed [arise together].
One should appoint women as witnesses for women; for the twice-born, those of similar status; for Śūdras, virtuous Śūdras; and for those of the lowest birth, those of the lowest origin.
Moreover, they cite this:
"A promissory note, a gift made in jest, what is due for gambling or liquor,
and what remains unpaid from fines or taxes— the son is not liable to pay these to the creditor."
"Speak the truth, witness; your ancestors are hanging there.
Waiting for your word, they are flying up and falling down."
Naked, shaven-headed, and carrying a skull-bowl, tormented by hunger and thirst,
blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy.
One kills five by lying about a maiden; one kills ten by lying about a cow;
one kills a hundred by lying about a horse; and one kills a thousand by lying about a human being.
When a husband has died during legal proceedings, there is an expiation for the woman of the family;
by the prior determination of those [matters], they are here cut off by the accusers.

At the time of marriage, during sexual union, when life is at stake, or when all one's wealth is being seized—one may speak untruth for the sake of a Brahmin; indeed, they say that these five kinds of untruth are not sinful.
If they speak of what ought to be done for the sake of their own people or their own interests, or even for the sake of wealth, by relying solely on their own faction,
they cause even those ancestors of their lineage and family who dwell in heaven to fall.
They also cause [them] to fall.
A father who beholds the face of his living son discharges his debt to him and attains immortality.
"Endless are the worlds for those who have sons; there is no world for one who has no son"—so it is heard in the sacred tradition.
"May they be childless, those devourers!"—this is a curse. (cf. ṚV. 1.21.5c:

*aprajāḥ santv atriṇaḥ*) "O Agni, through offspring may I attain immortality"—there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) thus: (cf. ṚV. 5.4.10c: *jātavedo yaśo asmāsu dhehi prajābhir agne amṛtatvam aśyām* ||) "Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity."
Then, by the grandson of the son, he reaches the highest heaven of the sun.
Regarding this, they dispute whether the son belongs to the owner of the field or to the progenitor.
Regarding this, they cite both examples:
"If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of others, those calves belong only to the owners of the cows; the bull's labor was in vain. (Va. 17.8)
"Be vigilant and guard this thread; let not another's seed be sown in your field. A son belongs to the one who begot him in the life hereafter; therefore, do not weave this thread in vain.
"If among many born of the same father, one man has a son, the sacred tradition declares that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that one son."
If among many wives who share one husband, one is possessed of a son,
the Vedic revelation states that they all become possessed of sons through that son.
Thus, there are twelve sons as seen in the Purāṇas.
The first [type of son] is one begotten by oneself upon his own wedded wife.
In the absence of that, a son born of a wife duly appointed [to bear a child] is the second.
Va.17.15 The third [type] is the *putrikā*.
It is known that a woman without a brother goes toward the ancestors of her husband; she goes back to them to become their son.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"I shall give you this brotherless maiden, adorned with ornaments;
whatever son is born of her shall be my son."
The fourth is the one who returns again to existence.

Va.17.19 She who, having abandoned her husband from childhood and having lived with others, returns to his very household, becomes a *punarbhū*. Va.17.20 And she who, having abandoned a husband who is impotent, fallen, or insane, takes another husband, or does so after he has died, becomes a *punarbhū*.
Va.17.21 The son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*) is the fifth.
Regarding the son whom a woman, not consecrated by marriage in her father's house, might bear out of desire, they say he belongs to his maternal grandfather.
Moreover, they cite this:

"If the unmarried daughter of one should obtain a son from a husband of equal status, by that son the maternal grandfather becomes a father of a son; he shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and inherit the wealth."
And the one secretly born in the house is the sixth.
"These are the heirs, the kinsmen, the saviors from great fear," so they say.
Now, among those who have no heirs or relatives, the son born of a woman pregnant at marriage (*sahoḍha*) is indeed the first.
If a pregnant woman undergoes the sacramental rite, the son born is a *sahoḍha* (son by a pregnant bride).
The adopted son is the second.
That which his mother and father may give.
The third is one who has been purchased.
That has been explained by means of the story of Śunaḥśepa.
King Hariścandra indeed purchased the son of Sajīgartasauyavasa.
The fourth [type of disciple] is one who has come of his own accord.
That has been explained by Śunaḥśepa.

Śunaḥśepa, having been bound to the sacrificial post, praised the deities. Thereupon, the deities released his bonds. The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) said to him, "Let this boy be ours! He did not agree to them. They then reached an agreement, saying, "Let him be the son of whomever he desires. Viśvāmitra was his *hotṛ* priest; thus, he went to become his son.
One who has been abandoned is the fifth.
He should accept one who has been abandoned by his mother and father.
"The son of a Śūdra woman is indeed the sixth," so they say; these are those who have neither inheritance nor kinship.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If none of the six preceding [relatives] should be an heir to anyone, these [others] shall take his inheritance."
Now follows the division of the inheritance among brothers.
And for those who are childless, [the period lasts] until they obtain a son.
The eldest shall take two shares.
And for cattle and horses, one-tenth less than ten [is the tax].
And the goats, sheep, and house belong to the youngest brother.
And for the middle [prince], there shall be implements of black iron and equipment for the mountain fastnesses.
The women shall divide the mother's dowry among themselves.
If a Brāhmaṇa has sons by a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyā wife...
The son of a Brāhmaṇī woman shall take a third share.
The son of a Kṣatriya woman [by a Brāhmaṇa father] receives two shares.
The others shall divide [the property] equally.
And whoever among them should have produced [the property] by himself shall take two shares.
But those who have entered another stage of life are without shares.
And those who are eunuchs, insane, or outcasts.
The support of the impotent and the insane [is the duty of their relatives].
The widow of a deceased man shall observe a vow for six months, eating food free from pungent seasonings and salt, and sleeping on the ground.

After six months have passed, having bathed and offered the *śrāddha* for her husband, and having assembled those related by learning, ritual action, or kinship from the father’s side, the father or brother should arrange the appointment (*niyoga*). One should not, however, appoint a woman who is insane, lacking self-control, or diseased.
Even if she is older.
Sixteen years.
Unless he should be ill, [he shall not do so].
During the *prājāpatya* hour, she should behave toward him as if he were her husband, except for laughing with him, verbal harshness, and physical violence.
In matters of food, clothing, bathing, and the application of ointments, she should be the first to approach [her husband].
Regarding one who has procreated with an unauthorized woman, they say: "The son belongs to the progenitor."
If there were those who are subject to necessity (niyogin).
There is no appointment (niyoga) out of greed for inheritance.
Some say that one should assign [the task] after first instructing him in the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
A maiden who has reached puberty shall wait for three years.
After three years, she may obtain a husband of equal status.
Moreover, they cite this example:
"If, here on earth, a maiden is given away by her father after she has passed the proper age due to his negligence, she,
having been delayed beyond the proper time, destroys the giver just as an excessive sacrificial fee destroys the teacher."
Out of fear that her daughter might reach the time of puberty, the father should give away an unmarried girl;
for if she remains beyond her season, guilt falls upon the father.

"As many seasons as touch a maiden who is of equal status, desirous, and being courted by [a suitor], so many embryos have been killed by those two, the mother and the father; such is the declaration of Dharma."
If the bridegroom dies after she has been given [in marriage] by water and word,
but before she has been led away with the sacred mantras, that maiden belongs to her father alone.
If a maiden has been forcibly abducted but not consecrated with the sacred mantras, she should be given to another according to the prescribed rule; for such a girl remains exactly as a maiden.
If the husband dies while she is still a young girl, having been consecrated by the sacred mantras alone,
and if her virginity remains intact, she deserves to undergo the sacramental rite once again.
A woman whose husband is away on a journey shall wait for five years.
After five years have passed, she shall go to her husband's presence.
If she should not be desirous of going abroad for the sake of dharma or wealth, she should be treated as if she were already dead.

Thus, a Brāhmaṇī woman who has borne children receives five [shares], while one who has not borne children receives four; a Rājanyā woman who has borne children receives five, while one who has not borne children receives three; a Vaiśyā woman who has borne children receives four, while one who has not borne children receives two; and a Śūdrā woman who has borne children receives three, while one who has not borne children receives one.
From this point forward, among those who share the same purpose, birth, funeral rice-ball offerings, water libations, and lineage, each preceding one is more venerable than the next.
But indeed, while a man of noble birth exists, she should not go to another.
If among the six preceding [categories of heirs] there should be no heir whatsoever, then those who are *sapiṇḍas* or those who stand in the position of sons shall divide his property.
In the absence of these, the teacher and the pupil shall take [the property].
In the absence of those two, the king shall take it.
But the king shall not take [the property] of a Brahmin.
But the property of a Brahmin is a terrible poison.
They do not say that poison is the true poison; it is said that the property of a Brahmin is poison.
Poison kills only a single person, but the property of a Brahmin destroys sons and grandsons.
One should bestow [it] upon those who are virtuous and possess the threefold knowledge; one should bestow it.
They say that one born from a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a Caṇḍāla.
From a Kṣatriya man and a Vaiśya woman, a Vaiṇa is born.
From a Vaiśya woman, an Antyāvasāyin is born.
They say that one born of a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is a Rāmakas.
From a Rājanya man and a Pukkasa woman, a Pukkasa is born.
They say that one born to a Brāhmaṇī woman by a Rājanya man becomes a Sūta.
Moreover, they cite this:
