"Whosoever among those born in secret have resorted to the qualities of their father's lineage,
one should recognize them by their actions, for they have fallen away from the conduct appropriate to those qualities."
Those born from women one, two, or three degrees lower than the fathers of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes become Ambaṣṭhas, Ugras, and Niṣādas respectively.
Among Śūdras, the Pāraśava is [the foremost].
"Like a *pāraśava* [son], he possesses strength even while living," so they say.
"Indeed, those who are Śūdras are this very cremation ground."
Therefore, one should not study in the presence of a Śūdra.
Moreover, they cite these verses sung by Yama:
"This cemetery is manifest before our eyes—those Śūdras who are evildoers.
Therefore, one should never study in the vicinity of a Śūdra."
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor the remains of food, nor that which has been prepared as an oblation;
nor should one teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him.

"Whoever should teach him the Dharma, and whoever should prescribe him a vow—he enters along with that person into a terrible, unmitigated darkness. Thus it is said. "Should a worm ever arise at the opening of his wound..."
One is purified by the Prājāpatya penance; the sacrificial fees consist of gold, a cow, and clothing.
Having piled the fire-altar, one should not approach a woman.
A woman who is black in complexion is for pleasure alone, not for dharma; she is not for dharma. Thus it is said.
Va.19.1 The specific duty of a king is the protection of living beings; from its performance comes his success.
Va.19.2 The learned say that this sacrificial session (*sattram*) is characterized by fear and compassion, and is subject to old age and death.
Va.19.3 Therefore, one should appoint a domestic priest (*purohita*) for those duties prescribed for the householder stage.
It is known: "The kingdom prospers when it has a domestic priest."
Because it protects both.
And because of incapacity.
Having entered into all these local, regional, caste, and family customs, the king should establish the four social orders in their respective duties.
If they act improperly toward them, he should inflict punishment.
But the punishment for injury or verbal abuse shall be determined according to the specific circumstances of place, time, social status, age, learning, and occupation.
From scripture and from examples.
One should not harm trees that bear flowers and fruit.
And he should destroy [the enemy] for the purpose of causing cultivation.
And for the constituent parts of the householder's life, the measures and weights shall be maintained.
Due to its dependence on a substratum, mist is not [the cause] of things in their own right.
Theft shall consist merely in taking away the value of the object. (It shall not be considered theft) if it is otherwise.
In the case of the words *mahā* and *mahaḥ*, there may optionally be the substitution of *path-*.
In a military expedition, an army consisting of ten divisions should be twice as effective [as one with fewer].
There should be water-stalls for each [of them].
And he should cause at least fifty men to be summoned.
Women shall not be unproductive.
If one's hands were like stones, if one's feet were like beans or like arrows, or if one's feet were like kārṣāpaṇa coins, [one would be reborn as such].
One who is without water is to be robbed of his speed.
A Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), a royal official, a person without a protector, a renunciant, a child, an elderly person, a youth, and those who have recently given birth.
24. Maidens who have gone abroad and women supported by their husbands [are not to be questioned].
With one's two arms, one should give a hundred times more than with the upper garment.
Burning down rivers, marshes, and forests, and the enjoyment of mountains shall be free of tolls.
Or those who depend upon him may give it.
Every month, he should cause the marriage-fee to be brought.
And when the king has passed away, one should give what is incidental.
By this, the conduct toward one's mother is explained.
The king shall support the paternal uncles and maternal uncles of the queen.
And [he should inform] his kinsmen and others as well.
The wives of the king shall receive food and clothing.
Or, not desiring [to remain], they may go forth into homelessness.
The king shall support those who are impotent or insane.
Because the inheritance goes to that [person].
Regarding customs duties as well, they cite this verse of Manu:
"There is no [duty] on a broken kārṣāpaṇa coin, nor on one who lives by his craft, nor on a child, nor on a messenger;
nor on what is obtained as alms, nor on the remnants of what has been seized, nor on a Śrotriya, nor on a wandering ascetic, nor at a sacrifice."
A thief is not considered guilty by reason of entering [a house].
One who carries weapons, one captured with stolen goods, or one who bears wounds—these are declared [as grounds for execution] by some authorities.
If a person deserving punishment is released, the king shall fast for one night.
The domestic priest shall fast for three nights.
The domestic chaplain shall undergo the *kṛcchra* penance for punishing those who do not deserve punishment.
The king [shall fast] for three nights.
Moreover, they cite this:
"The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife, to her husband;
a pupil and a sacrificer, to their teacher; and a thief, to the king."
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings become stainless and go to heaven, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.
Sin overtakes the king who releases a guilty person;
but if the king causes him to be slain, he destroys the evil deed through righteousness.
For kings, immediate purification is prescribed in the case of urgent business;
likewise, in the case of non-urgent matters, time alone is the determining factor here.
And in this regard, they cite a verse sung by Yama:
"Today there is no fault for kings, nor indeed for those observing vows or performing sacrificial sessions; for, seated in the station of Indra, they are always one with Brahman."
"For they are always yours."
Va.20.1 There is an expiation for an offense committed unintentionally.
Some say that [the offense] occurs even when it is done intentionally.
"For those who possess self-control, the teacher is the ruler; for the evil-minded, the king is the ruler;
and for those who commit secret sins, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the ruler."
And there, while the sun is rising, he should remain standing and mutter the Sāvitrī.
Thus he remained at night, having been dismissed by the sun.
One with deformed nails or blackened teeth, however, shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights.
A younger brother who has married before his elder brother shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, after which he may enter the household and marry that very woman.
Now, one who has been superseded by a younger brother, having performed the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances and having given his property to him, may marry again and take her as his wife.
The husband of an *agredidhiṣū* woman, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, may enter the household and marry her.
Having performed the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances, and having given her back to him, he may marry her again.
We shall explain the "slayer of heroes" (vīrahaṇ) later on.
Having performed the *brahmahatyā-kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, he may again receive the Veda from his teacher.

One who violates the teacher’s bed shall cut off his penis together with the testicles, place them in his joined palms, and walk facing south; wherever he meets with an obstacle, there he shall remain until his body perishes.
Or, having been stripped of his clothes and anointed with ghee, he shall embrace a red-hot iron image; it is known from tradition that he becomes purified through death.
And the same applies toward the wives of one's teacher, son, or pupil.

Having approached a woman who is a heavy relative by birth, a female friend of one's teacher, a female friend of one's teacher, an unworthy person, or one who has fallen from her caste, one shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for one-fourth of a year.
The same applies to eating the food of Caṇḍālas or outcasts; in those cases, there is a re-initiation (punar-upanayana), but with the exclusion of the shaving of the head and other such rites.
And in this regard, they cite this verse of Manu:
"Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
these are indeed discontinued during the rite of re-consecration."

But for intentionally drinking intoxicants—whether *asurā* or *surā*—if done unknowingly, one must perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, consume clarified butter, and undergo the rite of re-initiation (*punar-saṃskāra*).
And likewise for the consumption of urine, feces, and semen.

If any twice-born man should drink water that has stood in a vessel for liquor, he becomes pure in three nights alone after drinking water from the lotus, the *udumbara*, the *bilva*, and the *palāśa* trees.
But in the case of repeated consumption, that twice-born man shall drink it while it is fire-colored; he becomes purified through death.
We shall now declare [the penance for] the slayer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*): having killed a Brāhmaṇa, one becomes a slayer of an embryo; as does one who kills an embryo that is not yet discernible.

"For embryos that have not been discerned become males; therefore, they offer oblations for the sake of producing males. Therefore, the killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan), having kindled the fire, should offer these [oblations].

"I offer my body hairs to Death; with my body hairs, I drive away Death"—this is the first [offering]. "I offer my skin to Death; with my skin, I drive away Death"—this is the second. "I offer my blood to Death; with my blood, I drive away Death"—this is the third. "I offer my flesh to Death; with my flesh, I drive away Death"—this is the fourth.
"I offer my sinews to Death; with my sinews, I drive away Death"—this is the fifth.

"I offer the fat to Death; with fat I drive away Death"—this is the sixth [offering]. "I offer the bones to Death; with bones I drive away Death"—this is the seventh. "I offer the marrow to Death; with marrow I drive away Death"—this is the eighth.
For the sake of the king or for the sake of a Brahmin, one should cause oneself to be slain facing the enemy in battle.
It is known from tradition that one who has thrice failed [in the sacrifice] becomes purified by [the rite called] *ajita*.
For it is said that the sin of one who has uttered the truth becomes lessened.

Nevertheless, they cite this example: "Having said 'he is fallen' regarding one who is fallen, or 'he is a thief' regarding a thief, by such speech one incurs an equal fault; if it is false, one incurs double the fault."
Likewise, having killed a Kṣatriya woman, one should perform penance for eight years.
Va.20.32 There are six Vaiśyas.
Three [years] for a Śūdra.
And having killed a Brāhmaṇī woman of the Ātreya lineage, as well as a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has participated in a Soma sacrifice.
We shall now speak of the *ātreyī*: they call a woman who has bathed after her menses, while still menstruating, an *ātreyī*.
For in this case, it becomes the future offspring.
Va.20.37 For the killing of a Kṣatriya who is not the son of Atri, [the penance is] that of an Ātreya.
In the case of injuring a woman of the royal caste or a Vaiśya woman, [the same penalty applies].
Va.20.39: For the killing of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, [the penance is] the same.
Having killed a Śūdra woman, [one must perform penance] for one year.

In the case of stealing gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, having disheveled his hair, he should run toward the king, saying: "I am a thief; may your majesty punish me! To him the king should give a weapon made of Udumbara wood; with that he should destroy himself. It is known from tradition: "By death he becomes purified."

It is known from tradition: "Or, having smeared himself with clarified butter, he should burn himself starting from the feet by means of a fire of cow dung; he becomes purified upon death. (Va. 20.42)
Moreover, they cite this example:
"Listen to how that [karma] becomes a limb of those who, having died before their time due to various sinful deeds, have again entered a body."
A thief becomes one with deformed nails; a killer of a Brahmin becomes one with white leprosy; a drinker of liquor has black teeth; and one who violates the Guru’s bed suffers from skin disease.

And in the case of association with those who have fallen [from their status], whether through the Vedic [lineage] or through marriage, one must abandon whatever resources were obtained from them and must not live together with them.
It is traditionally known that by going to the northern direction and studying the *Saṃhitā* without eating, one becomes purified.
Nevertheless, they cite this example:
"By the austerity of bodily mortification, by penance, and by Vedic study, the doer of evil is released from evil; and by means of giving, he is likewise fully liberated."
Thus it is known; it is known.

If a Śūdra should have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in *vīraṇa* grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved and having smeared her all over with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a black donkey and cause her to be led along the great highway. It is traditionally known that she thus becomes purified.

If a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red Darbha grass and throw him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be performed and having anointed her thoroughly with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a white donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road. It is traditionally known that she thus becomes purified.

If a Kṣatriya should have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap that Kṣatriya in reed-leaves and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved and having anointed her all over with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a white donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road. It is traditionally known: "Thus she becomes purified."
In this same way, a Vaiśya [begets] on a Kṣatriya woman.
And a Śūdra [is the son] of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman.

Va.21.6: If a wife commits an infidelity against her husband through the mind, she shall subsist for three nights on either barley gruel or milk-rice and sleep on the ground. After the three nights, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with one hundred and eight repetitions of the *Sāvitrī* mantra, each preceded by the word "head" (*śiras*). It is traditionally taught that she thus becomes purified.

Regarding offenses involving speech, it is traditionally known that after performing this same penance for one month, she should, once the month has passed, remain submerged in water and offer oblations with four hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī verse; thus she becomes purified.

But in the case of sexual intercourse, she shall wear a cloth smeared with ghee for one year; she shall sleep on a bed of cow-dung or on a layer of *kuśa* grass. After one year has passed, she shall offer oblations with her head submerged in water, reciting the *Sāvitrī* mantra one hundred and eight times. It is traditionally known that she thus becomes purified.
In sexual intercourse and in visiting sacred bathing places, one turns away from the [specific] duties.
But four [wives] are to be abandoned: one who has gone to a disciple, one who has gone to a teacher, one who is specifically a wife-killer, and one who has approached a *juṅgita*.

The gods do not lead that Brahmin woman who drinks liquor to the world of her husband; having exhausted her merit, she wanders right here [in this world], becoming like a submerged leech or a pearl-oyster shell in the water.
Women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have had sexual intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; those who have conceived are not.
They should perform the penance in reverse order, beginning with the Kṛcchra and ending with the Cāndrāyaṇa.

For those women who are devoted to their husbands, who are householders, and who are faithful to the vow of truth and purity, their worlds are equal to those of their husbands; but for those who are unchaste, the worlds are like those of jackals.
If a wife drinks liquor, half of the husband's body falls [into sin];
for one whose body is thus fallen in half, no atonement is prescribed.
If a Brahmin should intentionally approach the wife of a Brahmin, it is a *kṛcchra* penance if the husband has not yet ceased his ritual duties, and an *atikṛcchra* if he has ceased them.
The same applies to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya.
If he should kill a cow, he shall remain for six months wrapped in her raw hide, performing either the *kṛcchra* or the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
The rule for those two is as follows.
One eats during the day for three days, and likewise eats at night for three days;
one observes the vow of not begging for three days, and does not eat for three days—this is the *kṛcchra*.
For three days one should drink hot water; for three days one should drink hot milk; having drunk hot ghee for three days, one should subsist on air for the final three days.
Thus concludes the Taptakṛcchra penance.
And one should give the Ṛṣabha-vehat oblation.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"In ancient times there were only three diseases: envy, lack of food, and old age. Having killed a spotted goat, one should offer ninety-eight [goats]."
Having killed a dog, a cat, a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a rat, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and give some small gift.
But having killed a heap of boneless beings as large as a cow, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and give some small gift.
But for those things possessing bone, one [part] each.
If one should abandon the sacred fires, he shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then have the fires re-established.
And in the case of persistent falsehood toward a guru, one should bathe with one's clothes on and propitiate the guru; it is traditionally known that through such propitiation, one becomes purified.
An atheist, having performed the twelve-night penance (kṛcchra), shall desist from atheism.
But for one who follows the conduct of an atheist, the penance is an *atikṛcchra*.
By this, the seller of Soma is explained.
If a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) violates his initiation vows, he shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and then increase the growth of the great thicket.

The mendicants (bhikṣukas) shall follow the rules of forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) regarding the increase of the Soma-plant and the refinement according to their own scriptures; [this applies to] the refinement according to their own scriptures.

Now, this person indeed gives false explanations; he causes one who should not be sacrificed for to sacrifice, or accepts what should not be accepted, or eats food that is unfit to be eaten, or performs exactly that which should not be performed.
Regarding this, they deliberate whether one should perform an expiation or not.
"One should not do it," they say.
For indeed, karma is not exhausted.
Therefore, based on this scriptural indication, one should indeed act [in accordance with it].
"He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice crosses over all evil, he crosses over even the murder of a Brāhmaṇa"— and one who is thus accused should perform the Gosava and Agniṣṭut sacrifices.
Its expiations are recitation, austerity, burnt offerings, fasting, and giving.

The Upaniṣads, the Vedas and so forth, the concluding portions of the Vedas, all the meters, the Saṃhitās, the Madhu-hymns, the Aghamarṣaṇa, the Atharvaśiras, the Rudras, the Puruṣasūkta, the Rājana and Rauhiṇa Sāmans, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Pāvamānīs, and the Sāvitrī—these are the purifiers.
Moreover, they cite this:
"One who performs the Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitra sacrifice even once during the [proper] season, purifies ten generations of his lineage."
According to the rule for fasting, subsisting on milk, eating fruits, consuming a handful of barley-gruel, ingesting gold, and drinking soma are means of purification.
All mountain peaks, all rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords, dwellings of sages, cow-pens, and forest thickets—these are the regions.
The years, months, twenty-four half-months, twelve days, six days, three days, a day and night—these are the divisions of time.
These very same [actions] may optionally be performed when there is no specific instruction.
In cases of heavy offenses, the penances shall be heavy; in cases of light offenses, they shall be light.
The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa—these constitute the universal penance (sarvaprāyaścitta), these constitute the universal penance.
If a religious student (brahmacārī) should approach a woman, he shall sacrifice a donkey dedicated to the Rakṣases as the deity, as an animal offering, in a common fire at a crossroads in the forest.
Or he should offer a pap (caru) to Nairṛta.
For him, one should offer oblations, saying: "To Desire, svāhā! To the desire for desire, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To the Rākṣasa deities, svāhā!"
This same [penance] applies to the intentional emission of semen during the daytime, in dreams, or during other observances prior to the *samāvartana*.
In the case of sexual intercourse with an animal, one should give a white bull as a gift.
Having gone to a cow, the fault is explained as being equal to that of killing a Śūdra woman.
Va.23.7 For a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), there is a cessation from the vow upon the performance of funeral rites.
Except in the case of one's mother and father.
If he should fall ill, he may at will eat all the leftovers of his teacher for the sake of medicine.
Va.23.10 If one who has been commissioned by his teacher should die, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
Va.23.11 If a religious student (*brahmacārī*) should eat meat or food that is the leavings of another, he shall perform a *kṛcchra* for twelve nights and then complete the remainder of his vow.
And likewise in the case of eating at a funeral feast (śrāddha) or during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka).
It is known from the Vājasaneyaka that honey offered unintentionally does not cause defilement.
If one who has committed suicide becomes an outcast, the funeral rites for his sapinda relatives are cut short.
He who destroys himself by means of wood, water, clods of earth, stones, weapons, poison, or ropes, is a self-destroyer.
Moreover, they cite this example:
"If a twice-born man, out of affection, should perform the funeral rites for one who has committed suicide,
he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow together with the Taptakṛcchra penance."
We shall explain the Cāndrāyaṇa penance further on.
In the case of an attempt to commit suicide, [the penance lasts] for three nights.

One who abandons his life while still living shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights; he shall fast for three nights, always wearing an oily garment, and restraining his breaths within himself, he shall recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times. Or else, by this same procedure, he may revolve the *Gāyatrī*.
Alternatively, having kindled the fire, one should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.
And whatever else besides the great sins (mahāpātaka) there may be—all this is purified by this [rite].

Moreover, having mentally contemplated a sin, one should sip water while reciting, "May Agni and Manyu [protect me]," and then mutter the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *satya*, or recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn.
Having touched human bone that is still moist, there is a period of impurity for three nights.
But if it is not moist, one should remain [in that state] for a day and night.
And the same applies when following after a corpse.
If one goes between those who are studying, there shall be a fast for a day and night.
For three nights, they shall remain without bathing and without clothing, each with the other.
For dogs, cats, mongooses, and swift-moving creatures, [the period of impurity lasts] for a day and a night.

For eating the flesh of a dog, a cock, a village pig, a heron, a vulture, a hawk, a pigeon, a human, a crow, or an owl, there shall be a fast for seven nights, becoming free from feces, consuming clarified butter, and undergoing the purificatory rite once again.
But a Brāhmaṇa who has been bitten by a dog, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean,
shall perform one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and, after consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*), he then becomes pure.
It is traditionally known that upon touching a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, or an outcaste (*patita*), one becomes pure immediately after bathing with one's clothes on.
Upon hearing the cry of an outcaste or a *caṇḍāla*, they shall remain for three nights observing silence and fasting.
"It is known from tradition that those who recite it up to a maximum of a thousand times become purified."

By this very same [rule], those who teach for a fee and those who officiate at sacrifices for a fee are explained; it is known from scripture that they become purified by the relinquishing of their sacrificial fees.
By this very [rule], one who is accused is explained.
Va.23.38 For killing an embryo, one shall subsist on water for twelve nights and fast for twelve nights.
Va.23.39 Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime involving loss of caste or a minor offense, one shall subsist on water for a month and repeat the Śuddhavatī verses.
Or he should go to the final purificatory bath of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By this very same [rule], sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman is explained.
Now, furthermore, there is another common arrangement of the Kṛcchra penance known as the Vyūḍha.
One day in the morning, one day at night, and one day without begging—this constitutes the *parāka* penance.
In this manner, four days constitute the subsequent [penances].
For the sake of favoring the brahmins, Manu, the best of the upholders of dharma,
likewise prescribed the Śiśukṛcchra for children, the elderly, and the sick.
Now follows the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
At the beginning of the dark fortnight of the month, one should eat fourteen morsels; increasing the number of morsels, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
Thus, at the beginning of the bright fortnight, one should eat only a single morsel;
eating with a reduction of morsels, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
In this very place, he should either sing the Sāman hymns or mutter the Vyāhṛtis.
This month-long Cāndrāyaṇa rite is a purifier praised by the seers;
it is prescribed as the expiation for all those [offenses] for which no specific penance has been ordained.
It is prescribed by means of the root *dhā* with the prefix *vi*.
Now follows the Atikṛcchra penance.

For three days eating only in the morning and likewise in the evening, and for three days eating only what is unasked for—this is the Parāka penance. The Kṛcchra consists of eating as much as one might take once; that same [practice] performed in the manner previously described is the Atikṛcchra.
Va.24.3 Subsisting on water for one day and eating [only] at night for six days constitutes the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
Va.24.4 These are the forms of the vows (*vrata*) for the *kṛcchra* penances.

He shall have his beard and hair shaved—except for the eyebrows, the eyelashes, and the topknot—and having clipped his nails, wearing a single garment and eating blameless food [consisting of a single meal of blameless alms], bathing three times a day, carrying a staff and a water-pot, avoiding conversation with women and Śūdras, and habituated to standing and sitting, he shall stand during the day and sit at night; thus says the venerable Vasiṣṭha.
Va.24.6 He shall not give this treatise on Dharma to one who is not his son, nor to one who is not his pupil, nor to one who has not lived with him for a year.
"A thousand [cows] with a bull as the eleventh is the teacher's fee, or rather, it is the teacher's favor."
I shall describe, without omission, the purification for all great sins whose faults have not been made public, as well as for all minor offenses.

For one who has maintained the sacred fires, who is disciplined, aged, and learned, the penance prescribed in secret [is appropriate]; for other people, that which was previously stated [should be applied].
Those who are constantly disciplined through breath-control, purifications, gifts, burnt offerings, and likewise recitations, are liberated from their sins; of this there is no doubt.
Performing breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the purifiers (pavitrāṇi), the vyāhṛtis, and likewise the praṇava,
with the purifier in hand and seated, one should practice the daily Veda-recitation (brahma).
Constantly engaged and practicing breath-restraints again and again,
let him perform the highest austerity from the tips of his hair to the tips of his nails.
From cessation wind is born; from wind, fire is indeed born;
by heat water is then born; thereafter, the interior is purified by these three.

Neither by intense austerity, nor by Vedic study, nor by sacrifice, are the twice-born able to attain that goal which they reach through yoga. Through yoga, knowledge is attained; yoga is the defining characteristic of dharma.
Yoga is the supreme austerity; therefore, one should always remain disciplined in it.
One should be constantly engaged with the *praṇava* and the seven *vyāhṛtis*, as well as with the three-footed *gāyatrī*; for such a person, no fear exists anywhere.
The Vedas arise from the *praṇava* and are established within the *praṇava*; the *praṇava* consists of all speech. Therefore, one should practice the *praṇava*.
The single syllable is known as the supreme Brahman, the highest purifier.
When a mixture of all sins has arisen,
the great purification for it is ten thousand repetitions of the Sāvitrī mantra.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while holding the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma.
It is said: "He speaks."
One should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the rule and without sloth;
the sin committed during a day and night perishes at that very moment.
Whatever sin has been committed by deed, thought, or word during the day,
one removes it while sitting during the evening twilight through breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
Whatever sin has been committed by deed, by mind, or by speech during the night,
one dispels it by means of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) upon rising at the morning twilight.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava,
performed day after day, purify even the killer of a learned Brahmin within a month.

Having recited the *kautsa* hymn beginning with *apa ita* and the three verses of Vasiṣṭha beginning with *prati* (*apa naḥ śośucad agham... prati stomebhir uṣasam...*), one who has drunk liquor is purified—even a drinker of *surā*—by means of the *māhitra* and the *śuddhavatī* verses.
Having recited the *Aśvavāmīya* and the *Śivasaṃkalpa* even once,
one becomes stainless in an instant, even after having stolen gold.
Having recited the *haviṣyantīya* hymn, the triplet beginning with "na tam aṃhaḥ" (RV 10.126.1–3),
and having muttered the *puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the teacher’s bed is liberated from that sin.
Alternatively, while submerged in water, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
Manu has declared that this is equal to the final purificatory bath of a horse sacrifice.
The sacrifice of silent recitation (*japayajña*) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual action (*ārambhayajña*).
The whispered (*upāṃśu*) sacrifice is said to be a hundredfold [superior], and the mental (*mānasa*) sacrifice is a thousandfold.
Those four types of cooked sacrifices (*pākayajña*), when accompanied by the ritual sacrifices (*vidhiyajña*),
all together do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of silent recitation (*japayajña*).
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other rites or not, a Brahmin is called one who is friendly (maitra).

Sins do not dwell with those who recite prayers, those who perform burnt offerings, those who practice meditation, those who reside at sacred fords, and those who have performed ritual ablutions accompanied by head-vows.
Just as a fire, fanned by the wind and fed with oblations, blazes up,
even so a Brahmin who is constantly devoted to the recitation of prayers shines forth brilliantly.
For those who constantly study their own sacred texts, whose souls are ever restrained,
and who likewise engage in silent recitation and burnt offerings, no downfall is known to exist.

One who desires purification, even if established in all manner of sins, should employ this divine [formula] which has a maximum of a thousand [repetitions], a middle of a hundred, and a minimum of ten.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune by the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra by wealth; but the highest of the twice-born by silent recitations and burnt offerings. Just as horses would be without a chariot, or as a chariot would be without horses;
Thus, there is no knowledge for one who lacks austerity, nor is there knowledge for one who lacks austerity.
Just as food mixed with honey, or honey mixed with food,
so too are austerity and knowledge combined into a great medicine.
Sin does not attach itself even to one who performs evil deeds, provided he is a Brahmin endowed with knowledge and austerity, and devoted to the constant recitation of sacred texts and daily rites.
"One is joined with sin. Thus it is said.
If even more than a hundred wrong deeds have been committed, yet the Veda is retained in memory,
the fire of that Veda burns them all away, just as ordinary fire consumes fuel.
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees,
so too does the fire of knowledge burn away the defects of the self born of karma.
Even having killed these worlds, and even while enjoying them from here and there,
the learned man who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.
One should not take pleasure in evil deeds by relying on the power of the Vedas;
for it is through ignorance and negligence that one is consumed by karma, and not otherwise.
A sage who performs austerities in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits,
and one who studies even a single verse of the Ṛgveda— these two are equal.
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will strike me."
The daily practice of Vedic study according to one's ability and the performance of the sequence of the great sacrifices quickly destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes.
One should constantly and untiringly perform one's own duty as declared in the Veda;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
Through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, matrimonial alliance, and likewise through the acceptance of improper gifts, no fault shall accrue to Brahmins; for they are equal to fire and the sun.
When a ground for doubt has arisen regarding what is fit or unfit to be eaten, I shall declare the purity of food; listen to me as I speak it.
A Brahmin should drink the *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* plants, which are alkaline, salty, and dry, for three nights; and he should likewise drink *śaṅkhapuṣpī* with milk for three nights.
Having boiled the leaves of the *palāśa* and *bilva*, as well as *kuśa* grass, lotuses, and *udumbara* figs, one should drink the water; by doing so, one becomes pure within three nights.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with a fast for one night, would purify even a dog-eater (*śvapāka*).
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise ghee—
by consuming these five products of the cow for five nights, one is purified by the *pañcagavya*.
One who consumes barley according to the prescribed rule is purified by direct perception alone;
when the state [of the recipient] is pure, they are pure, but if it is impure, they remain full of passion.
Three morning meals of sacrificial food, three evening meals likewise,
and three meals of unsolicited food— this constitutes a threefold fast.
If, however, one who subsists on air hastens to perform [the rite], he should remain by a body of water at night; that [fast] is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
Having performed the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra eight thousand times when the sun has risen,
one is released from all sins, provided that one is not a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
Whether one is a thief, a drinker of liquor, a killer of an embryo, or one who violates the teacher’s bed,
by merely studying the Dharmaśāstra, he is released from all sins.
For misfortunes, ill-performed rites, and likewise for great sins,
the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are the destroyers of all evil.
One should increase the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight;
on the new moon day, one should not eat at all—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
And thus is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa.
A woman is not defiled by her paramour, nor is a Brahmin by his Vedic rites;
water is not defiled by urine or excrement, nor is fire by the act of burning.
Whether she has herself committed misconduct, or has been banished,
or has been enjoyed by force, or has even fallen into the hands of a thief;
A woman who has been defiled must not be abandoned; her abandonment is not ordained.
She should wait for the time of her menses; she becomes pure through the period of her season.
Women are an incomparable purifier; they are never defiled. For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
Formerly, these women were enjoyed by the gods—Soma, Gandharva, and Agni;
afterwards, when they come among men, they do not incur any fault according to the Dharma. Soma granted them purity, and Gandharva taught them speech.
Fire possesses the quality of being entirely pure; therefore, women are free from stain.
Those who know the Dharma recognize three sins of women in this world:
the murder of a husband, the destruction of an embryo, and the causing of an abortion of one's own fetus.
A calf is pure when causing milk to flow; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
women are pure during sexual intercourse; and a dog is pure when seizing game.

Goats and horses are pure in their mouths; cows are pure in every part [or, according to Bhler’s reading: "Cows are pure behind"]. Hereafter, I shall declare all the purifiers of the Vedas, by whose recitations (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*) people are purified; of this there is no doubt.
The Aghamarṣaṇa, the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, the Taratsamās,
the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Pāvamānīs, and the Durgā-sāvitrī.
The *atiṣaṅgas*, the *padastobhas*, the *sāmans*, and likewise the *vyāhṛtis*;
the *bhāruṇḍa* *sāmans*, as well as the *gāyatra* and the *raivata*.
The Puruṣasūkta, the Bhāsa, and likewise the Devavratas; the Abliṅga, the Bārhaspatya, the Vāksūkta, and the Madhucchandas verses.
The Śatarudriya, the Atharvaśiras, the Triṣuparṇa, the Mahāvrata, the Go-sūkta, the Aśva-sūkta, and the two Sāmans, the Śuddha and the Aśuddhiya.
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agner-vrata, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—these, when recited, purify living beings; if one so desires, one obtains the memory of past births.
Gold is the first offspring of Agni; the earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun. He who should give even a single cow, or land, would obtain infinite fruit from them.
A cow, a horse, gold,
and land obstruct the giver who sees the hand of a Brahmin who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) and is devoid of sacred rites (*nirākṛta*).
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, however, one should [feed] seven or five Brahmins with sesame seeds—
either black or otherwise— mixed with honey.
"May the King of Dharma be pleased"— if one holds this in mind,
whatever sin has been committed throughout one's life perishes in that very instant.
Having fashioned a golden hub for a wheel made from black antelope skin together with its hoof,
and having covered it with sesame seeds, listen to the fruit of the merit of one who should give it.
By him, the earth—along with its golden caves, its mountains, forests, and groves, and its four faces—has been given; of this there is no doubt.
"He who gives a black antelope skin, sesame seeds, gold, honey,
and clarified butter to a Brahmin overcomes all evil deeds."
One overcomes all evil deeds.
Through giving, one obtains all desires.
He shall be long-lived, a celibate student, and handsome.
One who practices non-violence is reborn in heaven.
By entering the fire, one attains the world of Brahmā.
From silence comes good fortune.
The lord of the nāgas [is freed] from dwelling in the water.
Va.29.7 One who is free from debt and whose wealth is exhausted.
Va.29.8 He is one who possesses water, ten [treasures], and the fulfillment of all desires.
The giver of food becomes one with clear vision and a retentive memory.
The wise one is the giver of fearlessness in every respect.
If [the water] is drawn by a cow, one should perform ablutions at all sacred fords.
From the gift of beds and seats, one attains sovereignty over the inner apartments.
From the gift of an umbrella, one obtains a house.
A house-burner reaches the city.
Va.29.15 One who gives shoes provides a vehicle. {BṣPṣ vehicle}{E vehicle} Va.29.16 Furthermore, they also cite:
Whatever sin a man, distressed by his livelihood, commits, [he is purified from it].
Moreover, one is purified by the gift of land even if it is only the size of a cow-hide.
One should give a full water-pot to the Brahmin for the purpose of sipping;
having attained supreme satisfaction after death, he is born again as a drinker of Soma.
The gift of thousands of oxen, capable of bearing the yoke,
given according to the rules to a worthy recipient, is equal to the gift of a daughter in marriage.
They say there are three supreme gifts: cows, land, and Sarasvatī;
for among all gifts, the gift of knowledge is indeed superior to them.
He who, being free from malice, knows this and follows this conduct, attains that which bestows the ultimate fruit— the liberation from saṃsāra.
"One who has faith, who is pure and self-controlled, should uphold [this] and also listen to it;
having abandoned all evils, he is glorified on the back of the firmament. Thus [it is said].
"He is glorified on the back of the firmament. Thus it is said.
Practice the Dharma, not unrighteousness; speak the truth, not falsehood.
Look to the long-term, not the short-term; look to what is supreme, not the inferior.
A Brahmin becomes fire.
For it is stated in the Śruti: "The Brahmin is indeed Agni."
And how is that so?

In this regard, for the Brahmin, the body is the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), volition is the sacrifice, the animal victim is the self, the tethering rope is the intellect, the assembly hall (*sadas*) is the mouth, the *āhavanīya* fire is the navel, the stomach is the *gārhapatya* fire, the *adhvaryu* priest is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the *hotṛ* priest is the down-breath (*apāna*), the *brahmā* priest is the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the *udgātṛ* priest is the pervasive breath (*samāna*), the self and the senses are the sacrificial vessels. He who, knowing thus, offers the objects of the senses with the senses—this is also known in the *Kāṭhaka*.
Moreover, they cite this:

"The one who offers oblations into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins— fires well-fueled by the wood of the Vedas— protects the recipient, protects the giver, and indeed protects himself from sin."
That which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is superior even to the Agnihotra; it does not spill over, it does not cause distress, and no calamity shall befall it.
With meditation as the fire, truth as the fuel, patience as the oblation, modesty as the sacrificial ladle, non-violence as the sacrificial cake, contentment as the sacrificial post,
and the granting of fearlessness to all beings as the fee for the priests— the wise man, having thus performed the mental sacrifice, attains imperishability.
The hair of one who grows old decays, and the teeth of one who grows old decay;
yet the hope for life and the hope for wealth do not decay even as one grows old.
"That craving which is so difficult for those of evil intellect to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays—
that very craving which is a disease unto death— happiness belongs to him who abandons it."
"Homage be to Vasiṣṭha, the son of Urvaśī, born of Mitra and Varuṇa, the hundredfold walker—to Vasiṣṭha, to Vasiṣṭha! Thus [he said].
End of the Text
